domains.name: The EDA Landscape
domains.description: What electronic design automation is, the RTL-to-GDSII flow stage by stage, the representations each stage consumes and produces, PPA, the industry and its history.
covers: Electronic design automation, ECAD, computer-aided engineering
Integrated circuit design, VLSI, ULSI
ASIC, FPGA, SoC, semiconductor IP cores, standard cells and cell libraries as products
Design abstraction, hierarchy, top-down and bottom-up design, hardware-software co-design
The end-to-end flow: specification, architecture, RTL, verification, synthesis, DFT, floorplan, placement, CTS, routing, extraction, signoff, tape-out, fabrication, packaging, test
Why real flows are iterative: timing, power and verification recur at many stages; how errors propagate downstream
Representations and formats map: HDL/RTL, Boolean networks, BDD/AIG, gate netlists, Liberty, SDC, LEF/DEF, SPEF, GDSII/OASIS, SPICE netlists, PDK decks - what each preserves, abstracts and enables
PPA (power, performance, area) and the cost of a respin
Analog/mixed-signal, FPGA, PCB/package and manufacturing as adjacent branches with different flows
Industry: the major EDA vendors and their product lines; foundry model, fabless companies, the EDA industry structure
Major tools by role (custom layout, place and route, synthesis, logic and circuit simulation, timing signoff, physical verification, test, FPGA implementation) - what class of problem each solves
Research communities: DAC, ICCAD, DATE, ISPD, ITC, CAV; landmark history: structured VLSI design, SPICE, the university CAD tools behind today's logic synthesis and layout
Standards bodies for languages, formats, boards and manufacturing

concepts.label: What electronic design automation is
concepts.definition: Electronic design automation (EDA) is the software that turns an idea for an electronic system into something a factory can build and a tester can check.
key_ideas: Every tool is an algorithm on a model

sample.question:
A gate-sizing optimizer upsizes cells on failing paths and re-times after every few moves. What does this illustrate?

A) An implementation tool calling an analysis engine inside its loop

B) A verification tool proving functional correctness

C) An analysis tool that never changes the design

D) Two independent tools that never share data
sample.answer: An implementation tool calling an analysis engine inside its loop
sample.explanation: Optimizers transform the design but need an analyzer, here a timer, to score each change.

concepts.label: Integrated circuits and VLSI scale
concepts.definition: An integrated circuit puts transistors and their wiring on one piece of silicon.

sample.question: A chip family holds 6 billion transistors today. If the count doubles every 3 years, how many billion transistors will a chip of the same cost hold after 9 years?
sample.explanation: 9 years is 3 doubling periods, so the count is $6 \cdot 2^{3} = 48$ billion.

concepts.label: Abstraction levels from system to layout
concepts.definition: Designers describe a chip at several levels of abstraction: system, algorithm or behavior, register transfer, gate, transistor and layout.
key_ideas: What each level keeps and drops

sample.question:
A C++ model computes a video filter with no notion of clock cycles. At which level is it?

A) Behavioral or algorithmic level

B) Register-transfer level

C) System floorplan level

D) Gate level
sample.answer: Behavioral or algorithmic level
sample.explanation: An untimed algorithm is a behavioral description; RTL fixes cycle-by-cycle register behaviour.

concepts.label: Hierarchy, top-down and bottom-up design
concepts.definition: A chip is never designed as one flat list of billions of cells. It is a tree of modules: the top instantiates subsystems, which instantiate blocks, which instantiate library cells.

sample.question: The top module instantiates 6 copies of block A and 4 copies of block B. Block A contains 5 standard cells of its own plus 2 instances of block C. Block C contains 28 standard cells. Block B contains 31 standard cells. How many standard cells does the fully flattened design contain?
sample.explanation: Multiply along each path from the top: $6(5 + 2 \cdot 28) + 4 \cdot 31 = 490$ cells.

concepts.label: ASICs, FPGAs and systems on chip
concepts.definition: Three product kinds dominate digital hardware. An application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) is fabricated for one purpose.
key_ideas: Three ways to build digital logic

sample.question:
What does an ASIC team pay for that an FPGA team does not?

A) Functional verification

B) Synthesis of RTL into logic

C) Static timing analysis

D) A mask set and wafer fabrication for its own design
sample.answer: A mask set and wafer fabrication for its own design
sample.explanation: Both teams synthesize, time and verify; only the ASIC team fabricates its own masks.

concepts.label: IP cores and standard-cell libraries as products
concepts.definition: Almost nothing on a modern chip is designed from scratch. Standard cells, memories, I/O cells, PHYs and processor cores are bought or reused as intellectual-property (IP) products.

sample.question:
Why does hard IP give the integrator less risk but less freedom?

A) It must be redesigned for every use

B) It can be resynthesized at any frequency

C) It contains no timing information

D) Its timing and layout are proven but cannot be changed
sample.answer: Its timing and layout are proven but cannot be changed
sample.explanation: The more physical the delivery, the more is fixed and verified in advance, and the less the integrator can modify.

concepts.label: Hardware-software co-design
concepts.definition: A system's function can run in software on a processor or in dedicated hardware.

sample.question: Profiling shows that 65% of a program's runtime is a kernel that a hardware accelerator runs 2 times faster. The rest stays in software. What is the overall speedup? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: The RTL-to-GDSII flow end to end
concepts.definition: The RTL-to-GDSII flow is the chain of tools that turns register-transfer code into the mask layout a foundry manufactures.
key_ideas: What each stage hands the next
What becomes known at each stage

sample.question:
In a standard digital implementation flow, which stage comes directly after parasitic extraction?

A) Tape-out

B) Packaging

C) RTL design

D) Signoff

E) Routing
sample.answer: Signoff
sample.explanation: The chain runs RTL design, Logic synthesis, Scan insertion, Floorplanning, Placement, Clock tree synthesis, Routing, Parasitic extraction, Signoff, Tape-out, Fabrication, Packaging, Production test, so Signoff follows Parasitic extraction.

concepts.label: Specification, architecture and RTL
concepts.definition: The front of the flow decides what the chip is before any tool decides how to build it.

sample.question:
Which of these is an interface item in a specification?

A) The bus protocol and pin list a block must support

B) The OPC recipe of a mask layer

C) The global router's gcell size

D) The number of buffers in the clock tree
sample.answer: The bus protocol and pin list a block must support
sample.explanation: Interfaces define how the chip or block connects to the outside world.

concepts.label: Functional verification in the flow
concepts.definition: Functional verification asks whether the design does what the specification says.

sample.question: A small controller has 3 input bits and 6 bits of state. An exhaustive test must apply every input combination in every state. How many (state, input) pairs is that?
sample.explanation: There are $2^{6}$ states and $2^{3}$ input combinations, so $2^{9} = 512$ pairs, and reaching each state may itself take many cycles.

concepts.label: Logic synthesis
concepts.definition: Logic synthesis translates RTL into a netlist of cells from a target library, optimizing for timing, area and power under the constraints in an SDC file.
key_ideas: Correctness and what synthesis cannot see

sample.question:
During elaboration, what does synthesis infer from an always block triggered on a clock edge?

A) Clock buffers

B) Registers

C) Tristate buses

D) Latches
sample.answer: Registers
sample.explanation: Edge-triggered processes describe flip-flops.

concepts.label: Design for test and scan insertion
concepts.definition: A fabricated chip can have manufacturing defects that no design review could find, so each die is tested before it ships.
key_ideas: What DFT costs the rest of the flow

sample.question: A design has 13,800 scan flip-flops, divided as evenly as possible into 16 scan chains. How many flip-flops are in the longest chain?

concepts.label: Floorplanning and power planning
concepts.definition: Floorplanning is the first physical step. It chooses the die and core size, places the large blocks (memories, analog macros, hard IP), arranges the I/O, and lays down the power distribution network.

sample.question: Synthesis reports 560,000 square microns of standard cells and macros. The floorplan targets a utilization of 0.8. What core area does that require, in square microns? Round to the nearest whole number.
sample.explanation: Core area = cell area / utilization = 560000 / 0.8 = 700000 square microns.

concepts.label: Placement
concepts.definition: Placement assigns every standard cell a legal location in the rows of the floorplan.
key_ideas: Density, legality and what goes wrong

sample.question: A net connects pins at (29, 28), (27, 0), (12, 21), (22, 18), in microns. What is its half-perimeter wirelength, in microns?
sample.explanation: The bounding box width plus height is 45 microns.

concepts.label: Clock tree synthesis
concepts.definition: Every flip-flop needs the clock, and it needs it at nearly the same time as its neighbours.

sample.question: After clock tree synthesis, the clock latencies of a group of flip-flops are 417, 350, 437, 454, 415 ps. What is the global skew of the group, in picoseconds?
sample.explanation: Global skew is the maximum minus the minimum latency: $454 - 350 = 104$ ps.

concepts.label: Global and detailed routing
concepts.definition: Routing turns every net's connectivity into metal wires and vias on the available layers, without breaking design rules and without shorting nets together.

sample.question: A global router reports these gcell edges: edge 1: demand 16, capacity 14; edge 2: demand 12, capacity 13; edge 3: demand 22, capacity 17; edge 4: demand 10, capacity 8. What is the total overflow?
sample.explanation: Overflow sums $\max(0, \text{demand} - \text{capacity})$ over the edges, giving 9.

concepts.label: Extraction, timing and signoff
concepts.definition: Signoff is the set of final checks that must all pass before a design is sent to manufacturing.

sample.question: A chip is signed off in 2 functional modes, at 5 process-voltage-temperature corners and 3 interconnect RC corners, with every combination analyzed. How many timing scenarios must be run?
sample.explanation: Scenarios multiply: the product is 30.

concepts.label: Tape-out, fabrication, packaging and test
concepts.definition: Tape-out is the moment the design team releases final layout to the foundry. After it, the design leaves the EDA world for the factory: mask making, wafer fabrication, wafer test, dicing, packaging and final test.

sample.question:
What does the design team deliver to the foundry at tape-out?

A) Final layout in GDSII or OASIS with its documentation

B) Only the gate-level netlist

C) The Liberty files and SDC

D) The RTL and testbenches
sample.answer: Final layout in GDSII or OASIS with its documentation
sample.explanation: The foundry manufactures from layout; behavioural and timing files stay with the design team.

concepts.label: Why design flows iterate
concepts.definition: The flow diagram is a straight line, but no real project runs it once. Timing, power, area and verification are checked at many stages with better information each time, and when a later check fails, an earlier stage re-runs.
key_ideas: The same question asked many times

sample.question:
Why does a later stage keep finding surprises that an earlier stage did not?

A) Each stage optimized against an estimate that the next stage computes more accurately

B) Later tools use different logic functions

C) Earlier tools ignore constraints

D) The process changes between stages
sample.answer: Each stage optimized against an estimate that the next stage computes more accurately
sample.explanation: Estimation error at one stage becomes a violation discovered at the next.

concepts.label: How poor decisions propagate downstream
concepts.definition: A flow is a directed sequence of stages, and an error made in one stage is inherited by every stage after it.

sample.question: A flow runs synthesis, scan insertion, floorplanning, placement, CTS, routing, extraction, signoff in that order, and a change to a stage invalidates that stage and every later one. An engineer changes the floorplanning step. How many stages must re-run, counting the changed one?
sample.explanation: floorplanning is stage 3 of 8, so stages 3 through 8 re-run: 6 stages.

concepts.label: The map of design representations and formats
concepts.definition: A design passes through a dozen representations on its way from RTL to masks, and each one is stored in a file format that tools exchange.
key_ideas: The main formats and what they keep
Who writes and who reads each format
Choosing the format for a computation

sample.question:
Which format keeps power domains, supply nets, isolation and retention intent?

A) Liberty (.lib)

B) VCD or SAIF activity file

C) SDF

D) UPF
sample.answer: UPF
sample.explanation: UPF keeps power domains, supply nets, isolation and retention intent.

concepts.label: Netlists as the shared currency of the flow
concepts.definition: A netlist is the list of component instances in a design and the nets that connect their pins.

sample.question: A netlist has these nets, each written with its driver pin first: n1: U7/Y U5/A; n2: U2/Y U6/C U3/C U12/C U1/B U9/B; n3: U11/Y U3/C U4/A U10/B U6/A U9/B; n4: U1/Y U8/B U11/C; n5: U2/Y U11/C; n6: U3/Y U8/C U7/B U5/A U1/A U11/A. What is the total fanout, summed over all nets?
sample.explanation: Each net's fanout is its pin count minus the driver; the sum is 19.

concepts.label: Boolean networks, BDDs and AIGs
concepts.definition: Before logic becomes cells it lives in a technology-independent representation of Boolean functions.

sample.question: How many rows does the truth table of a 6-input Boolean function have?

concepts.label: Liberty cell libraries
concepts.definition: Liberty is the format that tells synthesis, timing and power tools how each library cell behaves.
key_ideas: Power, leakage and what tables miss

sample.question: A Liberty cell_rise table has index_1 (input slew) 0.02, 0.05, 0.1 ns and index_2 (output load) 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.04 pF. Its rows are slew 0.02 ns: 0.0585, 0.078, 0.117, 0.195; slew 0.05 ns: 0.0765, 0.096, 0.135, 0.213; slew 0.1 ns: 0.1065, 0.126, 0.165, 0.243. What rise delay does it give, in ns, at an input slew of 0.05 ns and a load of 0.02 pF?
sample.explanation: The point lies on the grid, so the delay is the table entry 0.135 ns.

concepts.label: SDC timing constraints
concepts.definition: SDC is the Tcl-based format in which designers state timing intent: which clocks exist and at what period, when inputs arrive and outputs are required relative to those clocks, and which paths are exceptions.

sample.question: An SDC file contains create_clock -name core_clk -period 2 [get_ports clk], with times in ns. What is the clock frequency, in MHz? Round to 1 decimal place.

concepts.label: LEF and DEF physical exchange
concepts.definition: LEF (Library Exchange Format) and DEF (Design Exchange Format) are the text formats in which physical-design tools exchange abstract layout.
key_ideas: LEF: abstracts of cells and layers
DEF: a design in database units

sample.question: A DEF file declares UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS 1000 and DIEAREA ( 0 0 ) ( 1300000 1200000 ). What is the die area, in square millimetres? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Dividing by 1000 units per micron gives a 1300 by 1200 micron die, 1.56 square millimetres.

concepts.label: SPEF parasitic exchange
concepts.definition: The Standard Parasitic Exchange Format (SPEF), defined in IEEE 1481, carries the resistances and capacitances that extraction computes from routed layout.
key_ideas: Resistance paths and use in timing

sample.question: A SPEF file with *C_UNIT 1 FF has a *D_NET for net *8 whose *CAP section reads: 1 *8:1 2.4; 2 *8:2 0.2; 3 *8:3 3.2; 4 *8:4 2; 5 *8:2 *14:3 1.4. The last entry couples *8 to another net. What total capacitance should the *D_NET line report, in fF? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: Ground and coupling capacitances add: 9.2 fF.

concepts.label: GDSII and OASIS mask layout
concepts.definition: GDSII and OASIS are the formats in which final layout is handed to the foundry. They store polygons on numbered layers, organized into a hierarchy of cells, and nothing else: no nets, no timing, no logic.

sample.question: A GDSII UNITS record says one database unit is 1E-9 metres. A BOUNDARY vertex has the integer coordinate 1287153. What is that coordinate in microns? Round to 4 decimal places.

concepts.label: SPICE netlists and PDK decks
concepts.definition: A process design kit (PDK) is the foundry's package that lets a design team use a process: device models, design rules, verification decks, extraction data, and often basic cells.
key_ideas: The PDK as the root of every abstraction

sample.question:
Where does a SPICE netlist appear in a digital flow?

A) Only in placement

B) Only in RTL simulation

C) In library characterization, custom design and LVS

D) Only in mask fracturing
sample.answer: In library characterization, custom design and LVS
sample.explanation: Cells are characterized by SPICE, custom blocks are simulated in it, and LVS compares SPICE netlists.

concepts.label: Power, performance and area
concepts.definition: Power, performance and area (PPA) are the three numbers by which a chip implementation, and the tools that produced it, are judged.
key_ideas: Voltage, frequency and the quadratic lever

sample.question: A block switches an effective capacitance of 250 pF with activity factor 0.2, at 0.9 V and 0.8 GHz. What is its dynamic power $\alpha C V^2 f$, in mW? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $0.2 \cdot 250 \times 10^{-12} \cdot 0.9^2 \cdot 0.8 \times 10^9$ W is 32.4 mW.

concepts.label: PPA trade-offs and Pareto fronts
concepts.definition: There is no single best implementation of a design, because power, performance and area cannot all be minimized at once.

sample.question:
Two implementations of a block are A: 17 mW, 1 ns, 1.8 square mm; B: 20 mW, 1.2 ns, 2 square mm. Lower is better for power, critical-path delay and area. Which statement is true?

A) A dominates B

B) B dominates A

C) Neither dominates the other

D) Each dominates the other
sample.answer: A dominates B
sample.explanation: A point dominates another when it is no worse on every metric and strictly better on at least one.

concepts.label: Dies per wafer
concepts.definition: A wafer is a disc, and dies are rectangles, so only a whole number of dies fit, and some area at the edge is always lost.

sample.question: Ignoring edge loss, how many dies of 439 square mm fit by area on a 300 mm wafer? Round to 1 decimal place.

concepts.label: Yield and cost per good die
concepts.definition: Not every die on a wafer works. Random defects, particles and process faults kill some fraction, and the probability that a die survives falls with its area.

sample.question: Defects are Poisson-distributed at 0.05 per square cm. Under $Y = e^{-D_0 A}$, what fraction of 277 square mm dies is defect-free, in percent? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: 277 square mm is 2.77 square cm, so $Y = e^{-0.05 \cdot 2.77} = 87.1\%$.

concepts.label: The cost of a respin
concepts.definition: A respin is a second (or third) fabrication of a chip after first silicon fails.
key_ideas: Expected cost and the value of verification

sample.question: A respin needs a new mask set costing 25 million dollars and 36 engineers for 2 months at 15 thousand dollars per engineer-month. What is its direct cost, in millions of dollars? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $25 + 36 \cdot 2 \cdot 15/1000 = 26.08$ million dollars.

concepts.label: Analog and mixed-signal design flows
concepts.definition: Analog and mixed-signal (AMS) circuits, such as amplifiers, data converters, PLLs, regulators and RF front ends, do not fit the RTL-to-GDSII flow.

sample.question:
What is the first design representation in a typical analog flow?

A) A transistor-level schematic

B) A gate-level netlist

C) A routed DEF

D) Synthesizable RTL
sample.answer: A transistor-level schematic
sample.explanation: Analog design starts from a schematic of devices that the designer sizes and simulates.

concepts.label: The FPGA implementation flow
concepts.definition: An FPGA flow starts from the same RTL as an ASIC flow but ends in a bitstream that configures a fixed chip.
key_ideas: Placement and routing on a fixed fabric
Vendor tools, open tools and trade-offs

sample.question:
What does FPGA technology mapping cover the logic with?

A) Library cells from a Liberty file

B) Mask polygons

C) k-feasible cones, each with at most k inputs

D) Transistor networks
sample.answer: k-feasible cones, each with at most k inputs
sample.explanation: Any function of k inputs fits one LUT, so mapping finds cones with at most k inputs.

concepts.label: PCB and package design
concepts.definition: A chip is useless until it is packaged and mounted on a board. Package design connects the die to the outside world through bumps, substrate traces and balls; printed circuit board (PCB) design connects packages, passives and connectors through layers of copper.

sample.question:
Why does advanced packaging make package design resemble chip design?

A) Packages are synthesized from RTL

B) Packages now contain transistors

C) Packages need clock trees

D) Thousands of die-to-die connections must be routed at fine pitch
sample.answer: Thousands of die-to-die connections must be routed at fine pitch
sample.explanation: Dense interposer and bridge wiring needs chip-like routing and verification.

concepts.label: Manufacturing, lithography and DFM
concepts.definition: Manufacturing is the branch where geometry becomes silicon, and its tools work on the far side of tape-out: mask synthesis, lithography simulation, process modelling and yield analysis.

sample.question:
A layer's pitch is too tight for one exposure. What resolution technique splits it?

A) Multiple patterning onto two or more masks

B) Metal fill

C) Scan insertion

D) Optical proximity correction alone
sample.answer: Multiple patterning onto two or more masks
sample.explanation: Splitting the layer into masks, a graph-colouring problem, relaxes the pitch per exposure.

concepts.label: The foundry and fabless model
concepts.definition: Most chips today are designed by companies that do not own a factory. A fabless company designs chips and sells them; a foundry manufactures chips that others design.

sample.question:
Besides models and rule decks, what do foundries often supply or reference for their process?

A) Validated standard-cell and memory libraries

B) Board-level layouts

C) The customer's testbench

D) The customer's floorplan
sample.answer: Validated standard-cell and memory libraries
sample.explanation: Libraries characterized on the process are part of design enablement.

concepts.label: EDA vendors and industry structure
concepts.definition: The EDA industry is small in revenue next to the semiconductor industry it serves, but it is indispensable: no advanced chip can be built without its tools.

sample.question:
Which barrier does a new EDA entrant face that a mature vendor already cleared?

A) The need for a user interface

B) The need to read Verilog

C) The need to run on Linux

D) Foundry certification of its tool on each process
sample.answer: Foundry certification of its tool on each process
sample.explanation: Without certification, signoff results are not accepted for manufacturing.

concepts.label: The commercial and open-source tool landscape
concepts.definition: Engineers name tools by product, but a tool designer should name them by the problem class they solve: simulation, synthesis, place and route, static timing, extraction, physical verification, test, custom layout.

concepts.label: Open-source EDA tools
concepts.definition: Open-source EDA has grown from academic prototypes into a complete RTL-to-GDSII flow that has taped out real chips.
key_ideas: What open tools are good for

sample.question:
What does the open-source tool nextpnr do?

A) Event-driven Verilog simulation

B) RTL synthesis to a gate-level netlist

C) Compiling Verilog into a fast cycle-based C++ model

D) FPGA placement and routing
sample.answer: FPGA placement and routing
sample.explanation: nextpnr: FPGA placement and routing.

concepts.label: Standards bodies and open formats
concepts.definition: EDA works only because tools from different vendors can read each other's files and agree on what a language means.

sample.question:
Which IEEE standard defines boundary scan (JTAG)?

A) IEEE 1481

B) IEEE 1801

C) IEEE 1149.1

D) IEEE 1364
sample.answer: IEEE 1149.1
sample.explanation: JTAG boundary scan is IEEE 1149.1.

concepts.label: Structured VLSI design, SPICE and the university CAD tools
concepts.definition: Modern EDA grew from a few landmark ideas of the 1970s and 1980s.

sample.question:
How does SPICE formulate the circuit equations?

A) Modified nodal analysis with sparse matrices

B) A timing graph of arrival times

C) An and-inverter graph

D) A routing-resource graph
sample.answer: Modified nodal analysis with sparse matrices
sample.explanation: Modified nodal analysis gives a sparse system solved by sparse LU factorization.

concepts.label: EDA research conferences and communities
concepts.definition: EDA research is published mainly at conferences, and each major conference has a distinct community and focus.

sample.question:
Which conference is research-focused and covers the whole of EDA without a large exhibition?

A) ISSCC

B) ICCAD

C) DAC

D) SEMICON
sample.answer: ICCAD
sample.explanation: ICCAD is the field-wide research conference.

concepts.label: The four-layer model across flow engines
concepts.definition: An agent that changes EDA tools on request needs to know which part of an engine a request touches.
key_ideas: The same four layers in every engine
Why the core must stay small

sample.question:
In a router, which part is strategy rather than core?

A) The definition of a short between nets

B) The rip-up and reroute ordering

C) The DRC-correct path model

D) Grid and layer legality
sample.answer: The rip-up and reroute ordering
sample.explanation: How the router searches is strategy; what counts as a legal route is core.

concepts.label: Routing a flow change request to a tier
concepts.definition: Requests to change a flow arrive in plain language: make placement less congested near the memories, time this block with an extra margin, route this bus on upper layers.
key_ideas: Proving a change at its tier

sample.question:
What defines a Tier 2 change?

A) A small implementation at a defined extension point, leaving the core untouched

B) A change to the foundry rule deck

C) A value in a configuration file

D) A change to the engine's core source
sample.answer: A small implementation at a defined extension point, leaving the core untouched
sample.explanation: Tier 2 adds code through a seam such as a plug-in interface.

concepts.label: Fast and accurate engines across the flow
concepts.definition: Every analysis in the flow exists at several accuracies: a fast placer and a full placer, a quick congestion estimate and a global router, a fast timer with lumped wires and a signoff timer with extracted parasitics.
key_ideas: The cost of a modeling loop
When to recurse to the accurate engine
What the fast mode gives up

sample.question: An agent runs 60 iterations of a fast place-and-time loop, each taking 15 minutes, and every 5th iteration it confirms the result with an accurate run taking 240 minutes. How many minutes does the whole loop take?
sample.explanation: $60 \cdot 15 + \lfloor 60/5 \rfloor \cdot 240 = 3780$ minutes.

concepts.label: Differential QoR checks on a flow change
concepts.definition: When an agent changes a flow, by a parameter, a plug-in or a script, someone must decide whether the change did what it claimed and nothing else.

sample.question: A differential timing check compares endpoint setup slacks (in ps, baseline to new) after a flow change: A: -10 to -9; B: -3 to 0; C: -5 to -3; D: 37 to 33; E: 32 to 29. With a tolerance of 5 ps, how many endpoints moved?
sample.explanation: Count endpoints whose slack changed by more than 5 ps: 0.

concepts.label: Agentic closure loops across the flow
concepts.definition: Design closure has always been a loop: read reports, decide a fix, run tools, check again.
key_ideas: The closure loop as an agent
Rewards, reward hacking and the human gate

sample.question:
A path fails timing by 6 ps. What should a well-designed closure agent try first?

A) Relaxing the clock constraint

B) Changing the floorplan

C) A local fix such as resizing a gate or inserting a buffer

D) Re-running synthesis from RTL
sample.answer: A local fix such as resizing a gate or inserting a buffer
sample.explanation: The most local fix re-runs the fewest stages, as an engineer would choose.

domains.name: Boolean Reasoning and Complexity
domains.description: Boolean functions, cofactors, Shannon expansion, covers and clauses, and the complexity theory that explains why every EDA problem needs heuristics.
covers: Boolean algebra and Boolean functions, propositional and predicate logic as used in hardware
Cofactors, Shannon expansion, Boolean difference, unate and binate functions, symmetry
Cubes, covers, SOP/POS, minterms, implicants, prime implicants
Boolean decomposition, functional dependence
Decision diagrams overview, constraint satisfaction problems
Partial orders and lattices in logic

Computational complexity: P vs NP, NP-completeness, NP-hardness, reductions (SAT, 3-SAT, clique, vertex cover), approximation algorithms, heuristics, parameterized complexity, randomized algorithms, amortized analysis, algorithm analysis
Data structures for Boolean reasoning (bit-parallel truth tables, hash-consing)

concepts.label: Boolean functions and truth tables
concepts.definition: A Boolean function $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ is the object every logic tool manipulates: synthesis rewrites it, a SAT solver searches its inputs, an equivalence checker compares two of them, and a test generator looks for inputs that expose a difference.
key_ideas: Functions from n bits to one bit
Comparing two functions row by row

sample.question: Let $f(a, b, c) = \overline{c} + ab$. On how many of the 8 rows of its truth table is $f = 1$?
sample.explanation: Evaluating the expression row by row gives the ON-set m(0, 2, 4, 6, 7), which has 5 rows.

concepts.label: Cofactors of a Boolean function
concepts.definition: The cofactor of $f$ with respect to a literal is the function left over when that variable is fixed.
key_ideas: Cofactor with respect to a cube

sample.question: Let $f(a, b, c) = \overline{a}c + b + \overline{b}\overline{c}$. Compute the cofactor $f_{\overline{b}}$ (set $b = 0$), a function of a, c. How many of its 4 rows are 1?
sample.explanation: Setting b = 0 keeps the 4 rows with that value. Of those, 3 have f = 1.

concepts.label: Shannon expansion
concepts.definition: Shannon expansion writes any Boolean function as a choice between its two cofactors: $f = x\, f_x + \overline{x}\, f_{\overline{x}}$.
key_ideas: Splitting a function on one variable
Rebuilding a function from its cofactors

sample.question: A function of a, b, c is built by Shannon expansion on $a$: $f = a\,(\overline{c} + \overline{b}) + \overline{a}\,(\overline{c} + \overline{b})$. On how many of the 8 rows of $f$ is $f = 1$?
sample.explanation: The two terms are disjoint, since one needs a = 1 and the other a = 0. The positive cofactor has 3 ON rows and the negative cofactor has 3, so f has 6.

concepts.label: Boolean difference and sensitivity
concepts.definition: The Boolean difference of $f$ with respect to $x$ is the function that is 1 exactly where changing $x$ changes $f$.
key_ideas: The XOR of the two cofactors

sample.question: Let $f(a, b, c) = \sum m(3, 4, 5, 6, 7)$. The Boolean difference $\partial f / \partial a = f_{a} \oplus f_{\overline{a}}$ is a function of b, c. On how many of its 4 rows is it 1?
sample.explanation: XOR the two cofactors row by row: they differ on 3 of the 4 rows.

concepts.label: Unate and binate functions
concepts.definition: A function is positive unate in $x$ when raising $x$ from 0 to 1 can never lower the output, negative unate when it can never raise it, and binate when it does both on different rows.

sample.question:
Let $f(a, b, c) = b\overline{c} + \overline{b}c$. How does $f$ depend on $c$? Compare $f_{c}$ with $f_{\overline{c}}$.

A) Independent of $c$

B) Positive unate in $c$

C) Binate in $c$

D) Negative unate in $c$
sample.answer: Binate in $c$
sample.explanation: Neither cofactor implies the other: some rows rise with c and others fall, so f is binate in c.

concepts.label: Symmetric functions
concepts.definition: A function is symmetric in a pair of variables when swapping them never changes the output, and totally symmetric when any permutation of its inputs leaves it unchanged.
key_ideas: Symmetry in a pair of variables

sample.question: A totally symmetric function of 3 inputs is 1 exactly when the number of inputs at 1 is one of {1, 2}. How many of its 8 rows are 1?
sample.explanation: Count the rows of each allowed weight: C(3,1) + C(3,2) = 6.

concepts.label: Existential and universal quantification
concepts.definition: Quantifying a Boolean variable removes it from a function. The existential quantification $\exists x\, f$ asks whether some value of $x$ makes $f$ true; the universal quantification $\forall x\, f$ asks whether every value does.
key_ideas: Existential quantification as an OR of cofactors
Universal quantification as an AND of cofactors

sample.question: Let $f(a, b, c) = b + a + a\overline{c}$. The property "there exists a value of $b$ that makes $f$ true" is $\exists b\, f$, a function of a, c. On how many of its 4 rows is it 1?
sample.explanation: Existential quantification is the OR of the cofactors: f with b = 0 OR f with b = 1. That OR is 1 on 4 rows.

concepts.label: Support and functional dependence
concepts.definition: The support of a function is the set of variables it really depends on. Expressions routinely mention variables the function ignores, and netlists routinely compute signals that are functions of other signals.
key_ideas: The true support of a function
Vacuous variables in a redundant expression
When one function is a function of others

sample.question: Let $f(a, b, c, d) = \sum m(0, 2, 4, 6)$. How many variables are in the true support of $f$, the variables whose Boolean difference is not identically 0?
sample.explanation: Compare the two cofactors of each variable. They differ only for a, d, so the support has 2 variables.

concepts.label: Simple disjoint decomposition
concepts.definition: A decomposition writes a function as a composition of smaller ones. The simple disjoint form is $f(A, B) = h(g(A), B)$: a sub-function $g$ reads only the bound set $A$, and the rest of the logic sees $A$ only through that single wire.
key_ideas: Searching for a good bound set

sample.question: Let $f(a, b, c, d) = \sum m(0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 10, 11, 14, 15)$. Draw the decomposition chart with bound set $\{a, d\}$ (one column per assignment of the bound set) and free set $\{b, c\}$. What is the column multiplicity, the number of distinct columns?
sample.explanation: Each column is the cofactor of f with respect to one assignment of (a, d), a function of b, c. There are 3 distinct cofactors. A simple disjoint decomposition f = h(g(a, d), b, c) exists exactly when this is at most 2.

concepts.label: Cubes and their minterms
concepts.definition: A cube is a product of literals, such as $a\overline{c}d$, and also the set of minterms it covers, a subcube of the Boolean hypercube.

sample.question: In positional notation over 5 variables (one position per variable, 0 for a complemented literal, 1 for a true literal, - for an absent variable), how many minterms does the cube 0--0- contain?
sample.explanation: The cube has 3 dashes, each free to be 0 or 1, so it contains 2^3 = 8 minterms.

concepts.label: Sum-of-products and product-of-sums forms
concepts.definition: Every Boolean function has two canonical two-level forms: the sum of its minterms and the product of its maxterms.

sample.question: Let $f(a, b, c) = b\overline{c} + b + \overline{a}\overline{b}$. How many literals does its canonical sum of minterms contain in total?
sample.explanation: There are 6 ON rows, each a minterm of 3 literals: 18 literals.

concepts.label: Cubes, implicants and prime implicants
concepts.definition: An implicant of $f$ is a cube that lies entirely inside the ON-set, so it implies $f$.

sample.question:
Let $f(a, b, c) = \sum m(0, 1, 3, 6)$. Classify the cube $\overline{b}$.

A) An implicant of $f$ but not prime

B) Not an implicant of $f$

C) An essential prime of the complement of $f$

D) A prime implicant of $f$
sample.answer: Not an implicant of $f$
sample.explanation: Some minterm of the cube is an OFF row of f, so the cube is not contained in the ON-set.

concepts.label: Essential prime implicants
concepts.definition: A prime implicant is essential when it is the only prime covering some ON minterm.

sample.question: Let $f(a, b, c) = \sum m(0, 7)$. How many prime implicants does $f$ have?
sample.explanation: The primes are $\overline{a}\overline{b}\overline{c}$, $abc$: 2.

concepts.label: Minimum covers and the covering problem
concepts.definition: Once the primes are known, two-level minimization becomes a covering problem: choose the cheapest set of primes whose union is the ON-set.

sample.question: Let $f(a, b, c) = \sum m(2, 6)$. What is the smallest number of product terms in any sum-of-products expression for $f$?
sample.explanation: A minimum SOP uses primes only. Of the 1 primes, 1 are essential, and the cheapest set covering every ON minterm has 1 cubes.

concepts.label: Incompletely specified functions
concepts.definition: Real specifications leave some outputs free. Inputs that never occur (an unused opcode, an unreachable state code) and outputs nobody observes are don't cares.
key_ideas: The ON, OFF and don't-care sets
Primes of an incompletely specified function

sample.question: An incompletely specified function of a, b, c has ON-set $\sum m(0, 3, 4, 6)$ and don't-care set $d(1, 2)$; every other row is OFF. How many completely specified functions agree with it on every care row?
sample.explanation: Each of the 2 don't-care rows may be 0 or 1: 2^2 = 4.

concepts.label: Tautology checking of a cover
concepts.definition: A cover is a tautology when its cubes together contain every minterm, so the function it represents is the constant 1.
key_ideas: A cover is a tautology when nothing is missed
Cube containment as a tautology question

sample.question: Over the variables a, b, c, in that order, a cover is $F = \{-0-, -00, -00, -00, 11-, 0-0, 0-1\}$ in positional notation. How many of the 8 minterms does $F$ miss? (Zero means $F$ is a tautology.)
sample.explanation: The cubes together cover 8 of the 8 minterms, so 0 are missed.

concepts.label: Bit-parallel truth tables
concepts.definition: For functions of up to about 16 inputs, the fastest representation is the explicit truth table packed into machine words.
key_ideas: A function as one machine word

sample.question:
A tool stores $f(a, b, c) = \overline{a}\overline{c} + a + \overline{b}$ as a 8-bit truth-table word. Bit $i$ of the word holds $f$ at minterm $i$, where $i$ is written in binary as $abc$ with $a$ the most significant bit; bit 0 is the least significant bit of the word. Which word is it?

A) 0xF6

B) 0xEF

C) 0xF7

D) 0x08
sample.answer: 0xF7
sample.explanation: The ON-set is m(0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7); set those bits and read the word in hex from bit 7 down to bit 0: 0xF7.

concepts.label: Hash-consing and structural hashing
concepts.definition: Hash-consing is the rule that a data structure never stores two copies of the same node: before creating a node, look up its key, the operator and its children's identifiers, in a unique table, and return the existing node if one is there.

sample.question: An and-inverter graph over inputs $a, b, c, d$ is built gate by gate: $g_{1} = c \land d$, $g_{2} = a \land d$, $g_{3} = g_{1} \land g_{2}$, $g_{4} = g_{1} \land g_{2}$, $g_{5} = b \land g_{2}$, $g_{6} = g_{3} \land g_{4}$. The builder hash-conses: before creating an AND node it looks up the pair of operands in a unique table. How many AND nodes does the table hold at the end?
sample.explanation: Of the 6 gate definitions, 4 produce new keys; the rest are duplicates or simplify away. Hash-consing gives each distinct structure exactly one node, so equality of nodes is a pointer comparison.

concepts.label: Decision diagrams overview
concepts.definition: A reduced ordered binary decision diagram (ROBDD) is the Shannon expansion tree of a function with identical subfunctions shared and pointless tests removed, under a fixed variable order.
key_ideas: From the Shannon tree to a reduced diagram
Counting reduced nodes level by level

sample.question: Let $f(a, b, c) = \sum m(1, 6)$. Build its reduced ordered BDD with the order a < b < c (first variable at the top). How many internal (non-terminal) nodes does it have?
sample.explanation: At each level, count the distinct subfunctions reached by fixing the variables above it that still depend on that level's variable; sum over levels: 5 nodes, plus the two terminals.

concepts.label: The Boolean lattice and implication order
concepts.definition: Bit vectors of length $n$, ordered componentwise, form the Boolean lattice $B^n$: the hypercube with 00...0 at the bottom and 11...1 at the top.

sample.question: In $B^{6}$ ordered componentwise, how many vectors are comparable to 011110 (above it, below it, or equal)?
sample.explanation: There are 2^2 vectors at or above and 2^4 at or below; the vector itself is counted twice: 19.

concepts.label: Monotone functions
concepts.definition: A monotone function is an order-preserving map from $B^n$ to $\{0, 1\}$: raising any input never lowers the output.
key_ideas: Minimal true points are the primes
Maximal false points give the clauses

sample.question: The monotone function $f(a, b, c, d) = ab + ad + c$ uses only positive literals. On how many of its 16 rows is $f = 1$?
sample.explanation: The ON-set is the up-set of the minimal true points: every vector at or above one of them. It has 11 rows.

concepts.label: Fixpoints on the subset lattice
concepts.definition: Many verification questions are answered by iterating a set operator until it stops changing.
key_ideas: The least fixpoint is the reachable set

sample.question: A transition system has states $s_0$ to $s_6$ and transitions $s_1 \to s_4,\ s_4 \to s_4,\ s_5 \to s_1,\ s_5 \to s_5,\ s_6 \to s_2,\ s_6 \to s_4$. Reachability iterates $R_0 = \{s_1, s_5\}$, $R_{k+1} = R_k \cup \mathrm{Img}(R_k)$ until nothing changes. How many steps add at least one new state?
sample.explanation: Breadth-first, each step adds the states one transition further out. The farthest reachable state is 1 transitions from the initial set, so 1 steps add states and the next step confirms the fixpoint.

concepts.label: Conjunctive normal form and clauses
concepts.definition: Conjunctive normal form is an AND of clauses, each clause an OR of literals. It is the input language of every SAT solver (the DIMACS format), so equivalence checking, bounded model checking, test generation and many scheduling and routing problems end up as CNF.

sample.question:
Under the assignment $x_{1} = 0, x_{2} = 1, x_{3} = 0, x_{4} = 0$, how many clauses of $(
eg x_{2} \lor 
eg x_{3}) \land (
eg x_{2} \lor 
eg x_{4}) \land (
eg x_{1} \lor x_{2} \lor 
eg x_{4}) \land (
eg x_{2} \lor 
eg x_{3})$ are falsified?
sample.explanation: A clause is falsified only when every one of its literals is false. 0 clauses are.

concepts.label: Tseitin encoding of a circuit
concepts.definition: The Tseitin encoding turns a circuit into CNF of linear size by giving every gate output its own variable and writing a few clauses that force that variable to equal the gate's function of its inputs.
key_ideas: Variables and the size of the encoding

sample.question: Use the standard Tseitin encoding: one fresh variable per gate output, the clauses of output if and only if gate function, and no simplification. How many clauses encode a single two-input XNOR gate?
sample.explanation: y = a XNOR b, like XOR, needs 4 three-literal clauses. Total: 4.

concepts.label: Counting satisfying assignments
concepts.definition: Model counting, written #SAT, asks how many assignments satisfy a formula rather than whether one exists.

sample.question:
Over $x_1$ to $x_{3}$, how many assignments satisfy $(
eg x_{2} \lor 
eg x_{3}) \land (x_{1} \lor 
eg x_{2} \lor 
eg x_{3}) \land (x_{1} \lor x_{2} \lor 
eg x_{3})$?
sample.explanation: Enumerate all 8 assignments and test every clause: 5 satisfy the formula.

concepts.label: Resolution and variable elimination
concepts.definition: Resolution is the single inference rule behind clause-based reasoning: from $(x \lor A)$ and $(\neg x \lor B)$ infer $(A \lor B)$.

sample.question: Resolve $(x_{1} \lor x_{4})$ with $(\neg x_{1} \lor x_{4})$ on $x_{1}$. How many distinct literals does the resolvent contain?
sample.explanation: Drop the clashing pair and take the union of what remains, merging repeated literals: $(x_{4})$, 1 literals.

concepts.label: Constraint satisfaction problems in CNF
concepts.definition: A constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) has variables with finite domains and constraints over subsets of them.
key_ideas: One-hot encoding of a finite domain

sample.question: A CSP has 11 variables, each with a domain of 3 values, encoded one-hot with an at-least-one clause and pairwise at-most-one clauses per variable. How many domain clauses are there in total, before any constraint clauses?
sample.explanation: Each variable needs 1 + C(3, 2) = 4 clauses; times 11 variables gives 44.

concepts.label: Tractable classes of SAT
concepts.definition: SAT is NP-complete, but several syntactic classes are solvable in polynomial time, and a surprising share of the constraints that EDA tools generate fall into them.
key_ideas: XOR constraints and where hardness begins

sample.question:
In a 2-SAT implication graph, $x$ and $\neg x$ lie in the same strongly connected component. What follows?

A) The formula has exactly two models

B) $x$ is true in every model

C) $x$ can be removed as a pure literal

D) The formula is unsatisfiable
sample.answer: The formula is unsatisfiable
sample.explanation: Paths $x \to \dots \to \neg x$ and $\neg x \to \dots \to x$ force $x$ to equal its own negation, so no assignment works.

concepts.label: Algorithm analysis for Boolean tools
concepts.definition: Boolean tools live on the edge between polynomial and exponential cost. A tool designer must predict, before writing code, whether an approach scales: how much memory an explicit representation takes, how many calls a recursion makes, and how a measured runtime will extrapolate to the next design size.
key_ideas: Memory of an explicit truth table

sample.question: A tool stores the complete truth table of a 17-variable function bit-parallel in 64-bit machine words. How many words does it need?
sample.explanation: The table has 2^17 bits; dividing by 2^6 bits per word leaves 2^11 = 2048 words. Each extra variable doubles it, which is why explicit tables stop near 16 to 20 inputs.

concepts.label: Amortized analysis
concepts.definition: Amortized analysis bounds the total cost of a sequence of operations, even when single operations are occasionally expensive.

sample.question: A binary counter starts at 0 and is incremented 147 times. Each increment flips the trailing 1s to 0 and one 0 to 1. How many bit flips happen in total?
sample.explanation: Bit j flips once every 2^j increments, so the total is 2N minus the number of 1s in N: 2(147) - 4 = 290, under 2 flips per increment.

concepts.label: Randomized algorithms and random simulation
concepts.definition: Randomized algorithms use coin flips to be faster or simpler than any known deterministic method, at the price of a bounded probability of error or a random running time.
key_ideas: The chance that random vectors miss a difference
Expected time to the first counterexample

sample.question: Two 6-input functions differ on exactly 1 of the $2^{6}$ input vectors. A simulator applies 19 independent, uniformly random vectors. What is the probability that none of them exposes the difference? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Each vector misses with probability 1 - 1/64. Independence gives (1 - p)^19 = 0.7414.

concepts.label: P, NP and coNP
concepts.definition: Complexity classes tell a tool designer what kind of algorithm to look for. A problem in P has an algorithm whose time is polynomial in the input size.
key_ideas: coNP and the shape of verification problems

sample.question:
Which of these is a decision problem?

A) Find the smallest circuit computing this truth table

B) List all satisfying assignments of this CNF

C) Count the models of this formula

D) Is there an input vector that sets this circuit's output to 1?
sample.answer: Is there an input vector that sets this circuit's output to 1?
sample.explanation: A decision problem has a yes or no answer. The others ask for an object, a list or a number.

concepts.label: Polynomial-time reductions
concepts.definition: A reduction from problem A to problem B is a polynomial-time transformation of every instance of A into an instance of B with the same yes or no answer.

sample.question:
What must a polynomial-time many-one reduction from problem A to problem B do?

A) Run in polynomial time on yes-instances only

B) Map instances of B to instances of A

C) Map yes-instances of A to yes-instances of B and no-instances to no-instances, in polynomial time

D) Preserve the number of solutions exactly
sample.answer: Map yes-instances of A to yes-instances of B and no-instances to no-instances, in polynomial time
sample.explanation: The reduction is a polynomial function f with x in A exactly when f(x) is in B. Counting solutions is a stronger, parsimonious requirement.

concepts.label: NP-completeness
concepts.definition: A problem is NP-complete when it is in NP and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time.
key_ideas: NP-hard, NP-complete and the problems a tool meets

sample.question:
Why does the Cook-Levin proof turn a verifier into a circuit?

A) A polynomial-time verifier on inputs of fixed size unrolls into a polynomial-size circuit, and asking whether some certificate makes it accept is a satisfiability question

B) Circuits remove the need for certificates

C) Circuits run faster than Turing machines

D) Only circuits can express polynomial time
sample.answer: A polynomial-time verifier on inputs of fixed size unrolls into a polynomial-size circuit, and asking whether some certificate makes it accept is a satisfiability question
sample.explanation: The circuit's free inputs are the certificate bits; satisfiability of the circuit is exactly the existence of an accepted certificate.

concepts.label: From SAT to 3-SAT
concepts.definition: 3-SAT, where every clause has at most three literals, is the standard starting point for NP-hardness proofs because its instances are uniform and small gadgets can simulate a clause.
key_ideas: Fresh variables for a whole formula

sample.question: The standard SAT-to-3-SAT reduction splits a clause of 5 literals into a chain of three-literal clauses. How many fresh linking variables does it introduce?
sample.explanation: A chain of k - 2 = 3 clauses has k - 3 = 2 links between consecutive clauses, one fresh variable each.

concepts.label: Vertex cover, independent set and clique
concepts.definition: Vertex cover, independent set and clique are three faces of one problem, and they appear throughout EDA: vertex cover in test-point selection and in breaking cycles, independent sets in conflict-free scheduling and in register binding, cliques in compatibility-based resource sharing.
key_ideas: Covers and independent sets are complements

sample.question: A graph $G$ has 26 vertices and its maximum independent set has 21 vertices. How large is the minimum vertex cover of $G$?
sample.explanation: Complement the largest independent set to get the smallest cover: 26 - 21 = 5.

concepts.label: Approximation algorithms and heuristics
concepts.definition: When a problem is NP-hard, a tool still has to return an answer quickly. An approximation algorithm runs in polynomial time and comes with a proven ratio: its cost is never worse than $\rho$ times the optimum.
key_ideas: Greedy set cover and heuristics without guarantees

sample.question: A graph on vertices 1 to 6 has edges (1,6), (3,6), (2,6), (1,4), (1,2), (4,6), (4,5), (1,3), (2,3), (1,5). The 2-approximation for vertex cover scans the edges in this order and, whenever an edge has neither endpoint in the cover, adds both endpoints. How many vertices does it return?
sample.explanation: The edges it picks form a maximal matching of 3 edges, and it returns both endpoints of each: 6 vertices.

concepts.label: Parameterized complexity
concepts.definition: Parameterized complexity measures running time in two quantities: the input size $n$ and a parameter $k$ such as the solution size or the treewidth.

sample.question: A refined vertex-cover search branches on a vertex $v$ of degree at least 3: take $v$ (budget drops by 1) or take all its neighbours (budget drops by at least 3). Its leaf count satisfies $L(k) = L(k-1) + L(k-3)$ with $L(0) = L(1) = L(2) = 1$. What is $L(9)$?
sample.explanation: Iterating gives L(9) = 19, against 2^9 = 512 for plain edge branching. Better branching lowers the base of the exponent, not the dependence on n.

concepts.label: SAT and BDD engines as agent tools
concepts.definition: In an agent-first flow, SAT solvers, BDD packages and simulators are not libraries buried inside one program; they are skills an agent calls through a typed tool interface, the way engines are exposed over MCP.

sample.question:
A SAT tool takes a CNF in DIMACS form. What else must each call carry so that results are reproducible?

A) The solver's source code

B) The resource limits and the random seed

C) The expected answer

D) The agent's chat history
sample.answer: The resource limits and the random seed
sample.explanation: CDCL runs depend on seeds and limits; recording them makes a verdict, and especially an UNKNOWN, repeatable.

concepts.label: Fast and exact Boolean reasoning modes
concepts.definition: Every Boolean engine has a fast mode and an exact mode. Random or guided simulation, structural hashing and cheap signatures run in microseconds and can only refute; SAT, BDDs and proof-producing checkers are complete but can take arbitrarily long.
key_ideas: Exact engines as the accurate mode

sample.question:
An agent proposes a rewrite of a 13-input block and runs 3072 independent uniformly random vectors through the original and the rewrite with no mismatch. Suppose the rewrite were in fact wrong on 8 of the $2^{13}$ inputs. Which statement is correct?

A) A difference that size would escape with probability about 0.9503, so equivalence is still unproven

B) A difference that size would escape with probability about 0.0497, so equivalence is still unproven

C) The clean run proves equivalence, so the exact check can be skipped

D) A difference that size would escape with probability about 0.001, so equivalence is still unproven
sample.answer: A difference that size would escape with probability about 0.0497, so equivalence is still unproven
sample.explanation: Each vector misses with probability 1 - 8/2^13, so all 3072 miss with probability (1 - p)^3072 = 0.0497. Simulation can refute equivalence, never prove it; an exact SAT or BDD check must follow.

concepts.label: Equivalence checking as the golden test
concepts.definition: When an agent proposes a logic transform, a rewrite, a resynthesized cone, a remapped block, the golden test is a combinational equivalence check between the original and the proposal.

sample.question: Over a, b, c, an agent proposes replacing $f = \overline{a}c + \overline{a}\overline{b}$ by $g = c + \overline{a}\overline{b}$. The golden test builds the miter $f \oplus g$ and asks a SAT solver for inputs that make it 1. How many of the 8 input vectors satisfy the miter? (Zero means the transform is correct.)
sample.explanation: Compare the two truth tables: they differ on m(5, 7). Any one of these is a counterexample the solver can return, and the transform is rejected unless the count is 0.

concepts.label: Change tiers in a Boolean reasoning engine
concepts.definition: When an agent or a user asks for a change in a SAT solver or BDD package, the first decision is where the change belongs.
key_ideas: Landing a request in a tier

sample.question:
In a BDD package, the unique table and the canonicity invariant (no duplicate nodes, no node with equal children) belong to which layer?

A) Parameters

B) Policy

C) Observation hooks

D) The core
sample.answer: The core
sample.explanation: Canonicity is what makes equivalence a pointer comparison; nothing outside the core may break it.

concepts.label: Tool-grounded rewards for logic transforms
concepts.definition: Training a model to propose logic rewrites with reinforcement learning needs a reward, and the natural reward comes from tools: an equivalence checker says whether the rewrite is correct, structural hashing and a node count say whether it helps.

sample.question:
A proven-equivalent rewrite raises logic depth from 18 to 26 levels on a timing-critical block. What should the reward include?

A) The number of SAT conflicts

B) A bonus for the added depth

C) Nothing more, since equivalence is enough

D) A depth or delay term alongside the node count
sample.answer: A depth or delay term alongside the node count
sample.explanation: A reward that sees only area will trade delay for nodes; the objective must contain what the design cares about.

domains.name: Graph Algorithms for EDA
domains.description: Netlists as hypergraphs, partitioning (KL, FM, multilevel, spectral), shortest paths and A*, flows, Steiner trees and the graph machinery under placement, routing and timing.
covers: Directed graphs, DAGs, hypergraphs; netlists as hypergraphs; clique and star net models
Topological sorting, strongly connected components, graph traversal

Graph partitioning, hypergraph partitioning, min-cut, Kernighan-Lin, Fiduccia-Mattheyses, multilevel partitioning (coarsen, partition, uncoarsen), spectral partitioning, graph Laplacian, spectral graph theory
Graph coloring, graph matching, bipartite matching
Network flow, maximum flow, minimum cut, minimum-cost flow
Shortest paths: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, A* search; longest paths in DAGs
Minimum spanning tree, Steiner tree problem, rectilinear Steiner tree, Hanan grid
Traveling salesman problem (scan-chain ordering), graph embedding, planarity, graph drawing

concepts.label: Netlists as hypergraphs
concepts.definition: A netlist is a set of cells joined by nets, and a net can join any number of cells.

sample.question: A netlist has cells c1 to c6 and nets n1 = {c2, c4, c6}; n2 = {c1, c3, c6}; n3 = {c1, c3, c4, c6}; n4 = {c1, c2, c4, c5}. Seen as a hypergraph, how many pins (vertex-hyperedge incidences) does it have?
sample.explanation: Each net contributes one pin per cell it touches. The net sizes are 3, 3, 4, 4, which sum to 14.

concepts.label: Directed pin graphs of drivers and sinks
concepts.definition: Timing analysis, levelization and loop detection need to know which way signals flow.
key_ideas: Direction as a source of structure

sample.question: Each cell has one output pin. The nets are: n1 driven by c2, sinks c4; n2 driven by c5, sinks c7; n3 driven by c6, sinks c7. Build the directed pin graph with one arc from each net's driver to each of its sinks. How many arcs does the graph have?
sample.explanation: A net with k pins has one driver and k - 1 sinks, so it contributes k - 1 arcs. Summing the sink counts gives 3.

concepts.label: Clique and star models of a net
concepts.definition: Many algorithms, from spectral partitioning to quadratic placement, need an ordinary weighted graph rather than a hypergraph.

sample.question: A netlist has nets with 7, 2, 8, 8 pins. Expanding every net as a clique, how many graph edges result (count parallel edges between the same pair separately)?
sample.explanation: A k-pin clique has k(k - 1)/2 edges. Summing over the nets gives 78. Large nets dominate: the clique count grows quadratically.

concepts.label: Compressed incidence storage for netlists
concepts.definition: A million-cell netlist has several million pins, and every pass of a partitioner or placer walks them.

sample.question: Nets: n1 = {c3, c4, c5}; n2 = {c2, c6}; n3 = {c1, c3, c4}; n4 = {c1, c2, c3, c4}. The tool stores net-to-pin incidence in compressed form: an offset array netStart of length m + 1 and a pin array listing each net's cells in order, so net j's pins are pin[netStart[j]] up to pin[netStart[j+1] - 1], with nets indexed from 0 (n1 is index 0). What is netStart[1]?
sample.explanation: netStart[1] is the number of pins in nets 0 to 0, which is 3. The offsets are 0, 3, 5, 8, 12.

concepts.label: Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree
concepts.definition: Routed nets, clock trees, Steiner trees and buffer trees are rooted trees: a driver at the root, sinks at the leaves.
key_ideas: Two passes on an RC tree

sample.question: A rooted tree has nodes 1 to 6 with root 1 and parent(2) = 1, parent(3) = 1, parent(4) = 1, parent(5) = 1, parent(6) = 2. Children are visited in increasing label order. Which node is visited in position 6 of the pre-order traversal? Answer with its label.
sample.explanation: Pre-order visits a node before its children: 1, 2, 6, 3, 4, 5. Position 6 holds node 5.

concepts.label: Topological sorting of a DAG
concepts.definition: A combinational netlist, cut at its registers, is a directed acyclic graph. A topological order lists its vertices so that every arc goes forward, which is exactly the order in which arrival times, logic values or signal probabilities can be computed in one pass.

sample.question: A combinational netlist graph has nodes v1 to v5 and arcs v3→v5, v3→v4, v5→v2, v5→v1. Run Kahn's algorithm, always removing the ready node (in-degree 0) with the smallest label. Which node is output in position 4? Answer with its number (for v3, answer 3).
sample.explanation: Kahn's algorithm repeatedly outputs a node with no remaining predecessors and deletes its arcs. With smallest-label tie-breaking the order is v3, v4, v5, v1, v2.

concepts.label: Levelization of a combinational netlist
concepts.definition: Levelization assigns each vertex of a combinational DAG a level: primary inputs and register outputs at level 0, and every other vertex one above its deepest fanin.

sample.question: A combinational netlist has nodes v1 to v8 and arcs v1→v4, v2→v4, v3→v4, v4→v5, v4→v7, v5→v6, v7→v8. Primary inputs (nodes with no incoming arc) are at level 0, and every other node sits one level above its highest fanin. What is the level of v6?
sample.explanation: Levels in topological order: v1:0, v2:0, v3:0, v4:1, v5:2, v6:3, v7:2, v8:3.

concepts.label: Strongly connected components and combinational loops
concepts.definition: A combinational loop, a cycle that passes through no register, breaks static timing, makes simulation oscillate or depend on order, and is almost always a design error.

sample.question: A gate-level netlist graph has nodes v1 to v7 and arcs v1→v5, v2→v6, v2→v3, v3→v5, v4→v2, v4→v7, v5→v1, v7→v3. How many strongly connected components does it have (a node on no cycle is a component by itself)?
sample.explanation: The strongly connected components are {v4} {v7} {v2} {v3} {v6} {v1, v5}.

concepts.label: Longest paths in a DAG
concepts.definition: Static timing analysis is, at its core, a longest-path computation on a DAG: the latest arrival time at a vertex is the longest path, by delay, from any timing start point.

sample.question: A timing graph has nodes v1 to v6 and arcs with delays in ps: v1→v3 (1), v2→v4 (6), v3→v6 (6), v4→v5 (2), v4→v6 (4). Both v1 and v2 are inputs with arrival 0 ps. What is the latest arrival time (longest-path length) at v4, in ps?
sample.explanation: Relax arcs in topological order, keeping the maximum: arrivals are 0, 0, 1, 6, 8, 10 for v1 onward.

concepts.label: Reverse-topological passes and node slack
concepts.definition: A forward pass computes the latest arrival at every vertex. A backward pass, in reverse topological order, computes the latest time each vertex may settle without violating any endpoint requirement.

sample.question: A timing graph has nodes v1 to v5 and arcs with delays in ps: v1→v3 (8), v1→v4 (3), v2→v3 (3), v3→v5 (3). Inputs v1 and v2 arrive at 0 ps, and every endpoint (node with no outgoing arc) is required by 11 ps. What is the required time at v3, in ps?
sample.explanation: Forward pass (max): arrivals 0, 0, 8, 3, 11. Backward pass in reverse topological order (min of successor required time minus arc delay): required 0, 5, 8, 11, 11.

concepts.label: Counting paths through a node
concepts.definition: The number of input-to-output paths in a netlist can be exponential in its size, which is why timers cannot enumerate paths and why path-based fault models and path coverage metrics need care.

sample.question: A netlist DAG has nodes v1 to v6 and arcs v1→v3, v1→v4, v1→v5, v1→v6, v2→v5. Sources are v1 and v2; sinks are the nodes with no outgoing arc. How many distinct source-to-sink paths are there?
sample.explanation: Count paths from the sources forward: N(v) = sum of N over predecessors, with N = 1 at each source. The counts are 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 1; summing over sinks gives 5.

concepts.label: Incremental updates on a DAG
concepts.definition: Optimization loops change one gate, one wire or one buffer at a time and need updated timing after each change.
key_ideas: The fanout cone bounds the work

sample.question: A timing graph has nodes v1 to v6 and arcs with delays in ps: v1→v3 (5), v2→v4 (6), v2→v6 (6), v3→v4 (9), v3→v5 (6), v4→v6 (4). Inputs v1 and v2 arrive at 0 ps. An ECO slows arc v1→v3 by 3 ps. An incremental timer marks dirty v3 and everything in its fanout cone. How many nodes are marked, including v3?
sample.explanation: Only nodes reachable from v3 can see a new arrival. Walking forward from it reaches 4 nodes, including itself.

concepts.label: Routing grids as graphs
concepts.definition: A router does not search the plane; it searches a graph. Global routers use a coarse grid of routing bins, and detailed routers use a fine grid of tracks on each metal layer, with vias between layers.

sample.question: A detailed-routing grid has 14 columns, 18 rows and 6 metal layers. Layer 1 runs horizontally and directions alternate layer by layer. Each layer has one vertex per grid point, wire edges join neighbouring points along that layer's preferred direction only, and via edges join the same point on adjacent layers. How many vertices does the grid graph have?
sample.explanation: One vertex per point per layer: 14 × 18 × 6 = 1512.

concepts.label: Breadth-first wavefront search on a grid
concepts.definition: Lee's maze-routing algorithm is breadth-first search on a grid graph: a wavefront expands from the source one step at a time, labelling each cell with its distance, until it reaches the target.

sample.question: A routing grid has columns 1 to 5 and rows 1 to 6; cells are written (column, row). Blocked cells: (2, 2), (2, 3), (2, 4), (2, 5), (2, 6), (3, 4). The source is at (1, 2) and the target at (5, 6). Moves go to the 4 neighbours. Lee's algorithm labels every reachable cell with its wavefront number, the source being 0. What label does cell (1, 5) receive?
sample.explanation: The wavefront expands one step at a time around blocked cells, so the label is the breadth-first distance: 3.

concepts.label: Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm
concepts.definition: Real routing costs are not uniform: vias cost more than wire, congested edges cost more than free ones, and wrong-way segments are penalized.
key_ideas: Settling vertices in order of distance

sample.question: An undirected routing graph has vertices v1 to v5 and edge costs v1-v4 (5), v2-v3 (4), v2-v5 (8), v3-v4 (9), v4-v5 (8). Run Dijkstra's algorithm from v1, breaking ties by the smaller vertex number. What is the shortest-path cost from v1 to v3?
sample.explanation: Settling order with final distances: v1 (0), v4 (5), v5 (13), v3 (14), v2 (18).

concepts.label: Bellman-Ford and negative edge weights
concepts.definition: Some EDA graphs carry negative weights: constraint graphs for layout compaction and retiming, timing graphs with hold constraints written as negative arcs, and residual graphs in min-cost flow.

sample.question: A directed constraint graph has vertices v1 to v6 and arcs, listed in this order, v1→v3 (4), v3→v4 (3), v4→v5 (-1), v2→v4 (8), v3→v5 (8), v1→v2 (7), v4→v6 (5). There is no negative cycle. What is the shortest-path distance from v1 to v6?
sample.explanation: After n - 1 rounds of relaxing every arc the distances are final: 0, 7, 4, 7, 6, 12.

concepts.label: Difference constraints as shortest paths
concepts.definition: Many layout and timing problems reduce to constraints of the form $x_j - x_i \le c$: minimum spacing between cell edges in compaction, register moves in retiming, and offsets in clock scheduling.

sample.question: Solve the difference constraints $x_1 - x_2 \le 0$, $x_2 - x_4 \le -1$, $x_3 - x_4 \le -4$, $x_1 - x_3 \le 0$, $x_1 - x_4 \le 5$ with the standard construction: an arc $x_i \to x_j$ of weight $c$ for each constraint $x_j - x_i \le c$, plus a source $x_0$ with weight-0 arcs to every variable, and $x_k$ = shortest distance from $x_0$. What value does $x_3$ get?
sample.explanation: Shortest distances satisfy every constraint because d(j) ≤ d(i) + c is exactly x_j - x_i ≤ c. Distances from the source: -4, -1, -4, 0.

concepts.label: A* search
concepts.definition: A* is Dijkstra's algorithm with a sense of direction. It orders the search by the cost so far plus an estimate of the cost to go, so a router expands vertices toward the target instead of in every direction.

sample.question: A* routes from (1, 1) to the target (6, 9) on a grid with unit step cost, using the Manhattan-distance heuristic. Node (9, 9) is in the open list with path cost g = 18. What is its priority f = g + h?

concepts.label: The cut size of a partition
concepts.definition: Partitioning splits a netlist into blocks so that few nets cross between them. It drives floorplanning, min-cut placement, multi-FPGA mapping, parallel simulation and the clustering steps inside modern placers.

sample.question: Nets: n1 = {c1, c2, c3, c5}; n2 = {c1, c2, c5}; n3 = {c1, c2, c3, c5}; n4 = {c2, c3, c4, c5}; n5 = {c2, c3}; n6 = {c1, c6}. The partition is A = {c2, c3, c4}, B = {c1, c5, c6}. How many nets are cut (have pins on both sides)?
sample.explanation: A net is cut when its pins are not all on one side. The cut nets are n1, n2, n3, n4, giving 4. A net counts once however many of its pins cross.

concepts.label: How net models distort cut size
concepts.definition: Graph partitioners and spectral methods work on ordinary graphs, so they replace each net by a clique or star.

sample.question: A net with 5 pins is modeled as a clique. A partition puts 2 of its pins on side A and the rest on side B. How many clique edges cross the cut?
sample.explanation: Every pin on A connects to every pin on B: 2 × 3 = 6 edges, though the hyperedge itself is cut only once.

concepts.label: Balance constraints on a bipartition
concepts.definition: Without a balance constraint, the best partition is trivial: put everything on one side and cut nothing.

sample.question: A bipartitioner must keep each side's cell area between $(1-\epsilon)A/2$ and $(1+\epsilon)A/2$, where $A$ is the total area. With A = 368 and an imbalance tolerance of 5%, what is the largest area one side may hold? Round to 1 decimal place.

concepts.label: Kernighan-Lin swap gain
concepts.definition: The Kernighan-Lin algorithm was the first effective partitioning heuristic, and its gain formula is the template for every move-based partitioner since.

sample.question: A weighted graph has edges v1-v5 (2), v2-v4 (5), v2-v5 (3), v3-v4 (2), v3-v5 (2), v3-v6 (4), v4-v6 (3), v5-v6 (2). The bisection is A = {v1, v3, v4}, B = {v2, v5, v6}. For a vertex v, D(v) = E(v) - I(v), the external minus internal edge weight. What is D(v3)?
sample.explanation: Edges from v3 to the other side weigh 6 and edges inside its side weigh 2, so D = 6 - 2 = 4.

concepts.label: Fiduccia-Mattheyses cell gain
concepts.definition: The Fiduccia-Mattheyses algorithm moves one cell at a time on the hypergraph itself, under a balance tolerance.
key_ideas: Nets that a move cuts, and the gain

sample.question: Nets: n1 = {c1, c2, c3, c5}; n2 = {c2, c3, c5}; n3 = {c1, c3, c5}; n4 = {c1, c2, c4, c6}; n5 = {c1, c2, c3, c4}. The partition is A = {c4, c5, c6}, B = {c1, c2, c3}. FS(c5) counts the nets on which c5 is the only cell on its side. What is FS(c5)?
sample.explanation: On those nets every other pin is already across, so moving c5 makes the net uncut. c5 has 3 such nets.

concepts.label: Gain buckets and incremental gain updates
concepts.definition: What makes FM linear per pass is not the gain formula but its data structure: an array of buckets indexed by gain, each a doubly linked list of cells, with a pointer to the highest non-empty bucket.

sample.question: Nets: n1 = {c3, c5, c6}; n2 = {c1, c2, c4, c6}; n3 = {c2, c3, c4, c7}; n4 = {c2, c4, c5, c7}; n5 = {c2, c4, c5, c6}; n6 = {c1, c6, c7}; n7 = {c2, c6}. An FM bucket array keeps one list per possible gain value, and a cell's gain lies between -p and p where p is its number of nets. How many buckets does one side's array need?
sample.explanation: The largest cell degree is p_max = 5 (degrees 2, 5, 2, 4, 3, 5, 3), so gains run from -5 to 5: 2 × 5 + 1 = 11 buckets.

concepts.label: The Fiduccia-Mattheyses algorithm
concepts.definition: The Fiduccia-Mattheyses algorithm is the local-search engine at the heart of almost every netlist partitioner, from flat bipartitioning to the refinement step of hMETIS and KaHyPar.

sample.question:
An FM pass starts from a cut of 14 nets and tentatively moves cells (each then locked) with gains 2, 1, 0, 2, -1, in that order. Which outcome does the pass commit?

A) Keep the first 5 moves, cut 10

B) Keep only the first move, cut 12

C) Keep the first 3 moves, cut 11

D) Keep the first 4 moves, cut 9
sample.answer: Keep the first 4 moves, cut 9
sample.explanation: The cumulative gains are 2, 3, 3, 5, 4. FM rolls back to the prefix with the largest cumulative gain, 5 after 4 moves, giving cut 14 - 5 = 9. Stopping at the first negative gain would miss later recoveries.

concepts.label: Coarsening by heavy-edge matching
concepts.definition: Multilevel partitioners shrink the netlist level by level, contracting groups of strongly connected cells into single vertices.

sample.question: A weighted graph has edges v1-v2 (6), v1-v4 (1), v2-v3 (5), v2-v4 (3), v2-v6 (3), v3-v4 (3), v3-v6 (8), v4-v5 (1), v5-v6 (4). Heavy-edge matching visits vertices in the order v1, v5, v3, v4, v2, v6; an unmatched vertex is matched to its unmatched neighbour with the heaviest edge (ties go to the smaller number), or stays single if none is left. Which vertex is v1 matched with? Answer with its number.
sample.explanation: The matching is {v1-v2, v3-v4, v5-v6}.

concepts.label: Multilevel partitioning
concepts.definition: Multilevel partitioning is the method behind hMETIS, KaHyPar and PaToH, and the reason partitioning million-cell netlists is fast and good.

sample.question:
A multilevel partitioner coarsens a netlist of 10000 cells. Each level shrinks the vertex count by a factor of 2, and coarsening stops at the first level with at most 200 vertices. How many coarsening levels run?

A) 9 levels

B) 7 levels

C) 4 levels

D) 5 levels

E) 6 levels
sample.answer: 6 levels
sample.explanation: The smallest L with 10000 / 2^L ≤ 200 is L = 6. The hierarchy depth grows only logarithmically in the netlist size, and each level costs time linear in its size, so the whole V-cycle stays near-linear.

concepts.label: The graph Laplacian
concepts.definition: The Laplacian matrix $L = D - A$ turns a weighted netlist graph into linear algebra.

sample.question: A weighted graph on v1 to v4 has edges v1-v3 (1), v1-v4 (4), v2-v3 (6), v2-v4 (6), v3-v4 (3). Its Laplacian is $L = D - A$. What is the diagonal entry $L_{33}$?
sample.explanation: The diagonal holds the weighted degree, the sum of the weights of edges at v3: 10.

concepts.label: Cut size as a Laplacian quadratic form
concepts.definition: The quadratic form $x^T L x$ is one formula with two EDA meanings. Evaluated on a $\pm 1$ vector it is four times the cut of a bisection; evaluated on real coordinates it is quadratic wirelength.

sample.question: A weighted graph has edges v1-v3 (1), v1-v4 (2), v2-v3 (3), v2-v4 (3), v2-v5 (4), v3-v5 (3). For the vector x = (-3, 1, -2, 3, 4), indexed by v1 onward, what is $x^T L x$?
sample.explanation: Use the identity $x^T L x = \sum_{(i,j)} w_{ij}(x_i - x_j)^2$ over edges rather than forming L: the sum is 256.

concepts.label: Ratio cut and normalized objectives
concepts.definition: A hard balance constraint is one way to stop a partitioner from cutting off a tiny block.

sample.question: A weighted graph has edges v1-v3 (2), v2-v3 (4), v2-v4 (3), v2-v6 (1), v3-v5 (4), v3-v6 (3), v4-v6 (4). For the partition A = {v1, v3, v4, v6}, B = {v2, v5}, what is the ratio cut $\text{cut}(A,B)/(|A|\,|B|)$? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The cut weight is 12 and |A||B| = 4 × 2 = 8, so the ratio cut is 1.5.

concepts.label: Spectral bisection with the Fiedler vector
concepts.definition: Spectral bisection relaxes the discrete cut problem to an eigenproblem: the eigenvector of the second-smallest Laplacian eigenvalue, the Fiedler vector, embeds the vertices on a line so that strongly connected vertices sit close together.

sample.question: Three cells form a path: c1-c2 with weight 9 and c2-c3 with weight 4. What is the algebraic connectivity $\lambda_2$ of its Laplacian? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is $\lambda(\lambda^2 - 2(w_1+w_2)\lambda + 3w_1w_2)$, so $\lambda_2 = (w_1+w_2) - \sqrt{w_1^2 - w_1w_2 + w_2^2} = 13 - \sqrt{61} = 5.19$.

concepts.label: Maximum flow and minimum cut
concepts.definition: The max-flow min-cut theorem turns a cut problem, which looks combinatorial, into a flow problem with fast exact algorithms.
