sample.question: A flow network has arcs with capacities s→a (6), s→b (6), a→t (1), b→c (1), c→t (9). What is the maximum flow value from s to t?
sample.explanation: Augmenting until no residual s-t path remains gives 2. The nodes still reachable from s in the residual graph, {s, a, b}, form a minimum cut whose capacity is also 2.

concepts.label: Residual graphs and augmenting paths
concepts.definition: Every max-flow and min-cost-flow algorithm works on the residual graph: the network of capacities that remain after the current flow, including backward arcs that let the algorithm undo flow already sent.

sample.question: Arc u→v has capacity 4 and carries flow 1. What is the residual capacity of the forward arc u→v?
sample.explanation: Forward residual = capacity - flow = 4 - 1 = 3.

concepts.label: Hypergraph min-cut through a flow network
concepts.definition: A partitioner that wants the minimum number of nets separating two groups of cells needs a minimum cut in a hypergraph, where cutting a net costs its weight once however many pins cross.
key_ideas: Why the minimum cut removes whole nets

sample.question: Nets: n1 = {c2, c3}; n2 = {c1, c3, c5, c6}; n3 = {c2, c3, c6}; n4 = {c1, c3, c4, c5}. Lawler's construction turns this 6-cell netlist into a flow network: each net becomes two nodes joined by one arc of capacity equal to the net weight, with infinite-capacity arcs from each of its cells into the first node and from the second node back to each cell. How many nodes does the network have?
sample.explanation: 6 cell nodes plus 2 per net: 6 + 2 × 4 = 14.

concepts.label: Minimum-cost flow
concepts.definition: Minimum-cost flow sends a required amount of flow at the least total cost, with a cost per unit on every arc.

sample.question: A network has arcs s→a (capacity 5, cost 4), a→b (capacity 6, cost 4), a→c (capacity 2, cost 7), a→t (capacity 2, cost 1), b→t (capacity 3, cost 2), c→t (capacity 5, cost 2). Costs are per unit of flow. What is the minimum cost of sending 1 unit from s to t?
sample.explanation: With one unit, min-cost flow is the cheapest s-t path by cost: 5.

concepts.label: Bipartite matching
concepts.definition: Many EDA assignment problems pair items of one kind with slots of another under compatibility rules: pins to package bumps, I/O signals to pads, cells to legal sites, registers to scan slots, nets to tracks.

sample.question: A pin assigner must place 4 pins P1 to P4 onto 4 slots S1 to S4. Each pin may use only these slots: P1: S2, S3, S4; P2: S2, S3, S4; P3: S1, S2, S3; P4: S1, S3. What is the largest number of pins that can be assigned, one pin per slot?
sample.explanation: This is a maximum bipartite matching; augmenting paths find size 4. Adding a source to every pin and every slot to a sink, all capacities 1, turns it into a max-flow problem with the same value.

concepts.label: Weighted assignment of cells to slots
concepts.definition: When every pairing has a cost, matching becomes the assignment problem: place $n$ cells into $n$ slots, one each, at minimum total cost.

sample.question: A detailed placer reassigns 3 cells to 3 free slots in a window. The wirelength cost of putting each cell in slots 1 to 3 is: cell 1: 1, 9, 4; cell 2: 2, 5, 8; cell 3: 7, 4, 3. What is the minimum total cost of a one-to-one assignment?
sample.explanation: The optimal assignment is cell 1 → slot 1, cell 2 → slot 2, cell 3 → slot 3, total 9. The Hungarian algorithm finds it in polynomial time; it is a min-cost perfect matching, a special min-cost flow.

concepts.label: Minimum spanning trees for net estimation
concepts.definition: Before a net is routed, placers and timers need an estimate of its wirelength and topology.
key_ideas: What the MST estimate is good for

sample.question: A net has pins p1 (6, 1), p2 (10, 9), p3 (1, 7), p4 (2, 2). Using Manhattan distance, what is the length of its rectilinear minimum spanning tree?
sample.explanation: Prim's or Kruskal's algorithm on the complete graph of Manhattan distances gives total length 22 (half-perimeter of the bounding box: 17).

concepts.label: The Hanan grid
concepts.definition: A Steiner tree may add junction points that are not pins, and in the plane there are infinitely many candidate points.
key_ideas: The Hanan grid as a graph

sample.question: A net has pins p1 (9, 3), p2 (9, 4), p3 (5, 5), p4 (8, 4), p5 (8, 2). The Hanan grid is formed by drawing a horizontal and a vertical line through every pin. How many Hanan grid points (line intersections) are there?
sample.explanation: There are 3 distinct x values and 4 distinct y values, so 3 × 4 = 12 points. Pins sharing a coordinate share a line.

concepts.label: Rectilinear Steiner minimum trees
concepts.definition: The shortest way to connect a net's pins with horizontal and vertical wires is a rectilinear Steiner minimum tree, which may branch at points that are not pins.
key_ideas: Three pins and the median point

sample.question: A 3-pin net has pins p1 (7, 12), p2 (6, 6), p3 (2, 9). What is the length of its rectilinear Steiner minimum tree?
sample.explanation: For three pins the RSMT meets at the Steiner point (median x, median y) and its length equals the half-perimeter of the bounding box: 11. The rectilinear MST is 14.

concepts.label: RSMT versus RMST and half-perimeter
concepts.definition: Placers and timers pick a wirelength estimate per net: half-perimeter, minimum spanning tree, or Steiner tree.

sample.question: A 4-pin net has pins p1 (6, 7), p2 (3, 9), p3 (2, 3), p4 (0, 1). What is the ratio of its rectilinear MST length to its RSMT length? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: MST 16 / RSMT 14 = 1.14. Hwang's theorem caps this ratio at 3/2 for any rectilinear net.

concepts.label: The iterated 1-Steiner heuristic
concepts.definition: Iterated 1-Steiner improves a minimum spanning tree by adding Steiner points one at a time, each time the Hanan point that shortens the MST most.
key_ideas: The gain of one Steiner point

sample.question: A net has pins p1 (6, 0), p2 (2, 3), p3 (3, 6), p4 (5, 4) and a rectilinear MST of length 13. Adding the Hanan point (5, 3) as a Steiner point and recomputing the MST, by how much does the tree length drop?
sample.explanation: MST with the point: 12. Gain 13 - 12 = 1. A point that does not help gives gain 0 or less.

concepts.label: Scan-chain ordering as a traveling salesman path
concepts.definition: Scan design threads every flip-flop of a block into shift-register chains for test.
key_ideas: Chain length as a path length

sample.question: Scan flip-flops sit at f1 (5, 11), f2 (11, 1), f3 (8, 12), f4 (1, 11), f5 (4, 11), f6 (2, 2). The chain starts at the scan-in port at (0, 0) and wires each flop to the next with Manhattan length. What is the total chain wirelength for the order f4, f3, f5, f2, f1, f6?
sample.explanation: Add the Manhattan distance of each hop, starting from the port: 70.

concepts.label: Graph coloring in EDA
concepts.definition: Graph coloring assigns labels to vertices so that adjacent vertices differ. In EDA the labels are resources: registers for values in high-level synthesis, tracks for nets in channel routing, masks for features in multiple patterning, time slots for operations, and test sessions for cores.
key_ideas: Counting colors and the effect of order

sample.question: A register allocator builds an interference graph: vertices v1 to v6 are values, and an edge joins two values that are live at the same time: v1-v3, v1-v4, v1-v5, v1-v6, v3-v4, v5-v6. Greedy coloring visits v4, v6, v3, v5, v2, v1 and gives each vertex the smallest color number (1, 2, ...) not used by an already-colored neighbour. What color does v5 receive?
sample.explanation: Greedy colors: v1:3, v2:1, v3:2, v4:1, v5:2, v6:1.

concepts.label: Interval graphs and track assignment
concepts.definition: When conflicts come from overlapping intervals, such as nets spanning column ranges in a channel or values live over time ranges in a schedule, the conflict graph is an interval graph.

sample.question: In a routing channel, each net occupies a closed column interval: N1 [1, 8], N2 [13, 14], N3 [15, 21], N4 [15, 19], N5 [9, 12]. Two nets conflict when their intervals share a column, so they cannot use the same track. What is the minimum number of tracks, equal to the channel density (the largest number of intervals covering one column)?
sample.explanation: Column 15 is covered by 2 intervals. Interval graphs are perfect, so the chromatic number equals this largest clique, and the left-edge algorithm achieves it.

concepts.label: Two-coloring for double patterning
concepts.definition: At advanced nodes, some layers are printed with two exposures, each on its own mask.
key_ideas: The conflict graph and its components

sample.question: On a double-patterning layer, features F1 to F7 that are closer than the same-mask spacing get a conflict edge: F1-F6, F2-F4, F2-F6, F3-F5, F3-F7, F4-F5, F6-F7. Each feature must go on mask A or mask B, and conflicting features need different masks. How many connected components does the conflict graph have (an isolated feature counts as one)?
sample.explanation: Components can be colored independently, which is how decomposition tools split the problem. There are 1.

concepts.label: Planarity and embedding in layout
concepts.definition: A graph is planar if it can be drawn in the plane without crossings. Planarity is the theory behind single-layer routing, river routing and the need for vias, and graph drawing methods are close relatives of placement.
key_ideas: Euler's bound as a quick test

sample.question:
A single-layer routing problem reduces to a conflict graph with v = 12 vertices and e = 34 edges. What does Euler's edge bound let you conclude?

A) Planar: e is within 3v - 6 = 30

B) Undecided: e is within 3v - 6 = 30, which is necessary but not sufficient

C) Not planar: e exceeds 3v - 6 = 30

D) Not planar: e exceeds v - 1 = 11, so the graph has a cycle
sample.answer: Not planar: e exceeds 3v - 6 = 30
sample.explanation: A simple planar graph with v ≥ 3 has at most 3v - 6 edges; 34 > 30 proves non-planarity, so a crossing (a via or second layer) is unavoidable.

concepts.label: A partitioner's core versus its change surface
concepts.definition: In an agent-first EDA flow, a model edits and configures engines on request, so each engine must be built so that the common requests never touch its correctness-critical code.
key_ideas: Which tier a request lands in
Keeping the core small and fast

sample.question:
The number of V-cycles and the vertex count at which coarsening stops belong to which layer?

A) Parameters: configuration with no recompile

B) The immutable core

C) Observation hooks

D) Strategy plug-ins
sample.answer: Parameters: configuration with no recompile
sample.explanation: They are numbers that tune an existing algorithm. Changing them needs no code.

concepts.label: A seam for custom net weighting
concepts.definition: The most common customer-specific request to a partitioner is to change what a cut net costs: timing-critical nets should cost more, clock nets nothing, buses as a group.
key_ideas: Weights through the seam, cut in the core
What the seam must expose and guarantee

sample.question:
Nets: n1 = {c5, c6}; n2 = {c2, c3, c5}; n3 = {c1, c3}; n4 = {c1, c4, c5}; n5 = {c1, c3, c5}; n6 = {c1, c2, c5}. The partition is A = {c1, c4, c6}, B = {c2, c3, c5}. A customer's NetWeightProvider plug-in returns weight 5 for timing-critical nets (n1, n3, n5), weight 0 for clock nets (n4, which clock-tree synthesis rebuilds anyway) and weight 1 otherwise. What weighted cut does the unchanged core report?

A) Weighted cut 4

B) Weighted cut 5

C) Weighted cut 17

D) Weighted cut 16

E) Weighted cut 21
sample.answer: Weighted cut 16
sample.explanation: Of 5 cut nets, each contributes its provider weight: critical nets 5 each, clock nets 0, others 1, for 16. The core's cut accounting is unchanged; only the weights arrive through the seam.

concepts.label: Differential tests on cut size
concepts.definition: When an agent edits a partitioner, the harness decides whether the change is safe.

sample.question:
Nets: n1 = {c1, c4, c5}; n2 = {c1, c4, c6}; n3 = {c2, c5, c6}; n4 = {c2, c3, c4}; n5 = {c1, c6}. After a refactor of FM's incremental gain updates, the engine returns A = {c2, c4}, B = {c1, c3, c5, c6} and its internal counter reports a cut of 3. The differential test recomputes the cut from the returned partition. What should it report?

A) Pass: the counter is the engine's own measurement, so it is trusted

B) Pass: the recomputed cut is 4, matching the counter

C) Pass: a difference of up to 2 nets is within normal tolerance

D) Fail: the recomputed cut is 4, so the counter is off by 1
sample.answer: Fail: the recomputed cut is 4, so the counter is off by 1
sample.explanation: The independent recount gives 4 but the counter says 3. A cut is an exact integer, so any mismatch is a bug in the incremental bookkeeping, not noise.

concepts.label: Fast multilevel modes in an agent's modeling loop
concepts.definition: An agent exploring floorplans or clusterings needs to evaluate many candidates quickly, so it runs a fast mode of the partitioner in a continuous loop and recurses to the accurate mode only when the decision demands it.
key_ideas: What a fast mode gives up

sample.question:
An agent's modeling loop uses a fast multilevel mode (one V-cycle, no refinement at the two finest levels). The last accurate run on this block cut 757 nets. Five fast runs with different seeds cut 799, 777, 776, 801, 775. Policy: keep using the fast mode only if its mean cut is within 5% of the accurate reference and its seed spread (max minus min) is at most 20 nets; otherwise recurse to the accurate mode. What does the loop do?

A) Recurse: the mean gap of 3.8% exceeds 5%, though the spread is fine

B) Recurse: the spread of 26 exceeds 20, though the gap is fine

C) Recurse: both the gap of 3.8% and the spread of 26 exceed their limits

D) Keep the fast mode: gap 3.8% and spread 26 are within limits
sample.answer: Recurse: the spread of 26 exceeds 20, though the gap is fine
sample.explanation: Mean fast cut 785.6, so the gap is (785.6 - 757)/757 = 3.8%. Spread 801 - 775 = 26. Gap test passes, spread test fails.

concepts.label: Tool-grounded rewards for graph engines
concepts.definition: Graph engines make excellent reward sources for training or tuning models: cut sizes, tree lengths, path costs and flow values are exact, cheap and reproducible.

sample.question:
A Steiner-tree generator is rewarded with minus the tree length. What is the hack?

A) Output a shorter tree that does not connect every pin

B) Round coordinates to the Hanan grid

C) Output the rectilinear MST

D) Use more Steiner points than pins
sample.answer: Output a shorter tree that does not connect every pin
sample.explanation: Length is meaningful only for a tree that spans all pins, so connectivity must be verified first.

domains.name: Computational Geometry for Layout
domains.description: Rectilinear geometry, polygon Booleans, plane sweep and spatial indexes: the kernels under DRC, extraction, fill and routing.
covers: Computational geometry for layout: orthogonal/rectilinear geometry, Manhattan distance, polygons
Polygon clipping and Boolean operations on polygons (AND/OR/NOT/XOR of layers), sizing (grow/shrink)
Line-segment intersection, sweep-line / plane-sweep algorithms, point location
Nearest-neighbor search, range searching, spatial indexing: R-tree, R*-tree, quadtree, k-d tree, interval tree, segment tree, bounding volume hierarchy
Voronoi diagrams, Delaunay triangulation, convex hull, Minkowski sum, geometric optimization
Rectangular decomposition of rectilinear polygons, spatial databases

concepts.label: Manhattan distance and rectilinear geometry
concepts.definition: Layout geometry is rectilinear: almost every wire, cell outline and via is a polygon whose edges run horizontally or vertically, on an integer grid.

sample.question: A driver pin sits at (60, 47) and a sink pin at (35, 39), in nm. What is the Manhattan (L1) distance between them, in nm?
sample.explanation: Add the absolute coordinate differences: |60 - 35| + |47 - 39| = 25 + 8 = 33 nm.

concepts.label: Bounding boxes and rectangle intersection
concepts.definition: The axis-parallel rectangle is the workhorse of layout geometry. Every shape has a bounding box, every spatial index stores boxes, and the first test in nearly every check is whether two boxes intersect.

sample.question: A net has pins at (28, 7), (20, 21), (29, 34), (36, 8) (um). What is the area of their bounding box, in square um?
sample.explanation: The box spans x from 20 to 36 and y from 7 to 34, so its area is 16 x 27 = 432.

concepts.label: The orientation predicate
concepts.definition: Almost every geometric algorithm, from convex hulls to polygon Booleans to segment intersection, branches on one question: given three points, do they make a left turn, a right turn, or lie on a line?

sample.question: For points $a = (0, -5)$, $b = (-2, -5)$ and $c = (-6, -2)$, compute the orientation determinant $(b_x - a_x)(c_y - a_y) - (b_y - a_y)(c_x - a_x)$.
sample.explanation: (-2)(3) - (0)(-6) = -6. A positive value means a left (counter-clockwise) turn, negative a right turn, zero collinear.

concepts.label: Integer coordinates and exact predicates
concepts.definition: A geometry engine for layout is only as trustworthy as its arithmetic. Layout data lives on an integer grid in database units, and the engine's decisions (is this point inside, do these edges cross, are these shapes touching) are signs of predicates.
key_ideas: Database units and the integer grid

sample.question:
Why do layout tools store geometry as integers in database units rather than as floating-point microns?

A) Integers take less memory than any floating-point type

B) Foundries forbid floating-point arithmetic in sign-off

C) Floating point cannot represent coordinates larger than 1 mm

D) Integer coordinates make equality, alignment and Boolean results exact and reproducible
sample.answer: Integer coordinates make equality, alignment and Boolean results exact and reproducible
sample.explanation: Manufacturing grids are discrete. Integers make two edges either exactly aligned or not, so the same input always gives the same polygons.

concepts.label: Spacing between rectangles
concepts.definition: Minimum spacing is the most common design rule: two shapes on a layer must be at least $s$ apart.
key_ideas: Checking a rule without square roots

sample.question: Two metal shapes are A = $[0, 60] \times [0, 60]$ and B = $[81, 107] \times [38, 54]$, in nm. What is the Euclidean edge-to-edge spacing between them, in nm?
sample.explanation: The projections overlap on one axis, so the closest points face each other straight across the gap of 21 nm.

concepts.label: Area of a rectilinear polygon by the shoelace formula
concepts.definition: A layout polygon is stored as a ring of integer vertices. Its area, needed for density, capacitance estimates, antenna ratios and fill, comes from the shoelace formula: a sum of cross products of consecutive vertices.

sample.question: A rectilinear polygon has vertices, in order, (2, 0), (3, 0), (3, 3), (6, 3), (6, 4), (8, 4), (8, 10), (6, 10), (6, 7), (3, 7), (3, 5), (2, 5). Use the shoelace formula to find its area.
sample.explanation: Summing $x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i$ around the ring gives 58, and half of it is the area 29. The listing is counter-clockwise, so the sum is positive.

concepts.label: Point-in-polygon tests and fill rules
concepts.definition: Deciding whether a point is inside a polygon underlies probing a net at a location, connectivity through vias, and the definition of what a self-overlapping or multi-ring shape even covers.

sample.question: A polygon has vertices (2, 3), (6, 3), (6, 4), (7, 4), (7, 12), (6, 12), (6, 6), (2, 6). A ray is cast from the query point (7.5, 3.5) towards +x. How many polygon edges does it cross?
sample.explanation: Only vertical edges to the right of the point whose y-span contains 3.5 can be crossed. There are 0, so the point is outside (even).

concepts.label: Boolean operations on layout polygons
concepts.definition: DRC rule decks, derived layers, extraction and mask preparation are written as Boolean expressions over layers: gate = poly AND diffusion, contacts NOT covered by metal, the XOR of two versions of a layer.

sample.question: Layer A holds $[5, 14] \times [14, 20]$ and layer B holds $[0, 9] \times [2, 15]$. What is the area of A AND B?
sample.explanation: AND keeps the region in both: the intersection box, with area 4.

concepts.label: Growing and shrinking polygons
concepts.definition: Sizing moves every edge of a polygon outward (grow) or inward (shrink) by a distance $d$.

sample.question: A 52 nm by 54 nm rectangle is grown (sized up) by 5 nm on every side. What is the area of the result, in square nm?
sample.explanation: Each dimension grows by 2d: (52 + 10)(54 + 10) = 3968.

concepts.label: Area after offsetting a rectilinear polygon
concepts.definition: Fill engines, keep-out generators and density estimators need the area of a grown or shrunk polygon without always building it.
key_ideas: The A plus P d plus 4 d squared law
Applying it to a vertex list
Round corners and the Euclidean offset

sample.question: A rectilinear polygon has area 120 and perimeter 64 (in um and square um). It is shrunk by 1 um, and every part of it is wider than 2 um so nothing collapses. What is the shrunk area, in square um?
sample.explanation: Shrinking removes a strip of length times d along each edge; strips overlap at convex corners and leave a d-by-d square at reflex corners, a net +4 d^2. So 120 - 64(1) + 4(1) = 60.

concepts.label: Minkowski sums and keep-out regions
concepts.definition: The Minkowski sum $A \oplus B = \{a + b : a \in A, b \in B\}$ is the operation behind sizing, keep-out regions and configuration spaces.

sample.question: What is the area of the Minkowski sum of A = $[15, 19] \times [11, 17]$ and B = $[-4, -3] \times [2, 8]$?
sample.explanation: The sum of two boxes is the box whose ranges are the sums of the ranges: $[11, 16] \times [13, 25]$, area 5 x 12 = 60.

concepts.label: Polygon representations in layout databases
concepts.definition: The same region can be stored as a vertex ring, a set of oriented edges, a stack of trapezoids, a bitmap or a hierarchy of placed cells.
key_ideas: Holes, cut lines and file formats

sample.question:
A polygon is given as a vertex ring with two consecutive collinear edges. What is the cleanest normalization?

A) Split the polygon at that vertex into two polygons

B) Reverse the ring

C) Insert another vertex between them

D) Drop the middle vertex so every stored vertex is a real corner
sample.answer: Drop the middle vertex so every stored vertex is a real corner
sample.explanation: A vertex between collinear edges carries no shape information. Removing it gives a canonical form that compares equal across tools.

concepts.label: The plane-sweep paradigm
concepts.definition: A plane sweep turns a two-dimensional problem into a sequence of one-dimensional ones.

sample.question: A vertical sweep line moves left to right over the rectangles R1 = $[23, 28] \times [6, 11]$, R2 = $[14, 26] \times [20, 25]$, R3 = $[12, 17] \times [3, 12]$, R4 = $[5, 17] \times [16, 28]$. Each left and right edge is an event; events at the same x are handled at one stop. How many stops does the sweep make?
sample.explanation: The 8 events have distinct x-coordinates 5, 12, 14, 17, 23, 26, 28, so the sweep stops 7 times.

concepts.label: Line-segment intersection by sweep
concepts.definition: Finding all crossings among wire segments is the textbook sweep problem and a direct layout need: crossings on the same layer are shorts, and crossings between layers are where vias may go and where coupling is computed.
key_ideas: Crossings of horizontal and vertical segments

sample.question: Wire segments on one layer are H1 from (4, 11) to (10, 11); H2 from (4, 3) to (8, 3); H3 from (0, 9) to (2, 9); V1 from (11, 6) to (11, 8); V2 from (5, 4) to (5, 12); V3 from (3, 6) to (3, 10); V4 from (9, 4) to (9, 10). How many horizontal-vertical crossings are there?
sample.explanation: A horizontal and a vertical segment cross when the vertical's x lies inside the horizontal's x-range and the horizontal's y lies inside the vertical's y-range. 1 pairs qualify.

concepts.label: Area of a union of rectangles by sweep
concepts.definition: The area covered by overlapping rectangles, counting overlaps once, is needed for density checks, fill targets and capacitance estimates on unmerged data.

sample.question: Metal shapes R1 = $[13, 17] \times [9, 16]$, R2 = $[6, 15] \times [4, 16]$, R3 = $[6, 15] \times [0, 11]$ may overlap. What is the area of their union?
sample.explanation: The shapes sum to 235, but overlaps would be double counted. Sweeping in x and multiplying each slab's covered y-length by its width gives 158.

concepts.label: Reporting overlapping rectangle pairs
concepts.definition: Many checks begin by finding every pair of shapes that overlap, or that come closer than a rule distance: shorts between nets, spacing candidates, enclosure pairs.

sample.question: Report all overlapping pairs among R1 = $[17, 27] \times [1, 8]$, R2 = $[2, 12] \times [1, 6]$, R3 = $[4, 8] \times [5, 8]$, R4 = $[19, 28] \times [18, 22]$, R5 = $[11, 14] \times [20, 26]$, R6 = $[6, 16] \times [10, 16]$. Pairs that merely touch do not count. How many pairs overlap with positive area?
sample.explanation: A pair overlaps when both its x-overlap and its y-overlap are positive. 1 pairs qualify; a sweep finds them in O(n log n + k).

concepts.label: Point location by slabs and trapezoidal maps
concepts.definition: Point location asks which region of a planar subdivision contains a query point: which polygon a probe lands on, which net a via hits, which tile of a partition a coordinate falls in.

sample.question: The slab method for point location draws a vertical line through every segment endpoint. For the non-crossing segments s1 from (12, 1) to (18, 2); s2 from (3, 5) to (20, 4); s3 from (0, 8) to (1, 7), how many slabs result, counting the two unbounded ones?
sample.explanation: The endpoints have 6 distinct x-coordinates (0, 1, 3, 12, 18, 20), which cut the plane into 7 slabs.

concepts.label: Interval trees
concepts.definition: An interval tree stores $n$ intervals and answers stabbing queries, all intervals containing a point, in $O(\log n + k)$ time with $O(n)$ storage.

sample.question: The y-extents of wires crossing a cut line are the closed intervals [34, 36], [24, 30], [3, 19], [11, 29], [32, 38], [38, 39]. A stabbing query asks which intervals contain y = 4. How many does it report?
sample.explanation: An interval [a, b] contains 4 when a <= 4 <= b. 1 intervals qualify.

concepts.label: Segment trees and canonical decomposition
concepts.definition: A segment tree stores intervals by splitting each into $O(\log n)$ canonical pieces that are nodes of a balanced tree over the elementary intervals.

sample.question: A segment tree is built over the intervals [12, 17], [16, 19], [16, 20], [5, 11]. Its leaves are the elementary intervals: the open gaps between consecutive distinct endpoints, the endpoints themselves as points, and the two unbounded ends. How many leaves are there?
sample.explanation: There are 7 distinct endpoints, giving 7 point leaves and 8 open intervals: 2m + 1 = 15.

concepts.label: R-trees for spatial queries
concepts.definition: The R-tree is the standard dynamic index for rectangles: a height-balanced tree whose nodes store the minimum bounding rectangles (MBRs) of their children.
key_ideas: Counting the work of a query

sample.question: An R-tree leaf node holds the entries E1 = $[14, 16] \times [12, 14]$, E2 = $[4, 8] \times [7, 10]$, E3 = $[8, 12] \times [10, 12]$. What is the area of the node's minimum bounding rectangle?
sample.explanation: Take the minimum and maximum of the entry edges: the MBR is $[4, 16] \times [7, 14]$, area 84.

concepts.label: R-tree node splitting
concepts.definition: When an R-tree node overflows, its entries must be divided between two nodes, and the division decides how much the resulting MBRs overlap and how much dead space they enclose.
key_ideas: Overlap and margin in the R*-tree

sample.question: Guttman's quadratic split scores a pair of entries by the area wasted if they shared a node: $d = \text{area}(\text{MBR}(E_1 \cup E_2)) - \text{area}(E_1) - \text{area}(E_2)$. Compute d for $E_1$ = $[11, 17] \times [3, 7]$ and $E_2$ = $[6, 10] \times [16, 20]$.
sample.explanation: The joint MBR has area 187; subtracting 24 and 16 gives 147. A negative d means the entries overlap.

concepts.label: k-d trees and nearest neighbors
concepts.definition: A k-d tree splits space recursively, alternating axes, at the median of the points: x at the root, y at the next level, and so on.

sample.question: A 2-d tree is built over the cell centres (40, 28), (19, 31), (1, 0), (36, 15), (2, 29), (23, 23), (32, 3). The root splits on x at the median point, which goes to the root. What is the x-coordinate of the root's split?
sample.explanation: Sorting by x, the middle (number 4 of 7) point is (23, 23), so the root splits at x = 23.

concepts.label: Quadtrees over the die
concepts.definition: A quadtree recursively divides a square region into four equal quadrants, stopping where a cell is simple enough: empty, or holding few objects.

sample.question: A region quadtree covers a 4096 by 4096 unit die; each level halves the cell side. What is the smallest depth (root at depth 0) whose cells have side at most 371 units?
sample.explanation: Cells at depth d have side 4096 / 2^d. That first reaches 371 or less at depth 4, where the side is 256.

concepts.label: Uniform grids and bins
concepts.definition: The simplest spatial index divides the die into equal bins and keeps, for each bin, the shapes that overlap it.

sample.question: A uniform grid of 40 by 40 nm bins has 9 columns and 18 rows, bins numbered row by row from 0 at the origin. Bins are half-open. Which bin index holds the point (15, 700)?
sample.explanation: Column = floor(15 / 40) = 0, row = floor(700 / 40) = 17, index = 17 x 9 + 0 = 153.

concepts.label: Choosing a spatial index
concepts.definition: Interval trees, segment trees, R-trees, k-d trees, quadtrees, bin grids and bounding volume hierarchies all answer "what is near here", but each is tuned to a different query, data shape and update pattern.
key_ideas: Matching the query to the structure
Hierarchy and why DRC stays tractable

sample.question:
A union-area sweep needs, at each x-stop, the total length covered by the active y-intervals, under insertions and deletions. Which structure is used?

A) A segment tree storing a cover count and covered length in each node

B) A hash set of active intervals

C) A heap ordered by interval length

D) An R-tree of the rectangles
sample.answer: A segment tree storing a cover count and covered length in each node
sample.explanation: A segment tree over the compressed y-coordinates updates covered length in O(log n) per insertion or deletion.

concepts.label: Convex hulls by monotone chain
concepts.definition: The convex hull of a point set is the smallest convex polygon containing it. Layout tools use hulls for blockage and keep-out outlines, for quick containment and separation tests, as a building block of Voronoi and Delaunay computations, and as a lower bound in packing and floorplanning.

sample.question: How many vertices does the convex hull of the points (7, 8), (3, 4), (8, 8), (4, 1), (6, 3), (2, 2), (8, 1) have? Points lying on a hull edge between two corners are not vertices.
sample.explanation: Andrew's monotone chain sorts by x and keeps only left turns. The hull is (2, 2), (4, 1), (8, 1), (8, 8), (7, 8), (3, 4): 6 vertices.

concepts.label: Voronoi diagrams
concepts.definition: The Voronoi diagram of a set of sites divides the plane into cells, each holding the points closer to one site than to any other.

sample.question: The Voronoi diagram of 729 sites (not all collinear) is a planar subdivision. What is the largest number of Voronoi edges it can have?
sample.explanation: Euler's formula with every vertex of degree at least 3 bounds the edges by 3n - 6 = 2181, so the diagram has linear size.

concepts.label: Delaunay triangulation
concepts.definition: The Delaunay triangulation connects sites whose Voronoi cells share an edge. It is the triangulation that avoids skinny triangles where it can: it maximizes the minimum angle over all triangulations.

sample.question: A Delaunay triangulation is built over 145 points, 14 of them on the convex hull. How many edges does it have?
sample.explanation: Every triangulation of the same point set has 3n - 3 - h = 418 edges.

concepts.label: Decomposing rectilinear polygons into rectangles
concepts.definition: Many consumers of layout geometry want rectangles, not polygons: mask writers, some extractors, fill generators, simple DRC engines and data compressors.
key_ideas: Chords and the r minus g plus 1 formula

sample.question: A rectilinear polygon has vertices (0, 0), (28, 0), (28, 3), (17, 3), (17, 9), (8, 9), (8, 22), (5, 22), (5, 27), (0, 27). How many of its vertices are reflex (interior angle 270 degrees)?
sample.explanation: The polygon has 10 vertices. Walking counter-clockwise, every left turn is convex and every right turn reflex, and convex minus reflex is 4, so reflex = (n - 4)/2 = 3.

concepts.label: Slab decomposition versus minimum partition
concepts.definition: The simplest way to cut a rectilinear polygon into rectangles is to slice it with horizontal lines from every reflex vertex: a sweep produces it directly, it is easy to make robust, and mask fracturers and trapezoid-based Boolean engines use it.

sample.question: A fracturing step cuts a polygon with horizontal lines extended from every reflex vertex across the interior, and keeps the pieces. The polygon has outer boundary (7, 0), (20, 0), (20, 10), (13, 10), (13, 14), (0, 14), (0, 5), (7, 5); hole 1: (14, 8), (14, 9), (19, 9), (19, 8). How many rectangles result?
sample.explanation: Between consecutive vertex y-values the polygon is a set of horizontal runs; stacking identical runs gives 6 rectangles.

concepts.label: Spacing checks over many shapes
concepts.definition: A full spacing check finds every pair of separated shapes on a layer closer than the rule, across billions of shapes, and with rules that depend on widths, run lengths and corners.

sample.question: Metal shapes are M1 = $[0, 3] \times [4, 7]$, M2 = $[11, 19] \times [20, 25]$, M3 = $[25, 29] \times [23, 27]$, M4 = $[3, 6] \times [19, 23]$, M5 = $[32, 36] \times [2, 7]$. The spacing rule is 4, measured Euclidean between separated shapes (touching or overlapping shapes merge and are not checked). How many pairs violate it?
sample.explanation: For each separated pair, compare gx^2 + gy^2 with 16. 0 pairs fall short. A sweep or spatial index finds the candidates without testing all 10 pairs.

concepts.label: Width checks by shrinking and regrowing
concepts.definition: A minimum-width rule says no part of a shape may be narrower than $w$. Width is not a property of a rectangle but of every neck and arm of a merged polygon, which makes it harder than it sounds.

sample.question: Separate shapes S1 = $[0, 6] \times [0, 8]$, S2 = $[40, 41] \times [0, 2]$, S3 = $[80, 82] \times [0, 1]$, S4 = $[120, 126] \times [0, 8]$ are shrunk by 2 and then grown by 2 (an opening). How much area is lost?
sample.explanation: A rectangle survives the shrink only if both sides exceed 2d = 4; then the grow restores it exactly. Rectangles narrower than 4 vanish and stay gone: 4 area lost. The lost shapes are the width violations for a rule of 4.

concepts.label: Density windows and fill
concepts.definition: Chemical-mechanical polishing removes material unevenly unless every region of every layer has similar metal density.

sample.question: A density window is $[0, 70] \times [0, 70]$ (um). Metal shapes M1 = $[27, 35] \times [22, 40]$, M2 = $[23, 36] \times [21, 35]$, M3 = $[31, 59] \times [45, 76]$ may overlap one another and may extend past the window. What is the metal density in the window, in percent? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: Clip each shape to the window, take the union area (922 square um, overlaps counted once) and divide by 4900: 18.8 percent.

concepts.label: Hierarchical layout and flat shape counts
concepts.definition: A chip layout is a hierarchy: standard cells placed in blocks, blocks in the top level, memories as arrays of bit cells.

sample.question: Cell C draws 25 shapes. Cell B draws 8 shapes and places 10 instances of C. Cell A draws 8 shapes and places 4 instances of B and 2 of C. The top cell draws 38 shapes and places 26 instances of A and 13 of B. How many shapes does the flattened layout contain?
sample.explanation: Flatten bottom-up: B holds 8 + 10 x 25 = 258, A holds 8 + 4 x 258 + 2 x 25 = 1090, top holds 38 + 26 x 1090 + 13 x 258 = 31732.

concepts.label: Overlap area and parallel run length
concepts.definition: Parasitic extraction turns geometry into capacitance and resistance. Its geometric inputs are simple: the overlap area between shapes on different layers (plate capacitance), the parallel run length and spacing between neighbouring wires on one layer (coupling capacitance), and the widths and lengths of wires (resistance).

sample.question: Two parallel horizontal wires are A = $[183, 346] \times [35, 47]$ and B = $[194, 448] \times [68, 80]$ (nm). What is their parallel run length, in nm?
sample.explanation: The run length is the overlap of the x-projections: min(346, 448) - max(183, 194) = 152 (zero if negative). Coupling capacitance grows with it.

concepts.label: Connectivity extraction with union-find
concepts.definition: Layout-versus-schematic and every net-aware check start by deciding which shapes are electrically connected: shapes that overlap or abut on a layer, joined across layers by vias and contacts.

sample.question: Shapes on one metal layer are M1 = $[13, 18] \times [10, 19]$, M2 = $[20, 25] \times [18, 23]$, M3 = $[1, 7] \times [8, 11]$, M4 = $[8, 17] \times [6, 8]$, M5 = $[7, 9] \times [2, 11]$. Shapes that overlap or share a boundary segment are electrically connected; touching only at a corner does not connect. How many separate nets (connected components) are there?
sample.explanation: Union every connected pair with a disjoint-set structure; 3 sets remain.

concepts.label: The geometry kernel as a protected core
concepts.definition: Every DRC, extraction, fill and LVS engine rests on a small geometry kernel: exact Booleans, sizing, edge and polygon predicates on integer coordinates.
key_ideas: What belongs in the geometry core
Policies, parameters and hooks around it
Keeping the hot loop inside the core

sample.question:
An agent wants to change how the engine computes intersection points of two diagonal edges. Which layer is that?

A) A hook, since it only observes results

B) A policy, since it is a heuristic

C) The core: it changes the numerical kernel every operation depends on

D) A parameter, since it only affects rounding
sample.answer: The core: it changes the numerical kernel every operation depends on
sample.explanation: Intersection arithmetic is part of the exact kernel. Changing it can alter every Boolean result, so it needs human review and full regression.

concepts.label: Change tiers for geometry-engine requests
concepts.definition: Requests to change a geometry engine arrive constantly: a new process value, a new rule shape, a performance problem, a bug.

sample.question:
An agent switches a check from Euclidean to square (L-infinity) measurement for a quick pre-check run. Which tier, assuming both metrics are already implemented?

A) It cannot be done without a new rule deck language

B) Tier 3: changing the predicate kernel

C) Tier 1: selecting an existing option

D) Tier 2: writing a new metric
sample.answer: Tier 1: selecting an existing option
sample.explanation: Choosing among built-in metrics is configuration. Only a metric the engine does not have would need a plug-in.

concepts.label: Spatial queries as agent tools
concepts.definition: An agent fixing violations or exploring a layout cannot read a billion shapes; it asks questions.
key_ideas: Cost and safety at the tool boundary

sample.question:
An agent needs the shapes on metal 3 inside a window. Which tool signature gives it what it needs without ambiguity?

A) query(text) taking a natural-language description

B) query_region(layer, x1, y1, x2, y2) with coordinates in stated database units

C) dump_layer(layer) returning every shape

D) query_region(x, y) taking one point in microns
sample.answer: query_region(layer, x1, y1, x2, y2) with coordinates in stated database units
sample.explanation: Typed, unit-explicit inputs make the query exact and checkable. A free-text or whole-layer interface pushes parsing and filtering onto the model.

concepts.label: Tiled parallel geometry with halos
concepts.definition: The standard way to run geometry checks on many cores, many machines or a GPU is to cut the die into tiles and process them independently.
key_ideas: Halo overhead and the fast-accurate loop

sample.question: A parallel DRC engine cuts a 5517 by 2098 um die into 200 by 200 um tiles (the last row and column may be partial) and hands one tile to each worker. How many tiles are there?
sample.explanation: ceil(5517 / 200) = 28 columns and ceil(2098 / 200) = 11 rows give 308 tiles.

concepts.label: Differential testing of geometry engines
concepts.definition: When an agent or an engineer changes a geometry engine, the proof that nothing broke is differential: run the old and new versions on reference layouts and compare the outputs geometrically.
key_ideas: Reading the signature of a change

sample.question: A regression compares a golden output shape $[7, 13] \times [12, 20]$ with a new engine's output $[0, 9] \times [2, 13]$. What is the area of their XOR, the region the differential check reports?
sample.explanation: XOR = 48 + 99 - 2(2) = 143. A correct change to a geometry kernel must leave this at zero unless the change was meant to move shapes.

domains.name: Optimization for EDA
domains.description: LP, ILP, convex and nonconvex optimization, Lagrangian relaxation, metaheuristics, dynamic programming and Bayesian optimization, each tied to the EDA problem it solves.
covers: Mathematical optimization, operations research, combinatorial vs continuous optimization
Linear programming, duality, integer programming, MILP, branch and bound, branch and cut, Benders decomposition
Quadratic programming, QCQP, nonlinear programming, convex and nonconvex optimization, constrained optimization
Lagrange multipliers, KKT conditions, Lagrangian relaxation (as in gate sizing), penalty methods, augmented Lagrangian, ADMM
Gradient descent, conjugate gradient as an optimizer, Newton and quasi-Newton (BFGS, L-BFGS), Nesterov acceleration, coordinate descent
Metaheuristics: simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, evolutionary computation, tabu search, local search
Dynamic programming, constraint programming and constraint satisfaction
Multi-objective optimization, Pareto efficiency, robust and stochastic optimization, Bayesian optimization
Problem formulation discipline: decision variables, objective, constraints, why exact optimization is hard, relax/approximate/decompose/search

concepts.label: Formulating an optimization problem
concepts.definition: Every EDA engine is an optimizer wearing a domain costume. A placer, a sizer, a router and a scheduler each choose values for some unknowns to make a cost small while respecting rules.

sample.question:
An HLS scheduler assigns operations to clock cycles under a resource limit. Which encoding of the decision makes an ILP possible?

A) A real number per operation equal to its delay

B) A binary per pair of resources

C) One integer for the total latency only

D) A binary $x_{i,t}$ that is 1 when operation i starts in cycle t
sample.answer: A binary $x_{i,t}$ that is 1 when operation i starts in cycle t
sample.explanation: Time-indexed binaries let both precedence and per-cycle resource limits be written as linear constraints.

concepts.label: Continuous versus combinatorial optimization
concepts.definition: Once the variables are fixed, the problem falls into a class: linear, quadratic, convex, integer, mixed-integer, nonconvex, combinatorial or black-box.
key_ideas: Why EDA alternates continuous and discrete

sample.question:
A detailed placer assigns 6 cells to 6 legal slots, one cell per slot. How many assignments are possible?

A) 36

B) 64

C) 46656

D) 720
sample.explanation: An assignment is a permutation, so there are $6! = 720$. This is a combinatorial problem: no gradient exists between permutations.

concepts.label: Why exact optimization is hard
concepts.definition: Most EDA problems worth solving are NP-hard: partitioning, floorplanning, placement, routing, covering, scheduling under resources.
key_ideas: What NP-hardness does and does not say

sample.question:
An exhaustive optimizer evaluates $10^{6}$ configurations per second. Roughly how long does it take to enumerate all $4^{111}$ sizings of 111 gates with 4 sizes each?

A) About $10^{66}$ seconds

B) About $10^{63}$ seconds

C) About $10^{30}$ seconds

D) About $10^{60}$ seconds

E) About $10^{54}$ seconds
sample.answer: About $10^{60}$ seconds
sample.explanation: The space has about $10^{66.8}$ points; dividing by $10^{6}$ per second leaves about $10^{60}$ seconds. For scale, the age of the universe is about $4 \times 10^{17}$ seconds.

concepts.label: Relax, decompose, approximate or search
concepts.definition: Faced with an NP-hard model, a tool designer has four moves: relax a hard constraint to get a bound and a starting point, decompose the problem into smaller coupled pieces, approximate by rounding or a simpler model, or search the discrete space directly.

sample.question:
Which is a relaxation of a 0-1 ILP?

A) Adding a cutting plane

B) Fixing some variables to 1

C) Replacing $x \in \{0, 1\}$ with $0 \le x \le 1$

D) Branching on a fractional variable
sample.answer: Replacing $x \in \{0, 1\}$ with $0 \le x \le 1$
sample.explanation: A relaxation enlarges the feasible set, so its optimum bounds the original from the optimistic side.

concepts.label: Linear programming and its geometry
concepts.definition: A linear program minimizes or maximizes a linear objective over a region cut out by linear inequalities.
key_ideas: The optimum is at a vertex

sample.question: A linearized budget LP allots x and y units of two resources to two blocks. Maximize $z = 2x + 6y$ subject to (1) $2x + y \le 6$, (2) $2x + 4y \le 18$, and $x, y \ge 0$. What is the objective value at the vertex where constraints (1) and (2) are both tight? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: Solve the two tight constraints together: $x = 1$, $y = 4$. Then $z = 2 \cdot 1 + 6 \cdot 4 = 26$.

concepts.label: Standard form and the simplex pivot
concepts.definition: The simplex method is the algebra behind the vertex walk. It rewrites inequalities as equations with slack variables, represents a vertex as a basic solution, and moves to an adjacent vertex by a pivot that swaps one basic variable out and one nonbasic variable in.
key_ideas: Reduced costs and the objective step

sample.question: A routing-capacity LP has 2 variables and 4 inequality constraints of the form $Ax \le b$, plus $x \ge 0$. After adding one slack variable per inequality to reach standard form, what is the largest possible number of basic solutions (choices of the basic variables)? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: Standard form has 2 + 4 = 6 variables and 4 equality rows. A basic solution picks 4 basic variables, so there are at most $\binom{6}{4} = 15$ of them. Simplex visits only a few, which is why it is fast in practice.

concepts.label: Linear programming duality
concepts.definition: Every LP has a dual LP whose optimum equals the primal's. The dual is not a curiosity: its variables are prices on the primal's constraints, its feasible points are certificates that bound the primal, and its structure drives Lagrangian relaxation in gate sizing, Benders cuts, shadow prices on routing capacity and the stopping tests in every solver.
key_ideas: Optimal dual values at a vertex

sample.question: A linearized budget LP allots x and y units of two resources to two blocks. Maximize $z = 7x + 5y$ subject to (1) $4x + y \le 28$, (2) $x + 4y \le 22$, and $x, y \ge 0$. The dual is: minimize $28y_1 + 22y_2$ subject to $4y_1 + y_2 \ge 7$, $y_1 + 4y_2 \ge 5$, $y \ge 0$. The point $y_1 = 5$, $y_2 = 2$ is dual feasible. What upper bound on the primal optimum does it certify? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: Weak duality: every dual-feasible point bounds the primal maximum from above. The bound is $28 \cdot 5 + 22 \cdot 2 = 184$.

concepts.label: Shadow prices and complementary slackness
concepts.definition: A dual value is a price: how much the optimal objective improves per extra unit of a constraint's right-hand side.

sample.question: A linearized budget LP allots x and y units of two resources to two blocks. Maximize $z = 4x + 8y$ subject to (1) $2x + 3y \le 12$, (2) $2x + 5y \le 16$, (3) $x \le 7$, and $x, y \ge 0$. The optimum is at $x = 3$, $y = 2$. What is the slack of constraint (3) at the optimum? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: Slack is right-hand side minus left-hand side at the optimum: 4. A constraint with positive slack is not binding.

concepts.label: Difference constraints and longest paths
concepts.definition: A system of constraints $x_j - x_i \le w_{ij}$ is an LP with a special structure: it is the dual of a shortest-path problem, so it is solved by graph algorithms in place of a general LP solver.
key_ideas: Negative cycles and the clock-skew bound

sample.question: A one-dimensional layout compactor places 5 edges left to right with $x_0 = 0$ and minimum-spacing constraints $x_1 \ge x_0 + 3$, $x_2 \ge x_1 + 3$, $x_3 \ge x_2 + 2$, $x_4 \ge x_3 + 2$ (in nm). What is the smallest feasible value of $x_4$? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: Each constraint is an edge of weight d in the constraint graph, and the minimum position of a node is its longest-path distance from $x_0$. Relaxing the edges in topological order gives positions 0, 3, 6, 8, 10, so $x_4 = 10$.

concepts.label: LP relaxation and the integrality gap
concepts.definition: An integer program becomes an LP when its integrality requirements are dropped. That LP relaxation is the engine of every MILP solver: it bounds the optimum, guides branching and suggests roundings.

sample.question: A timing-repair pass chooses a subset of candidate upsizes under an area budget of 12 units: upsize 1 recovers 20 ps of TNS for 4 area units; upsize 2 recovers 22 ps of TNS for 5 area units; upsize 3 recovers 5 ps of TNS for 12 area units. Each upsize is taken whole ($x_i \in \{0,1\}$). Relax each $x_i$ to $0 \le x_i \le 1$. What is the LP relaxation's optimal value, an upper bound on the recoverable TNS, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The relaxed knapsack is solved greedily: take upsizes in decreasing order of ps per area unit and take a fraction of the first one that does not fit. That gives 43.25 ps.

concepts.label: Integer programming and branch and bound
concepts.definition: Branch and bound solves integer programs exactly by building a tree: each node is a subproblem with some variables fixed, its relaxation gives a bound, and any node whose bound cannot beat the best known solution is pruned.

sample.question: A branch-and-bound search for a minimum test-set cover (covering in ATPG compaction) has an incumbent cover of 44 patterns. The open nodes have LP lower bounds 39, 41, 52, 51. A node is pruned when its bound cannot strictly beat the incumbent. How many open nodes can be pruned? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: For minimization a node whose lower bound is at least the incumbent 44 cannot contain a smaller cover. 2 of the bounds satisfy that.

concepts.label: Big-M and disjunctive constraints
concepts.definition: Many EDA rules are either-or: block i is left of, right of, below or above block j; a cell sits in one of two regions; a wire uses one of two layers.

sample.question: An ILP floorplanner keeps block i left of block j unless binary $p = 1$: $x_i + w_i \le x_j + Mp$. Block i has width 14 um and its fence allows $0 \le x_i \le 64$; block j's fence requires $x_j \ge 37$. What is the smallest M, in um, that makes $p = 1$ switch the constraint off for every feasible placement? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: With p = 1 the constraint must hold for the worst case, largest $x_i$ and smallest $x_j$: $M \ge 64 + 14 - 37 = 41$. A larger M is still valid but weakens the LP relaxation.

concepts.label: ILP formulation of operation scheduling
concepts.definition: High-level synthesis must assign operations of a dataflow graph to control steps so that dependences hold and the number of functional units stays within a limit.

sample.question: A time-indexed ILP schedules 4 operations into 5 control steps with binaries $x_{i,t} = 1$ when operation i starts in step t. Variables exist only inside each operation's [ASAP, ALAP] window: op1 [3, 5], op2 [2, 5], op3 [2, 4], op4 [4, 4]. How many binary variables does the model have? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: Each operation contributes ALAP - ASAP + 1 variables. Summing the windows gives 11, against 20 without mobility pruning.

concepts.label: Global routing as an integer program
concepts.definition: Global routing assigns each net a route through a coarse grid of routing regions so that no edge carries more wires than its capacity and total wirelength stays small.

sample.question: A global router picks one candidate route per net. Edge capacities: e1 = 1, e2 = 2, e3 = 1, e4 = 1. Candidates: net 1: route A uses e1+e2+e3 (length 33), route B uses e1+e2+e4 (length 35); net 2: route A uses e3+e4 (length 22), route B uses e3 (length 12); net 3: route A uses e1+e2+e3 (length 32), route B uses e2 (length 14). The current solution: net 1 takes B, net 2 takes B, net 3 takes A. What is the total overflow, the sum over edges of usage above capacity? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: Count how many chosen routes cross each edge, subtract the capacity where usage exceeds it, and add. The total overflow is 2.

concepts.label: Cutting planes and branch and cut
concepts.definition: A cutting plane is an inequality that every integer solution satisfies but the current LP solution violates.

sample.question: A binary knapsack row from a placement-legalization ILP reads $9x_1 + 7x_2 + 2x_3 + 3x_4 + 2x_5 \le 16$. The LP relaxation returns $x_1 = 0.3$, $x_2 = 0.9$, $x_3 = 0.9$, $x_4 = 1$, $x_5 = 0.4$. The set {x_1, x_2, x_4} is a cover (its weights exceed 16), giving the cover inequality $x_1 + x_2 + x_4 \le 2$. By how much does the LP point violate it? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: No integer solution can take every item of a cover, so at most 2 of them are 1. The LP point sums to 2.2 over the cover, exceeding 2 by 0.2, so the cut removes it.

concepts.label: Benders decomposition
concepts.definition: Benders decomposition splits a mixed-integer program into a master problem over the complicating integer variables and an LP subproblem over the continuous rest.

sample.question:
What does the master's auxiliary variable $\theta$ represent?

A) The integer part of the objective

B) An underestimate of the subproblem's optimal cost as a function of the master variables

C) The duality gap

D) The number of cuts so far
sample.answer: An underestimate of the subproblem's optimal cost as a function of the master variables
sample.explanation: Optimality cuts bound $\theta$ from below; at convergence $\theta$ equals the true subproblem cost at the master's choice.

concepts.label: Testing convexity with the Hessian
concepts.definition: Convexity is the property that makes continuous optimization trustworthy: every local minimum of a convex function over a convex set is global, so descent methods cannot get trapped.
key_ideas: Classifying a quadratic by its Hessian

sample.question:
A placement cost term is $f(x, y) = 3x^2 - 4xy + 4y^2 + 2x$. Its Hessian is constant. How is f classified on all of the plane?

A) Strictly concave

B) Strictly convex

C) Convex but not strictly convex

D) Neither convex nor concave
sample.answer: Strictly convex
sample.explanation: The Hessian is $\begin{pmatrix} 6 & -4 \\ -4 & 8 \end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $4ac - b^2 = 32$ and leading entry 6. Positive determinant with a positive leading entry is positive definite; zero determinant is semidefinite; a negative determinant means one positive and one negative eigenvalue, a saddle.

concepts.label: The KKT conditions
concepts.definition: The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions are the optimality conditions of constrained optimization: stationarity of the Lagrangian, feasibility, nonnegative multipliers and complementary slackness.

sample.question: A sizing step wants gate sizes near $a = 3$ and $b = 3$ but shares an area budget. It solves $\min\ 2(x - 3)^2 + 2(y - 3)^2$ subject to $x + y \le 5$. What is the optimal x? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Stationarity gives $2 \cdot 2(x - 3) + \lambda = 0$ and $2 \cdot 2(y - 3) + \lambda = 0$, so $x = 3 - \lambda/4$ and $y = 3 - \lambda/4$. The unconstrained point violates the budget, so the constraint is active: $x + y = 5$ gives $\lambda = (3 + 3 - 5)/0.5 = 2$, $x = 2.5$, $y = 2.5$.

concepts.label: Quadratic placement as a convex QP
concepts.definition: Quadratic placement models every two-pin connection as a spring and minimizes the total squared length.
key_ideas: One movable cell between fixed pins
Coupled cells and the linear system
Building A and b for a netlist

sample.question: One movable cell connects by two-pin nets to fixed pins: a pin at x = 46 with weight 2, a pin at x = 64 with weight 2, a pin at x = 36 with weight 3. Quadratic placement minimizes $\sum w_k (x - p_k)^2$. Where does the cell land, in um? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Setting the derivative $2\sum w_k (x - p_k)$ to zero gives the weighted mean $x = 328/7 = 46.86$.

concepts.label: Posynomials and geometric programming in sizing
concepts.definition: Delays under the Elmore model are posynomials in the gate and wire sizes: sums of positive terms that are products of powers of the variables.
key_ideas: Balancing a size against its load

sample.question: Sizing one gate by a factor x adds input load to its driver and divides its own drive resistance, giving a path delay $D(x) = 2x + 50/x$ ps for $x > 0$. What size $x^*$ minimizes the delay? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $D'(x) = 2 - 50/x^2 = 0$ gives $x^* = \sqrt{50/2} = 5$, and then both terms are equal, $D^* = 2\sqrt{2 \cdot 50} = 20$ ps. In $u = \ln x$ the posynomial becomes a convex sum of exponentials, so this stationary point is global.

concepts.label: Nonconvex landscapes, QCQP and local optima
concepts.definition: Most real EDA formulations are nonconvex: non-overlap, discrete sizes, density, bilinear capacitance terms, and nonlinear equalities.

sample.question:
A one-dimensional density-penalty landscape f is a quartic with a positive leading term and $f'(x) = (x - 3)(x - 4)(x - 5)$. Gradient descent with a small step starts at $x_0 = 3.1$. Where does it converge?

A) x = 5

B) It diverges to infinity

C) x = 3

D) x = 4
sample.explanation: f' is negative below 3, positive between 3 and 4, negative between 4 and 5, and positive above 5, so 3 and 5 are local minima and 4 is a local maximum. Descent never crosses the maximum: from 3.1 it slides to x = 3.

concepts.label: Gradient descent
concepts.definition: Gradient descent moves the variables a small step against the gradient, the direction of steepest local increase.
key_ideas: The gradient of a quadratic cost
Iterates on a quadratic and the contraction factor

sample.question: A quadratic wirelength model for one cell is $f(x, y) = \tfrac{1}{2}(3x^2 + 4xy + 3y^2) - 10x - 7y$. The cell sits at $(5, 3)$. What is the y-component of the gradient there? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: $\partial f/\partial x = 3x + 2y - 10$ and $\partial f/\partial y = 2x + 3y - 7$. At the cell this is $(11, 12)$.

concepts.label: Step size, smoothness and line search
concepts.definition: The step size decides whether gradient descent converges, how fast, and how robustly.
key_ideas: The stability limit two over L
The best fixed step and conditioning

sample.question: A placer's quadratic objective has constant Hessian $\begin{pmatrix} 11 & -3 \\ -3 & 8 \end{pmatrix}$. Fixed-step gradient descent converges only if $\eta < 2/L$, where L is the largest eigenvalue. What is $2/L$? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The eigenvalues are $\frac{a + b}{2} \pm \sqrt{(\frac{a - b}{2})^2 + h^2}$ = 6.146 and 12.854. With $L = 12.854$, the limit is $2/L = 0.156$. Along the stiffest direction the error factor is $1 - \eta L$, which leaves $(-1, 1)$ beyond that step.

concepts.label: Nesterov's accelerated gradient
concepts.definition: Nesterov's accelerated gradient adds a look-ahead extrapolation to gradient descent and improves the worst-case convergence on smooth convex problems from order $1/k$ to order $1/k^2$.
key_ideas: The gradient step from the look-ahead

sample.question: An ePlace-style placer runs Nesterov's method on $f(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}(x - 4)^2$ with step $\eta = 0.15$ and momentum $\beta = 0.5$: $y_k = x_k + \beta(x_k - x_{k-1})$, then $x_{k+1} = y_k - \eta f'(y_k)$. With $x_k = 20$ and $x_{k-1} = -5$, what is the look-ahead point $y_k$? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $y_k = 20 + 0.5(20 - (-5)) = 32.5$. The gradient is then evaluated at this extrapolated point, not at $x_k$; that is the difference from heavy-ball momentum.

concepts.label: Conjugate gradient for placement systems
concepts.definition: Conjugate gradient minimizes a convex quadratic, or equivalently solves a symmetric positive definite system $Ax = b$, using only matrix-vector products.
key_ideas: The first iterate and the next direction

sample.question: A quadratic placer solves $Ax = b$ with $A = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ 1 & 8 \end{pmatrix}$ and $b = (-6, 9)$ by conjugate gradient from $x_0 = 0$, so $r_0 = d_0 = b$. What is the first step length $\alpha_0 = r_0^T r_0 / d_0^T A d_0$? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $r_0^T r_0 = 117$, $A d_0 = (-21, 66)$, $d_0^T A d_0 = 720$, so $\alpha_0 = 0.1625$. This is the exact line minimum along $d_0$.

concepts.label: Newton's method for minimization
concepts.definition: Newton's method for minimization replaces the function by its second-order Taylor model and jumps to that model's minimum.
key_ideas: The Newton step in one dimension

sample.question: Newton's method minimizes $f(x) = e^x - 3x$ from $x_0 = 1.5$. What is $x_1 = x_0 - f'(x_0)/f''(x_0)$? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $f'(x) = e^x - 3$ and $f''(x) = e^x$, so $x_1 = x_0 - 1 + 3 e^{-x_0} = 1.169$. The true minimizer is $\ln 3 = 1.099$.

concepts.label: Quasi-Newton methods: BFGS and L-BFGS
concepts.definition: Quasi-Newton methods build a Hessian approximation from successive gradients instead of computing second derivatives.
key_ideas: The secant condition in one dimension

sample.question: In one dimension, BFGS reduces to the secant method. A sizing knob has derivative values $f'(2) = -8$ and $f'(9) = 3$. Using the secant curvature estimate, what is the next iterate $x_2$? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The curvature estimate is $B = (3 - (-8))/(9 - 2) = 1.5714$, which satisfies the secant condition $B s = y$. Then $x_2 = 9 - (3)/1.5714 = 7.091$.

concepts.label: Coordinate descent
concepts.definition: Coordinate descent minimizes over one variable at a time, holding the others fixed.

sample.question: Coordinate descent minimizes $f(x, y) = \tfrac{1}{2}(5x^2 + 2xy + 6y^2) - 3x + 8y$ exactly along one coordinate at a time, x first, from $(-1, 0)$. What is x after the first coordinate update? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Hold $y = 0$ and set $\partial f/\partial x = 5x + 1 \cdot (0) - (3) = 0$: $x = 0.6$.

concepts.label: Smoothing nonsmooth objectives
concepts.definition: HPWL, the half-perimeter wirelength, is convex but not differentiable: it is a max minus a min of pin coordinates.
key_ideas: Error bounds and the gamma schedule

sample.question: A net's pins sit at x = 25, 9 um. An analytical placer smooths HPWL with the log-sum-exp model and $\gamma = 9$ um. What is the smooth maximum $\gamma \ln \sum_i e^{x_i/\gamma}$, in um? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Summing the exponentials and taking the log gives 26.405 um, slightly above the true maximum 25. The smooth version is differentiable everywhere, which gradient-based placers need.

concepts.label: The Lagrangian dual function
concepts.definition: The Lagrangian dual function minimizes the Lagrangian over the primal variables for fixed multipliers.

sample.question: A power-minimizing sizing model solves $\min\ 2x^2 + y^2$ subject to a speed requirement $x + y \ge 2$. Its Lagrangian is $L = 2x^2 + y^2 + \lambda(2 - x - y)$ with $\lambda \ge 0$. What is the dual function value $g(\lambda) = \min_{x,y} L$ at $\lambda = 4.5$? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Minimizing L over x and y gives $x = \lambda/4$, $y = \lambda/2$, so $g(\lambda) = 2\lambda - (\tfrac{1}{8} + \tfrac{1}{4})\lambda^2 = 2\lambda - 0.375\lambda^2$. At $\lambda = 4.5$ that is 1.406, a lower bound on the minimum power.

concepts.label: Lagrangian relaxation
concepts.definition: Lagrangian relaxation moves hard coupling constraints into the objective with multipliers.
key_ideas: Upstream load and the lower bound

sample.question: In Lagrangian-relaxation gate sizing, each timing arc carries a multiplier $\lambda \ge 0$, and optimality requires flow conservation at every gate: incoming multipliers sum to outgoing ones. A gate's 1 incoming arcs carry 1.5; 1 of its 2 outgoing arcs carry 0.8. What multiplier must the last outgoing arc carry? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: The KKT conditions of the relaxed sizing problem force $\sum \lambda_{in} = \sum \lambda_{out}$ at each node. Incoming total 1.5, minus the known outgoing 0.8, leaves 0.7. That lets the solver keep only one multiplier set that lives on the flow polytope.

concepts.label: Subgradient updates of multipliers
concepts.definition: The dual function of a relaxed problem is concave but often not differentiable, especially when the primal has discrete choices.
key_ideas: A multiplier update from the violation

sample.question: A Lagrangian-relaxation sizer updates the multiplier of the timing constraint $a \le T$ at a sink by $\lambda \leftarrow \max(0, \lambda + t(a - T))$. Now $\lambda = 1.6$, step $t = 0.004$ per ps, the required time is T = 730 ps and the current arrival is a = 820 ps. What is the new $\lambda$? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The constraint value $a - T = 90$ ps is a subgradient of the dual. The raw update is $1.6 + 0.004 \cdot 90 = 1.96$; the projection onto $\lambda \ge 0$ gives 1.96. Slack paths lose weight and violating paths gain it.

concepts.label: Quadratic penalty methods
concepts.definition: A penalty method replaces a hard constraint with a cost that grows with the violation, then increases the penalty weight until the violation is small.

sample.question: Wirelength pulls a cell toward x = 37 um, but a fence requires $x \le 24$. A quadratic-penalty placer minimizes $(x - 37)^2 + \rho\,\max(0, x - 24)^2$. With $\rho = 2$, where is the penalized minimizer, in um? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The minimizer is beyond the fence, so set $2(x - 37) + 2\rho(x - 24) = 0$: $x = (37 + 2 \cdot 24)/(1 + 2) = 28.333$ um.

concepts.label: Augmented Lagrangian method
concepts.definition: The augmented Lagrangian method, also called the method of multipliers, adds both a multiplier term and a quadratic penalty to the objective, then updates the multiplier from the remaining violation.

sample.question: A pin must sit exactly on a track at x = 0 while wirelength pulls it toward -10. The augmented Lagrangian method with $\rho = 1$ minimizes $(x + 10)^2 + \lambdax + \tfrac{\rho}{2}x^2$ over x, then updates $\lambda \leftarrow \lambda + \rhox$. With $\lambda = -3.5$, what x minimizes the augmented Lagrangian? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Set the derivative to zero: $2(x + 10) + \lambda + \rhox = 0$, so $x = (2a - \lambda + \rho c)/(2 + \rho) = (2 \cdot (-10) - (-3.5) + 1 \cdot 0)/(2 + 1) = -5.5$.

concepts.label: ADMM and splitting
concepts.definition: The alternating direction method of multipliers splits a problem into pieces that each own some variables, solves the pieces separately, and drives shared copies to agree through scaled dual variables.
key_ideas: The z-update with the new x

sample.question: Two placement partitions each own a copy of a shared boundary cell's coordinate: partition 1 prefers 22 um, partition 2 prefers 7 um. ADMM solves $\min (x - 22)^2 + (z - 7)^2$ subject to $x = z$ with scaled updates $x \leftarrow \arg\min_x (x - 22)^2 + \tfrac{\rho}{2}(x - z + u)^2$, $z \leftarrow \arg\min_z (z - 7)^2 + \tfrac{\rho}{2}(x - z + u)^2$, $u \leftarrow u + x - z$, with $\rho = 2$, $z_0 = 10$, $u_0 = 0$. What is $x_1$? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $x_1 = (2 \cdot 22 + \rho(z_0 - u_0))/(2 + \rho) = 16$. $z_1 = (2 \cdot 7 + \rho(x_1 + u_0))/(2 + \rho) = 11.5$. $u_1 = u_0 + x_1 - z_1 = 4.5$. Each partition solves only its own small problem; u accumulates the disagreement.

concepts.label: Local search, neighborhoods and tabu search
concepts.definition: Local search starts from a solution and repeatedly moves to a neighbour chosen by a rule.
key_ideas: Steepest descent and where it stops

sample.question: Configurations 0 to 9 of a partitioner have costs 29, 14, 88, 60, 13, 33, 87, 99, 59, 68. The move set changes the configuration index by plus or minus 1. How many local minima (no neighbour is cheaper) are there? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: A configuration is a local minimum when every neighbour costs more; the endpoints have one neighbour. The local minima are at configurations 1, 4, 8: 3 in all. Only one of them is global, which is why plain descent is not enough.

concepts.label: Simulated annealing
concepts.definition: Simulated annealing is local search that sometimes accepts a worse move, with a probability that falls as a temperature parameter cools.

sample.question: A simulated-annealing placer proposes a swap that raises HPWL by $\Delta = 33$ um at temperature T = 55 um. With the Metropolis rule, what is the probability the swap is accepted? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Uphill moves are accepted with probability $e^{-\Delta/T} = e^{-33/55} = 0.549$. Downhill moves are always accepted.

concepts.label: Cooling schedules and equilibrium
concepts.definition: The cooling schedule decides how the temperature falls and how many moves run at each temperature.

sample.question: A geometric cooling schedule sets $T_{k+1} = \alpha T_k$ with $T_0 = 360$ and $\alpha = 0.8$. What is $T_{6}$? Round to 3 decimal places.

concepts.label: Slicing floorplans and annealing moves
concepts.definition: A slicing floorplan recursively cuts the chip into rectangles, and a Polish expression writes that cutting tree in postfix form.
key_ideas: Accepting a move and the representation's limits

sample.question: Blocks (width x height): block 1 is 4 x 1, block 2 is 1 x 5, block 3 is 1 x 6. In the Polish expression 1 3 V 2 V, operator V places its two operands side by side (widths add, height is the larger) and H stacks them (heights add, width is the larger). What is the area of the enclosing rectangle? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: Evaluate the postfix expression with a stack, combining the top two sub-floorplans at each operator. The final rectangle is 6 x 6, area 36.

concepts.label: Genetic algorithms and evolutionary search
concepts.definition: Genetic algorithms evolve a population of candidate solutions by selection, crossover and mutation.

sample.question: A genetic floorplanner's population has fitness values 12, 5, 39, 35 (individuals 1 to 4). With roulette-wheel (fitness-proportional) selection, what is the probability that one draw picks individual 1? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Probability is fitness over total fitness: 12/91 = 0.132.

concepts.label: Dynamic programming
concepts.definition: Dynamic programming solves a problem by combining optimal solutions of overlapping subproblems, computed once and stored.

sample.question: A chain of 3 gates picks one of 3 sizes per gate (S, M, L). Each choice has a delay cost (gate 1 costs S = 7, M = 4, L = 4; gate 2 costs S = 7, M = 7, L = 5; gate 3 costs S = 8, M = 8, L = 4) and each adjacent pair adds a loading cost by (driver size, load size) (gates 1 to 2: SS = 5, SM = 1, SL = 3, MS = 6, MM = 6, ML = 1, LS = 6, LM = 3, LL = 0; gates 2 to 3: SS = 2, SM = 0, SL = 6, MS = 3, MM = 3, ML = 4, LS = 4, LM = 2, LL = 4). The cost-to-go of the last gate is its own cost (S = 8, M = 8, L = 4). What is the cost-to-go of gate 2 at size S, $V_{2}(S) = c_{2}(S) + \min_b [t(S, b) + V_{3}(b)]$? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: Add gate 2's own cost 7 to the best transition-plus-cost-to-go over the next gate's sizes. That gives 15. Bellman's principle: the best completion from here does not depend on how we got here.

concepts.label: Tree covering in technology mapping
concepts.definition: Technology mapping covers a subject graph of simple gates with library cells. When the subject graph is a tree, minimum-area covering is solved exactly by dynamic programming: for every node, the best cover of the subtree rooted there is the best pattern match at that node plus the best covers of the subtrees the pattern leaves exposed.
key_ideas: One DP step at a node
Trees, subtrees and the DAG problem

sample.question: A tree mapper covers a NAND2/INV subject chain, listed from the input side: n1 INV, n2 NAND2, n3 INV, n4 INV. Each NAND2's other input is a primary input. Library areas: INV = 1, NAND2 = 2, AND2 (an INV fed by a NAND2) = 3, BUF (an INV fed by an INV) = 3. The DP has best(n1) = 1, best(n2) = 3, best(n3) = 4. What is best(n4), the cheapest cover of the chain up to and including n4? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: At n4 either a 1-node INV covers it (best(n3) + 1) or a 2-node pattern rooted at n4 covers it and n3 (best(n2) + its area). The cheaper option gives 5.

concepts.label: Van Ginneken buffer insertion
concepts.definition: Van Ginneken's algorithm inserts buffers on a routing tree to maximize slack at the driver.
key_ideas: Propagating a candidate through a wire
Pruning and choosing at the driver

sample.question: Van Ginneken's DP carries candidates (load C, required time q) up the tree. A candidate (C = 42 fF, q = 140 ps) passes up through a wire with R = 132 ohm and C = 36 fF (pi model). What is the candidate's new required time, in ps? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The wire's Elmore delay is $R(C_w/2 + C) = 132(18 + 42)$ ohm fF = 7.92 ps, so $q' = 140 - 7.92 = 132.08$ ps and the load grows to 78 fF.

concepts.label: Constraint satisfaction and propagation
concepts.definition: Constraint programming states a problem as variables with finite domains and constraints between them, then alternates propagation, which removes values that cannot appear in any solution, with search over what is left.
key_ideas: Counting solutions of a small CSP

sample.question: A scheduling CSP has start-time domains $s_1 \in \{0..12\}$, $s_2 \in \{0..10\}$, $s_3 \in \{0..12\}$, $s_4 \in \{0..12\}$ and precedence constraints $s_1 + 1 \le s_2$, $s_2 + 1 \le s_3$, $s_3 + 2 \le s_4$. After arc consistency, how many values remain in the domain of $s_3$? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: Bounds propagation pushes lower bounds forward along the chain and upper bounds backward until nothing changes: $s_1 \in \{0..8\}$, $s_2 \in \{1..9\}$, $s_3 \in \{2..10\}$, $s_4 \in \{4..12\}$. For these binary precedence constraints that is exactly arc consistency.

concepts.label: Pareto optimality
concepts.definition: Chip design never optimizes one number. Power, performance and area (PPA) pull against each other, as do wirelength and congestion, or yield and speed.

sample.question: A flow sweep produced designs, both objectives to be minimized: D1 (delay 7, power 8); D2 (delay 5, power 8); D3 (delay 12, power 2); D4 (delay 11, power 11); D5 (delay 1, power 11); D6 (delay 11, power 7); D7 (delay 8, power 3). How many designs dominate D1 (no worse in both objectives and strictly better in at least one)? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: The designs dominating D1 are D2, so the count is 1. Equal values in both objectives do not dominate.

concepts.label: Weighted sums, epsilon constraints and hypervolume
concepts.definition: To compute a single answer from a multi-objective problem, tools scalarize: combine the objectives with weights, or optimize one objective with the others bounded.

sample.question: Designs (minimize both): D1 (delay 10, power 1); D2 (delay 7, power 5); D3 (delay 5, power 10); D4 (delay 2, power 10). A flow script scores $s = 0.2 \cdot \text{delay} + 0.8 \cdot \text{power}$. What is the lowest score? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Score every design; D1 is lowest at 2.8. A weighted sum with positive weights always picks a Pareto-optimal design, but only those on the convex hull of the front.

concepts.label: Robust and stochastic optimization
concepts.definition: Designs must work across process corners, voltages, temperatures and operating modes, and their parameters vary randomly.

sample.question: A sizing choice is evaluated at corners SS, TT, FF with probabilities 0.25, 0.5, 0.25. Costs per corner, in that order: option 1: 20, 12, 16; option 2: 15, 20, 3; option 3: 19, 12, 14. A robust (min-max) formulation picks the option with the best worst case. What is that worst-case cost? Give an integer.
sample.explanation: The worst cases are 20, 20, 19; the smallest is 19 (option 3). Robust optimization protects the worst corner and ignores the probabilities.

concepts.label: Gaussian process surrogates
concepts.definition: A Gaussian process is a probability model over functions, used as the surrogate in Bayesian optimization.
key_ideas: The posterior mean from one observation

sample.question: A Bayesian flow tuner models QoR versus a utilization knob with a zero-mean Gaussian process and squared-exponential kernel $k(x, x') = 3\exp(-(x - x')^2 / (2 \cdot 1^2))$. What is the covariance $k(0.2, 0.6)$? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The distance is 0.4, so $k = 3 \exp(-0.4^2/(2 \cdot 1^2)) = 2.769$. Nearby inputs are strongly correlated; at a few length scales the correlation vanishes.

concepts.label: Bayesian optimization
concepts.definition: Bayesian optimization finds a good input for an expensive black-box function in few evaluations.

sample.question: An analog-sizing BO loop maximizes gain margin. The surrogate predicts at candidate points x1: mean 3, sd 0.6; x2: mean 0.6, sd 1.3; x3: mean 4.8, sd 0.6; x4: mean 0.1, sd 2; x5: mean 3.8, sd 0.3. With the upper confidence bound $\mu + \kappa\sigma$ and $\kappa = 2$, what acquisition value does the chosen point have? Round to 2 decimal places.
