sample.explanation: Compute $\mu + 2\sigma$ for each and take the largest: x3 with 6. Larger $\kappa$ favours uncertain points (exploration).

concepts.label: Bayesian optimization for analog sizing and flow tuning
concepts.definition: Textbook Bayesian optimization assumes a few continuous inputs, noise-free evaluations and one at a time.
key_ideas: When BO fits an EDA tuning problem

sample.question:
Some flow knobs are categorical (which placer mode, which CTS strategy). What does BO need?

A) A kernel or encoding that handles categorical inputs, such as one-hot or a dedicated categorical kernel

B) A larger noise variance

C) Nothing: categories are treated as reals

D) To drop all categorical knobs
sample.answer: A kernel or encoding that handles categorical inputs, such as one-hot or a dedicated categorical kernel
sample.explanation: Treating category labels as real numbers invents a false ordering; mixed-variable kernels avoid that.

concepts.label: Objective weights as Tier 1 parameters
concepts.definition: In an agent-first engine, an optimizer's objective weights are its most important change surface.
key_ideas: Which tier a request lands in

sample.question:
Why does pushing most requests into Tier 1 objective weights make an optimization engine easier for agents to drive?

A) Tier 1 changes skip all testing

B) Weight changes are fast, safe and reversible, and need no compile-test cycle

C) Weights are invisible to QoR

D) Weights change the core algorithm
sample.answer: Weight changes are fast, safe and reversible, and need no compile-test cycle
sample.explanation: A well-placed seam turns the common request into configuration, so the agent's loop is seconds long and low risk.

concepts.label: Move sets and cost functions as Tier 2 policies
concepts.definition: Search-based optimizers, annealers, local search, rip-up and reroute, are defined by their move sets and cost functions.

sample.question:
What context must a move-set seam expose to a plug-in so it can propose useful moves?

A) Write access to the legalizer's internals

B) Read access to current positions, connectivity and local cost deltas, plus a way to return proposed moves

C) Nothing but a random seed

D) The engine's source code
sample.answer: Read access to current positions, connectivity and local cost deltas, plus a way to return proposed moves
sample.explanation: A narrow interface gives the plug-in the state it reads and a typed way to propose; the core still applies and checks the move.

concepts.label: Tool-grounded reward design for optimization agents
concepts.definition: Agents that learn to optimize, choosing placements, routes, sizes or flow settings, are trained and judged by rewards computed by tools.

sample.question:
An RL routing agent is rewarded by the tool with $R = -\text{WL ratio} - 10 \cdot \text{overflow}/100 - 0.08 \cdot \text{DRC violations}$. Candidate results: Run 1: wirelength ratio 0.85, overflow 4 edges, DRC violations 0; Run 2: wirelength ratio 0.92, overflow 2 edges, DRC violations 0; Run 3: wirelength ratio 1.05, overflow 0 edges, DRC violations 0; Run 4: wirelength ratio 0.95, overflow 3 edges, DRC violations 0. Which run earns the highest reward?

A) Run 1

B) Run 2

C) Run 3

D) Run 4
sample.answer: Run 3
sample.explanation: Compute R for each run; Run 3 scores highest at -1.05. Note how the penalty weights decide whether a short but dirty route can beat a longer clean one.

concepts.label: Agent-driven design-space exploration
concepts.definition: A design-space exploration agent runs many flow experiments in parallel, chooses the next ones from the results so far, and recommends configurations.

sample.question:
A design-space exploration agent starts 8 flow configurations with 20 minutes each, then repeatedly keeps the better half and doubles each survivor's budget, until one configuration remains and gets its run. How many machine-minutes does the whole exploration use?

A) 640

B) 480

C) 1280

D) 160
sample.explanation: Each round costs (configs times minutes): 160, 160, 160, 160. With halving and doubling every round costs the same, 4 rounds of 160, total 640, against 1280 for running every configuration at the final budget.

concepts.label: Golden and differential tests for optimizers
concepts.definition: When agents edit and tune optimization engines, every change needs proof that it does what it claims and nothing else.

sample.question:
A new optimizer skill is compared with the baseline on 3 golden designs. The wirelength ratios (new over baseline) are 1.06, 1.06, 0.92. What is the geometric-mean ratio?

A) 1.011

B) 1.034

C) 0.999

D) 1.017

E) 1.021
sample.explanation: Multiply the ratios and take the 3-th root: 1.011. The geometric mean treats a 10% gain and a 10% loss symmetrically in log terms, so one large design cannot dominate.

domains.name: Numerical Methods for EDA
domains.description: Sparse linear algebra, Newton's method, stiff ODE integration, Krylov solvers, PDE discretization and model order reduction for simulators and analyzers.
covers: Sparse matrices and sparse linear systems, storage formats (CSR), fill-in, orderings (minimum degree, AMD, nested dissection)
LU and Cholesky factorization, pivoting, numerical stability, conditioning, floating-point arithmetic
Iterative methods, Krylov subspaces, conjugate gradient, GMRES, preconditioning, multigrid
Nonlinear equations: Newton-Raphson for systems, damping, fixed-point iteration, convergence
ODEs, DAEs, stiff equations, numerical integration: backward Euler, trapezoidal rule, BDF/Gear, Runge-Kutta, stability regions, local truncation error
PDE discretization: finite difference, finite element, finite volume, boundary element methods
Eigenvalue problems, SVD, model order reduction and reduced-order models (as numerics)
Automatic differentiation, scientific computing, HPC, parallel computing, distributed computing, GPU computing

concepts.label: Nonzero pattern of a nodal matrix
concepts.definition: Every circuit simulator, IR-drop analyzer and extractor ends up solving a linear system whose matrix comes from a netlist.
key_ideas: One unknown per node, one entry per connection
Why circuit matrices are so sparse

sample.question: A resistor network has 5 non-ground nodes: R9 from node 3 to ground; R11 from node 1 to ground; R6 between nodes 2 and 5; R3 between nodes 1 and 4; R8 between nodes 5 and 1; R2 between nodes 1 and 3; R4 between nodes 1 and 5; R7 between nodes 3 and 4; R5 between nodes 2 and 4; R10 from node 4 to ground; R1 between nodes 1 and 2. In the nodal conductance matrix $G$ (one row and column per non-ground node), how many nonzero entries does row 1 have?
sample.explanation: Row 1 has its diagonal entry plus one off-diagonal entry for each distinct non-ground neighbour of node 1 (4 of them). Resistors to ground only add to the diagonal, and parallel resistors share one entry: 5 nonzeros.

concepts.label: Sparse matrix storage
concepts.definition: A sparse matrix is stored as lists of its nonzeros, never as a dense array. The format decides what is cheap: appending entries while stamping, walking a row for a matrix-vector product, or walking a column during factorization.
key_ideas: Coordinate and compressed sparse row formats

sample.question: Store the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 7 & 0 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & 5 & 2 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ in compressed sparse row (CSR) format with arrays val, col_idx and row_ptr. What is the total number of array entries across the three arrays?
sample.explanation: The matrix has 9 nonzeros, so val and col_idx each hold 9 entries and row_ptr holds n + 1 = 5: total 23.

concepts.label: Sparse matrix-vector product in CSR
concepts.definition: The sparse matrix-vector product $y = Ax$ is the inner kernel of every Krylov solver, every power-grid iteration and every explicit time step.
key_ideas: The row loop over the row pointer
Cost and memory traffic of SpMV

sample.question: Rows and columns are numbered from 0. The matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 & 8 \end{pmatrix}$ is stored in CSR with nonzeros of each row kept in increasing column order. At which position (0-based) of the val array is the entry in row 3, column 2?
sample.explanation: Row 3 starts at row_ptr[3] = 4. Count the nonzeros of row 3 to the left of column 2 and add: position 5.

concepts.label: Fill-in and reordering
concepts.definition: Gaussian elimination on a sparse matrix creates new nonzeros, called fill, in positions that were zero.
key_ideas: Counting fill for an elimination order
Why order changes fill: the arrow matrix

sample.question: A symmetric sparse matrix has a nonzero diagonal and off-diagonal nonzeros at the vertex pairs 1-3, 1-4, 2-4, 2-5, 3-4, 4-5 (the graph of the matrix, vertices 1 to 5). Gaussian elimination eliminates vertex 2 first. How many fill edges (new off-diagonal nonzero pairs) does that step create?
sample.explanation: Eliminating 2 makes its neighbours a clique. Count the neighbour pairs that were not already joined: 0.

concepts.label: Markowitz pivot selection
concepts.definition: Circuit matrices from modified nodal analysis are unsymmetric, and their pivots must also be numerically safe.
key_ideas: Choosing the pivot with least predicted fill
Markowitz count as a bound on actual fill

sample.question: An unsymmetric sparse matrix has this nonzero pattern: row 1: columns 1, 4; row 2: columns 1, 2; row 3: columns 3; row 4: columns 1, 4. What is the Markowitz count of the entry in row 4, column 4?
sample.explanation: Row 4 has 2 nonzeros and column 4 has 2, so the count is (2 - 1)(2 - 1) = 1.

concepts.label: Minimum degree ordering
concepts.definition: Minimum degree is the symmetric version of Markowitz pivoting and the most widely used fill-reducing ordering.
key_ideas: Greedy elimination of the lowest-degree vertex
Tracing the ordering and its fill

sample.question: A symmetric matrix has the graph with edges 1-3, 1-6, 2-3, 2-4, 2-5, 2-6, 3-5, 3-6, 4-6 on vertices 1 to 6. Minimum degree ordering always eliminates a vertex of least current degree, breaking ties by the lowest label. Which vertex is eliminated second?
sample.explanation: The minimum degree order is 1, 4, 5, 2, 3, 6, so the answer is 4.

concepts.label: Nested dissection and separators
concepts.definition: Nested dissection orders a mesh-like graph by cutting it with small separators and numbering each separator after the pieces it separates.
key_ideas: Asymptotic fill for grids and why it matters

sample.question:
A 11-by-11 grid graph (a five-point power-grid mesh) is split by nested dissection with its middle column as the separator. How many vertices does each of the two remaining halves contain?

A) 50

B) 55

C) 60

D) 66
sample.explanation: The separator is the middle column of 11 vertices. The other 110 vertices split evenly: 55 per half.

concepts.label: LU factorization for circuit matrices
concepts.definition: A transient simulation of a large circuit solves a sparse linear system at every Newton iteration of every timestep, often millions of times.
key_ideas: Eliminating a nodal matrix row by row

sample.question: Gaussian elimination without pivoting factors the nodal matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 9 & -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 10 & -4 \\ -2 & -4 & 10 \end{pmatrix}$ as $A = LU$ with unit lower-triangular $L$. What is the multiplier $l_{21}$? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The multiplier is the entry being eliminated over the pivot: $l_{21} = a_{21}/a_{11} = -2/9 = -0.2222$.

concepts.label: Small pivots and element growth
concepts.definition: Gaussian elimination is only as stable as its pivots. A tiny pivot, which in a circuit can come from a nearly floating node, a minimum gmin conductance or a transistor switched almost off, produces huge multipliers that swamp the rest of the matrix in rounding error.
key_ideas: A tiny pivot creates a huge multiplier

sample.question: A nodal matrix has a nearly floating node: $A = \begin{pmatrix} 10^{-3} & 1 \\ 1 & 9 \end{pmatrix}$. Eliminating without pivoting, what is the multiplier $l_{21}$?
sample.explanation: $l_{21} = a_{21}/a_{11} = 1 / 10^{-3} = 1000$, a huge multiplier from a tiny pivot.

concepts.label: Threshold partial pivoting
concepts.definition: Sparse LU must serve two masters: pivots large enough for stability and pivots placed to minimize fill.
key_ideas: Choosing among eligible pivots by Markowitz count

sample.question: The active pivot column of a sparse LU has these candidates: row 1: value 7.2, 2 nonzeros in its row; row 2: value -1, 2 nonzeros in its row; row 3: value -4.8, 2 nonzeros in its row; row 4: value -7.4, 4 nonzeros in its row; row 5: value 8.5, 5 nonzeros in its row. With threshold $u = 0.01$, how many candidates pass the test $|a_{ij}| \ge u \max_k |a_{kj}|$?
sample.explanation: The largest magnitude is 8.5, so the cutoff is 0.085. 5 candidates reach it.

concepts.label: Conditioning of circuit matrices
concepts.definition: Even a perfectly stable solver cannot recover digits that the problem itself does not determine.
key_ideas: Condition number of a conductance matrix
Conductance spread, gmin and digits lost

sample.question: Node 1 connects to ground through 5 mS and to node 2 through 15 mS; node 2 connects to ground through 9 mS. Its conductance matrix is $\begin{pmatrix} 20 & -15 \\ -15 & 24 \end{pmatrix}$ mS. What is the condition number $\kappa_\infty(G) = \|G\|_\infty \|G^{-1}\|_\infty$? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $\|G\|_\infty = 39$ (largest row sum), $\det G = 255$, $\|G^{-1}\|_\infty = 0.152941$, so $\kappa_\infty = 5.96$.

concepts.label: Cholesky for conductance matrices
concepts.definition: Resistive networks, RC interconnect and power grids give symmetric positive definite conductance matrices.
key_ideas: Why grounded conductance matrices are SPD
Half the work and no pivoting

sample.question: Two nodes are joined by 9 mS; node 1 has 9 mS and node 2 has 9 mS to ground, so $G =$ $\begin{pmatrix} 18 & -9 \\ -9 & 18 \end{pmatrix}$ mS. For $v = (2, 0.2)$ V, compute $v^T G v$ in mW (it equals the power the resistors dissipate). Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $v^T G v = g_{12}(v_1 - v_2)^2 + g_1 v_1^2 + g_2 v_2^2 = 65.52$ mW, positive for every nonzero $v$, which is why $G$ is positive definite.

concepts.label: Newton-Raphson for nonlinear systems
concepts.definition: A DC operating point, and every implicit timestep of a transient, is a system of nonlinear equations $F(x) = 0$, one KCL equation per node with device currents that depend nonlinearly on node voltages.
key_ideas: The Jacobian and the linearized system
One Newton step on a two-equation system
Residual norms and when to stop

sample.question: Solve $F_1 = x^2 + y - 5 = 0$, $F_2 = 2x + y^2 - 5 = 0$ by Newton-Raphson from $(x_0, y_0) = (1.5, 1.3)$. What is the determinant of the Jacobian at the starting point? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $J = \begin{pmatrix} 2x & 1 \\ 2 & 2y \end{pmatrix}$, so $\det J = 4x_0y_0 - 2 = 5.8$.

concepts.label: Newton on exponential device laws
concepts.definition: Semiconductor devices obey exponential laws: diode and bipolar currents grow like $e^{V/V_T}$, and MOSFETs do in subthreshold.
key_ideas: One Newton update from an initial guess

sample.question: A source of 3.5 V drives a 2.5 kΩ resistor into a diode to ground with $I_s = 10^{-14}$ A and $V_T = 25$ mV. The node equation is $f(V) = (V - 3.5)/R + I_s(e^{V/V_T} - 1) = 0$. At the guess $V_0 = 0.71$ V, what is the residual $f(V_0)$ in mA? Round to 4 decimal places.

concepts.label: Damped Newton and step limiting
concepts.definition: Newton's method converges only near the solution. Far from it, the full step can overshoot, oscillate or diverge, especially with exponential devices.
key_ideas: Limiting the voltage change per iteration

sample.question: Damped Newton solves $x^3 - 14 = 0$ from $x_0 = 0.5$ with damping factor $\lambda = 0.5$, so $x_1 = x_0 + \lambda\,\Delta x$ with the full Newton step $\Delta x$. What is $x_1$? Round to 4 decimal places.

concepts.label: Newton convergence criteria
concepts.definition: A Newton loop needs a precise rule for when to stop. Stop too early and the answer is wrong; demand too much and the simulator wastes iterations or never terminates because of roundoff.
key_ideas: Reading quadratic convergence from the iterates

sample.question: A SPICE-style test accepts a node update when $|v_{k+1} - v_k| \le \text{reltol} \cdot \max(|v_{k+1}|, |v_k|) + \text{vntol}$ with reltol = 0.001 and vntol = 1 µV. Two iterates are $v_k = 2.893$ V and $v_{k+1} = 2.89415$ V. What is the allowed change, in µV? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $0.001 \cdot 2.89415$ V $+ 1$ µV $= 2895.15$ µV. The actual change is 1150 µV.

concepts.label: Continuation and homotopy methods
concepts.definition: When Newton fails even with damping, simulators solve an easier problem first and deform it into the real one.
key_ideas: Embedding the problem in a parameter family
Source stepping and gmin stepping as homotopies
Step size along the path and turning points

sample.question:
Why does continuation use the solution at the previous parameter value as the Newton starting guess?

A) Newton converges only locally, and the solution path moves continuously with s, so the previous point lies inside the basin of attraction

B) It guarantees quadratic convergence from any point

C) It makes the Jacobian symmetric

D) It removes the need to factor the Jacobian
sample.answer: Newton converges only locally, and the solution path moves continuously with s, so the previous point lies inside the basin of attraction
sample.explanation: Newton's quadratic convergence is local. Continuation keeps each new problem close to one already solved.

concepts.label: Backward Euler
concepts.definition: Transient circuit simulation integrates the circuit equations in time, and the workhorse integrator is backward Euler.
key_ideas: One step for an RC circuit
Backward Euler on a coupled system

sample.question: Apply one backward Euler step of size $h = 0.6$ to $y' = -9.5y - 4.5$ from $y_0 = 3.5$. What is $y_1$? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Backward Euler evaluates the slope at the new point: $y_1 = y_0 + h(-ay_1 + b)$, so $y_1 = (y_0 + hb)/(1 + ah) = (0.8)/(6.7) = 0.1194$.

concepts.label: The trapezoidal rule for ODEs
concepts.definition: The trapezoidal rule averages the slopes at both ends of a step. It is second-order accurate and A-stable, so it is SPICE's default transient method.
key_ideas: Averaging the slopes at both ends
One trapezoidal step for an RC circuit

sample.question: Apply one trapezoidal step of size $h = 0.4$ to $y' = -0.5y + 0$ from $y_0 = -1.5$. What is $y_1$? Round to 4 decimal places.

concepts.label: Companion models of integration steps
concepts.definition: A simulator does not integrate capacitor and inductor equations separately from the circuit.
key_ideas: A capacitor becomes a conductance and a current source
Trapezoidal companion with the history current
Inductor companions and the solve per step

sample.question: Backward Euler replaces a 162 fF capacitor by a companion conductance in parallel with a current source. With timestep $h = 41$ ps, what is the companion conductance, in mS? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $G_{eq} = C/h = 162\text{ fF}/41\text{ ps} = 3.9512$ mS (1 fF/ps is 1 mS).

concepts.label: BDF2 and Gear methods
concepts.definition: Backward differentiation formulas (BDF), known in circuit simulation as Gear's methods, generalize backward Euler by using several past points.
key_ideas: Differentiating an interpolant through past points
One BDF2 step on a linear test equation
Starting the method and its order limits

sample.question: BDF2 estimates $y'(t_{n+1})$ by differentiating the quadratic through three equally spaced samples. With step $h = 0.8$ and $y_{n-1} = -1.9$, $y_n = -0.8$, $y_{n+1} = 1.6$, what is that derivative estimate $(3y_{n+1} - 4y_n + y_{n-1})/(2h)$? Round to 4 decimal places.

concepts.label: Stability regions of integration methods
concepts.definition: Whether an integration method is safe on a circuit depends on the eigenvalues of the circuit's linearization and on the method's stability region.
key_ideas: The test equation and the amplification factor
Comparing forward Euler, backward Euler and trapezoidal

sample.question: For the test equation $y' = \lambda y$, one step of a method multiplies $y$ by its amplification factor $R(z)$, $z = h\lambda$. What is $R(z)$ for trapezoidal at $z = -8.5$? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Forward Euler $R = 1 + z$, backward Euler $R = 1/(1 - z)$, trapezoidal $R = (1 + z/2)/(1 - z/2)$. For trapezoidal at $z = -8.5$: -0.619.

concepts.label: Stiff equations
concepts.definition: Circuits are stiff: a femtofarad parasitic on a small resistor has a picosecond time constant, while the signals of interest evolve over nanoseconds or microseconds.
key_ideas: The explicit step limit on a stiff circuit
Why implicit methods win despite the solve

sample.question: Two coupled RC nodes obey $x' = Ax$ with $A =$ $\begin{pmatrix} -1439 & 3 \\ 3 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ per ns. Its eigenvalues are real and negative. What is the stiffness ratio $|\lambda|_{max}/|\lambda|_{min}$? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: For the symmetric matrix the eigenvalues are $-(720.5 \pm 718.5063)$, i.e. -1439.0063 and -1.9937 per ns. Ratio 721.8.

concepts.label: Local truncation error
concepts.definition: The local truncation error (LTE) of an integration step is the error it would make starting from exact data.
key_ideas: Estimating the error from divided differences
Error constants of BE, trapezoidal and BDF2

sample.question: A node voltage has $|v''| \approx 3.9$ V/ns$^2$ near $t_n$. What is the backward Euler local truncation error of a step $h = 0.12$ ns, in mV? Round to 4 decimal places.

concepts.label: LTE-based timestep control
concepts.definition: A transient simulator never uses a fixed timestep. After each step it compares the LTE estimate with a tolerance, rejects bad steps, and chooses the next step from the error.

sample.question: A timestep controller accepts a step when its LTE estimate is at most the tolerance of 0.7 mV. The last 4 attempted steps had estimates 1.54, 0.84, 0.84, 0.63 mV. How many were rejected?
sample.explanation: Each estimate above 0.7 mV fails: 3 rejections, each retried with a smaller step.

concepts.label: Differential-algebraic equations in circuits
concepts.definition: The equations a circuit simulator integrates are not ordinary differential equations.
key_ideas: Why BDF methods handle index-1 DAEs

sample.question:
Why can a simulator not hand $C x' + G x = u$ to a standard explicit ODE solver by writing $x' = C^{-1}(u - Gx)$?

A) C is always diagonal

B) Explicit solvers cannot handle linear systems

C) G must be inverted instead of C

D) C is generally singular in MNA, so its inverse does not exist
sample.answer: C is generally singular in MNA, so its inverse does not exist
sample.explanation: Nodes without capacitance and source branch currents give zero rows in C, so the ODE form does not exist.

concepts.label: Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel on power grids
concepts.definition: The simplest iterative solvers update one node at a time from its neighbours. On a power grid each update is a local KCL balance, so Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel are easy to implement, trivially parallel (Jacobi) and memory-light.
key_ideas: A node update averages its neighbours
One sweep on a resistive grid

sample.question: A power-grid node connects through 2 S to a node at 0.942 V, 15 S to a node at 0.983 V, 18 S to a node at 0.947 V, and its cells draw 0.8 A. Holding the neighbours fixed, what voltage does one Jacobi update assign to the node, in volts? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: KCL: $\sum g_j(v_j - v_i) = I_{load}$, so $v_i = (\sum g_j v_j - I_{load})/\sum g_j = (33.675 - 0.8)/35 = 0.9393$ V.

concepts.label: The conjugate gradient method
concepts.definition: Conjugate gradients (CG) is the iterative method for symmetric positive definite systems, the matrices of resistive power grids, RC interconnect and thermal networks.
key_ideas: Minimizing the energy along conjugate directions
Exact termination and the Krylov subspace

sample.question: For $A =$ $\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 8 \end{pmatrix}$ and $b =$ $\begin{pmatrix} -5 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$, CG minimizes the energy $\phi(x) = \tfrac12 x^TAx - b^Tx$. What is $\phi$ at $x = (0, 2)$? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $x^TAx = 32$ and $b^Tx = 12$, so $\phi = 4$.

concepts.label: CG convergence and the condition number
concepts.definition: How many CG iterations a power-grid solve needs is set by the condition number of the matrix.

sample.question: The CG error bound is $\|e_k\|_A \le 2\rho^k\|e_0\|_A$ with $\rho = (\sqrt\kappa - 1)/(\sqrt\kappa + 1)$. For $\kappa =$ $7 \times 10^{1}$, what is $\rho$? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $\sqrt\kappa = 8.367$, so $\rho = 0.7865$. Compare $(\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)$ for steepest descent, much closer to 1.

concepts.label: GMRES
concepts.definition: MNA matrices with controlled sources, inductor branches and voltage sources are unsymmetric, so CG does not apply.
key_ideas: Minimal residual over the Krylov subspace
The first GMRES step by hand

sample.question: GMRES solves $Ax = b$ with the nonsymmetric $A =$ $\begin{pmatrix} 6 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $b =$ $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ from $x_0 = 0$. The first Krylov subspace is span$\{b\}$, so $x_1 = \alpha b$. For the trial value $\alpha = 0.2$, what is the residual norm $\|b - \alpha Ab\|_2$? Round to 4 decimal places.

concepts.label: Preconditioning
concepts.definition: Krylov methods are only as fast as the spectrum of the matrix allows, and power-grid and thermal matrices have bad spectra.
key_ideas: Solving an equivalent system that converges faster
Jacobi scaling of a badly scaled matrix
Cost per iteration against iterations saved

sample.question: Unpreconditioned CG on a grid matrix with $\kappa = 10^{7}$ takes 810 iterations. A preconditioner brings the effective condition number to $10^{3}$. If iterations scale like $\sqrt\kappa$, about how many iterations remain? Round to the nearest integer.

concepts.label: Incomplete LU and incomplete Cholesky
concepts.definition: Incomplete LU and incomplete Cholesky factorizations run Gaussian elimination but throw away most of the fill.
key_ideas: Factor but keep the original pattern
Levels of fill and drop tolerances

sample.question: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 7 & -1 & -3 \\ -1 & 9 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$ has zeros at positions (2,3) and (3,2). Exact Gaussian elimination of column 1 makes position (2,3) nonzero. What value appears there? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $a_{23} - l_{21}a_{13} = 0 - (-1/7)(-3) = -0.4286$. ILU(0) discards this fill because (2,3) is outside the pattern of $A$.

concepts.label: Multigrid for power grids
concepts.definition: Multigrid solves grid problems in work proportional to the number of unknowns, with an iteration count that does not grow with grid size.
key_ideas: Grid-independent convergence on large power grids

sample.question: Damped Jacobi with weight $\omega = 1$ on the 1D Laplacian with 27 interior points multiplies the Fourier error mode $k$ (frequency $\theta = k\pi/(n+1)$) by $1 - \omega(1 - \cos\theta)$ per sweep. By what factor is mode $k = 15$ multiplied after 1 sweep(s)? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $\theta = 1.683$ rad, one sweep gives -0.112, and 1 sweep(s) give -0.112. High modes shrink fast; low modes (small $\theta$) barely change.

concepts.label: Finite difference discretization
concepts.definition: Thermal analysis of a die, substrate noise and some field problems are partial differential equations.
key_ideas: The five-point Laplacian on a thermal grid

sample.question: Temperatures along a line at spacing $h = 0.5$ mm are 30.9, 28 and 30.9 °C. What is the central second-difference estimate of $T''$ at the middle point, in K/mm$^2$? Round to 4 decimal places.

concepts.label: Boundary conditions in thermal grids
concepts.definition: A thermal model is only as good as its boundaries: a heat sink, an insulated package edge, a convective surface.
key_ideas: Neumann: insulated edges and ghost nodes
Robin: convection to a heat sink

sample.question: A rod of length 6 mm with uniform heating obeys $-T'' = Q$ with $Q = q/k = 0.6$ K/mm$^2$, and its ends are held at 43.4 °C and 39.2 °C (Dirichlet). A finite-difference grid has 7 equal intervals. What temperature does it compute at node 5 (node 0 is the first end), in °C? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The exact solution $T = T_a + (T_b - T_a)x/L + Qx(L - x)/2$ is quadratic, so the second difference reproduces it exactly at the nodes. At $x = 4.2857$ mm: 42.6041 °C.

concepts.label: Explicit time stepping of heat flow
concepts.definition: Transient thermal analysis, such as a hot spot heating during a power burst, integrates the heat equation in time.
key_ideas: Method of lines: the grid becomes an ODE system
One explicit step and why implicit is preferred

sample.question: The method of lines turns $T_t = \alpha T_{xx}$ into $dT_i/dt = \alpha(T_{i-1} - 2T_i + T_{i+1})/h^2$. With $\alpha = 21$ mm$^2$/s, $h = 1$ mm and neighbouring temperatures 45.3, 43, 44.3 °C, what is $dT_i/dt$ at the middle node, in K/s? Round to 4 decimal places.

concepts.label: The finite element method
concepts.definition: The finite element method discretizes PDEs on unstructured meshes, which fit the irregular geometry of packages, TSVs and interposers far better than grids.
key_ideas: The weak form and hat functions
Load vectors and solving a small mesh

sample.question: A 1D linear finite element of length 1.1 mm, cross-section 0.6 mm$^2$ and conductivity 20 W/(m K) has element matrix $(kA/h)\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. What is its off-diagonal entry, in mW/K? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $kA/h = 20 \cdot 0.6\text{ mm}^2/1.1\text{ mm} = 10.9091$ mW/K, so the off-diagonal entry is -10.9091.

concepts.label: Finite volume and flux conservation
concepts.definition: The finite volume method integrates the conservation law over each cell, so heat leaving one cell exactly enters its neighbour.
key_ideas: Balancing fluxes over a control volume

sample.question: Two control volumes of a material with $k = 2$ W/(m K) share a face of area 0.05 mm$^2$; their centres are 0.12 mm apart and sit at 58.6 and 49.3 °C. What heat flows through the face, in mW? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $q = kA(T_i - T_j)/d = 2 \cdot 0.05/0.12 \cdot 9.3 = 7.75$ mW (with mm units, W/(m K) times mm gives mW/K).

concepts.label: Boundary element methods for extraction
concepts.definition: Capacitance extraction solves Laplace's equation in the dielectric around conductors, an unbounded region.

sample.question:
A BEM capacitance extractor models 4 identical box-shaped wires. Each box is meshed with 4-by-4 panels on its top and bottom faces, 4-by-2 on its front and back, and 4-by-2 on its two ends. How many unknowns (panel charges) does the system have?

A) 256

B) 384

C) 64

D) 128
sample.explanation: Each box has $2(16 + 8 + 8) = 64$ panels; 4 boxes give 256 unknowns, one charge per panel.

concepts.label: Transfer-function moments of RC networks
concepts.definition: Interconnect networks extracted from layout have millions of RC elements, far too many to simulate with every gate.
key_ideas: Expanding H(s) in powers of s
Moments, Elmore delay and a one-pole fit

sample.question: A single RC section has $H(s) = 1/(1 + s\tau)$ with $R = 3$ kΩ and $C = 0.5$ pF. Expanding $H(s) = \sum_k m_k s^k$, what is the moment $m_3$, in ns$^3$? Round to 4 decimal places.

concepts.label: Model order reduction by Krylov projection
concepts.definition: Krylov projection builds reduced interconnect models that match moments without ever forming them explicitly.
key_ideas: How many moments a projection matches

sample.question:
A Krylov basis for reduction starts from $r =$ $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ with $A =$ $\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 \end{pmatrix}$. The subspace $K_2(A, r) = \mathrm{span}\{r, Ar\}$. What is the second Krylov vector $Ar$ (before orthogonalization)?

A) $(1, -3)$

B) $(17, -18)$

C) $(-6, -1)$

D) $(1, 6)$

E) $(-1, -6)$
sample.explanation: Multiply row by row: $Ar = (-1, -6)$.

concepts.label: Truncation by singular values
concepts.definition: Krylov methods match moments; singular-value methods rank directions by importance and throw away the weak ones with a computable error bound.
key_ideas: Singular values rank the important directions
The Eckart-Young error of a truncation
Choosing the reduced order for a tolerance

sample.question: A snapshot matrix of a thermal model has singular values 19.7, 3.349, 2.344, 0.821, 0.336. What percentage of the total energy $\sum\sigma_i^2$ do the first 1 singular directions capture? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Forward-mode automatic differentiation
concepts.definition: Newton iteration needs Jacobians, sensitivity analysis needs gradients, and analytical placers optimize by gradient.
key_ideas: Dual numbers carry a value and a derivative
Cost: one pass per input direction

sample.question: Forward-mode AD evaluates $f(x) = (x^2 + 4x)(x - 4)$ on the dual number $x = -4 + 1\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon^2 = 0$. The result is $f + f'\varepsilon$. What is the $\varepsilon$ coefficient?
sample.explanation: $u = x^2 + 4x = 0 - 4\varepsilon$, $w = x - 4 = -8 + 1\varepsilon$, and $(u_0 + u_1\varepsilon)(w_0 + w_1\varepsilon) = u_0w_0 + (u_0w_1 + u_1w_0)\varepsilon = 0 + 32\varepsilon$.

concepts.label: Reverse mode and adjoint sensitivity
concepts.definition: When a single scalar, a delay, an IR drop or a placement cost, depends on many parameters, its gradient is best computed backwards.
key_ideas: Sweeping adjoints backwards through the graph
Adjoint sensitivity of a linear circuit

sample.question: A reverse-mode sweep records $f = x^2 y + 3y$ at $(x, y) = (-2, 2)$, seeds $\bar f = 1$ and propagates adjoints backward through each operation. What adjoint $\bar y = \partial f/\partial y$ does it produce?
sample.explanation: Each node passes its adjoint times the local partial derivative to its inputs, and contributions to a shared input add: $\bar y = 7$.

concepts.label: GPU computing for EDA kernels
concepts.definition: GPUs offer far more arithmetic and memory bandwidth than CPUs, but EDA kernels benefit only when they fit the hardware.
key_ideas: Mapping solver kernels to GPU threads

sample.question: A CSR SpMV on n = 4031000 rows with 8 nonzeros per row does 2 flops per nonzero and moves $12\,\text{nnz} + 4(n + 1) + 16n$ bytes (values, indices, row pointers, $x$ and $y$). What is its arithmetic intensity, in flop/byte? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: nnz = 32248000, flops = 64496000, bytes = 467596004, intensity 0.1379 flop/byte, far below the balance point of any processor.

concepts.label: Parallel speedup and its limits
concepts.definition: Parallel hardware speeds up EDA engines only as far as their serial parts allow.
key_ideas: Amdahl's law for a fixed problem

sample.question: A transient simulation spends 83 percent of its single-thread time in device evaluation and the sparse solve, which parallelize perfectly, and the rest in serial bookkeeping. By Amdahl's law, what speedup do 64 threads give? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $S = 1/((1 - p) + p/N) = 1/(0.17 + 0.83/64) = 5.47$; the limit for infinite threads is 5.88.

concepts.label: Reduction order and reproducibility
concepts.definition: Floating-point addition is not associative, so a parallel sum gives slightly different answers depending on how it is split across threads.
key_ideas: Computing a sum in two orders

sample.question: In IEEE single precision (24-bit significand, round to nearest even), compute $(2^{25} + 2) + 3$ exactly as the hardware would, rounding after each addition. What is the result? ($2^{25} = 33554432$.)
sample.explanation: Near $2^{25}$ the spacing of float32 numbers is 4, so small additions round to the nearest representable value at each step; the result is 33554436.

concepts.label: Numerical kernels as an immutable core
concepts.definition: In an agent-first EDA engine, the numerical kernels are the immutable core: the code every analysis trusts and every agent calls but rarely edits.
key_ideas: What belongs in the solver core
Policies, parameters and hooks around a solver
The determinism contract of a kernel

sample.question:
Why keep the hot numerical kernels (SpMV, triangular solve, element evaluation) inside the core rather than behind fine-grained plug-in calls?

A) The kernels change too often to be core

B) Agents cannot call core code

C) Plug-ins cannot perform floating-point arithmetic

D) Per-entry calls across a plug-in boundary block inlining and vectorization and would dominate run time
sample.answer: Per-entry calls across a plug-in boundary block inlining and vectorization and would dominate run time
sample.explanation: Seams should be coarse, per solve or per batch, so the compiler can optimize the inner loops.

concepts.label: Seams for solvers and preconditioners
concepts.definition: A seam is the narrow, stable interface where new behaviour plugs into an engine without touching its core.
key_ideas: The linear solver and preconditioner seams
What context the seam must expose
Classifying solver change requests by tier

sample.question:
Which interface makes a good seam for plugging new linear solvers into a circuit simulator?

A) analyze(pattern), factor(values), solve(rhs): coarse calls per matrix and per solve

B) A global variable holding the current matrix

C) get(i, j) and set(i, j) called for each matrix entry

D) One function that parses the netlist and returns waveforms
sample.answer: analyze(pattern), factor(values), solve(rhs): coarse calls per matrix and per solve
sample.explanation: Splitting symbolic analysis from numeric factorization lets the simulator reuse the analysis across Newton iterations; coarse calls keep the hot loops inside the solver.

concepts.label: Differential tests for solver changes
concepts.definition: Every change to a numerical engine, by an agent or a person, must be proven before promotion.
key_ideas: Golden circuits and what must not move

sample.question:
A solver change is tested on $A =$ $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -3 \\ -3 & 9 \end{pmatrix}$, $b =$ $\begin{pmatrix} -21 \\ 39 \end{pmatrix}$. It returns $\hat x = (-3.99994, 2.99994)$. What is the normwise backward error $\eta = \|b - A\hat x\|_\infty/(\|A\|_\infty\|\hat x\|_\infty + \|b\|_\infty)$?

A) $8.28 \times 10^{-5}$

B) $1.5 \times 10^{-5}$

C) $8.28 \times 10^{-6}$

D) $7.2 \times 10^{-4}$

E) $1.85 \times 10^{-5}$
sample.explanation: $\|r\|_\infty = 0.00072$, $\|A\|_\infty = 12$, $\|\hat x\|_\infty = 3.99994$, $\|b\|_\infty = 39$. A stable solver in double precision gives $\eta$ near $10^{-16}$; this one is far above, so the test fails.

concepts.label: GPU solvers inside agent loops
concepts.definition: Agents exploring power-grid straps, decap placements or thermal floorplans issue hundreds of similar solves.
key_ideas: When to recurse to the accurate solver

sample.question:
An agent evaluates 203 candidate power-grid variants that share one sparsity pattern. Each solve on its own costs 30 ms of setup (symbolic analysis, transfer, launch) plus 4.5 ms of numeric work. Batched, the setup is paid once and the numeric work stays 4.5 ms per candidate. What does batching gain?

A) 1.15 times faster

B) 14.85 times faster

C) 7.42 times faster

D) 203 times faster

E) 6.67 times faster
sample.answer: 7.42 times faster

concepts.label: Fast and accurate solver modes
concepts.definition: Every numerical engine can trade accuracy for speed: looser tolerances, lower precision, coarser meshes, larger timesteps, reduced models.
key_ideas: Loose tolerances and what they buy
Promoting a fast result to signoff

sample.question:
The accurate mode of an IR-drop solver runs CG to a relative tolerance of $10^{-10}$ in 590 iterations. A fast mode stops at $10^{-2}$. If iterations scale like $\ln(2/\varepsilon)$ at a fixed condition number, about how many iterations does the fast mode take?

A) 132

B) 264

C) 590

D) 59

E) 295
sample.explanation: $590 \cdot \ln(2 \cdot 10^{2})/\ln(2 \cdot 10^{10}) = 132$ iterations.

domains.name: Variability, Yield and Reliability Statistics
domains.description: Monte Carlo and rare-event estimation, process variation, statistical timing mathematics, yield models and lifetime statistics.
covers: Monte Carlo method, quasi-Monte Carlo, importance sampling, rare-event simulation (SRAM failure rates)
Regression analysis, design of experiments, response surface methodology, surrogate fitting
Uncertainty quantification, sensitivity analysis, worst-case analysis
Statistical process control, process variation (global, local, systematic, random), spatial correlation, PCA of variation
Extreme value theory, Weibull distribution, lifetime modeling, reliability engineering, failure analysis, fault tolerance
Yield and yield optimization, statistical timing analysis as a statistics problem (sum and max of Gaussians)

concepts.label: Process variation
concepts.definition: No two transistors come out of a fab identical. Gate length, oxide thickness, dopant count and line-edge shape all scatter, and so do the delays, leakages and margins built from them.

sample.question:
Which variation is not a manufacturing variation at all, yet still enters a variability budget?

A) Line-edge roughness

B) Random dopant fluctuation

C) Supply and temperature variation during operation

D) Wafer-level oxide thickness drift
sample.answer: Supply and temperature variation during operation
sample.explanation: Voltage and temperature vary in the field (environmental variation). They are budgeted alongside process variation but have different statistics and correlation.

concepts.label: Pelgrom mismatch scaling
concepts.definition: The local random part of process variation has a remarkably simple law. Pelgrom's law states that the mismatch between two identically drawn, closely spaced transistors shrinks with the square root of their gate area.

sample.question: A process has a Pelgrom coefficient $A_{V_T} = 2.7$ mV$\cdot\mu$m. A matched pair uses devices with $W = 0.6\ \mu$m and $L = 0.04\ \mu$m. What is the standard deviation of the threshold-voltage difference between the two devices, in mV? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $\sigma(\Delta V_T) = A_{V_T}/\sqrt{WL} = 2.7/\sqrt{0.024} = 17.43$ mV.

concepts.label: Spatially correlated variation
concepts.definition: Within-die variation is not purely random from device to device. Lithography focus, etch loading and wafer-level gradients produce slow spatial trends, so neighbouring gates are more alike than distant ones.

sample.question: Within-die variation of gate length is modeled with the exponential correlation $\rho(d) = e^{-d/\lambda}$ and correlation length $\lambda = 1000\ \mu$m. What is the correlation between two gates $850\ \mu$m apart? Round to 3 decimal places.

concepts.label: Principal components of correlated variation
concepts.definition: A statistical timer that tracks a separate random variable for every grid cell of a die, all correlated with each other, would carry thousands of dependent variables through every addition and max.

sample.question: The gate-length variations of two regions of a die have covariance matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 10 & 3 \\ 3 & 10 \end{pmatrix}$ in nm$^2$. What is the variance carried by the first principal component, in nm$^2$? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Eigenvalues of a symmetric 2x2: $\frac{a+b}{2} \pm \sqrt{(\frac{a-b}{2})^2 + c^2} = 10 \pm 3$. The larger is 13.

concepts.label: Statistical process control
concepts.definition: A fab does not wait for yield loss to notice that its process drifted. It measures critical dimensions, film thicknesses and electrical test structures on every lot and plots them on control charts.
key_ideas: How fast a chart detects a shift

sample.question: A fab monitors gate critical dimension with an $\bar{X}$ chart. The in-control process has mean 38.3 nm and standard deviation 1.3 nm, and each plotted point averages 25 sites. What is the upper control limit, in nm? Round to 3 decimal places.

concepts.label: Sigma level and failure probability
concepts.definition: Designers state margins in sigmas: a 3-sigma corner, a 6-sigma bitcell. A tool designer must be able to convert that language into probabilities and back, instantly and in both directions, because every rare-event target, array-yield budget and sample-size estimate in variation analysis is set in sigmas and checked in probabilities.
key_ideas: From array yield back to a cell sigma

sample.question: A cell fails when a Gaussian margin falls more than 3.25 standard deviations below its mean. What is the failure probability, in parts per million? Round to the nearest integer.

concepts.label: Sums of correlated Gaussians
concepts.definition: A path delay is a sum of stage delays, and a statistical timer must know its mean and spread.
key_ideas: A path of n correlated stages

sample.question: Two stage delays on a path have standard deviations 6 ps and 14 ps and correlation coefficient 0.1. What is the standard deviation of their sum, in ps? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $\mathrm{Var} = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + 2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2 = 36 + 196 + 16.8 = 248.8$, so $\sigma = 15.773$ ps.

concepts.label: Sums and maxima of Gaussian variables
concepts.definition: Statistical static timing propagates arrival-time distributions through a timing graph with two operations: add a gate delay along an edge, and take the maximum where paths reconverge.
key_ideas: The variance, and why max is not Gaussian

sample.question: Two arrival times at a gate input are jointly Gaussian: $A \sim N(115, 8^2)$ ps and $B \sim N(104, 8^2)$ ps with correlation 0.3. What is the probability that $A$ is the larger (the tightness probability of $A$)? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $\theta = \sqrt{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2 - 2\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B} = 9.4657$ and $\alpha = (\mu_A - \mu_B)/\theta = 1.1621$. The tightness probability is $\Phi(\alpha) = 0.8774$.

concepts.label: Canonical first-order delay forms
concepts.definition: A block-based statistical timer must store every arrival time in a representation that is closed under addition, approximately closed under max, and that remembers correlation.

sample.question: In first-order canonical form, with $\Delta X_1, \Delta X_2$ shared principal components and each $\Delta R$ an independent random term (all standard normal), two arrival times are $A = 112 + 2\,\Delta X_1 + 3\,\Delta X_2 + 1\,\Delta R$ and $B = 103 + 3\,\Delta X_1 + 2\,\Delta X_2 + 4\,\Delta R$ ps. What is the standard deviation of $A$, in ps? Round to 3 decimal places.

concepts.label: Timing yield from a delay distribution
concepts.definition: A statistical timer's output is not a slack but a distribution, and the number that matters to the business is the fraction of manufactured dies that meet the target frequency.

sample.question: Statistical timing gives the circuit delay as Gaussian with mean 609 ps and standard deviation 29 ps. What percentage of dies meet a clock period of 609 ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Monte Carlo estimation
concepts.definition: Monte Carlo is the reference method of variation analysis: draw process parameters from their distributions, simulate the circuit for each draw, and count.
key_ideas: The estimator and its standard error
Cost scales as one over the square root of N

sample.question: A Monte Carlo run simulates 2000 random instances of a circuit and 9 of them fail a spec. What is the standard error of the estimated yield, in percentage points? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $\hat{Y} = 1991/2000 = 0.9955$. $SE = \sqrt{\hat{Y}(1-\hat{Y})/N} = 0.0015$, which is 0.15 percentage points.

concepts.label: Monte Carlo sample size for a failure rate
concepts.definition: Before launching a Monte Carlo run, a flow must decide how many samples to ask for.
key_ideas: Demonstrating a bound with zero failures
Why plain Monte Carlo fails at high sigma

sample.question: A failure rate near $p = 0.005$ is to be estimated by plain Monte Carlo with a relative error of at most 20 percent at 90 percent confidence ($z = 1.645$). Using $N = z^2(1-p)/(p\,\varepsilon^2)$, how many samples are needed? Give the smallest integer.

concepts.label: Quasi-Monte Carlo sequences
concepts.definition: Plain Monte Carlo spends its samples at random, so they clump and leave gaps. Quasi-Monte Carlo replaces random points with deterministic low-discrepancy sequences that fill the space evenly.

sample.question: What is point number 22 of the base-2 van der Corput sequence (the radical inverse of 22 in base 2)? Round to 6 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $22 = 10110_2$. Mirroring the digits about the radix point gives $0.01101_2 = 0.40625$.

concepts.label: Importance sampling
concepts.definition: Importance sampling is the workhorse of rare-event estimation in circuit variability.
key_ideas: Several dimensions and the choice of shift

sample.question: A failure rate under $X \sim N(0,1)$ is estimated by drawing from the shifted proposal $N(3, 1)$. What is the likelihood-ratio weight of the sample $x = 2.5$? Round to 4 decimal places.

concepts.label: Most probable failure point
concepts.definition: Where in parameter space does a circuit most likely fail? In standard-normal coordinates the answer is the point of the failure region closest to the origin, because the Gaussian density falls off with distance.
key_ideas: Scaling and the search in practice

sample.question: In standard-normal parameter space a cell fails when $6 x_1 + 4 x_2 > 40$. How far from the origin, in sigmas, is the most probable failure point? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The closest point of the plane $a\cdot x = b$ is at distance $\beta = b/\|a\| = 40/7.2111 = 5.547$, along the direction of $a$.

concepts.label: Rare-event estimation
concepts.definition: Memory bitcells, sense amplifiers, flip-flops in safety-critical logic and high-volume analog blocks all need failure rates far below what plain Monte Carlo can measure.
key_ideas: The cost of the naive approach

sample.question:
A bitcell fails at the 4-sigma tail ($p \approx 3.17 \times 10^{-5}$). Roughly how many plain Monte Carlo simulations does a 10 percent relative error at 95 percent confidence need?

A) About $3.16 \times 10^{4}$

B) About $6.19 \times 10^{5}$

C) About $3.16 \times 10^{6}$

D) About $1.21 \times 10^{7}$

E) About $1.21 \times 10^{5}$
sample.answer: About $1.21 \times 10^{7}$
sample.explanation: Relative standard error is $\sqrt{(1-p)/(Np)}$, so $N \approx z^2/(p\,\varepsilon^2) = 1.21 \times 10^{7}$. That is why rare-event methods exist.

concepts.label: Extreme value tails
concepts.definition: When the question is about the far tail of a distribution, the body of the distribution is irrelevant and often misleading.

sample.question: Simulated read delays above a threshold $u = 75$ ps occur with probability 0.02. The excesses over $u$ fit a generalized Pareto distribution with scale $\sigma = 10$ ps and shape $\xi = 0.3$. What is the probability that a delay exceeds 88 ps, in parts per million? Round to the nearest integer.

concepts.label: Sensitivity analysis
concepts.definition: Before spending a Monte Carlo budget, an engine wants to know which variation sources matter.

sample.question: A gate delay depends on independent process parameters, linearized about nominal. $V_{th}$: sensitivity -2.25 ps per mV, $\sigma = 8.5$ mV; $L_{eff}$: sensitivity 0.25 ps per nm, $\sigma = 1.5$ nm. What is the first-order standard deviation of the delay, in ps? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $\sigma_D^2 = \sum_i (\partial D/\partial p_i)^2\sigma_i^2 = 365.7656 + 0.1406 = 365.9062$, so $\sigma_D = 19.129$ ps.

concepts.label: Variance-based sensitivity indices
concepts.definition: First-order sensitivities assume the response is linear. When parameters interact, for example when a mismatch matters only at low supply, derivatives at nominal under-report importance.

sample.question: A response is $Y = 3 X_1 + 3 X_2 + 1 X_3$ with independent zero-mean inputs of standard deviations 1, 1 and 4. What is the first-order Sobol index of $X_1$? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: For an additive linear model $S_1 = a_1^2\sigma_1^2/\mathrm{Var}(Y) = 9/34 = 0.265$.

concepts.label: Worst-case versus statistical analysis
concepts.definition: Worst-case analysis pushes every parameter to its bad limit at once and checks the circuit there.
key_ideas: How rare the worst case really is

sample.question: A delay depends linearly on independent Gaussian parameters. $V_{th}$: sensitivity 2 ps per mV, $\sigma = 4$ mV; $L_{eff}$: sensitivity -1.75 ps per nm, $\sigma = 1.5$ nm; $t_{ox}$: sensitivity -2.75 ps per nm, $\sigma = 1.5$ nm. A worst-case analysis pushes every parameter 2 sigma in its delay-increasing direction at once. How much does the delay rise, in ps? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Each parameter adds $k|a_i|\sigma_i$: the total is $2 \times 14.75 = 29.5$ ps.

concepts.label: Process corners
concepts.definition: A process corner is a set of device models with every global parameter moved to a chosen statistical extreme.

sample.question:
A process corner such as SS is defined how, statistically?

A) The mean of all dies at high temperature

B) Device model parameters shifted together to a chosen sigma level of the global distribution

C) A Monte Carlo sample of local mismatch

D) The slowest die ever measured
sample.answer: Device model parameters shifted together to a chosen sigma level of the global distribution
sample.explanation: Corner models move the global parameters jointly, typically near 3 sigma, so every transistor on the die is equally slow.

concepts.label: Regression for model fitting
concepts.definition: Variation-aware EDA runs on fitted models: delay against load and slew, leakage against threshold voltage, a performance metric against process parameters.

sample.question: A characterization run measures cell delay (ps) against output load (fF) at the points (2, 45.8), (20, 76.5), (22, 76.8), (40, 114). What is the least-squares slope, in ps per fF? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $b_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx} = 1.79$ ps per fF.

concepts.label: Factorial designs and run counts
concepts.definition: Every characterization study, every process-sensitivity experiment and every surrogate model is built from a set of simulation or silicon runs.

sample.question: A characterization study varies 5 process and environment factors, each at 4 levels. How many simulations does a full factorial design need?
sample.explanation: Every combination is run: $4^{5} = 1024$.

concepts.label: Main effects and interactions
concepts.definition: Once the runs of a two-level design are simulated, the analysis is arithmetic on contrasts.

sample.question: A $2^2$ experiment varies A (temperature) and B (threshold implant dose) between coded levels -1 and $+1$ and measures a delay in ps: $(-,-) = 51$, $(+,-) = 46.5$, $(-,+) = 55$, $(+,+) = 46.5$. What is the main effect of A, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Average at A high minus average at A low: $(46.5 + 46.5)/2 - (51 + 55)/2 = -6.5$ ps.

concepts.label: Response surface methods
concepts.definition: Response surface methodology fits a low-order polynomial to a few well-chosen simulations and then optimizes the polynomial instead of the circuit.
key_ideas: A quadratic through three coded runs
Two factors and the canonical analysis

sample.question: A leakage-versus-delay figure of merit is simulated at a sizing factor coded $x = -1, 0, +1$, giving 57.5, 58 and 63.5. Fit $y = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 x^2$ through the three points. At what coded $x$ is the fitted surface stationary? Round to 3 decimal places.

concepts.label: Validating a surrogate model
concepts.definition: A surrogate replaces an expensive simulation with a cheap fitted model inside an optimization or a Monte Carlo loop.

sample.question: A delay surrogate is checked on 5 held-out SPICE runs (ps): predicted 83.3, simulated 84.6; predicted 64.9, simulated 67.6; predicted 60.3, simulated 59.7; predicted 64.6, simulated 64.9; predicted 79.8, simulated 77.6. What is the hold-out root-mean-square error, in ps? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The sum of squared errors is 14.27; dividing by 5 and taking the root gives 1.689 ps.

concepts.label: Yield as a probability
concepts.definition: Yield is the fraction of manufactured dies that work and meet spec, and it is the number that turns variation statistics into cost.

sample.question: A ring-oscillator frequency is Gaussian with mean 109 MHz and standard deviation 7 MHz. A die passes if the frequency lies between 91 and 123 MHz. What is the parametric yield, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Poisson defect yield
concepts.definition: Random particles and pattern defects kill dies independently of process variation.

sample.question: A die of 532 mm$^2$ is made in a process with 0.35 killer defects per cm$^2$, spread at random. Under the Poisson model, what is the die yield, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Clustered defects and negative binomial yield
concepts.definition: Real defects are not spread uniformly: they cluster on some wafers and some regions.

sample.question: A die of 150 mm$^2$ sees 0.27 defects per cm$^2$, clustered with negative binomial parameter $\alpha = 2$. What is the die yield, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $AD_0 = 0.405$, so $Y = (1 + AD_0/\alpha)^{-\alpha} = 69.16$ percent.

concepts.label: Redundancy and repairable yield
concepts.definition: Large memories would rarely work if every cell had to be perfect. Instead they carry spare rows and columns, and a die whose faults can be mapped onto spares is repaired at test.

sample.question: An SRAM array expects $\lambda = 0.5$ random faults (Poisson). It has 3 spare rows, each able to repair one fault, and the spares themselves are fault-free. What is the repaired yield, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The array is good with at most 3 faults: $\sum_{k=0}^{3} e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k! = 99.82$ percent. With no spares it would be 60.65 percent.

concepts.label: Design centering for yield
concepts.definition: Given a variation model and a spec, the nominal design point can be moved to maximize the fraction of dies that pass.
key_ideas: The sigma a spec can afford

sample.question: A performance spec runs from 80 to 110. The performance is Gaussian with standard deviation 5 and its mean currently sits at 91. How many percentage points of yield does moving the mean to the centre of the spec gain? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: At mean 91 the yield is 98.602 percent; at the centre 95 it is 99.73 percent. The gain is 1.13 points.

concepts.label: The Weibull distribution and lifetime
concepts.definition: A chip that works at test can still fail in the field: oxides break down, wires electromigrate, transistors drift under bias.

sample.question: Oxide breakdown times of a device population follow a Weibull distribution with scale $\eta = 24$ years and shape $\beta = 1.8$. What percentage of devices survive 17 years? Round to 3 decimal places.

concepts.label: Hazard rate and FIT
concepts.definition: Reliability is quoted in rates: how often units fail per hour of operation among those still working.
key_ideas: From FIT to mean time to failure

sample.question: A failure mechanism follows a Weibull law with $\eta = 1.60 \times 10^{7}$ hours and $\beta = 1.6$. What is the hazard rate after 13 years of operation (8760 hours per year), in FIT (failures per $10^9$ device-hours)? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $h(t) = (\beta/\eta)(t/\eta)^{\beta-1}$ with $t = 113880$ h gives $5.15 \times 10^{-9}$ per hour, which is 5.15 FIT. With $\beta > 1$ the rate is rising: wear-out.

concepts.label: Accelerated life testing
concepts.definition: Nobody can wait ten years to qualify a chip. Life tests run at elevated temperature, voltage or current so that failures appear in hundreds of hours, and a physical model of each mechanism translates stress time into field time.

sample.question: A failure mechanism has activation energy 0.9 eV. What is the Arrhenius acceleration factor between a stress temperature of 125 C and a use temperature of 55 C? Use $k = 8.617 \times 10^{-5}$ eV/K and add 273.15 to convert to kelvin. Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Fitting Weibull life data
concepts.definition: Life tests produce a list of failure times, often with some units still running when the test stops.

sample.question: On a Weibull plot the vertical coordinate is $\ln(-\ln(1-F))$. What is it for a cumulative failure fraction $F = 0.83$? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $-\ln(1-0.83) = 1.77196$ and its natural log is 0.5721. Weibull data plot as a straight line with slope $\beta$ against $\ln t$.

concepts.label: System reliability and fault tolerance
concepts.definition: A chip is a system of many parts, each with its own lifetime, and its reliability follows from how they are connected: in series, any failure kills the system; with redundancy, some failures are tolerated.

sample.question: A chip contains 4 identical, independent wear-out sites, and it fails when any one fails. Each site has a Weibull life with $\eta = 171$ years and $\beta = 2.8$. What is the probability, in percent, that the chip survives 12 years? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Series reliabilities multiply: $R = e^{-n(t/\eta)^\beta} = e^{-0.00235} = 99.765$ percent. A series of $n$ Weibull parts is Weibull with scale $\eta n^{-1/\beta}$.

concepts.label: Variance-aware surrogates in an agent loop
concepts.definition: In an agent-first flow, fast engines run continuously and accurate engines are called only where they change a decision.

sample.question: A fast timing surrogate predicts a path's slack as 24 ps with a Gaussian predictive standard deviation of 8 ps. What probability, in percent, does it give that the accurate timer would report negative slack? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $P(\text{slack} < 0) = \Phi(-\hat{\mu}/\hat{\sigma}) = \Phi(-3) = 0.13$ percent.

concepts.label: Allocating a Monte Carlo budget
concepts.definition: An agent that runs variation analysis has a fixed simulation budget and many places to spend it: several corners, several process splits, several candidate designs.

sample.question: An agent estimates mean leakage over a product that mixes three process splits (split A: fraction 0.5, sigma 1 nA; split B: fraction 0.4, sigma 1 nA; split C: fraction 0.1, sigma 1 nA). It has 1000 simulations and stratifies by split. Under Neyman allocation, how many go to split A? Round to the nearest integer.
sample.explanation: $n_h = n W_h\sigma_h/\sum_j W_j\sigma_j = 1000 \times 0.5 / 1 = 500$.

concepts.label: Rare-event estimation as a skill
concepts.definition: In an agent-first flow, a rare-event estimator is not a script someone runs by hand.

sample.question:
What must the skill return besides the point estimate of the failure rate, for a downstream agent to act on it?

A) The raw waveform of every simulation

B) A confidence interval, the effective sample size and the number of simulator calls

C) The random seed only

D) Only the estimate, rounded to one digit
sample.answer: A confidence interval, the effective sample size and the number of simulator calls
sample.explanation: An agent decides whether to spend more budget from the interval width and the health of the weights. A bare point estimate hides both.

concepts.label: Golden tests for statistical engines
concepts.definition: Every engine change in an agent-first flow is promoted only if golden and differential tests pass.
key_ideas: Tolerance bands from the standard error

sample.question: A golden test feeds a Monte Carlo yield skill a synthetic limit state whose exact failure probability is 0.048, runs 10000 samples with a fresh seed, and passes if the estimate lands within 3 standard errors of the truth. What is the half-width of the acceptance band, in percentage points? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $SE = \sqrt{p(1-p)/N} = 0.002138$, so the half-width is $3 \times SE = 0.641$ percentage points.

concepts.label: Agentic yield loops and reward gaming
concepts.definition: Yield closure is a natural agent loop: read per-spec failure statistics and sensitivities, propose a sizing or biasing change, verify it with variation analysis, iterate, and hand a human a verified diff.
key_ideas: What the loop reads, proposes and verifies
How a yield reward is gamed
Rewards and reports that resist gaming

sample.question:
The agent watches yield estimates for several variants. What tells it a variant needs more samples before it can be ranked?

A) Its point estimate is the highest

B) Its netlist is largest

C) Its confidence interval overlaps the intervals of competing variants or the yield target

D) It was simulated most recently
sample.answer: Its confidence interval overlaps the intervals of competing variants or the yield target
sample.explanation: Budget should go where the decision is still uncertain: where intervals overlap the comparison that matters.

domains.name: Circuits and Electromagnetics
domains.description: Circuit laws, RC and RLC dynamics, transfer functions, transmission lines, S-parameters and the field physics behind parasitics and signal integrity.
covers: Circuit theory: Kirchhoff's laws, nodal analysis, mesh analysis, network analysis, Thevenin/Norton
RC and RLC circuits, time constants, step responses
Signals and systems, linear systems, Fourier, Laplace and Z transforms, transfer functions, poles/zeros, feedback, control theory, stability theory
Impedance, admittance, resonance
Transmission lines, telegrapher's equations, characteristic impedance, reflection coefficient, impedance matching, scattering parameters
Electromagnetism: Maxwell's equations, electrostatics, magnetostatics, capacitance and inductance of conductors
Electromagnetic field solvers, computational electromagnetics, method of moments, FDTD
EMC/EMI, grounding, shielding, return current, skin effect, proximity effect, dielectric loss

concepts.label: Charge, current, voltage and power
concepts.definition: Every number a circuit simulator, timer or power tool reports is built from four quantities: charge, current, voltage and power.
key_ideas: Current as the rate of charge flow

sample.question: A driver's output current ramps linearly from 0 to 36 mA over 9 ns and then stops. How much charge does it deliver during the ramp, in picocoulombs? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: Charge is the integral of current: the area under a triangle, 36 mA times 9 ns over 2, which is 162 pC (one mA for one ns is one pC).

concepts.label: Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws
concepts.definition: Kirchhoff's two laws are the constraints every circuit simulator writes down before it solves anything.
key_ideas: Kirchhoff's current law at a node
Kirchhoff's voltage law around a loop

sample.question: At a node, 20 mA leaves through branch 1, 22 mA enters through branch 2, 8 mA enters through branch 3. One more branch, branch 4, connects to the node. What current leaves the node through branch 4, in mA? A negative answer means the current actually enters.
sample.explanation: KCL says the currents leaving a node sum to zero, so branch 4 must carry away the net inflow of the other branches: 10 mA.

concepts.label: Series, parallel and divider networks
concepts.definition: Series and parallel reduction and the divider rules are KCL and KVL applied to the two simplest topologies.

sample.question: A resistor of 410 ohm is in series with the parallel pair of 150 ohm and 40 ohm. What is the equivalent resistance, in ohms? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: The parallel pair is $150 \cdot 40/(150 + 40) = 31.58$ ohm; adding the series resistor gives 441.6 ohm.

concepts.label: Nodal analysis
concepts.definition: Nodal analysis chooses the node voltages as unknowns and writes KCL at every non-reference node.

sample.question: A 0.8 V source connects through $R_1 = 1$ kohm to node A. Node A has $R_2 = 6$ kohm to ground and a current source injecting 0.2 mA into it. What is the voltage at node A, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.

concepts.label: Modified nodal analysis and element stamps
concepts.definition: Plain nodal analysis cannot express an ideal voltage source or an inductor's DC short, so SPICE-class simulators use modified nodal analysis (MNA): node voltages plus selected branch currents as unknowns.

sample.question: A resistive network with ground as the reference node has 0.5 kohm from node 3 to ground, 5 kohm from node 2 to ground, 4 kohm between nodes 1 and 2, 1 kohm between nodes 2 and 3. In the nodal conductance matrix $G$ (rows and columns ordered by node 1, 2, 3), what is the entry $G_{22}$, in millisiemens? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Each conductance stamps $+g$ on the diagonals of its two nodes and $-g$ on the off-diagonal pair between them (a branch to ground stamps only its diagonal). Summing the stamps that touch entry (2, 2) gives 1.45 mS.

concepts.label: Mesh analysis
concepts.definition: Mesh analysis is the dual of nodal analysis: it takes a current circulating in each window of a planar circuit as the unknown and writes KVL around each window.

sample.question: A single loop contains a 4.5 V source aiding the clockwise direction, a 1.5 V source opposing it, and resistors of 1 kohm and 6 kohm. What is the clockwise loop current, in mA? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: KVL around the loop: $4.5 - 1.5 = (1 + 6) I$, so $I = 0.429$ mA (volts over kilohms gives mA).

concepts.label: Thevenin and Norton equivalents
concepts.definition: Any linear network seen from two terminals behaves like one voltage source in series with one resistor (Thevenin) or one current source in parallel with one resistor (Norton).
key_ideas: Norton current and maximum power transfer

sample.question: A 1.8 V source drives $R_1 = 3$ kohm into node a; $R_2 = 0.5$ kohm runs from a to ground, and $R_3 = 10$ kohm runs from a to the output terminal. What is the Thevenin (open-circuit) voltage at the output terminal, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: With the output open, no current flows in $R_3$, so the output sits at the divider voltage $1.8 \cdot 0.5/3.5 = 0.257$ V.

concepts.label: Capacitors and inductors as circuit elements
concepts.definition: Capacitors and inductors are the elements that give circuits memory. A capacitor relates current to the rate of change of voltage, an inductor relates voltage to the rate of change of current.

sample.question: A 41 pF load is slewed by 0.8 V in 2.4 ns at a constant rate. What current does the driver supply during the ramp, in mA? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $i = C\,dV/dt = 41\text{ pF} \cdot 0.8\text{ V}/2.4\text{ ns} = 13.67$ mA (pF times V per ns is mA).

concepts.label: RC circuits and time constants
concepts.definition: A resistor charging a capacitor is the most important waveform in digital design: every gate driving a wire and every wire charging a gate input is, to first order, an RC stage.

sample.question: A 20 kohm driver resistance charges a 25 fF load. What is the time constant, in picoseconds? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: $\tau = RC = 20\text{ kohm} \cdot 25\text{ fF} = 500$ ps (one kohm times one fF is one ps).

concepts.label: Rise time and 50 percent delay of an RC stage
concepts.definition: Timing libraries characterize every cell by two numbers per transition: the delay to the 50% point and the output transition time, usually measured between 10% and 90% (or 20% and 80%).

sample.question: A gate with an effective drive resistance of 2.5 kohm switches a 85 fF load, modeled as one RC stage driven by a step. What is the 50% delay, in picoseconds? Round to 1 decimal place.

concepts.label: RLC circuits
concepts.definition: Add inductance to an RC stage and the step response can ring. Series RLC behavior appears in package and bond-wire models, power-delivery networks, clock lines and long on-chip wires at high frequency.

sample.question: A series RLC circuit has $L = 4$ nH and $C = 15$ pF. What is its undamped natural frequency $f_0 = \omega_0/(2\pi)$, in GHz? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}$, so $f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{4 \times 10^{-9} \cdot 15 \times 10^{-12}}) = 0.65$ GHz.

concepts.label: Distributed RC lines and wire delay
concepts.definition: An on-chip wire is not one resistor and one capacitor; its resistance and capacitance are spread along its length.
key_ideas: A wire as a distributed RC line

sample.question: A wire of length 1100 um has resistance 0.2 ohm/um and capacitance 0.3 fF/um to ground. Modeling it as a distributed RC line driven by an ideal source, what is its Elmore delay at the far end, in picoseconds? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $R = 220$ ohm and $C = 330$ fF. Each element of capacitance sees the resistance up to it, so the Elmore sum becomes $\int_0^L r x\, c\, dx = RC/2 = 36.3$ ps.

concepts.label: Phasors and sinusoidal steady state
concepts.definition: In sinusoidal steady state every voltage and current in a linear circuit oscillates at the source frequency, differing only in amplitude and phase.

sample.question: Two currents of the same frequency meet at a node: $10\cos(\omega t - 45^\circ)$ mA and $9\cos(\omega t + 45^\circ)$ mA. What is the amplitude of their sum, in mA? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Add the phasors: $10\angle -45^\circ + 9\angle 45^\circ = 13.435 - j0.707$, whose magnitude is 13.454 mA. Amplitudes add directly only when the phases match.

concepts.label: Impedance and admittance
concepts.definition: Impedance generalizes resistance to sinusoidal steady state, and admittance is its reciprocal.

sample.question: A series circuit of $R = 30$ ohm, $L = 36$ nH and $C = 96$ pF is driven at 500 MHz. What is the magnitude of its impedance, in ohms? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Resonance and quality factor
concepts.definition: At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances of a circuit cancel. A series resonance makes impedance minimal; a parallel resonance makes it maximal.
key_ideas: Anti-resonance in a power delivery network

sample.question: A series LC circuit has $L = 16$ nH and $C = 45$ pF. What is its resonant frequency, in MHz? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: At resonance $X_L = X_C$, so $f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}) = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{16 \times 10^{-9} \cdot 45 \times 10^{-12}}) = 187.6$ MHz.

concepts.label: Linear time-invariant systems and convolution
concepts.definition: Linear time-invariant (LTI) systems are the reason circuit and interconnect analysis is tractable.
key_ideas: Pulse response from the step response

sample.question: A linear time-invariant interconnect model responds to input $x_1(t)$ with an output of 0.55 V at $t = 48$ ps, and to input $x_2(t)$ with 0.75 V at the same time. What is its output at $t = 48$ ps for the input $1\,x_1(t) + 3\,x_2(t)$, in volts? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Linearity gives superposition with scaling: $1 \cdot 0.55 + 3 \cdot 0.75 = 2.8$ V.

concepts.label: Fourier spectra of digital signals
concepts.definition: A digital signal is not a single frequency. Its spectrum, given by Fourier analysis, decides how much bandwidth every interconnect model, package model and measurement must cover.

sample.question: A clock is an ideal square wave from 0 to 1.8 V at 100 MHz with 50% duty cycle. What is the amplitude of its spectral component at 900 MHz, in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: A 0 to V square wave at 50% duty has only odd harmonics, of amplitude $2V/(n\pi)$. 900 MHz is harmonic $n = 9$, so its amplitude is $2 \cdot 1.8/(9\pi) = 0.127$ V.

concepts.label: Transfer functions and the Laplace domain
concepts.definition: The Laplace transform turns a linear circuit's differential equations into algebra in the complex frequency $s$.
key_ideas: The pole of an RC divider
Initial and final values of a step response

sample.question: A network has $R_1 = 8$ kohm in series from input to output, and $R_2 = 0.5$ kohm in parallel with $C = 75$ fF from output to ground. What is its DC gain $H(0)$? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: At $s = 0$ the capacitor's impedance $1/(sC)$ is infinite, so it drops out and $H(0) = R_2/(R_1 + R_2) = 0.0588$.

concepts.label: Poles, zeros and stability
concepts.definition: The poles of a transfer function are the natural frequencies of the system; the zeros are the frequencies it blocks.
key_ideas: Poles as roots of the denominator

sample.question: A transfer function has denominator $s^2 + 20s + 99$, with $s$ in units of $10^9$ per second. What is the pole closest to the origin, in those units?
sample.explanation: The roots of $s^2 + 20s + 99$ are $s = -11$ and $s = -9$. The closer one, -9, is the dominant (slowest) pole.

concepts.label: Bode magnitude and phase
concepts.definition: A Bode plot shows a transfer function's magnitude in decibels and its phase against log frequency.
key_ideas: Asymptotes of minus 20 dB per decade per pole

sample.question: An amplifier has $H(f) = 1/(1 + jf/f_p)$ with $f_p = 50$ MHz. What is its exact gain at 1000 MHz, in dB? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Feedback, loop gain and phase margin
concepts.definition: Feedback makes gain precise and insensitive to device variation, but it can also make a system oscillate.
key_ideas: Phase margin of a two-pole loop

sample.question: An amplifier with open-loop gain 5000 is wrapped in negative feedback with feedback factor $\beta = 0.1$. What is the closed-loop gain? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $A_{cl} = A/(1 + A\beta) = 5000/(1 + 500) = 9.98$, close to $1/\beta = 10$ because the loop gain $A\beta = 500$ is large.

concepts.label: The Z transform and discrete-time stability
concepts.definition: Simulators do not solve differential equations; they solve difference equations produced by an integration method.
key_ideas: Difference equations and the Z transform
Forward Euler and the stability limit

sample.question: A discrete-time filter obeys $y[n] = 0.8\,y[n-1] + 0.5\,x[n]$ with $y[-1] = 0$. The input is a unit step, $x[n] = 1$ for $n \ge 0$. What is $y[3]$? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Iterate from $n = 0$: 0.5, 0.9, 1.22, 1.476. The pole of $H(z) = 0.5/(1 - 0.8 z^{-1})$ is $z = 0.8$, inside the unit circle, so the output converges to $0.5/(1 - 0.8) = 2.5$.

concepts.label: Moments, Elmore delay and moment matching
concepts.definition: Moments are the Taylor coefficients of a transfer function around $s = 0$. The first moment of an RC tree is the Elmore delay; matching the first few moments with a low-order rational function is the idea behind asymptotic waveform evaluation (AWE) and later Krylov-based model order reduction.
