A placer needs a memory macro's size, pin locations and routing blockages, but not its transistors. Which view supplies them?

A) The abstract physical view (LEF)

B) The GDSII layout read transistor by transistor

C) The behavioral Verilog model

D) The Liberty timing model
sample.answer: The abstract physical view (LEF)
sample.explanation: LEF abstracts the macro to its outline, pins and obstructions, which is all placement and routing need.

concepts.label: Datapath and control
concepts.definition: A processor, and most accelerators, splits into a datapath, which holds and transforms data (registers, ALUs, shifters, muxes, memories), and a control unit, which decides each cycle what the datapath does by driving its mux selects, register enables and operation codes.

sample.question:
Which of these is a control signal rather than a datapath element?

A) The ALU's adder

B) The data memory

C) The register file's storage array

D) The register file's write enable
sample.answer: The register file's write enable
sample.explanation: Datapath elements hold or transform data; control signals such as enables and mux selects tell them what to do each cycle.

concepts.label: The processor performance equation
concepts.definition: Execution time factors into instruction count, cycles per instruction (CPI) and clock period.
key_ideas: Time equals count times CPI times period

sample.question: A program executes 790 million instructions with an average CPI of 2.5 on a 4 GHz clock. How long does it run, in milliseconds? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $T = IC \cdot CPI / f = 790 \times 10^6 \cdot 2.5 / (4 \times 10^9)$ s $= 493.75$ ms.

concepts.label: Pipelining
concepts.definition: Pipelining splits a long combinational computation into stages separated by registers, so several operations are in flight at once.

sample.question: Logic is split into 3 pipeline stages with delays 120, 200, 400 ps. Each pipeline register adds 65 ps (clock-to-q plus setup). What is the clock period, in ps?
sample.explanation: The slowest stage is 400 ps; plus 65 ps of register overhead gives 465 ps (against 785 ps unpipelined).

concepts.label: Pipeline hazards and stalls
concepts.definition: In a processor pipeline, instructions depend on each other, and a dependent instruction may need a value its predecessor has not yet written.
key_ideas: The five-stage pipeline and data hazards

sample.question: A classic five-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) writes the register file in the first half of a cycle and reads it in the second half. There is no forwarding. How many stall cycles does it insert for the sequence: add r5, r6, r6; lw r7, 20(r5); add r6, r2, r3?
sample.explanation: A dependent instruction must decode at least 3 cycles after its producer decodes. The sequence takes 9 cycles against 7 without hazards: 2 stalls.

concepts.label: Branch penalties and prediction
concepts.definition: Branches are about one instruction in five, and every mispredicted branch flushes the work fetched behind it.
key_ideas: One bit versus two bits on loops

sample.question: A pipeline has base CPI 1.2. Branches are 30% of instructions, 10% of them are mispredicted, and each misprediction costs 20 cycles. What is the CPI? Round to 3 decimal places.

concepts.label: Cache organization and address fields
concepts.definition: A cache is an SRAM data array plus a tag array that remembers which memory blocks it holds.

sample.question: A cache of 1024 KB, 4-way set-associative, with 32-byte blocks serves 48-bit byte addresses. How many index bits does the address use?
sample.explanation: $1024 \cdot 1024 / (32 \cdot 4) = 8192$ sets, so $\log_2 8192 = 13$ index bits.

concepts.label: Cache hits, misses and AMAT
concepts.definition: A cache's value is measured by how often it hits and how much a miss costs. Average memory access time combines the two, and tracing an address stream through a small cache shows where misses come from: cold starts, limited capacity, and conflicts between addresses that share a set.

sample.question: A cache has a hit time of 2 cycles, a miss rate of 3% and a miss penalty of 60 cycles. What is the average memory access time, in cycles? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Spec-to-RTL agent loops
concepts.definition: Language models can now write plausible RTL from a plain-language specification.

sample.question:
A simulation of generated RTL fails. What is the most useful feedback for the next iteration?

A) A request to regenerate the whole module from scratch

B) The total number of cycles simulated

C) The waveform of every signal in the design

D) The first failing cycle, the inputs that led to it, and the expected and actual outputs
sample.answer: The first failing cycle, the inputs that led to it, and the expected and actual outputs
sample.explanation: A minimal failing trace localizes the bug, which is what the model needs to propose a small edit.

concepts.label: Golden and differential checks for generated RTL
concepts.definition: When an agent changes RTL, two questions need evidence: is the new design correct against the specification (golden), and did it change only what was intended (differential)?

sample.question:
What does a passing directed testbench prove about a design?

A) That it is correct for all inputs

B) That it is equivalent to the previous version

C) That it matches the specification

D) That it behaves correctly on the vectors applied, and nothing more
sample.answer: That it behaves correctly on the vectors applied, and nothing more
sample.explanation: Simulation is evidence on the tested inputs only; completeness needs exhaustive or formal methods.

concepts.label: Agent design-space exploration of arithmetic
concepts.definition: Adders and multipliers have a rich, well-understood architecture space: ripple, carry-select, Sklansky, Brent-Kung, Kogge-Stone and hybrids for addition; array, Booth, Wallace, Dadda and compressor trees for multiplication.

sample.question:
An agent explores 32-bit adder architectures. Its fast model treats each level as 50 ps and uses: ripple-carry, 32 levels and 32 nodes; Brent-Kung, $2\log_2 n - 1$ levels and $2n - 2 - \log_2 n$ nodes, fanout 2; Sklansky, $\log_2 n$ levels and $\frac{n}{2}\log_2 n$ nodes, fanout $n/2$; Kogge-Stone, $\log_2 n$ levels and $n\log_2 n - n + 1$ nodes, fanout 2. The budget is 450 ps and the library allows a fanout of at most 8. Which architecture should it send to synthesis first, as the cheapest candidate meeting both limits?

A) Brent-Kung

B) Sklansky

C) Ripple-carry

D) Kogge-Stone
sample.answer: Brent-Kung
sample.explanation: At n = 32 the candidates have (levels, nodes, fanout) of ripple (32, 32, 2), Brent-Kung (9, 57, 2), Sklansky (5, 80, 16), Kogge-Stone (5, 129, 2). The depth budget allows 9 levels; the cheapest feasible one is Brent-Kung with 57 nodes.

concepts.label: Change tiers for parameterized RTL generators
concepts.definition: Much RTL is not written by hand but generated: parameterized modules, Chisel or other hardware-construction-language generators, memory compilers, arithmetic generators.
key_ideas: Tier 2: a new policy at a seam

sample.question:
A customer wants the FIFO generator's depth changed from 16 to 64. Which tier does the change land in?

A) Tier 3: a core edit

B) Tier 1: a parameter change, re-run with golden tests

C) None: it needs a new generator

D) Tier 2: a new plug-in
sample.answer: Tier 1: a parameter change, re-run with golden tests
sample.explanation: Depth is a parameter the generator exposes; no code changes.

concepts.label: Tool-grounded rewards for RTL agents
concepts.definition: Training or tuning a model to write RTL needs a reward, and the natural one is tool-grounded: compile it, test it, prove it, synthesize it, and score the outcome.

sample.question:
Why should a QoR term in an RTL reward be granted only to designs that already pass functional checks?

A) Otherwise an empty or wrong design wins on area

B) QoR is always zero for correct designs

C) QoR cannot be measured on failing designs

D) Functional checks are too expensive
sample.answer: Otherwise an empty or wrong design wins on area
sample.explanation: A design that does nothing is tiny; gating prevents rewarding it.

domains.name: Fabrication and Design-Technology Co-optimization
domains.description: Process steps, lithography, OPC and multiple patterning, the interconnect stack, PDKs and design rules, DTCO and yield.
covers: Semiconductor device fabrication, wafers, silicon wafers, semiconductor substrates
Epitaxy, oxidation, diffusion, ion implantation, CVD, PVD, ALD, etching, chemical-mechanical polishing

Photolithography, resolution limits (Rayleigh), extreme ultraviolet lithography, optical proximity correction, resolution enhancement technology, inverse lithography, multiple patterning (LELE, SADP, SAQP), mask synthesis, photomasks, mask data preparation
Process integration, FEOL, MOL, BEOL, interconnect, copper interconnect, damascene, low-k dielectrics, contact resistance, vias
Process design kits, design rules, design-rule manuals
Design-technology co-optimization (DTCO), system-technology co-optimization (STCO), standard-cell architecture (track height, fin depopulation, buried power rails, backside power delivery)
Design for manufacturability, design for yield, critical area analysis, defect density

concepts.label: The CMOS process flow
concepts.definition: A chip is built by repeating a small set of unit operations several hundred times on a silicon wafer: deposit a film, pattern it with lithography, etch or implant through the pattern, clean, and sometimes polish.
key_ideas: Modules repeated in a fixed order
From drawn layers to process steps
What the flow hides from the layout

sample.question:
Why is the gate stack of a modern high-k metal-gate flow often formed after the source and drain anneals (gate-last, or replacement gate)?

A) Because the gate must be patterned with EUV

B) Because the source and drain are built on the back of the wafer

C) Because polysilicon cannot be etched

D) The final metal gate and high-k stack cannot survive the high-temperature dopant activation
sample.answer: The final metal gate and high-k stack cannot survive the high-temperature dopant activation
sample.explanation: A sacrificial polysilicon gate holds the place through the hot steps and is then replaced, protecting the work-function metals from the thermal budget.

concepts.label: Silicon wafers and substrates
concepts.definition: Every chip starts as a slice of a single silicon crystal. Wafer diameter, orientation and substrate type are fixed before any design exists, yet they decide how many dies a fab can make per wafer, how much area is lost at the edge, and which transistor structures are available.

sample.question: A lot holds 7 silicon wafers of 300 mm diameter. What is the total silicon area of the lot, in square centimetres? Round to the nearest whole number.
sample.explanation: Each wafer has radius 15.0 cm, so area $\pi r^2 = 706.86$ square cm. Times 7 wafers gives 4948 square cm.

concepts.label: Thermal oxidation and the Deal-Grove model
concepts.definition: Heating silicon in oxygen or steam grows silicon dioxide that is consumed from the wafer itself.

sample.question: A thermal oxide of 500 nm is grown on bare silicon. How much silicon thickness does the growth consume, in nanometres? Use the consumption ratio 0.44. Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: Oxide grows partly into the silicon: each nanometre of oxide consumes 0.44 nm of silicon, so 500 nm consumes 220 nm.

concepts.label: Dopant diffusion and thermal budget
concepts.definition: Dopants placed by implantation do not stay put. Every hot step afterwards lets them spread by diffusion, which moves junctions, widens doped regions and shortens effective channel length.
key_ideas: Fick's law and the diffusion length

sample.question: A dopant has diffusivity $D = 5 \times 10^{-14}$ cm^2/s at the anneal temperature. What is its characteristic diffusion length $2\sqrt{Dt}$ after a 100-minute anneal, in nanometres? Round to 1 decimal place.

concepts.label: Ion implantation profiles
concepts.definition: Ion implantation shoots ionized dopant atoms into the wafer at a chosen energy and dose.
key_ideas: Dose, range and the Gaussian profile

sample.question: An implant delivers a dose of $4 \times 10^{15}$ cm^-2 with projected range $R_p = 75$ nm and straggle $\Delta R_p = 22$ nm (Gaussian profile). What is the peak concentration, in units of $10^{18}$ cm^-3? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $N_p = Q/(\sqrt{2\pi}\,\Delta R_p)$ with $\Delta R_p = 22 \times 10^{-7}$ cm gives 7.253e+20 cm^-3, which is 725.35 in units of $10^{18}$.

concepts.label: Epitaxy and strained layers
concepts.definition: Epitaxy grows a crystalline film that continues the lattice of the crystal beneath it.

sample.question:
What distinguishes epitaxy from ordinary chemical vapour deposition of a film?

A) The film is always amorphous

B) The film grows only on metal surfaces

C) The film grows as a single crystal that continues the substrate's lattice

D) The film is deposited by sputtering a target
sample.answer: The film grows as a single crystal that continues the substrate's lattice
sample.explanation: Epitaxial growth is templated by the crystal underneath, so the new layer is single-crystal and aligned to it.

concepts.label: CVD, PVD and ALD
concepts.definition: Most layers in a chip are deposited films: dielectrics between wires, barriers and seeds for copper, spacers that set feature widths, high-k gate dielectrics and work-function metals.
key_ideas: Three ways to put down a film
Choosing a method by what the layer must do

sample.question:
Which deposition method builds a film one self-limiting monolayer reaction at a time?

A) Electroplating

B) Thermal oxidation

C) Physical vapour deposition (PVD)

D) Atomic layer deposition (ALD)
sample.answer: Atomic layer deposition (ALD)
sample.explanation: ALD alternates two precursors; each surface reaction saturates, so each cycle adds a fixed, small thickness.

concepts.label: Etching: anisotropy, selectivity and over-etch
concepts.definition: Etching transfers a lithographic pattern into the film below by removing exposed material.

sample.question: A plasma etch removes material vertically at 360 nm/min and laterally at 34 nm/min. What is its anisotropy $A = 1 - r_{lat}/r_{vert}$? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $A = 1 - 34/360 = 0.906$. A wet isotropic etch has $A = 0$; a perfectly directional etch has $A = 1$.

concepts.label: Chemical-mechanical polishing and density
concepts.definition: Chemical-mechanical polishing (CMP) flattens the wafer after deposition so that the next lithography step stays in focus, and it defines damascene copper lines by removing excess metal.

sample.question: A CMP step removes 140 nm/min at 26 kPa down-force and 1.9 m/s pad velocity. By Preston's law, what removal rate is expected at 24 kPa and 0.9 m/s, in nm/min? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: Preston: rate $= K_p P v$, so the rate scales by $(24 \times 0.9)/(26 \times 1.9)$, giving 61.2 nm/min.

concepts.label: Lithographic resolution
concepts.definition: Lithography projects a mask pattern onto photoresist through a lens, and the finest pattern it can print sets the pitch of every critical layer.
key_ideas: Wavelength and numerical aperture as levers

sample.question: Using the Rayleigh criterion $R = k_1 \lambda / NA$ with $k_1 = 0.46$, what minimum half-pitch can a dry ArF scanner (193 nm, NA 0.93) print, in nanometres? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: $R = 0.46 \times 193 / 0.93 = 95.5$ nm, so the densest printable line pitch is twice that.

concepts.label: Depth of focus and the focus budget
concepts.definition: A pattern prints correctly only within a narrow range of focus. That range, the depth of focus, shrinks as numerical aperture rises, and everything that moves the wafer surface out of the focal plane must fit inside it: wafer flatness, leftover topography from polishing, and the scanner's own focus control.

sample.question: With $DOF = k_2 \lambda / NA^2$ and $k_2 = 0.75$, what is the depth of focus of an ArF immersion scanner (193 nm, NA 1.35), in nanometres? Round to 1 decimal place.

concepts.label: Photomasks, reduction and MEEF
concepts.definition: A photomask, or reticle, is a quartz plate carrying the pattern of one layer, written by an electron-beam or laser writer.

sample.question: A scanner projects the mask at 4x reduction. A line must print 90 nm wide on the wafer. How wide is it on the mask, in nanometres (ignoring OPC bias)?
sample.explanation: Mask dimensions are 4 times wafer dimensions: 360 nm.

concepts.label: Resolution enhancement techniques
concepts.definition: At low $k_1$ an ordinary mask under ordinary illumination prints a blurred, low-contrast image.

sample.question:
Why does dense, one-directional layout benefit most from dipole illumination?

A) Dipole poles are aligned to image one pitch in one direction very well

B) Dipoles remove line-end shortening

C) Dipoles change the photon energy

D) Dipoles work equally well for all orientations
sample.answer: Dipole poles are aligned to image one pitch in one direction very well
sample.explanation: A dipole source is optimized for gratings perpendicular to the pole axis and images the other orientation poorly, which pushes layouts toward unidirectional metal.

concepts.label: Optical proximity correction
concepts.definition: The image of a drawn rectangle is not a rectangle: corners round, line ends pull back, and widths shift with their neighbours.
key_ideas: Why printed shapes differ from drawn ones

sample.question:
Serifs added at the outer corners of a mask shape do what?

A) Connect two nets

B) Mark the cell boundary

C) Reduce the dose

D) Compensate corner rounding by adding light where the image loses it
sample.answer: Compensate corner rounding by adding light where the image loses it
sample.explanation: Corners lose intensity because they have neighbours on fewer sides; serifs add area there.

concepts.label: Model-based OPC iteration
concepts.definition: Model-based OPC is a numerical loop: simulate the print, measure edge placement errors, move mask fragments, repeat.
key_ideas: A feedback update for each fragment

sample.question: After one OPC pass, the simulated edge placement errors (printed minus target, in nm) at the 3 fragments of a polygon are -3, -6, -1. What is the RMS edge placement error, in nanometres? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Square, average and take the root: $\sqrt{46/3} = 3.92$ nm. OPC tools report both RMS and maximum EPE because a single bad fragment can still cause a bridge.

concepts.label: Extreme ultraviolet lithography
concepts.definition: Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography uses 13.5 nm light, about fourteen times shorter than ArF, so one exposure prints pitches that 193 nm immersion needs three or four masks to reach.
key_ideas: What a single EUV exposure replaces

sample.question: An EUV scanner uses 13.5 nm light at NA 0.33. At $k_1 = 0.47$, what half-pitch does one exposure print, in nanometres? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $R = 0.47 \times 13.5 / 0.33 = 19.23$ nm. The same $k_1$ on 193 nm immersion at NA 1.35 gives 67.2 nm.

concepts.label: Multiple patterning
concepts.definition: When a layer's pitch is below what one exposure can resolve, the pattern is split across several masks, each printing a sparser subset, and the results are combined on the wafer.
key_ideas: How many exposures a pitch needs

sample.question: A metal layer has a 54 nm line pitch and is split by four litho-etch exposures, with lines assigned to masks in rotation. What line pitch must each individual mask print, in nanometres?
sample.explanation: Each mask takes one line in every 4, so its pitch is $4 \times 54 = 216$ nm. The combined pattern interleaves them.

concepts.label: Layout decomposition as graph coloring
concepts.definition: To print a layer with several masks, every shape must be assigned to one mask so that shapes too close for one mask land on different masks.

sample.question: Small via shapes sit on one line at x positions (nm): A at 0, B at 60, C at 80, D at 140, E at 220. Two shapes on the same mask must be at least 60 nm apart, centre to centre. How many conflict edges does the decomposition graph have?
sample.explanation: Every pair closer than 60 nm must go on different masks, so each such pair is an edge, including non-neighbours. There are 1.

concepts.label: Self-aligned double and quadruple patterning
concepts.definition: Self-aligned patterning halves the pitch without a second critical exposure. Mandrel lines are printed at a relaxed pitch, a conformal spacer film is deposited and etched back, and the mandrels are removed, leaving two spacer lines per mandrel.

sample.question: SAQP starts from a mandrel pitch of 80 nm and applies the spacer process twice. What final line pitch results, in nanometres?
sample.explanation: Each spacer pass halves the pitch: 80 / 4 = 20 nm.

concepts.label: Mask data preparation
concepts.definition: Between tapeout and a finished mask, the layout is transformed several times: layers are derived, corrected, verified, broken into writer primitives and written.
key_ideas: The data path from tapeout to mask
Data volume, hierarchy and multi-beam writing

sample.question:
Which order is right for mask data preparation after tapeout?

A) Fracturing, OPC, then layer derivation

B) Boolean layer derivation, OPC and RET, verification, fracturing, then writing

C) Verification, then layer derivation, then OPC

D) Writing, then OPC
sample.answer: Boolean layer derivation, OPC and RET, verification, fracturing, then writing
sample.explanation: Mask layers are derived from drawn layers, corrected, verified by simulation, fractured into writer format and then written.

concepts.label: Process integration: FEOL, MOL and BEOL
concepts.definition: Process integration is the art of ordering hundreds of unit steps so that each one leaves the wafer in a state the next can use.
key_ideas: Why the middle of line became its own segment

sample.question:
Which segment contains the copper wiring layers and the vias between them?

A) Epitaxy

B) FEOL

C) MOL

D) BEOL
sample.answer: BEOL
sample.explanation: The back end of line is the multilevel interconnect stack, built after the devices and contacts.

concepts.label: The interconnect stack
concepts.definition: Above the transistors sit ten to twenty wiring levels. The lowest are thin, dense and resistive, for local connections inside and between cells; higher levels are progressively wider and thicker, for long routes, clocks and power.

sample.question: A block is 12 um wide. A vertical routing layer has a 42 nm pitch. How many vertical tracks cross the block?
sample.explanation: $\lfloor 12 \times 1000 / 42 \rfloor = 285$ tracks.

concepts.label: Damascene copper and barriers
concepts.definition: Copper cannot be plasma-etched cleanly, so copper wires are made by damascene: etch trenches and via holes in dielectric, line them with a barrier, fill with copper, and polish the excess away.
key_ideas: A barrier that does not scale

sample.question: A dual-damascene copper trench is 12 nm wide and 18 nm tall. A barrier and liner of 4 nm lines both sidewalls and the bottom. What percentage of the trench cross-section is copper? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: Copper fills $(12 - 2 \times 4) \times (18 - 4) = 56$ nm^2 of 216 nm^2, which is 25.9%.

concepts.label: Wire RC per unit length and scaling
concepts.definition: Every routed net is, electrically, a distributed resistance and capacitance. Resistance per unit length comes from resistivity and cross-section; capacitance per unit length from geometry and dielectric.

sample.question: A wire is 18 nm wide and 45 nm thick with effective resistivity 5.8 micro-ohm cm. What is its resistance per micrometre, in ohms? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $r = \rho/(w t) = 58$ ohm nm $\times 1000$ nm $/ 810$ nm^2 $= 71.6$ ohm per um.

concepts.label: Low-k dielectrics and air gaps
concepts.definition: Wire capacitance is proportional to the permittivity of the insulator around it.
key_ideas: Effective k of a real stack
Air gaps and the limits of low-k

sample.question: A wire has 0.17 fF/um of capacitance in a dielectric of $k = 3$. If every dielectric around it is replaced by one of $k = 2.7$ with the same geometry, what is the new capacitance per micrometre, in fF? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Capacitance is proportional to permittivity at fixed geometry: $0.17 \times 2.7 / 3 = 0.153$ fF/um.

concepts.label: Contact and via resistance
concepts.definition: Current enters a transistor through a contact to silicide on its source or drain and climbs to the wiring through a chain of vias.
key_ideas: Via stacks in series and parallel

sample.question: A contact to silicide has specific contact resistivity $\rho_c = 2.5 \times 10^{-9}$ ohm cm^2 and an interface of 35 nm by 29 nm. What is its interface resistance $\rho_c / A$, in ohms? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: $A = 1015$ nm^2 $= 1.015e-11$ cm^2, so $R = 2.5 \times 10^{-9} / 1.015e-11 = 246.3$ ohm. Halving the area doubles it.

concepts.label: What a process design kit contains
concepts.definition: A process design kit (PDK) is the foundry's description of a process, packaged for design tools.

sample.question:
Which PDK file tells extraction tools how thick each layer is and what dielectric surrounds it?

A) The interconnect technology or extraction rule file

B) The GDS layer map only

C) The PCell library

D) The DRC deck
sample.answer: The interconnect technology or extraction rule file
sample.explanation: Extractors use the layer stack description (thicknesses, permittivities, resistivities, width-dependent tables) to compute parasitics.

concepts.label: Design rules
concepts.definition: Design rules are geometric constraints a layout must satisfy so that it can be manufactured with acceptable yield: minimum widths, spacings, enclosures, extensions, areas and densities.

sample.question: A metal layer has a minimum width of 20 nm and a minimum spacing of 27 nm. What is the tightest legal line pitch, in nanometres?
sample.explanation: Pitch is width plus space: 20 + 27 = 47 nm.

concepts.label: Design-rule manuals and rule decks
concepts.definition: The design-rule manual (DRM) is the foundry's human-readable definition of every rule, with figures and conditions.
key_ideas: From simple numbers to conditional rules
How a deck computes a check

sample.question:
A rule says spacing between two metal lines must be 32 nm if the parallel run length exceeds 100 nm, else 28 nm. What kind of rule is this?

A) A density rule

B) A conditional, context-dependent spacing rule

C) An enclosure rule

D) A minimum width rule
sample.answer: A conditional, context-dependent spacing rule
sample.explanation: Modern decks are full of rules whose value depends on width, run length or neighbourhood, not single numbers.

concepts.label: Device models and corners in a PDK
concepts.definition: A PDK's device models describe how each transistor behaves across voltage, temperature and process variation.
key_ideas: Layout dependence, aging and model maturity

sample.question:
Why do PDKs include skewed corners such as SF and FS?

A) They are needed for DRC

B) Some circuits fail when NMOS and PMOS move in opposite directions, such as ratioed logic and SRAM

C) They model packaging only

D) They set the metal resistance
sample.answer: Some circuits fail when NMOS and PMOS move in opposite directions, such as ratioed logic and SRAM
sample.explanation: Global variation of NMOS and PMOS is not perfectly correlated; skewed corners stress circuits sensitive to their ratio.

concepts.label: Dies per wafer and edge loss
concepts.definition: How many dies a wafer holds is the denominator of every cost-per-die calculation and an input to yield and DTCO trade-offs.
key_ideas: Area ratio as an upper bound
Edge exclusion, scribe lanes and exact counts

sample.question: A die measures 14.5 mm by 24 mm. Dividing the area of a 300 mm wafer by the die area, how many dies would fit if edges did not matter? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: Wafer area is $\pi (300)^2/4 = 70686$ mm^2; die area is 348 mm^2; the ratio is 203.1. Real counts are lower because square dies do not tile a circle.

concepts.label: Defect density and yield models
concepts.definition: Random particles and process defects land on wafers with some average density. A die that receives a killer defect fails.
key_ideas: Inverting yield to learn defect density

sample.question: Killer defects land at random with density 0.17 per cm^2. What is the expected number of killer defects on a 550 mm^2 die? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Convert: 550 mm^2 = 5.5 cm^2. The mean is $\lambda = A D_0 = 0.935$.

concepts.label: Clustered defects and negative binomial yield
concepts.definition: Real defects are not spread uniformly: they cluster on some wafers, in some regions and on some dies.

sample.question: Using the negative binomial yield model $Y = (1 + A D_0/\alpha)^{-\alpha}$ with clustering parameter $\alpha = 5$, what is the yield of a 570 mm^2 die at 0.31 defects per cm^2, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Critical area analysis
concepts.definition: Not every defect that lands on a die kills it. A small extra particle between widely spaced wires is harmless; the same particle between two minimum-spaced wires is a short.

sample.question: Two parallel wires run side by side for 1700 um with a 49 nm space between them. A circular conducting defect of diameter 67 nm shorts them if it touches both. Ignoring end effects, what is the critical area for shorts, in um^2? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The defect centre must lie in a band of width $\max(0, x - s) = 18$ nm along the gap, so $A_c = L \max(0, x - s) = 30.6$ um^2.

concepts.label: Average critical area over defect sizes
concepts.definition: Critical area depends on defect size, and defects come in a distribution of sizes.
key_ideas: From average critical area to yield

sample.question: Defect diameters follow $f(x) = 2 x_0^2 / x^3$ for $x \ge x_0$ with $x_0 = 28$ nm. What percentage of defects are larger than 56 nm? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Cost per good die
concepts.definition: The economic figure of merit for silicon is the cost of a die that works. It combines wafer cost, dies per wafer and yield in one ratio.
key_ideas: From wafer cost to die cost

sample.question: A processed 300 mm wafer costs 6000 US dollars and holds 300 candidate dies. What is the cost per candidate die, in dollars, before yield? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Design for manufacturability and yield
concepts.definition: Design for manufacturability (DFM) changes a legal layout to make it more robust: fewer shapes sensitive to random defects, fewer patterns that print poorly, more redundancy where a single failure would kill the chip.

sample.question:
Why are DFM fixes usually applied only where they do not cost timing or area?

A) They are optional yield improvements, traded against PPA

B) They break LVS

C) They always make timing better

D) They are illegal elsewhere
sample.answer: They are optional yield improvements, traded against PPA
sample.explanation: Recommended-rule fixes help yield but add capacitance or area, so tools apply them opportunistically.

concepts.label: Standard-cell architecture and DTCO
concepts.definition: A standard-cell library fixes a cell height, a set of routing tracks inside each cell, power rails at the top and bottom, and a gate grid along the width.
key_ideas: Cell height as tracks times pitch
Why track height is a DTCO variable
Area arithmetic of a track reduction

sample.question: A standard-cell library is a 6.5-track library on a 46 nm horizontal metal pitch. What is the cell height, in nanometres? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: Cell height is tracks times metal pitch: $6.5 \times 46 = 299$ nm.

concepts.label: Contacted poly pitch and cell width
concepts.definition: The width of a standard cell is counted in contacted poly pitches (CPP): the pitch of the gate lines, including room for a source-drain contact between neighbouring gates.
key_ideas: Row length from a cell list

sample.question: A cell has 8 gate (poly) tracks and uses a double diffusion break (two CPP of boundary per cell). The contacted poly pitch is 62 nm. What is the cell width, in nanometres?
sample.explanation: Width is $(8 + 2) \times 62 = 620$ nm.

concepts.label: Fin depopulation
concepts.definition: In a FinFET library, each transistor's drive comes from a whole number of fins. Fin depopulation reduces the fin count per device, for example from three to two or from two to one, so that the active area, and the cell height, can shrink.
key_ideas: Cell height on the fin grid

sample.question: A library depopulates its transistors from 4 fins to 3 fins each. To first order, drive current is proportional to fin count. What percentage of the original drive current remains? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: $3/4 = 75$%. Lower drive also means lower input capacitance, so delay into a light load falls less than this.

concepts.label: Buried power rails
concepts.definition: In a conventional cell, the power and ground rails run along the top and bottom edges on the lowest metal layer and take up track space.
key_ideas: What buried rails change in the flow

sample.question: A cell is 7.5 tracks tall on a 32 nm pitch: 6 signal tracks plus power rails that together occupy 1.5 tracks. Burying the power rails below the devices removes the rail tracks without changing the signal tracks. What is the new cell height, in nanometres? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: Only the 6 signal tracks remain: $6 \times 32 = 192$ nm.

concepts.label: Backside power delivery
concepts.definition: Backside power delivery (BSPDN) builds the power distribution network on the back of a thinned wafer and feeds the transistors from below.
key_ideas: Power from the back of the wafer
IR drop with and without backside power

sample.question:
What does backside power delivery move to the back of the wafer?

A) The signal routing layers

B) The clock tree only

C) The transistors themselves

D) The power distribution network, connected to the devices from below
sample.answer: The power distribution network, connected to the devices from below
sample.explanation: Power rails and the global power grid are built on the thinned wafer back, so front-side metal carries only signals.

concepts.label: The DTCO evaluation loop
concepts.definition: Design-technology co-optimization is an engineering loop, not a single calculation.

sample.question:
Which of these is a typical DTCO knob?

A) The bug tracker

B) Cell track height, fins per device, contacted poly pitch and metal pitch

C) The RTL coding style

D) The verification testbench
sample.answer: Cell track height, fins per device, contacted poly pitch and metal pitch
sample.explanation: These are the parameters that couple process capability to standard-cell and block layout.

concepts.label: System-technology co-optimization and chiplets
concepts.definition: System-technology co-optimization asks how to split a system across dies and packages.

sample.question: A monolithic 420 mm^2 die is made on 300 mm wafers costing 20000 US dollars, with 135 dies per wafer and Poisson yield at 0.18 defects per cm^2. What is the cost per good die, in dollars? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: PDK-aware agents and change tiers
concepts.definition: An agent that edits or drives physical-design engines must know the process: rules, layers, models and their versions.
key_ideas: Reading process facts instead of recalling them
Which tier a process change lands in
Guarding against invented and gamed process data

sample.question:
A PDK-aware agent sees that a design was built against PDK version 1.2 but the installed PDK is 1.4. What should it do first?

A) Proceed silently with 1.4

B) Delete the older layouts

C) Report the mismatch and diff the rule and model changes between the versions before acting

D) Rewrite the 1.4 deck to match 1.2
sample.answer: Report the mismatch and diff the rule and model changes between the versions before acting
sample.explanation: Version drift changes rules and models; making it explicit is the precondition for any trustworthy fix or report.

concepts.label: Fast versus accurate litho simulation
concepts.definition: Computational lithography has a natural pair of engines. Fast ones, such as calibrated compact optical and resist models, pattern matching and machine-learned hotspot detectors, run at full-chip scale.
key_ideas: When to recurse to the accurate engine

sample.question:
A machine-learning hotspot detector flags layout clips as risky. What is its role in a fast-accurate loop?

A) A replacement for all litho verification

B) A mask writer

C) A cheap filter that decides where to spend rigorous simulation

D) A tool that changes the illumination
sample.answer: A cheap filter that decides where to spend rigorous simulation
sample.explanation: The fast detector screens millions of clips; flagged ones go to accurate simulation, which is the ground truth.

concepts.label: Golden tests for rule-deck changes
concepts.definition: Rule decks are software, and agents will increasingly edit them: adding a rule, tightening a value, speeding up a check.

sample.question:
A spacing rule requires at least 28 nm. Which clips should the golden suite contain?

A) Only a clip at 0 nm

B) Only a clip at 100 nm

C) No clips; the value is enough

D) Clips at 27, 28 and 29 nm, among others, to check the boundary exactly
sample.answer: Clips at 27, 28 and 29 nm, among others, to check the boundary exactly
sample.explanation: Off-by-one and inclusive-versus-exclusive errors live at the boundary; golden tests must probe it on both sides.

concepts.label: The IP boundary around process data
concepts.definition: Foundry process data is among the most protected information in the industry: device models, rule decks, process recipes and yield data are covered by non-disclosure agreements.
key_ideas: What is confidential and why it is architecture
Narrow interfaces instead of shared text

sample.question:
Which of these is typically foundry-confidential process data?

A) Open-source router code

B) The Rayleigh equation

C) Textbook yield models

D) SPICE model parameters, rule decks and measured yield data
sample.answer: SPICE model parameters, rule decks and measured yield data
sample.explanation: Models, rules and fab data are protected under non-disclosure agreements; general physics and algorithms are not.

concepts.label: Agent-driven DTCO loops and their rewards
concepts.definition: DTCO is a search over coupled design and technology knobs, scored by expensive flows.
key_ideas: The agent proposes, the engines compute

sample.question:
Which inputs define one candidate in an automated DTCO sweep?

A) Cell height, fin count, CPP, metal pitches, rail scheme and rule values

B) The agent's prompt length

C) The RTL of the benchmark only

D) The number of compute nodes
sample.answer: Cell height, fin count, CPP, metal pitches, rail scheme and rule values
sample.explanation: These are the coupled design-technology knobs whose combination the loop explores.

domains.name: CMOS Circuits and Cell Libraries
domains.description: Static CMOS, logical effort, power, standard-cell layout and the Liberty abstraction every digital tool consumes.
covers: Static CMOS gates: pull-up/pull-down networks, NAND/NOR/AOI/OAI, transmission gates, dynamic logic
Inverter characteristics, noise margins, transistor sizing
RC delay models, logical effort, parasitic delay, path effort and optimal sizing
Power: dynamic switching power, short-circuit power, leakage power, activity factors, multi-Vt
Sequential cell circuits and their timing characterization
Standard cells, cell libraries, standard-cell layout (rows, rails, tracks), cell characterization
Liberty timing format: NLDM tables, CCS, LVF, power and noise views; what Liberty preserves and abstracts
Special cells: level shifters, isolation cells, retention cells, always-on cells, tie cells, fillers, decaps

concepts.label: The MOSFET as a switch
concepts.definition: Before a tool can time, size or characterize a gate, it needs the simplest faithful picture of a transistor: a switch controlled by its gate voltage.
key_ideas: Gate voltage opens and closes the channel
Series means AND, parallel means OR

sample.question:
In the switch model of a MOSFET, when does an nMOS conduct?

A) When its gate is low

B) Whenever its drain is above its source

C) When its source is high

D) When its gate is high
sample.answer: When its gate is high
sample.explanation: An nMOS turns on when its gate-source voltage exceeds the threshold, which for a source near ground means a high gate.

concepts.label: Static CMOS gate structure
concepts.definition: Every combinational standard cell in a digital library, from an inverter to an AOI222, is a static CMOS gate: an nMOS pull-down network and a dual pMOS pull-up network sharing one output.
key_ideas: The pull-down network from the function
The pull-up network is the dual
Why the structure is worth its cost

sample.question:
A static CMOS gate computes $Y = \overline{AB + CD}$. Write S(...) for transistors in series and P(...) for transistors in parallel. Which nMOS pull-down network implements it?

A) S(S(A, B), S(C, D))

B) S(P(A, B), P(C, D))

C) P(S(A, B), S(C, D))

D) P(P(A, B), P(C, D))
sample.answer: P(S(A, B), S(C, D))
sample.explanation: The pull-down network conducts exactly when the un-inverted expression is true: AND becomes series and OR becomes parallel, giving P(S(A, B), S(C, D)).

concepts.label: Transistor counts and series stacks
concepts.definition: Area, input capacitance and worst-case delay of a static gate all follow from two numbers that can be read straight off its Boolean expression: how many transistors it has, and how tall its tallest series stack is.

sample.question: How many transistors does a single-stage static CMOS gate for $Y = \overline{AB + CD}$ use?
sample.explanation: Every input literal drives one nMOS in the pull-down network and one pMOS in the pull-up network. With 4 literals the gate has 8 transistors.

concepts.label: AOI and OAI compound gates
concepts.definition: Compound AND-OR-invert (AOI) and OR-AND-invert (OAI) cells implement a two-level function in one static stage.

sample.question:
A standard-cell library contains the cell AOI21, with inputs lettered A, B, C, ... in group order. Which function does it compute?

A) $Y = AB + C$

B) $Y = \overline{AB + C}$

C) $Y = \overline{(A + B)C}$
sample.answer: $Y = \overline{AB + C}$
sample.explanation: In AOI the groups are ANDed, the results ORed, and the output inverted; OAI swaps AND and OR. Each digit is the size of one group, so AOI21 computes $Y = \overline{AB + C}$.

concepts.label: Transmission gates and pass-transistor logic
concepts.definition: A transmission gate is an nMOS and a pMOS in parallel, driven by complementary controls, that passes a signal in either direction without restoring it.

sample.question:
A transmission gate (an nMOS and a pMOS in parallel, both on) passes a logic 1 from a node held at $V_{DD} = 0.9$ V into a load at 0 V. Each device has a threshold magnitude of 0.3 V. What voltage does the load settle at?

A) 0.3 V

B) 0.6 V

C) 0.9 V

D) 0.45 V
sample.explanation: When the nMOS cuts off near VDD minus Vt, the pMOS is still fully on and pulls the load the rest of the way, so a transmission gate passes a full-swing 1.

concepts.label: The CMOS inverter transfer characteristic
concepts.definition: The voltage transfer characteristic (VTC) of the CMOS inverter, output voltage against input voltage, is the reference curve for every static gate.

sample.question: A long-channel CMOS inverter obeys the square law with $V_{DD} = 1.2$ V, $V_{tn} = 0.35$ V, $|V_{tp}| = 0.45$ V and $k_p / k_n = 1$. At its switching threshold $V_M$ both devices are saturated and carry equal current. What is $V_M$ in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Equating the saturation currents gives $V_M = (V_{tn} + r(V_{DD} - |V_{tp}|))/(1 + r)$ with $r = \sqrt{k_p/k_n} = 1$. That is 0.55 V.

concepts.label: Noise margins
concepts.definition: Noise margins quantify how much a logic level can be disturbed, by crosstalk, supply bounce or leakage, before the receiving gate misreads it.

sample.question: An inverter's VTC has $V_{OH} = 780$ mV, $V_{OL} = 10$ mV, and unity-gain points $V_{IL} = 304$ mV and $V_{IH} = 512$ mV. What is $NM_L$ in millivolts?
sample.explanation: $NM_H = V_{OH} - V_{IH} = 268$ mV and $NM_L = V_{IL} - V_{OL} = 294$ mV: the room between what a driver guarantees and what a receiver needs.

concepts.label: Dynamic and domino logic
concepts.definition: Dynamic logic replaces the pMOS pull-up network with a single clocked precharge device and evaluates through the nMOS network alone.

sample.question:
Why can one dynamic gate not directly drive another dynamic gate's input in the same clock phase?

A) The two clocks would short together

B) Dynamic outputs cannot drive any capacitance

C) The first gate's output starts high and only falls, so the second gate would see a falling input and may wrongly discharge

D) The second gate would precharge too early
sample.answer: The first gate's output starts high and only falls, so the second gate would see a falling input and may wrongly discharge
sample.explanation: During precharge the first output is high, so at the start of evaluation the second gate's input is high and starts discharging before the first gate settles. Domino logic inserts an inverter to fix this.

concepts.label: RC delay models of a gate
concepts.definition: The RC model replaces each conducting transistor by an effective resistance and each node by a capacitance to ground, so a gate's delay becomes an RC time constant.
key_ideas: Effective resistance and capacitance per unit width
The delay of a gate driving a load

sample.question: An inverter's pull-down has an effective resistance of 11 kOhm. Its own drain diffusion adds 6 fF at the output and it drives a load of 5 fF. Using the RC (Elmore) model $t = R(C_{par} + C_{load})$, what is the falling delay in picoseconds?
sample.explanation: The resistance charges both capacitances: $11 \times (6 + 5) = 121$ kOhm fF, and one kOhm times one fF is one ps.

concepts.label: Sizing for equal rise and fall
concepts.definition: Libraries size each gate so that its worst-case pull-up and pull-down match the drive of a reference inverter.

sample.question: A unit inverter has an nMOS of width 1 and a pMOS of width 2 (holes are 2 times slower). Size every gate so that its worst-case pull-down and pull-up resistances equal the unit inverter's. What width does each pMOS of a NOR3 get?
sample.explanation: The 3 pMOS devices are in series, so each must be 3 times the inverter's pMOS width: 6.

concepts.label: Elmore delay of a transistor stack
concepts.definition: A series transistor stack is a small RC ladder: every internal node between stacked devices carries diffusion capacitance that must also be discharged.
key_ideas: The stack as an RC ladder
Elmore delay of the falling output

sample.question: A NAND2 pull-down stack has 2 series nMOS transistors, each 4 kOhm when on. Number the internal nodes from the ground end: $C_1 = 3$ fF (node $j$ sits above $j$ transistors). The output carries 5 fF. All internal nodes start charged high. What is the Elmore delay of the falling output, in picoseconds?
sample.explanation: Each node's capacitance is multiplied by the resistance between it and ground: internal node $j$ sees $jR$ and the output sees $2R$. The internal terms give 12 ps and the output term 40 ps, for 52 ps.

concepts.label: Logical effort
concepts.definition: Logical effort measures how much worse a gate is than an inverter at driving a load, purely because of its topology.

sample.question: With pMOS twice as wide as nMOS for equal drive ($\gamma = 2$), what is the logical effort of one input of a NAND2? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Each input drives an nMOS of width 2 and a pMOS of width 2, so its capacitance is 4 against the inverter's 3: $g = 4/3 = 1.33$.

concepts.label: Parasitic delay
concepts.definition: A gate's delay has a part that depends on its load and a part that does not. The load-independent part, the parasitic delay, comes from the gate charging its own diffusion capacitance.

sample.question: In a process with $\gamma = 2$ and an inverter parasitic delay $p_{inv} = 0.8$, what is the parasitic delay of a NOR3 sized for unit-inverter drive, counting only diffusion on the output node? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The NOR3 output touches 3 parallel nMOS of width 1 and one pMOS of width 6: total 9, against the inverter's 3, so $p = 3 p_{inv}$.

concepts.label: Stage delay d = gh + p
concepts.definition: The logical-effort stage delay $d = gh + p$ condenses the RC model into one line: a topology term, a load term and a self-loading term.

sample.question: A gate has logical effort $g = 1.333$ and parasitic delay $p = 2$. Its input capacitance is 7 fF and it drives 7 fF. What is its stage delay $d$ in units of $\tau$? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Electrical effort is $h = C_{out}/C_{in} = 1$, so $d = gh + p = 1.333 \times 1 + 2 = 3.33$.

concepts.label: The FO4 delay as a process yardstick
concepts.definition: The fanout-of-four (FO4) delay, an inverter driving four copies of itself, is the standard yardstick of a process's speed.

sample.question: A process has $\tau = 4$ ps and $p_{inv} = 0.8$. What is the delay of an inverter driving four copies of itself (its FO4 delay), in picoseconds? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: An inverter has $g = 1$, and four identical loads give $h = 4$, so $d = 4 + p_{inv} = 4.8$ and the delay is 19.2 ps.

concepts.label: Path effort and minimum path delay
concepts.definition: A path of gates has an optimum: there is a minimum delay, achieved when every stage bears the same effort.
key_ideas: Path logical, electrical and branching effort

sample.question: A path is an inverter, then a NOR2, then a NAND3. Its first input is 3 fF and its last output drives 71 fF, with no branching. Use $\gamma = 2$ and $p_{inv} = 1$: inverter $g = 1, p = 1$; NAND2 $g = 4/3, p = 2$; NAND3 $g = 5/3, p = 3$; NOR2 $g = 5/3, p = 2$; NOR3 $g = 7/3, p = 3$. What is the path effort $F$? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: The optimal number of stages
concepts.definition: When a small gate must drive a large load, adding inverter stages can make the path faster, up to a point.
key_ideas: Choosing the integer and its uses

sample.question: A buffer chain must drive a load whose path effort is $F = 30$. Using the rule of thumb that each stage should bear an effort of about 4, estimate the number of stages $\log_4 F$. Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $\log_4 30 = \ln 30/\ln 4 = 2.45$. Round to a nearby integer and compare the neighbours.

concepts.label: Sizing a path at equal stage effort
concepts.definition: Knowing the optimal stage effort is not yet a design: each gate needs a size. Working backward from the load, each gate's input capacitance follows from its logical effort and the stage effort.
key_ideas: The optimal stage effort for the path
From continuous sizes to a real netlist

sample.question: A path is a NOR3, then a NAND2, then an inverter. The first input is 8 fF and the last output drives 76 fF, with no branching. Use $\gamma = 2$ and $p_{inv} = 1$: inverter $g = 1, p = 1$; NAND2 $g = 4/3, p = 2$; NAND3 $g = 5/3, p = 3$; NOR2 $g = 5/3, p = 2$; NOR3 $g = 7/3, p = 3$. What stage effort $\hat f$ minimizes the path delay? Round to 3 decimal places.

concepts.label: Input slew and the limits of the RC model
concepts.definition: The RC model assumes a step input, but every real input ramps, and a gate's delay depends strongly on how fast its input moves.

sample.question:
A gate's output transition time feeds the next gate. What does that mean for a timer?

A) Slew must be propagated along with arrival time, because each stage's delay depends on the previous stage's output slew

B) Slew can be ignored after the first stage

C) Slew and delay are the same quantity

D) Only the last stage's slew matters
sample.answer: Slew must be propagated along with arrival time, because each stage's delay depends on the previous stage's output slew
sample.explanation: Delay of stage k depends on the slew out of stage k-1, so a timer computes and carries a slew at every pin.

concepts.label: Dynamic power
concepts.definition: Dynamic power is the energy spent charging and discharging capacitance as signals switch.
key_ideas: The alpha C V squared f formula

sample.question: A block has 560 pF of switched capacitance, runs at $V_{DD} = 0.8$ V and $f = 2$ GHz, and has an activity factor $\alpha = 0.15$. Here $\alpha$ is the probability that a node makes a 0-to-1 transition in a cycle, so $P = \alpha C V^2 f$. What is its dynamic power in milliwatts? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $P = 0.15 \times 560\ \text{pF} \times 0.8^2 \times 2\ \text{GHz}$. Since pF times GHz is $10^{-3}$, the result is 107.52 mW.

concepts.label: Signal probability and activity factors
concepts.definition: The activity factor is the term in $\alpha C V^2 f$ that a power tool must estimate from the design itself.

sample.question: The inputs of a NAND2 are independent, with probabilities $p_A = 0.1$ and $p_B = 0.2$ of being 1 in any cycle, and successive cycles are independent. What is the probability that the output is 1? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: For a NAND2 the output-1 probability is $1 - p_A p_B = 0.98$.

concepts.label: Short-circuit power
concepts.definition: During an input transition there is an interval when both the pull-up and pull-down conduct, and current flows straight from the supply to ground.

sample.question:
Is short-circuit current present when an inverter's input is static?

A) No: one device is off whenever the input sits at a rail

B) Only in the subthreshold region

C) Yes, but only for a high input

D) Yes, it flows continuously
sample.answer: No: one device is off whenever the input sits at a rail
sample.explanation: Short-circuit current is a switching phenomenon. With the input at 0 or VDD one device is off (apart from leakage).

concepts.label: Leakage power and multi-Vt
concepts.definition: Leakage is the power a circuit burns while doing nothing: current through transistors that are nominally off.
key_ideas: Subthreshold current is exponential in Vt
DIBL and the cost of speed

sample.question: A library offers LVT and HVT flavours whose thresholds differ by 40 mV. The subthreshold swing is 85 mV per decade. By what factor does the off-current of an LVT device exceed that of the matching HVT device? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Subthreshold current falls one decade for every $S$ of threshold, so the ratio is $10^{\Delta V_t/S} = 10^{40/85} = 2.96$.

concepts.label: Multi-Vt assignment trade-offs
concepts.definition: A multi-Vt library gives every cell several threshold flavours with identical footprints.

sample.question: A block has 30000 LVT cells leaking 6 nW each and 129000 HVT cells. HVT cells leak 15 times less than LVT cells. What is the block's leakage power in microwatts? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: LVT: 30000 x 6 nW; HVT: 129000 x 0.4 nW. The sum is 231.6 uW.

concepts.label: Energy per operation
concepts.definition: Power tells you how fast energy is spent; energy per operation tells you what each computation costs.

sample.question: A datapath switches 34 pF of capacitance with activity $\alpha = 0.1$ (0-to-1 probability per operation) at $V_{DD} = 0.6$ V, one operation per cycle. What is the dynamic energy per operation, in picojoules? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $E = \alpha C V^2 = 0.1 \times 34 \times 0.36 = 1.224$ pJ (pF times volts squared is pJ).

concepts.label: Transistor-level latches and flip-flops
concepts.definition: Every register in a digital design is a library flip-flop, and every flip-flop is built from latches made of inverters and transmission gates.
key_ideas: Where setup, hold and clock-to-q come from

sample.question:
What is the job of the transmission gates in a transmission-gate latch?

A) Both pass the input at the same time

B) One passes the input when the latch is transparent and the other closes the feedback loop when it is opaque

C) They drive the output to the supply rails

D) They generate the inverted clock
sample.answer: One passes the input when the latch is transparent and the other closes the feedback loop when it is opaque
sample.explanation: Clocked complementary switches alternate between connecting the input and closing the storage loop.

concepts.label: Characterizing setup, hold and clock-to-q
concepts.definition: A flip-flop has no single correct setup time. Its clock-to-q grows smoothly as data arrives closer to the clock edge, until it fails outright.

sample.question: A characterization run sweeps how long before the clock edge the data input changes. Setup skew (data-to-clock) versus measured clock-to-q, in ps: 45 ps: 87; 40 ps: 92; 35 ps: 98; 30 ps: 105; 25 ps: 116; 20 ps: 130; 15 ps: 149; 10 ps: 174. Take the nominal clock-to-q as the value at the largest skew. The setup criterion allows a 20% push-out. What is the largest acceptable clock-to-q, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The nominal value is 87 ps, so the limit is $87 \times 1.2 = 104.4$ ps.

concepts.label: Integrated clock-gating cells
concepts.definition: The clock has an activity factor of 1 and a large capacitance, so stopping it where registers would hold their values anyway is the single most effective dynamic-power optimization in digital design.

sample.question:
Which flops can be clock-gated without changing behaviour?

A) Flops whose next state equals their current state whenever the enable is off

B) Only flops on the critical path

C) Any flop, at any time

D) Only flops with asynchronous reset
sample.answer: Flops whose next state equals their current state whenever the enable is off
sample.explanation: A gated flop holds its value. Gating is safe exactly where the original logic recirculated the value through a hold mux.

concepts.label: Latch regeneration and synchronizer MTBF
concepts.definition: When a flop samples an asynchronous signal, data sometimes changes within the tiny window around the clock edge, and the flop's internal latch is left balanced between 0 and 1.

sample.question: A synchronizer flop has regeneration time constant $\tau = 12$ ps and metastability window $T_w = 26$ ps. It samples data toggling at 100 MHz with a 1 GHz clock and allows 585 ps of resolution time. With $\text{MTBF} = e^{t_r/\tau}/(T_w f_c f_d)$, what is $\log_{10}$ of the MTBF in seconds? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Standard-cell layout
concepts.definition: A standard cell is a gate laid out on a fixed template: a common height, power rails along the top and bottom, and a width that is a whole number of placement sites.
key_ideas: The template: rails, wells and devices
Height in tracks, width in poly pitches
What the template buys the tools

sample.question: A library is built on a 6-track cell height, where a track is the horizontal metal routing pitch of 32 nm. What is the cell height in nm?
sample.explanation: Cell height is tracks times pitch: $6 \times 32 = 192$ nm.

concepts.label: The views of a cell library
concepts.definition: A cell library is not one file. It is a set of views of the same cells, each an abstraction tailored to one class of tool: the layout for manufacturing, a physical abstract for placement and routing, a timing and power model for analysis, a netlist for verification, and a behavioural model for simulation.

sample.question:
Which view does a layout-versus-schematic check compare the extracted layout against?

A) The Liberty file

B) The timing constraints

C) The transistor-level netlist (CDL or SPICE)

D) The LEF abstract
sample.answer: The transistor-level netlist (CDL or SPICE)
sample.explanation: LVS extracts transistors from the full layout and compares them with the reference transistor netlist.

concepts.label: Rows, sites, rails and utilization
concepts.definition: Before a placer moves a single cell, the floorplan fixes the placement grid: how many rows fit in the core, how many sites each row holds, where the rails go and what fraction of the sites cells will fill.
key_ideas: Utilization and why it is not 100%

sample.question: A core area is 32759 nm tall and the library's row height is 320 nm. Rows are stacked from the bottom edge with no gaps. How many complete placement rows fit?
sample.explanation: $\lfloor 32759 / 320 \rfloor = 102$ rows.

concepts.label: Drive strengths within a cell family
concepts.definition: A library offers each function in several drive strengths, such as X1, X2, X4 and X8.
key_ideas: The smallest size that meets a target

sample.question: In a cell family, the X1 size has output resistance 7 kOhm, output parasitic capacitance 3 fF and input capacitance 1 fF. Size Xk has $1/k$ the resistance and $k$ times both capacitances. What is the RC delay of the X4 size driving 27 fF, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $t = (R_1/k)(k C_p + C_L) = R_1 C_p + R_1 C_L / k = 21 + 47.25 = 68.25$ ps. The parasitic term does not shrink with size.

concepts.label: Liberty structure: cells, pins and arcs
concepts.definition: Liberty is the text format in which a cell library tells synthesis, timing and power tools what each cell does.
key_ideas: What the structure hides and assumes

sample.question:
What timing_sense should the Liberty timing group carry for the arc of an AO22 from input D to Y?

A) combinational

B) non_unate

C) positive_unate

D) negative_unate
sample.answer: positive_unate
sample.explanation: It is positive_unate because AND-OR without inversion is monotone increasing.

concepts.label: Liberty NLDM timing tables
concepts.definition: The nonlinear delay model (NLDM) is the classic Liberty timing model: for each arc and output edge, a two-dimensional table of delay and a table of output transition, indexed by input transition and output load.
key_ideas: Choosing the table from the edges

sample.question: Table cell_fall: index_1 (input transition, ps) = 5, 15, 45, 135; index_2 (output load, fF) = 1, 3, 9, 27. Row input transition = 5: 16, 22, 42, 100. Row input transition = 15: 17, 24, 46, 110. Row input transition = 45: 21, 30, 57, 137. Row input transition = 135: 34, 48, 91, 220. Values are in ps. Which value does the table give at an input transition of 45 ps and an output load of 27 fF?
sample.explanation: index_1 selects the row (input transition 45 ps) and index_2 the column (load 27 fF); the entry there is 137 ps.

concepts.label: What NLDM preserves and abstracts
concepts.definition: NLDM reduces a cell to a few numbers per grid point: one delay and one transition for a ramp input into a lumped capacitor.
key_ideas: Waveforms, receivers and the range of validity

sample.question:
What does NLDM assume about the load a cell drives?

A) It is a single lumped capacitance

B) It is a current source

C) It is an inductor in series with a capacitor

D) It is a distributed RC line
sample.answer: It is a single lumped capacitance
sample.explanation: The load index is total output capacitance; resistance between the driver and the far capacitance is not represented.

concepts.label: CCS and LVF models
concepts.definition: Two Liberty extensions carry what NLDM drops. Composite current source (CCS) models store the current a driver delivers as a function of time, so a timer can reconstruct waveforms into any load.
key_ideas: CCS: the driver as a current waveform
LVF: a sigma for every table entry
Asymmetric sigmas and what LVF assumes

sample.question: A CCS driver model gives the output current into a 10 fF load as samples held constant over successive 2 ps intervals: 64, 29, 76, 24 uA. Starting from 0 V, what is the output voltage after these intervals, in millivolts? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: The delivered charge is $\sum i \Delta t = 386$ uA ps $= 386$ aC, and $V = Q/C$; aC per fF is mV, so 38.6 mV.

concepts.label: Liberty power and noise views
concepts.definition: Liberty describes power and noise as well as timing. Leakage is given per cell and per input state, internal energy per transition is given in tables like delay, and noise views describe how a cell rejects and propagates glitches.
key_ideas: Total pin power and noise views

sample.question: A NAND2's Liberty leakage_power groups give, by input state: when "!A & !B" 4 nW, when "!A & B" 9 nW, when "A & !B" 14 nW, when "A & B" 28 nW. Inputs are independent with $P(A = 1) = 0.9$ and $P(B = 1) = 0.2$. What is the expected leakage in nW? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Weight each state's leakage by its probability: the state probabilities are 0.08, 0.02, 0.72 and 0.18, giving 15.62 nW.

concepts.label: Cell characterization
concepts.definition: Characterization turns transistor netlists and foundry device models into Liberty: it simulates every arc of every cell at every grid point and corner, measures delays, transitions, constraints, power and capacitances, and writes the tables.

sample.question: A library of 390 cells averages 7 delay arcs per cell. Each arc is characterized for a rising and a falling output on a 7 by 5 grid of input transition and load, at 10 PVT corners, one SPICE transient per point. How many transient simulations is that?
sample.explanation: Multiply: 390 cells x 7 arcs x 2 edges x 35 grid points x 10 corners = 1911000.

concepts.label: PVT corners and library sets
concepts.definition: A library is characterized at one operating point: a process condition, a supply voltage and a temperature (PVT).

sample.question:
Which corner gives the highest leakage power?

A) Fast process, high voltage, high temperature

B) Typical process at room temperature

C) Slow process, low voltage, low temperature

D) Fast process, low voltage, low temperature
sample.answer: Fast process, high voltage, high temperature
sample.explanation: Fast devices have low thresholds, higher voltage raises DIBL and current, and subthreshold leakage rises steeply with temperature.

concepts.label: Sequential constraint arcs in Liberty
concepts.definition: A flip-flop's Liberty description has delay arcs from the clock to the outputs and constraint arcs from the clock to the data and control inputs.

sample.question: A flop's Liberty constraint arc from CK (related_pin) to D. Table rise_constraint (timing_type setup_rising): index_1 (data transition, ps) = 10, 30, 90; index_2 (clock transition, ps) = 20, 60, 180. Row data transition = 10: 40, 36, 22. Row data transition = 30: 45, 40, 27. Row data transition = 90: 59, 54, 41. Values are in ps. What setup time applies when D rises with a 90 ps transition and CK a 180 ps transition?
sample.explanation: index_1 is the data transition and index_2 the clock transition here, so the entry at (90, 180) is 41 ps.

concepts.label: Level shifters, isolation and retention cells
concepts.definition: Designs with several supply voltages or with blocks that power down need cells that ordinary logic libraries do not provide: level shifters between voltage domains, isolation cells at the outputs of switchable domains, retention flops that keep state through power-down, and always-on buffers.

sample.question:
Why is a level shifter for a low-to-high crossing more complex than one for high-to-low?

A) Both are identical inverters

B) Going up only needs a resistor

C) Going up needs a cross-coupled or differential stage to reach the higher rail; going down a simple buffer on the lower supply suffices

D) Going down needs two supplies and going up needs one
sample.answer: Going up needs a cross-coupled or differential stage to reach the higher rail; going down a simple buffer on the lower supply suffices
sample.explanation: A higher-voltage input can safely drive a lower-supply inverter, but a lower-voltage input cannot fully switch a higher-supply one.

concepts.label: Power switches and power gating
concepts.definition: Power gating cuts a block's leakage by disconnecting it from the supply when it is idle.

sample.question: A switchable domain draws 71 mA through 3190 identical header switches in parallel, each with an on-resistance of 1300 Ohm. Assuming the current divides evenly, what is the voltage drop across the switches, in mV? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The switches act as one resistor of $1300 / 3190$ Ohm, so the drop is $71 \times 1300 / 3190 = 28.93$ mV (mA times Ohm is mV).

concepts.label: Tie, filler, tap, endcap and decap cells
concepts.definition: Some library cells have no logic function at all, or only a constant one: tie cells, fillers, well taps, endcaps, decoupling capacitors and spare cells.

sample.question:
What is a spare cell?

A) A copy of a cell kept for timing

B) A filler with decap

C) An unused gate placed in advance so a later metal-only fix can be wired to it

D) A cell with no inputs
sample.answer: An unused gate placed in advance so a later metal-only fix can be wired to it
sample.explanation: Spare gates scattered across the die let an engineering change be made by changing only metal masks.

concepts.label: Characterization as an agent skill
concepts.definition: Characterization is a natural first target for agent-driven engineering: it is compute-heavy, rule-bound and full of library-specific choices, and its outputs can be checked against SPICE.
key_ideas: The four layers of a characterizer

sample.question:
A characterization engine is split into the four-layer model. Which part belongs in the immutable core?

A) The list of corners to run tonight

B) The choice of index values for a new library

C) The measurement definitions and the netlist-to-SPICE deck generation that every table depends on

D) The logging hook that reports progress
sample.answer: The measurement definitions and the netlist-to-SPICE deck generation that every table depends on
sample.explanation: How delay, transition and constraints are measured is the correctness kernel; changing it silently changes every table, so it needs human approval and full regression.

concepts.label: Golden SPICE checks for library tables
concepts.definition: A golden SPICE check is the test that decides whether a characterization change is allowed to ship.
key_ideas: Relative error at a grid point

sample.question: A characterization skill under test reports a delay of 41 ps at one grid point where the golden SPICE reference gives 42 ps. What is the relative error, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $|41 - 42| / 42 = 2.38\%$, measured against the golden value.

concepts.label: Fast characterization surrogates
concepts.definition: Full characterization of a new corner or a new cell variant costs millions of SPICE transients.
key_ideas: What the fast engine trades away

sample.question:
Why should a surrogate's predictions never be written directly into a signoff library?

A) Surrogate tables are always too pessimistic

B) Liberty forbids predicted numbers

C) Signoff libraries cannot be edited

D) Signoff numbers must be traceable to accurate simulation within the agreed tolerance
sample.answer: Signoff numbers must be traceable to accurate simulation within the agreed tolerance
sample.explanation: The fast mode guides work; the accurate engine provides the numbers a design is signed off on.

concepts.label: Agents choosing cell architectures in DTCO
concepts.definition: Design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) chooses the cell architecture, track height, fins or sheets per device, pin layers and similar template parameters, jointly with the process.
key_ideas: The architecture choice and its scoring
Proxies and the danger of overfitting

sample.question:
In a DTCO loop, what is an agent choosing when it chooses a cell architecture?

A) The clock period of one design

B) The SDC constraints

C) The RTL of the design

D) Track height, fins or sheets per device, pin layers and similar parameters that set every cell's layout
sample.answer: Track height, fins or sheets per device, pin layers and similar parameters that set every cell's layout
sample.explanation: Design-technology co-optimization explores how the process and the cell template interact, before a library is fixed.

concepts.label: Tool-grounded rewards for library agents
concepts.definition: Reinforcement learning with tools as judges, tool-grounded RL, is how a model can learn to configure and run characterization: deterministic simulators score its output against ground truth and that score is the reward.

sample.question:
A reward checks tables only at the grid points that the golden suite covers. What behaviour might the model learn?

A) To refuse to produce tables

B) To produce uniformly accurate tables

C) To simulate only the golden cells correctly by luck

D) To be accurate at the checked points and careless elsewhere
sample.answer: To be accurate at the checked points and careless elsewhere
sample.explanation: Optimizing a reward that sees a fixed subset invites fitting that subset; checks must sample unseen points.

domains.name: HDLs and Hardware Compilers
domains.description: Verilog, SystemVerilog and VHDL semantics, elaboration, ASTs, IRs, SSA and dataflow analysis, RTLIL, MLIR and CIRCT.
covers: Hardware description languages; RTL; behavioral vs structural modeling
Verilog, SystemVerilog, VHDL, SystemC, Verilog-AMS, VHDL-AMS: semantics that matter for synthesis and simulation
Blocking vs nonblocking assignment, always_ff/always_comb, inferred latches, synthesizable subset
Elaboration, parameters, generate, hierarchy flattening
Compilers for hardware: lexing/parsing, abstract syntax trees, intermediate representations, static single assignment, control-flow graphs, data-flow analysis
Classical optimizations on IR: constant propagation, common subexpression elimination, dead-code elimination
Open-source front ends: Verilator, Icarus Verilog, GHDL, Surelog, UHDM, slang, Yosys frontend (RTLIL)
CIRCT and MLIR: dialects (HW, Comb, Seq, FIRRTL), lowering; Chisel/FIRRTL
Domain-specific languages for hardware

concepts.label: Register-transfer level design
concepts.definition: Register-transfer level (RTL) is the abstraction at which almost all digital hardware is written and at which the EDA flow begins.

sample.question:
An RTL block has three registers and no inputs. What determines the values they hold after 10 clock cycles?

A) Nothing: without inputs RTL cannot change state

B) Their reset values and the next-state functions, applied 10 times

C) The gate delays of the combinational logic

D) The order in which the registers are declared
sample.answer: Their reset values and the next-state functions, applied 10 times
sample.explanation: RTL is a synchronous state machine: state at cycle n+1 is a function of state and inputs at cycle n.

concepts.label: Behavioral versus structural modeling
concepts.definition: Hardware description languages let a designer say what a circuit does (behavioral style) or what it is made of (structural style), with continuous-assignment dataflow in between.
key_ideas: What each style costs a tool

sample.question:
Gate-level output from synthesis is written in Verilog. In which style?

A) Dataflow, with continuous assignments only

B) Structural: instances of library cells connected by wires

C) Behavioral, with always blocks

D) Transaction-level
sample.answer: Structural: instances of library cells connected by wires
sample.explanation: A synthesized netlist is a list of cell instances and their connections, with no behavioral code.

concepts.label: Four-state logic values
concepts.definition: Verilog and SystemVerilog simulate with four values per bit: 0, 1, x (unknown) and z (high impedance).
key_ideas: Bitwise operators on x and z

sample.question:
In Verilog, a = 4'b0x10 and b = 4'b11xx. What is the value of a | b?

A) 4'b111x

B) 4'b1110

C) 4'b1xxx

D) 4'b011x
sample.explanation: Work lane by lane. z behaves as x at a logic-operator input, a 0 controls AND and a 1 controls OR even against an unknown, and any unknown into XOR gives x. The result is 4'b111x.

concepts.label: Modules, ports and design hierarchy
concepts.definition: A module is the unit of definition in Verilog and SystemVerilog, and instances of modules form the design hierarchy.

sample.question:
What does an inout port model?

A) An input that can also be a parameter

B) A bidirectional connection, such as a tristate pad driven from either side

C) A port with no direction, ignored by synthesis

D) A port that is both a clock and a reset
sample.answer: A bidirectional connection, such as a tristate pad driven from either side
sample.explanation: inout ports carry signals in both directions and are typically resolved with tristate drivers.

concepts.label: The Verilog event scheduler
concepts.definition: Verilog simulation semantics are defined by an event scheduler: processes wake on events, run, and schedule further events into ordered regions of each time step.

sample.question:
Why does the strobe system task show final values for a time step, while the display task may show intermediate ones?

A) Strobe runs before everything else

B) Strobe executes in the region at the end of the time step, after all updates; display executes immediately when reached

C) Display runs in the NBA region

D) They are identical
sample.answer: Strobe executes in the region at the end of the time step, after all updates; display executes immediately when reached
sample.explanation: Monitor and strobe output happens in the last region of the time step, once values have settled.

concepts.label: Blocking and nonblocking assignments
concepts.definition: Verilog has two procedural assignments. Blocking assignment (=) updates its variable immediately; nonblocking assignment (<=) samples its right-hand side now and updates after the block has run.
key_ideas: Mixing the two in one block

sample.explanation: Execute the statements in order. A blocking assignment (=) updates its variable immediately, so later statements read the new value; a nonblocking assignment (<=) samples its right-hand side now and updates only after the whole block has run. Doing that for one rising clock edge gives b = 9. Treating every statement the other way would give 13.

concepts.label: Flip-flop inference from clocked blocks
concepts.definition: Synthesis does not see flip-flops in RTL; it infers them. The rule is about lifetimes: a variable needs storage when its value must survive from one clock cycle to the next.
key_ideas: Every nonblocking target is a register

sample.explanation: A variable assigned in a clocked block needs storage when its value must survive to the next cycle: every nonblocking target does, and a blocking temporary does only if some read sees the previous cycle's value. Continuous assigns infer no flops. Bits: q1: 8; q2: 12; q3: 8. Total 28.

concepts.label: Inferred latches
