A) A bound on the trip count so the tool can budget and report worst-case latency

B) Nothing, because HLS ignores while-loops

C) A switch to double precision

D) A directive to unroll it fully
sample.answer: A bound on the trip count so the tool can budget and report worst-case latency
sample.explanation: A data-dependent loop can be synthesized, but without a bound its latency is unknown and it may never terminate on bad data.

concepts.label: Co-simulation as the golden test
concepts.definition: In an HLS flow the C model is the specification, and C/RTL co-simulation is the test that checks the generated hardware against it.
key_ideas: Golden and differential tests for engine changes
Where the golden test is weak

sample.question:
Co-simulation passes. What has it not shown?

A) That the RTL finishes on those inputs

B) That the interface handshakes work on those tests

C) That outputs match the C model on the tested vectors

D) That the design meets timing after implementation
sample.answer: That the design meets timing after implementation
sample.explanation: Co-simulation is functional and cycle-level at RTL; physical timing needs implementation and static timing analysis.

concepts.label: Fast QoR surrogates for exploration
concepts.definition: Every HLS run costs minutes; every implementation run costs far more. Design-space explorers therefore use surrogate models that predict latency, II and resources from a configuration in milliseconds, and spend real runs only on promising points.
key_ideas: Ranking quality matters more than error

sample.question: A fast QoR surrogate predicts 3980 cycles of latency for a pragma configuration; full HLS synthesis reports 3700 cycles. What is the absolute percentage error of the prediction? Round to 1 decimal place.

domains.name: Static Timing Analysis
domains.description: Timing graphs, delay models, clocks and constraints, OCV, AOCV, POCV and SSTA, incremental timing and timing closure.
covers: Static timing analysis as graph propagation: timing graph, arcs, arrival time, required time, slack, WNS, TNS
Setup and hold checks, clock-to-q, recovery/removal, latches and time borrowing
Delay models: Elmore delay, NLDM table interpolation (slew and load), effective capacitance, slew propagation, wire delay
Clocks: definitions, generated clocks, clock latency and uncertainty, skew, jitter, CPPR/CRPR
Timing constraints and SDC: create_clock, set_input_delay, set_output_delay, false paths, multicycle paths, clock groups
Critical paths, path-based vs graph-based analysis, path enumeration
Corners and modes: PVT corners, MCMM
On-chip variation: flat OCV derates, AOCV, POCV, LVF; statistical STA (canonical first-order form, sum and max)
Incremental timing, timing closure, timing ECOs
OpenSTA: Liberty + Verilog netlist + SDC + SPEF in, reports out

concepts.label: The timing graph
concepts.definition: A static timer never simulates a circuit. It turns the netlist into a directed graph and propagates numbers along it.
key_ideas: Pins as nodes, arcs as edges
Counting cell arcs and net arcs
Loops, disabled arcs and why a DAG matters

sample.question:
Where do the delays on cell arcs come from?

A) The SPEF file alone

B) The Verilog netlist

C) The Liberty timing arcs of each cell, evaluated at the pin's slew and load

D) The SDC file
sample.answer: The Liberty timing arcs of each cell, evaluated at the pin's slew and load
sample.explanation: Liberty describes each input-to-output timing arc with delay and slew tables. Parasitics feed the load, and SDC sets clocks and constraints.

concepts.label: Timing sense and unateness of arcs
concepts.definition: A timer does not propagate one arrival time per pin but two, one for a rising and one for a falling transition.
key_ideas: Following a transition through a chain

sample.question:
A falling transition enters a chain of gates in this order: buffer. It passes through one input of each gate, and side inputs may hold any value. Which output transitions must the timer propagate at the end of the chain?

A) No transition, because the side inputs block it

B) A falling transition only

C) Both a rising and a falling transition

D) A rising transition only
sample.answer: A falling transition only
sample.explanation: Positive-unate arcs keep the direction, negative-unate arcs flip it, and a non-unate arc such as XOR can produce either, after which both directions travel on. The result is: a falling transition only.

concepts.label: Levelizing the timing graph
concepts.definition: Before a timer propagates anything it levelizes the graph: it assigns every node a level so that each arc goes from a lower level to a higher one.
key_ideas: Depth is the longest path in arcs
Levels as batches of independent work

sample.question: A timing graph has the arcs L→B, N→B, Q→N, T→F, T→M, N→M, Q→L. Sources are at level 0, and every other node is at one plus the largest level among its fanins. What is the level of node B?
sample.explanation: Sources sit at level 0 and every other node at one more than its deepest fanin. Levels: T = 0, Q = 0, F = 1, L = 1, N = 1, B = 2, M = 2.

concepts.label: Forward propagation of arrival times
concepts.definition: The arrival time at a pin is when the signal there settles, measured from the launching clock edge.

sample.question: A timing graph has the arcs Q→M (9 ps), U→A (10 ps), A→M (8 ps), Q→U (16 ps). Signals leave the sources Q at 20 ps. What is the latest arrival time at node M, in ps?
sample.explanation: Visit nodes in topological order and take the max over fanins of arrival plus arc delay. Arrivals: Q = 20, U = 36, A = 46, M = 54. At M the latest arrival is 54 ps.

concepts.label: Arrival and required times
concepts.definition: Arrival times say when data settles; required times say when it must settle. A timer computes the first forward from the startpoints and the second backward from the endpoints, and their difference is slack.

sample.question: A capture flip-flop is clocked with period 700 ps. Its clock pin sees the capturing edge 5 ps late (clock latency), and its setup time is 44 ps. Data launches from a flop on the edge at 0 ps with ideal latency. What is the required time at the capture flop's D pin, in ps?
sample.explanation: Required time is the capturing edge plus its latency minus setup: 700 + 5 - 44 = 661 ps.

concepts.label: What slack measures
concepts.definition: Static timing analysis reduces a chip's timing to one signed number per endpoint: slack.
key_ideas: Hold slack runs the other way

sample.question:
A path launches on a clock edge at 0 ps. The capture edge is at 800 ps, setup time is 30 ps and data arrives at 790 ps. What is the setup slack?

A) -20 ps

B) -50 ps

C) 10 ps

D) 20 ps
sample.answer: -20 ps
sample.explanation: Required time is 800 - 30 = 770 ps. Slack is required minus arrival: 770 - 790 = -20 ps.

concepts.label: Node slack and the critical path
concepts.definition: Slack is defined at every pin, not only at endpoints. Once arrivals and required times are known everywhere, the slack of a pin is the slack of the worst path through it.
key_ideas: The critical path shares one slack

sample.question: A timing graph has the arcs D→S (22 ps), R→W (26 ps), E→R (36 ps), R→D (13 ps), G→S (12 ps). Sources launch E at 10 ps, G at 10 ps. Endpoint required times are W at 82 ps, S at 56 ps. What is the slack at endpoint S, in ps?
sample.explanation: Arrivals (forward max): E = 10, G = 10, R = 46, D = 59, W = 72, S = 81. Required times (backward min): E = -15, G = 44, R = 21, D = 34, W = 82, S = 56. Slack is required minus arrival: E = -25, G = 34, R = -25, D = -25, W = 10, S = -25.

concepts.label: Worst and total negative slack
concepts.definition: A chip has millions of endpoints, each with a slack. Two summary numbers reduce them to something a team can track from run to run: worst negative slack and total negative slack.

sample.question: The setup slacks of a design's endpoints, in ps, are E1: -12, E2: 44, E3: -6, E4: 34, E5: -31, E6: -5, E7: -2. What is the worst negative slack (WNS), in ps?
sample.explanation: WNS is the most negative endpoint slack, -31 ps.

concepts.label: Elmore delay of an RC tree
concepts.definition: A routed net is not a wire with one delay. It is a tree: one driver, a trunk, branches and several sinks, each piece carrying resistance along its length and capacitance to ground.
key_ideas: The first moment of the impulse response
Computing it in one tree traversal

sample.question: An RC chain runs from the driver through $R_1 = 250\ \Omega$ then $C_1 = 35$ fF, $R_2 = 250\ \Omega$ then $C_2 = 25$ fF, $R_3 = 250\ \Omega$ then $C_3 = 15$ fF, each capacitor to ground. What is the Elmore delay at the far end, node 3, in picoseconds?
sample.explanation: Each capacitor sees all the resistance between it and the driver. Summing shared resistance times capacitance gives 32500 ohm-femtofarads, which is 32.5 ps.

concepts.label: Delay of a distributed RC wire
concepts.definition: A wire is not a lumped resistor and capacitor: its resistance and capacitance are spread along its length.
key_ideas: The distributed line halves the lumped delay

sample.question: A wire of length 350 um has resistance 1 ohm/um and capacitance 0.2 fF/um, distributed uniformly. Ignoring the driver and any load, what is its Elmore delay from one end to the other, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: A distributed line has Elmore delay $rcL^2/2$, half the lumped value: 1 x 0.2 x 350^2 / 2 = 12250 ohm-fF, which is 12.25 ps.

concepts.label: Interpolating NLDM tables
concepts.definition: Liberty's non-linear delay model stores each timing arc as small tables of delay and output slew, indexed by the input slew and the output load.

sample.question: A Liberty cell_rise table is indexed by input slew (index_1) and output load (index_2). Its window around the query holds: at slew 20 ps, load 4 fF the delay is 39 ps; at slew 20 ps, load 8 fF it is 60 ps; at slew 40 ps, load 4 fF it is 48 ps; at slew 40 ps, load 8 fF it is 71 ps. Using bilinear interpolation (extrapolating linearly from this window if the point lies outside it), what delay does the timer compute at slew 20 ps and load 5 fF? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The fractional positions are $t_s = 0$ along slew and $t_c = 0.25$ along load. Interpolate along load at each slew, then along slew: the result is 44.25 ps.

concepts.label: Stage delay: cell arc plus net arc
concepts.definition: A timing path alternates cell arcs and net arcs. A stage is one driving cell plus the net it drives up to a sink pin, and its delay is what a delay calculator computes in one call.
key_ideas: Cell delay from drive resistance and load
Summing stages into a path arrival

sample.question: Model each cell delay as intrinsic delay plus drive resistance times its total load (wire plus pin), and each wire as a pi model whose Elmore delay is wire resistance times (half the wire capacitance plus the pin capacitance). One kohm times one fF is one ps. Stage 1: the cell has intrinsic delay 7 ps and drive resistance 0.5 kohm; its output wire has capacitance 2 fF and resistance 0.2 kohm; the sink pin it drives has capacitance 3 fF. What is the cell delay of stage 1, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Cell delay = 7 + 0.5 x (2 + 3) = 9.5 ps.

concepts.label: Slew propagation: worst slew versus path slew
concepts.definition: Delay depends on input slew, so every stage's output slew must be carried to the next stage.

sample.question: Gate G has inputs A and B. Input A arrives at 60 ps with slew 150 ps; input B arrives at 160 ps with slew 150 ps. The arc from input X has delay $a_X + 0.4 s_X$ and output slew $b_X + 0.6 s_X$, where $s_X$ is the input slew, with $a_A = 28$, $a_B = 17$, $b_A = 28$, $b_B = 25$ (all ps). G drives gate H, whose arc delay is $22 + 0.3 s$ for input slew s. A graph-based timer keeps one slew per pin, the worst over all arcs into it. What slew does it store at G's output, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The arc from A gives output slew 118 ps and the arc from B gives 115 ps. Worst-slew merging keeps the larger, 118 ps, even though it may not belong to the latest-arriving input.

concepts.label: Effective capacitance of a resistive load
concepts.definition: Liberty tables assume a cell drives a pure capacitor. A real routed net has resistance between the driver and the far capacitance, which shields part of it: during the fast output transition the driver does not see the full load.

sample.question: A driver sees a pi load: 11 fF at its pin, then 850 ohm of wire resistance, then 42 fF at the far end. The resistance shields the far capacitance with time constant $\tau = R C_2$. What is $\tau$, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: 850 ohm x 42 fF = 35700 ohm-fF, which is 35.7 ps. A ramp much shorter than this sees mostly the near capacitance.

concepts.label: Setup and hold checks
concepts.definition: Every flop-to-flop path is checked twice. The setup check asks whether the slowest data reaches the capture flop before the next capturing edge; the hold check asks whether the fastest data stays away long enough not to corrupt the value being captured on the current edge.

sample.question: A flop-to-flop path is clocked with period 850 ps. The launch flop's clock arrives at 145 ps and the capture flop's clock at 75 ps after the source edge. Clock-to-Q is 74 ps, the longest combinational delay is 740 ps and the shortest is 113 ps. The capture flop's setup time is 55 ps and its hold time is 50 ps. What is the setup required time at the capture flop's D pin, in ps?
sample.explanation: The next capturing edge reaches the capture flop at 850 + 75 ps; setup must be met 55 ps before it: 870 ps.

concepts.label: Minimum clock period of a register path
concepts.definition: The setup check can be turned around: instead of asking whether a path meets a given period, ask for the smallest period it meets.
key_ideas: The smallest period one path meets

sample.question: In a register-to-register path, path 1 has clock-to-Q 72 ps, logic delay 440 ps, setup 58 ps and skew +30 ps. Skew is the capture clock arrival minus the launch clock arrival. What is the smallest clock period this path meets, in ps?
sample.explanation: Setup holds when $T \ge t_{cq} + d + t_{su} - skew$ = 72 + 440 + 58 - (+30) = 540 ps.

concepts.label: Half-cycle paths between opposite edges
concepts.definition: Not every path runs between rising edges. A path from a rising-edge flop to a falling-edge flop, or the reverse, has only part of a cycle for setup, and an unusually easy hold check.
key_ideas: Time between launch and capture edges
Setup slack of a half-cycle path
Hold is easy for half-cycle paths

sample.question: A clock has period 700 ps and is high for the first 315 ps of each cycle (rising at 0). A path launches on the rising edge at 0 ps and is captured by a falling-edge flop. Clock-to-Q is 38 ps, the longest logic delay 100 ps and the shortest 76 ps; setup is 47 ps and hold 22 ps. Clocks are ideal. How much time separates the launch edge from the setup capture edge, in ps?
sample.explanation: The setup capture edge is the first opposite edge after launch, 315 ps later.

concepts.label: Recovery and removal checks
concepts.definition: Asynchronous set and reset pins act immediately, without the clock, but releasing them is not instantaneous in effect: if a reset deasserts too close to a clock edge, the flop may not leave reset cleanly on that edge, and different flops may leave reset on different cycles.

sample.question: A reset synchronizer flop, clocked at period 1150 ps with clock arrival 140 ps, drives the asynchronous reset pin of a capture flop whose clock arrives at 130 ps. The synchronizer's clock-to-Q is 48 ps, and the reset net delay is at most 720 ps and at least 147 ps. The capture flop's recovery time is 36 ps and its removal time is 39 ps. What is the required time for the reset deassertion at the capture flop (the recovery check), in ps?
sample.explanation: Recovery is setup for the deasserting edge: 1150 + 130 - 36 = 1244 ps.

concepts.label: Latches and time borrowing
concepts.definition: A level-sensitive latch is transparent while its clock is active, so data may arrive after the latch opens and still pass through.

sample.question: A rising-edge flop launches data at 0 ps into a positive level-sensitive latch. The clock has period 700 ps with a 50% duty cycle, so the latch opens at 700 ps and closes at 1050 ps; the latch setup time before closing is 43 ps. Data arrives at the latch D pin at 880 ps. How much time does the path borrow from the next stage, in ps?
sample.explanation: Borrowing is the time past the opening edge: max(0, 880 - 700) = 180 ps.

concepts.label: Choosing the right timing check
concepts.definition: A timer applies different checks at different pins: setup and hold at flop data pins, recovery and removal at asynchronous controls, clock-gating checks at gates that combine a clock with an enable, minimum pulse width at clock pins, and data-to-data checks where two signals must stay aligned.

sample.question:
A reset signal deasserts close to a clock edge at a flop's asynchronous clear pin. Which check makes sure the flop leaves reset cleanly on that edge?

A) Minimum pulse width on the clear pin only

B) Setup on the D pin

C) No check: asynchronous pins are untimed

D) Recovery, with removal as its hold-like partner
sample.answer: Recovery, with removal as its hold-like partner
sample.explanation: Deassertion of an asynchronous control is timed against the clock: recovery is the setup-like check and removal the hold-like one.

concepts.label: Clock waveforms and create_clock
concepts.definition: Every check in a timer is measured against clock edges, and those edges come from the clock definitions in SDC.
key_ideas: Finding the next edge after a time

sample.question: The SDC command `create_clock -name clk -period 16 -waveform {4 8} [get_ports clk]` defines a clock in ns. What is its duty cycle, in percent? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: The clock is high from 4 to 8 ns, 4 ns of every 16 ns: 25%.

concepts.label: Clock source and network latency
concepts.definition: A clock edge does not reach every flop at the same time. It first travels from its true origin, an oscillator or PLL, to the point where the clock is defined, and then through the on-chip clock tree to each sink.
key_ideas: Propagated clocks in the setup check

sample.question: A clock has source latency 120 ps. Its tree first passes through shared buffers with delays 49 ps. One branch then passes buffers of 21 ps to the launch flop FF1; the other passes buffers of 56, 23, 38 ps to the capture flop FF2. With propagated clocks, when does the clock edge launched at 0 ps reach FF1, in ps?
sample.explanation: Clock arrival is source latency plus network latency, the sum of buffer delays along the path to FF1: 190 ps.

concepts.label: Clock skew and jitter
concepts.definition: Two effects move clock edges away from their ideal times: skew, a fixed spatial difference in arrival between two flops, and jitter, a random temporal variation of the edges themselves.
key_ideas: Setup slack with skew and jitter

sample.question: A flop-to-flop path is clocked with period 700 ps. The launch flop's clock arrives at 65 ps and the capture flop's clock at 105 ps after the source edge. Clock-to-Q is 51 ps, the longest combinational delay is 750 ps and the shortest is 24 ps. The capture flop's setup time is 52 ps and its hold time is 44 ps. What is the clock skew of this path (capture arrival minus launch arrival), in ps?
sample.explanation: Skew = 105 - 65 = 40 ps. Positive skew gives setup more time and hold less.

concepts.label: Clock uncertainty in setup and hold
concepts.definition: set_clock_uncertainty is the SDC knob that reserves margin on clock edges. Setup uncertainty makes the capturing edge effectively earlier; hold uncertainty makes the hold requirement larger.

sample.question: Before clock tree synthesis, a team budgets setup uncertainty as jitter plus an estimate of the skew the tree will add plus a design margin. The jitter is 29 ps, the skew estimate 65 ps and the margin 20 ps. What value should set_clock_uncertainty -setup carry, in ps?
sample.explanation: The terms add: 29 + 65 + 20 = 114 ps. After CTS, propagated clocks model the real skew, so the skew term is removed.

concepts.label: Generated clocks
concepts.definition: Many clocks on a chip are derived from others: divided by a counter, multiplied by a PLL, or shaped by selecting particular master edges.
key_ideas: Building a waveform from master edges

sample.question: A master clock has period 14 ns. A divider output is declared with create_generated_clock -source [get_ports clk] -divide_by 2. What is the generated clock's period, in ns?
sample.explanation: Dividing by 2 multiplies the period: 2 x 14 = 28 ns.

concepts.label: Setup and hold relationships between clocks
concepts.definition: When launch and capture flops are clocked by different but synchronous clocks, there is no single period to plug into the setup check.
key_ideas: General periods over the common period

sample.question: Data launches from a rising-edge flop on clock CLKA (period 12 ns) and is captured by a rising-edge flop on clock CLKB (period 6 ns). Both clocks come from one source and rise together at 0 ns. Over all launch edges, the setup check uses the nearest later capture edge. What is the most restrictive setup relationship (capture time minus launch time), in ns?
sample.explanation: The edge pattern repeats every lcm(12, 6) = 12 ns. For each CLKA edge in that window, find the first CLKB edge strictly later; the smallest gap is 6 ns.

concepts.label: Clock reconvergence pessimism removal
concepts.definition: Under on-chip variation, a timer takes the launch clock path late and the capture clock path early for setup.
key_ideas: The common point and its arrivals

sample.question: A clock tree is analyzed with early/late (min/max) delays per buffer, written early/late in ps. The common segment from the clock root to the branch point has buffers 29/40, 26/31, 46/50. The launch branch adds 53/57 to FF1, and the capture branch adds 26/38 to FF2. What is the late arrival of the clock at the branch point (the common point), in ps?
sample.explanation: Sum the late delays of the common buffers: 121 ps.

concepts.label: SDC timing constraints
concepts.definition: A timer knows nothing about intent until it reads constraints. The SDC format is a set of Tcl commands that define clocks, the environment at the block boundary, and the exceptions to single-cycle timing.

sample.question:
Which SDC command defines a clock with a period and waveform on a port?

A) set_input_delay

B) set_clock_latency

C) create_generated_clock

D) create_clock
sample.answer: create_clock
sample.explanation: create_clock names a clock source, its period and its edge times. Generated clocks are derived from a master with create_generated_clock.

concepts.label: Input and output delays
concepts.definition: A block is timed in isolation, but its ports connect to logic outside it. Input and output delays describe that outside logic as time budgets relative to a clock, so paths that enter or leave the block get proper setup checks.

sample.question: create_clock -period 700 sets the clock in ps, and clocks are ideal. Input port din has set_input_delay 280 -clock clk. From din, logic of 240 ps reaches a flop with setup 56 ps. What is the setup slack of this input path, in ps?
sample.explanation: The input delay models the external launch: data reaches din at 280 ps. Slack = 700 - 56 - (280 + 240) = 124 ps.

concepts.label: False and multicycle paths
concepts.definition: By default a timer assumes every path launched on one edge must be captured on the next.

sample.question:
A mux selects either clkA or clkB onto one clock net, never both at once. Which constraint fits?

A) set_false_path from clkA to clkA

B) set_clock_groups -asynchronous

C) A single clock with the faster period

D) set_clock_groups -logically_exclusive between clkA and clkB
sample.answer: set_clock_groups -logically_exclusive between clkA and clkB
sample.explanation: Exclusive clocks cannot coexist, so paths between them are not real. Asynchronous would also stop timing but misdescribes the design and changes crosstalk analysis.

concepts.label: Multicycle paths and the hold adjustment
concepts.definition: A multicycle path gives data more than one cycle to settle. The setup half of the exception is intuitive; the hold half is where mistakes happen, because moving the setup check also moves the default hold check.
key_ideas: The default hold check moves too

sample.question: A path between two flops on clock clk (period 700 ps, ideal) has clock-to-Q 59 ps, longest logic delay 1040 ps and shortest 117 ps; setup is 35 ps and hold 34 ps. The SDC has set_multicycle_path 2 -setup -from [get_cells FF1] -to [get_cells FF2]. What is the setup slack, in ps?
sample.explanation: Setup now captures at edge 2, at 1400 ps. Slack = 1400 - 35 - (59 + 1040) = 266 ps.

concepts.label: Counting paths in a timing graph
concepts.definition: Why can a timer not simply list every path and time each one? Because the number of paths grows exponentially with depth while the graph grows only linearly.

sample.question: A timing graph has the arcs Q→L, G→J, G→B, U→A, J→B, G→A, L→U, A→E, J→L. How many distinct paths run from the sources to node E?
sample.explanation: Count in topological order: a source has one path and every other node sums its fanins. Counts: G = 1, Q = 1, J = 1, L = 2, U = 2, B = 2, A = 3, E = 3.

concepts.label: Enumerating the k worst paths
concepts.definition: Block-based propagation gives each endpoint its worst arrival, but reports, path-based re-timing and optimizers need actual paths, and often more than one per endpoint.
key_ideas: The worst path to an endpoint

sample.question: A timing graph with a single source R has the arcs R→A (12 ps), R→E (26 ps), D→H (27 ps), A→E (32 ps), B→H (31 ps), R→B (29 ps), E→T (26 ps), T→D (10 ps). What is the delay of the worst (longest) path from R to H, in ps?
sample.explanation: The path delays into H, from worst down, are 107, 89, 60.

concepts.label: Graph-based versus path-based analysis
concepts.definition: A timer can analyze in two modes. Graph-based analysis keeps one worst value per pin and times the whole design in one pass.

sample.question:
A design has billions of paths but only a few million pins. Which analysis can time the whole design in one linear pass?

A) Path-based analysis of every path

B) Graph-based analysis

C) Exhaustive path enumeration with exact slews

D) Monte Carlo SPICE of every path
sample.answer: Graph-based analysis
sample.explanation: GBA keeps one value per pin and transition, so its work grows with the graph, not with the exponential number of paths.

concepts.label: Reading a timing path report
concepts.definition: A path report is the timer's explanation of one slack. It lists the launch clock, every cell and net increment along the data path, and then the capture clock with its adjustments.
key_ideas: Slack and what to read next

sample.question:
A setup path report lists these increments in ps:

clock clk (rise edge) 0
clock network delay (propagated) 125
FF1/CK -> FF1/Q (DFF_X1) 43
U1 (BUF_X4) 12 + 75 (net + cell)
U2 (XOR2_X1) 22 + 40 (net + cell)
U3 (INV_X2) 17 + 37 (net + cell)
U4 (BUF_X4) 3 + 64 (net + cell)
FF2/D net 22
---
clock clk (rise edge) 1050
clock network delay (propagated) 190
clock reconvergence pessimism 19
clock uncertainty -20
library setup time -45

What is the data arrival time at FF2/D, in ps?
sample.explanation: Add the launch clock network delay, clock-to-Q and every net and cell increment: 460 ps.

concepts.label: PVT corners
concepts.definition: A chip must work across manufacturing variation, supply voltage and temperature.

sample.question: A flop-to-flop path with ideal clocks at period 1100 ps is characterized at several PVT corners (path delays include clock-to-Q): ff_0p88v_m40c: max path 392 ps, min path 41 ps, setup 22 ps, hold 15 ps; ss_0p72v_m40c: max path 694 ps, min path 73 ps, setup 39 ps, hold 26 ps; ss_0p72v_125c: max path 706 ps, min path 75 ps, setup 40 ps, hold 27 ps. What is the setup slack at corner ff_0p88v_m40c, in ps?
sample.explanation: Per corner, setup slack = T - setup - max path and hold slack = min path - hold: ff_0p88v_m40c setup 686, hold 26; ss_0p72v_m40c setup 367, hold 47; ss_0p72v_125c setup 354, hold 48 (ps).

concepts.label: Multi-corner multi-mode analysis
concepts.definition: A chip has several modes, functional, test, low-power, each with its own clocks and constraints, and must work at several PVT and extraction corners.

sample.question: A chip has 3 functional and test modes and is signed off at 5 PVT and extraction corners. 0 mode-corner pairs are pruned because they can never dominate. How many scenarios does the MCMM run analyze?
sample.explanation: Scenarios are mode-corner pairs: 3 x 5 - 0 = 15.

concepts.label: On-chip variation derates
concepts.definition: Corners model chip-to-chip variation: a whole die is slow or fast. Within one die, delays still vary from cell to cell, because of local process variation, voltage drop and temperature gradients.
key_ideas: Removing pessimism on the common clock path

sample.question: A setup check uses a late derate of 1.09 on the launch clock path and data path and an early derate of 0.97 on the capture clock path. The launch clock path is 300 ps, the data path (including clock-to-Q) 500 ps, the capture clock path 210 ps, the period 850 ps and setup 36 ps (setup is not derated). What is the derated data arrival time at the capture flop, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Advanced OCV derates by depth and distance
concepts.definition: Flat OCV applies the same derate to a one-cell path and a forty-cell path. But random variation partly cancels along a path: the relative spread of a sum of $N$ independent delays shrinks like $1/\sqrt{N}$.
key_ideas: Looking up the derate by depth

sample.question: An AOCV late-derate table by logic depth reads depth 1: 1.15, depth 2: 1.13, depth 4: 1.12, depth 8: 1.11, depth 16: 1.1. A data path of depth 4 has a non-derated delay of 330 ps. What is its derated delay, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Depth 4 is on the table axis, so the derate is 1.12: 330 x 1.12 = 369.6 ps.

concepts.label: Parametric OCV and LVF sigma accumulation
concepts.definition: Parametric OCV models each arc's delay not as a number scaled by a derate but as a distribution with a mean and a sigma.

sample.question: A data path has 3 arcs. Their LVF (mean, sigma) delays in ps are (43, 5), (61, 8), (31, 8), and their random variations are independent. What is the sigma of the path delay, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Independent variances add: $\sigma = \sqrt{153}$ = 12.37 ps.

concepts.label: Statistical static timing analysis
concepts.definition: POCV treats each path's random variation statistically but keeps corners for correlated variation.
key_ideas: The canonical form and its sigma

sample.question: In first-order canonical form, $X_1$ and $X_2$ are shared global variation sources and each R is a private random term; all are independent standard normals, and coefficients are in ps. An arrival time is $A = 250 + 9 X_1 + 10 X_2 + 1 R$. What is its standard deviation, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Clark's max of two Gaussian arrivals
concepts.definition: Sums keep canonical forms Gaussian; maxima do not. At every merge pin a statistical timer must take the max of two random arrivals and approximate the result again by a Gaussian in canonical form.

sample.question: Two arrival times converge at a gate: A has mean 450 ps and sigma 7 ps, B has mean 480 ps and sigma 20 ps, and their correlation is 0.2. Clark's method uses $\theta = \sqrt{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2 - 2\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B}$ and $\alpha = (\mu_A - \mu_B)/\theta$. What is $\theta$, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Timing yield from a Gaussian delay
concepts.definition: Statistical timing changes the question from whether a path passes to how many dies pass.
key_ideas: The period for a target yield

sample.question: SSTA gives a circuit delay with mean 850 ps and sigma 16 ps. The clock period is 861 ps. What is the z-score of the period? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Incremental timing analysis
concepts.definition: An optimizer changes a design thousands of times, resizing a cell, inserting a buffer, moving an instance, and after each change it needs new slacks.
key_ideas: Arrivals change in the forward cone
Required times change in the backward cone
Slack changes in the union, lazily

sample.question: A timing graph has the arcs N→J, W→L, W→U, W→R, U→N, T→R, R→L, J→G. An ECO resizes a cell, and only the delay of arc N→J changes. How many nodes can have a changed arrival time (count every node whose arrival must be re-evaluated)?
sample.explanation: Arrivals flow forward, so only J and its fanout cone can change: J, G (2 in all).

concepts.label: Early termination in incremental propagation
concepts.definition: The fanout cone of a change is an upper bound on what must be recomputed, not the actual amount.
key_ideas: The new arrival at the changed node
Counting the nodes that actually change

sample.question: A timing graph has the arcs N→W (28 ps), E→W (25 ps), E→B (40 ps), N→A (16 ps), F→E (35 ps), H→N (6 ps), and sources launch H at 0 ps, F at 0 ps. An ECO changes the delay of arc H→N from 6 ps to 11 ps. What is the new arrival time at N, in ps?
sample.explanation: Arrivals before: H = 0, F = 0, N = 6, A = 22, E = 35, W = 60, B = 75. After: H = 0, F = 0, N = 11, A = 27, E = 35, W = 60, B = 75. Propagation stops wherever a node's new arrival equals its old one, because a max that did not change hides the edit from everything downstream.

concepts.label: Timing closure
concepts.definition: Timing closure is the iterative process of bringing a design from its first timing estimate to a netlist and layout that pass signoff in every scenario.
key_ideas: Reading the shape of the problem

sample.question:
Why do teams carry extra margin, such as a tighter clock, in early implementation stages?

A) To make the tools run faster

B) Because Liberty data is less accurate at signoff

C) Later stages add delay the early models cannot see, so early slack must cover it

D) To create hold violations deliberately
sample.answer: Later stages add delay the early models cannot see, so early slack must cover it
sample.explanation: Each stage's estimate is optimistic relative to the next. Over-constraining early leaves room for routing, crosstalk and variation effects.

concepts.label: Gate sizing in a timing ECO
concepts.definition: Upsizing a gate on a failing path is the most common timing fix, and the one most often over-estimated.

sample.question: On a failing path, driver D (drive resistance 1 kohm) drives only gate G's input (3 fF). G has intrinsic delay 15 ps and drive resistance 4 kohm and drives a load of 36 fF. Cell delay is intrinsic delay plus drive resistance times load (kohm times fF is ps). The ECO replaces G with a size 2x larger, which divides its drive resistance by 2 and multiplies its input capacitance by 2; the intrinsic delay is unchanged. What is G's new delay, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: 15 + 4 / 2 x 36 = 87 ps, down from 159 ps.

concepts.label: Hold fixing with delay buffers
concepts.definition: Hold violations are fixed by adding delay to the short paths, usually by inserting delay buffers.
key_ideas: Buffers needed at the fast corner
Setup cost at the slow corner

sample.question: A path fails hold by 58 ps at the fast corner (hold slack -58 ps) and has 108 ps of setup slack at the slow corner. A delay buffer adds 18 ps at the fast corner and 23 ps at the slow corner. What is the fewest buffers that fixes the hold violation?
sample.explanation: Each buffer adds 18 ps at the fast corner: ceil(58 / 18) = 4.

concepts.label: Useful skew
concepts.definition: Zero skew is not the goal of a clock tree; meeting timing is. Deliberately delaying or advancing the clock of a flop moves time between the stages before and after it.

sample.question: In a pipeline FF1 → FF2 → FF3, the stage into FF2 has setup slack -40 ps and the stage out of FF2 has setup slack 112 ps. Delaying FF2's clock by $\delta$ gives the first stage $\delta$ more and the second stage $\delta$ less. With $\delta$ = 35 ps, what is the worse of the two setup slacks, in ps?
sample.explanation: Stage 1: -40 + 35 = -5 ps. Stage 2: 112 - 35 = 77 ps. The worse is -5 ps.

concepts.label: The OpenSTA flow: inputs and reports
concepts.definition: OpenSTA is the open-source static timer used inside OpenROAD and in many research flows.
key_ideas: Running the analysis and reading results
A timer embedded in a flow

sample.question:
Which OpenSTA command loads the cell timing models that give arcs their delays?

A) read_spef

B) read_sdc

C) read_liberty

D) read_verilog
sample.answer: read_liberty
sample.explanation: Liberty files hold the cells' timing arcs, delay and slew tables, pin capacitances and checks.

concepts.label: The DerateProvider seam
concepts.definition: Timing derating is the clearest example of where an agent-first timer needs a seam.
key_ideas: Keeping the seam fast and safe

sample.question:
What does a POCV provider return through the seam, compared with a flat OCV provider?

A) The same factor for every arc

B) A mean and sigma adjustment rather than a single multiplicative factor

C) A list of false paths

D) A required time
sample.answer: A mean and sigma adjustment rather than a single multiplicative factor
sample.explanation: Flat OCV and AOCV scale a delay. POCV works with distributions, so the seam must carry a mean and a sigma that the core combines statistically.

concepts.label: Change tiers for timing requests
concepts.definition: Requests to change a timer arrive constantly: a new sigma count, a different derate scheme, a margin rule from silicon correlation, a reporting change.
key_ideas: Tier 2: a plug-in at the seam

sample.question:
A customer asks the timer to report the 20 worst paths per endpoint instead of 5. Which tier is this?

A) Tier 3, a change to propagation

B) Tier 2, a new path enumerator plug-in

C) It requires a new SDC command

D) Tier 1, a reporting parameter
sample.answer: Tier 1, a reporting parameter
sample.explanation: Which paths and how many to report is part of the timer's change surface, set by parameters.

concepts.label: Differential timing reports as golden tests
concepts.definition: How do you prove that a change to a timer did what it claimed and nothing else? Not by checking that the worst slack improved, and not by checking that the code compiles.
key_ideas: Intended endpoints and the promotion rule

sample.question: A new derate provider should lower the slack of the paths ending at E1, E2, E4, E6, E8, E9 by exactly 5 ps and leave every other endpoint unchanged, with a tolerance of 0.5 ps. The differential report lists before → after slacks in ps: E1: 42 → 35, E2: 32 → 27, E3: 72 → 72, E4: -10 → -15, E5: -6 → -8, E6: 31 → 26, E7: 27 → 27, E8: 64 → 59, E9: 72 → 67. How many endpoints moved by more than the tolerance?
sample.explanation: Compare after with before at each endpoint: 7 moved.

concepts.label: Surrogate fast timers in an agent loop
concepts.definition: An agent exploring placements, sizings or ECOs may evaluate thousands of candidates, too many for a signoff timer.

sample.question: A fast surrogate timer inside an agent's optimization loop predicts these endpoint setup slacks, in ps: E1: -36.5, E2: -13.5, E3: 32.5, E4: 56.5, E5: -18.5, E6: 50.5, E7: 7.5, E8: 54.5. Validation shows its error never exceeds 12 ps. An endpoint must be re-timed by the accurate timer when its true slack could have either sign. How many endpoints must be re-timed?
sample.explanation: True slack lies within 12 ps of the prediction, so the sign is uncertain when |predicted slack| < 12 ps: 1 endpoints.

concepts.label: Agentic timing ECO loops
concepts.definition: An agentic ECO loop reads timing reports, proposes fixes, applies them through the engines, verifies the result and iterates, with a human approving the final change.
key_ideas: What the loop reads and proposes

sample.question:
Why must the loop re-time incrementally after each proposed change?

A) To change the clock definitions

B) Each change shifts arrivals and slews in its cone, and the next proposal must see the updated state

C) To recompute the whole netlist from RTL

D) Because reports are cached forever otherwise
sample.answer: Each change shifts arrivals and slews in its cone, and the next proposal must see the updated state
sample.explanation: Incremental timing gives the updated slacks cheaply, so the loop proposes against the real current state.

concepts.label: Tool-grounded rewards from slack
concepts.definition: Training a model to fix timing needs a reward, and a static timer can provide one: deterministic, cheap enough to run per episode, and grounded in the same numbers signoff uses.
key_ideas: Reward hacking and the grounded check

sample.question: An RL environment scores an agent's timing ECO with reward $R = 2 \min(WNS, 0) + 0.01\,TNS - 10\,\Delta A$, where WNS and TNS are in ps and $\Delta A$ is the area increase in percent. The signoff timer reports WNS 3 ps and TNS 0 ps, and area grew 2.4%. What is the reward? Round to 2 decimal places.

domains.name: Test and Design for Test
domains.description: Fault models, fault simulation, ATPG, scan and compression, BIST, JTAG, diagnosis and yield learning.
covers: Design for testing, semiconductor testing, manufacturing defects vs faults
Fault models: stuck-at, transition, path delay, bridging, cell-aware
Fault simulation (serial, parallel, deductive, concurrent), fault coverage, test coverage, fault collapsing, equivalence and dominance
ATPG: D-algorithm, PODEM, FAN, SAT-based ATPG, controllability/observability (SCOAP)
Scan design: scan cells, scan chains, scan insertion, scan chain ordering, launch-on-capture vs launch-on-shift
Scan compression (EDT-style decompressors and compactors)
BIST: LFSRs, MISRs, logic BIST, memory BIST (March tests)
Boundary scan, JTAG, IEEE 1149.1, IEEE 1500, IEEE 1687, STIL
Automatic test equipment, wafer probing, burn-in, yield analysis, diagnosis, silicon debug, post-silicon validation
Error correction, redundancy and repair (memory repair)

concepts.label: Defects, faults, errors and failures
concepts.definition: Manufacturing test exists because fabrication is imperfect: particles, missing vias, shorts and drifted devices make some dies bad.

sample.question:
A metal particle shorts two adjacent wires on one die. In test terminology, what is the particle and what is the stuck-at or bridging description?

A) Both are failures

B) The particle is a defect; the logical description is a fault model

C) The particle is a fault; the logical description is a defect

D) The particle is an error; the description is a failure
sample.answer: The particle is a defect; the logical description is a fault model
sample.explanation: A defect is the physical imperfection. A fault is its abstraction at a level the tools can reason about, such as a bridge or a stuck line.

concepts.label: The stuck-at fault model
concepts.definition: The single stuck-at model is the workhorse of digital test: each line of a gate-level netlist may be permanently fixed at logic 0 or logic 1, one line at a time.

sample.question: Inputs a, b, c; g1 = NOR(a, c); g2 = OR(b, g1); g3 = NAND(a, g2); g4 = NOR(c, g3); primary output g4. Treat every fanout branch of a signal that feeds two or more gate inputs as a line of its own. How many single stuck-at faults does the circuit have?
sample.explanation: There are 7 stems (3 inputs and 4 gate outputs) and 4 fanout branches, so 11 lines. Each line can be stuck-at-0 or stuck-at-1: 22 faults.

concepts.label: Transition faults
concepts.definition: Many real defects do not fix a line at a constant: a resistive via or a weak transistor makes a signal switch too slowly.

sample.question:
Inputs a, b, c; g1 = NOR(b, c); g2 = NAND(a, g1); g3 = AND(a, g1); primary outputs g2 and g3. Counting every fanout branch as its own line, how many transition faults (slow-to-rise and slow-to-fall) does the transition fault model define?

A) 12

B) 40

C) 10

D) 20
sample.explanation: Each of the 10 lines gets a slow-to-rise and a slow-to-fall fault: 20, the same count as single stuck-at faults.

concepts.label: Path delay faults
concepts.definition: A path delay fault says that the cumulative delay along one specific path from an input to an output exceeds the clock period, even if no single gate is grossly slow.

sample.question: Inputs a, b, c; g1 = OR(b, c); g2 = NAND(a, c); g3 = OR(g1, g2); g4 = AND(a, g3); g5 = AND(b, g4); primary output g5. A path runs from a primary input through gates to a primary output. Each path carries a rising and a falling path delay fault. How many path delay faults does the circuit have?
sample.explanation: Counting paths by dynamic programming (paths into a gate are the sum over its inputs) gives 6 input-to-output paths, so 12 path delay faults.

concepts.label: Bridging faults
concepts.definition: Shorts between neighbouring wires are among the most common real defects, and they do not behave like a stuck line: the shorted nets fight, and the result depends on their values and on the drivers' strengths.

sample.question: A block has 21 nets and no layout data, so every unordered pair of distinct nets is a candidate bridge, each modeled as a wired-AND and as a wired-OR. How many bridging faults is that?
sample.explanation: $\binom{21}{2} = 210$ pairs times 2 models is 420. Real flows extract only physically adjacent pairs from the layout, which cuts this quadratic count to roughly linear.

concepts.label: Cell-aware fault models
concepts.definition: Stuck-at and transition faults sit on cell pins, but many defects sit inside cells: a short between transistor terminals, an open in a diffusion contact, a resistive bridge in local interconnect.

sample.question:
Why is cell-aware characterization done once per library cell and not per design instance?

A) Each instance has a different layout

B) The defect behaviour depends on the cell's layout and function, which every instance shares

C) Characterization requires the full chip netlist

D) Instances never contain defects
sample.answer: The defect behaviour depends on the cell's layout and function, which every instance shares
sample.explanation: Characterization is expensive transistor-level simulation; amortizing it over every instance of the cell is what makes it practical.

concepts.label: Fault collapsing
concepts.definition: A raw fault list has two faults per line, but many of them are indistinguishable or implied by others.

sample.question: Inputs a, b, c; g1 = NAND(a, c); g2 = NOT(g1); g3 = NAND(b, c); g4 = AND(g2, g3); primary output g4. Count every fanout branch as its own line, so the circuit has 18 single stuck-at faults. Collapse gate by gate: an input stuck at the controlling value is equivalent to the output stuck at the resulting value, and a NOT gate's input and output faults pair up with inverted values; equivalence is transitive. How many equivalence classes remain?
sample.explanation: Merging the gate-local equivalences reduces 18 faults to 10 classes; one representative per class is enough for test generation.

concepts.label: Detecting a fault with a test vector
concepts.definition: Fault simulation answers one question many times: does this input vector detect this fault?

sample.question: Inputs a, b, c; g1 = NAND(b, c); g2 = AND(a, c); g3 = NAND(g1, g2); g4 = AND(c, g3); primary output g4. Apply a=0, b=0, c=1. Of the faults g2 stuck-at-0; g4 stuck-at-1; b stuck-at-1; c stuck-at-0; b stuck-at-0, how many does this vector detect?
sample.explanation: A fault is detected when its line carries the opposite of the stuck value and the difference reaches an output. Detected: c stuck-at-0.

concepts.label: Serial fault simulation and fault dropping
concepts.definition: The simplest fault simulator copies the circuit, injects one fault, simulates every pattern, and repeats for every fault.

sample.question: A serial fault simulator applies 6 patterns to 5 faults. One run simulates one faulty circuit for one pattern. The first pattern that detects each fault is: f1 at pattern 5, f2 at pattern 4, f3 never, f4 at pattern 1, f5 at pattern 3. With fault dropping (a fault is removed after its first detection), how many faulty-circuit runs are needed?
sample.explanation: A detected fault costs runs up to and including its first detecting pattern; an undetected fault costs all 6. The sum is 19, against 30 without dropping.

concepts.label: Parallel-fault and parallel-pattern simulation
concepts.definition: A machine word holds 32 or 64 bits, and a bitwise AND evaluates all of them at once.

sample.question: A parallel-fault simulator packs machines into 32-bit words, one bit for the fault-free circuit and the rest for faulty circuits. With 1698 faults and 48 patterns and no fault dropping, how many simulation passes over the circuit are needed?
sample.explanation: Each pass carries 31 faults, so a pattern needs $\lceil 1698/31 \rceil = 55$ passes; for 48 patterns that is 2640.

concepts.label: Deductive fault simulation
concepts.definition: Deductive fault simulation computes, in one pass of the fault-free circuit, the complete set of faults that each pattern detects.

sample.question: In deductive fault simulation, a 2-input AND gate has inputs a = 0 with $L_a = \{5, 7\}$, b = 0 with $L_b = \{1, 2, 7\}$. Each list holds the faults (numbered 1 to 7) that complement that input under the current vector. Which faults are in the output list, ignoring the output's own local fault? Answer with the fault numbers separated by commas.
sample.explanation: Inputs at the controlling value 0: the output flips only if a fault flips all of them and none of the others, so intersect the controlling inputs' lists and remove the other lists. Result: {7}.

concepts.label: Concurrent fault simulation
concepts.definition: Concurrent fault simulation keeps the fault-free circuit and, at each gate, a list of faulty copies of that gate that differ from it.

sample.question:
What is the main cost of concurrent fault simulation?

A) It cannot drop detected faults

B) It needs SAT solving per pattern

C) Memory: the fault lists at busy gates can grow large and change dynamically

D) It needs one pass per fault
sample.answer: Memory: the fault lists at busy gates can grow large and change dynamically
sample.explanation: Storage per gate grows with the number of divergent faults, and list management dominates run time in large designs.

concepts.label: Fault simulation and coverage
concepts.definition: Coverage is the number a test program is judged by: what fraction of the modeled faults the pattern set detects.

sample.question: After ATPG on 29753 collapsed stuck-at faults: 28029 detected, 1071 proven untestable (redundant or blocked by tied logic), 267 aborted at the backtrack limit, and 386 not detected for other reasons. What is the fault coverage, detected faults over all faults, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: D-calculus and five-valued logic
concepts.definition: Automatic test pattern generation needs to reason about two circuits at once, the fault-free one and the faulty one, while most lines are still unassigned.

sample.question:
In the five-valued D-calculus, what is the output of a NAND gate with a = X, b = D?

A) 1

B) 0

C) X

D) $\overline{D}$

E) D
sample.answer: X
sample.explanation: Evaluate the fault-free and faulty machines separately: (X, 1) and (X, 0) give X.

concepts.label: Fault activation and path sensitization
concepts.definition: Every test for a stuck-at fault does two jobs: it activates the fault by driving the line to the opposite of the stuck value, and it sensitizes a path so that the resulting error reaches an output.
key_ideas: Branch faults and choosing a test

sample.question:
Inputs a, b, c; g1 = OR(b, c); g2 = NOR(a, g1); g3 = AND(b, g2); g4 = OR(g2, g3); primary output g4. Inputs in the order abc. Which vector activates (excites) g1 stuck-at-1, ignoring whether the error reaches an output?

A) 011

B) 110

C) 000

D) 001
sample.explanation: Activation needs the fault-free value of g1 to be 0, the opposite of the stuck value.

concepts.label: The D-algorithm
concepts.definition: The D-algorithm was the first complete algorithm for combinational test generation: for any detectable stuck-at fault it finds a test, and for an undetectable one it eventually proves none exists.

sample.explanation: The D-frontier is the set of gates whose output is still X while at least one input carries D or $\overline{D}$; they are the places where the error can be pushed forward.

concepts.label: SCOAP testability measures
concepts.definition: ATPG and test-point insertion need a cheap estimate of how hard it is to set a line to 0 or 1.

sample.question: Inputs a, b, c; g1 = NAND(a, c); g2 = NAND(c, g1); g3 = NAND(b, g2); primary output g3. Using SCOAP combinational controllability (inputs have CC0 = CC1 = 1, and each gate adds 1), what is CC1 of g2?
sample.explanation: Propagating (CC0, CC1) forward in topological order: g1 (3, 2); g2 (4, 2).

concepts.label: SCOAP observability
concepts.definition: Controllability says how hard it is to set a line; observability says how hard it is to see it, that is, to propagate a change on the line to a primary output.

sample.question: Inputs a, b, c; g1 = NAND(a, b); g2 = OR(c, g1); g3 = AND(a, g2); g4 = NOR(b, g3); primary output g4. SCOAP (CC0, CC1): a (1, 1); b (1, 1); c (1, 1); g1 (3, 2); g2 (5, 2); g3 (2, 4); g4 (2, 4). Primary outputs have CO = 0; an input of an AND or NAND has CO = CO(output) + the CC1 of the other inputs + 1 (CC0 for OR and NOR); NOT adds 1; a fanout stem takes the minimum over its branches. What is CO(b)?
sample.explanation: Working backward from the outputs: CO(g4) = 0, CO(g3) = 2, CO(g2) = 4, CO(g1) = 6, CO(c) = 8, CO(b) = 3, CO(a) = 5.

concepts.label: PODEM
concepts.definition: PODEM, path-oriented decision making, reformulated test generation so that decisions are made only on primary inputs.

sample.question:
Inputs a, b, c; g1 = NAND(a, b); g2 = NAND(b, c); g3 = OR(a, g1); g4 = AND(g2, g3); g5 = OR(c, g4); primary output g5. PODEM targets g1 stuck-at-0. The current input assignment is a = X, b = 1, c = 1, with all values implied. If the fault is activated, PODEM chooses the first D-frontier gate in netlist order and its first X input. What objective does PODEM set next?

A) g4 = 0

B) g3 = 1

C) g1 = 1

D) g1 = 0
sample.explanation: The fault is not yet activated, so the objective is to set the fault site to the opposite of the stuck value.

concepts.label: The FAN algorithm
concepts.definition: FAN, fanout-oriented test generation, kept PODEM's idea of deciding only where decisions are safe, but noticed that most decisions are wasted inside fanout-free regions where justification can never fail.

sample.question:
Why can FAN stop backtrace at head lines instead of primary inputs?

A) The cone feeding a head line is fanout-free, so any value on it can later be justified without conflict

B) Head lines are always primary inputs

C) Head lines carry D values

D) Head lines are never observable
sample.answer: The cone feeding a head line is fanout-free, so any value on it can later be justified without conflict
sample.explanation: With no reconvergent fanout behind a head line, justification is guaranteed to succeed, so deciding there shrinks the search.

concepts.label: SAT-based ATPG
concepts.definition: SAT-based ATPG turns test generation into Boolean satisfiability: build a formula that is satisfiable exactly when some input vector makes the fault-free and faulty circuits differ at an output, and hand it to a CDCL solver.

sample.question: Inputs a, b, c; g1 = XOR(a, c); g2 = OR(b, g1); g3 = AND(a, g2); g4 = NOR(a, g3); g5 = AND(a, g4); primary output g5. Tseitin encoding: a k-input AND, NAND, OR or NOR gives k + 1 clauses, a NOT gives 2, a two-input XOR gives 4. How many clauses encode the fault-free circuit?
sample.explanation: Summing per gate gives 16 clauses; the encoding is linear in circuit size.

concepts.label: Random-pattern testability
concepts.definition: Many faults are detected by almost any pattern, and some by almost none. The detection probability of a fault under uniformly random patterns decides how many random patterns a test needs, whether logic BIST is practical, and where ATPG must take over.

sample.question: Inputs a, b, c, d; g1 = NAND(a, d); g2 = OR(b, g1); g3 = NOR(c, g2); g4 = NOR(c, d); primary outputs g3 and g4. Inputs are independent and uniformly random. What is the probability that one random vector detects d stuck-at-0? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: 4 of the 16 vectors detect it, so $p = 4/16 = 0.25$.

concepts.label: Test compaction
concepts.definition: ATPG generates one test cube per targeted fault, with many inputs left as don't-cares.

sample.question: ATPG produced test cubes t1 = 11XXXX, t2 = X1XXXX, t3 = X001XX, t4 = X1XX01, t5 = 1XXX0X (X is don't care). Static compaction processes them in order and merges each cube into the first already-merged cube it is compatible with (no position where one has 0 and the other 1), otherwise it starts a new pattern. How many patterns result?
sample.explanation: Merged patterns: 11XX01, X001XX. Unspecified bits are what make compaction possible.

concepts.label: Scan chains
concepts.definition: Sequential ATPG is hard because flip-flop states can only be reached through many clock cycles.

sample.question: A design has 7424 mux-D scan flip-flops stitched into 8 equal-as-possible chains. With scan enable held at 1, how many shift clock cycles does it take to load one complete pattern into every chain?
sample.explanation: Chains shift in parallel, so the load takes as many cycles as the longest chain: $\lceil 7424/8 \rceil = 928$.

concepts.label: Scan insertion and chain balancing
concepts.definition: Scan insertion is the synthesis-stage transformation that replaces flip-flops with scan cells, fixes scan design-rule violations, and stitches the cells into chains.

sample.question: Scan insertion must stitch 9850 scan flip-flops into 37 chains as evenly as possible. How long is the longest chain?
sample.explanation: Balanced chains differ by at most one flop: $\lceil 9850/37 \rceil = 267$.

concepts.label: Scan-chain ordering
concepts.definition: Which flop follows which in a chain has no effect on test quality, so the order is free to minimize the chain's routing.

sample.question: Scan-in is at (0, 0) and scan-out at (11, 7). The flops are F1 (8, 12), F2 (11, 9), F3 (8, 5), F4 (0, 1), F5 (5, 11). Wirelength is the Manhattan distance summed along the chain from scan-in, through every flop, to scan-out. What is the wirelength of the order F4, F1, F3, F5, F2?
sample.explanation: Summing the Manhattan hops gives 46.

concepts.label: Launch-on-capture and launch-on-shift
concepts.definition: A transition test needs two vectors applied at speed, but a scan design can only load one state at a time.

sample.question:
A scan chain runs scan-in → $Q_1$ → ... → $Q_3$ → scan-out. In functional mode $D_1$ = $Q_2 + Q_3$, $D_2$ = $\overline{Q_2 Q_3}$, $D_3$ = $Q_1 Q_2$. The last shift leaves $V_1 = Q_1 \ldots Q_3$ = 100, and the scan-in pin holds 0. Under launch-on-shift, what launch state $V_2 = Q_1 \ldots Q_3$ does the final at-speed shift create?

A) 010

B) 000

C) 100

D) 011
sample.explanation: Launch-on-shift makes the second vector by shifting once more: $Q_1$ takes the scan-in bit and each other flop takes its predecessor's value.

concepts.label: Scan compression
concepts.definition: Tester channels are few and expensive, while designs have millions of scan flops.

sample.question: A design has 174809 scan flops and 16 scan-in channels on the tester. Without compression the channels drive 16 chains directly; with an EDT-style decompressor they feed 160 internal chains. By what factor does the shift length per pattern fall? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Uncompressed chains are $\lceil 174809/16 \rceil = 10926$ long, internal chains $\lceil 174809/160 \rceil = 1093$; the ratio is 10.

concepts.label: Linear decompressors
concepts.definition: A linear decompressor turns a few tester bits per cycle into many scan-cell values, each a GF(2) linear combination (an XOR) of the free variables the tester injected.

sample.question: A linear decompressor drives scan cells with XORs of the free variables: $s_1 = x_2 \oplus x_3 \oplus x_4$, $s_2 = x_2 \oplus x_3 \oplus x_4$, $s_3 = x_4$, $s_4 = x_1 \oplus x_2 \oplus x_4$. With $x_1 = 1$, $x_2 = 0$, $x_3 = 1$, $x_4 = 0$, what values do $s_1 \ldots s_4$ receive? Answer with the bits in order.
sample.explanation: Each cell is the parity of the variables it lists: 1101.

concepts.label: Response compactors and X-masking
concepts.definition: On the output side of a compressed design, many internal chains feed a few tester channels through a compactor.

sample.question: A space compactor folds 8 scan-chain outputs c1 to c8 into 3 tester outputs: $z_1$ = XOR(c1, c5, c8); $z_2$ = XOR(c3, c4, c7); $z_3$ = XOR(c2, c6). In one shift cycle the chains present c1 to c8 = 11011000. What do $z_1 \ldots z_3$ show? Answer with the bits in order.
sample.explanation: Each output is the parity of its group: 011.

concepts.label: LFSRs and MISRs
concepts.definition: Built-in self-test puts the pattern generator and the response checker on the chip.

sample.question: An external-XOR LFSR with 6 stages shifts $Q_1 \to Q_2 \to \ldots \to Q_6$ on each clock while $Q_1$ takes the feedback $Q_3 \oplus Q_6$. The state $Q_1 \ldots Q_6$ is 000110. What is the state after one clock? Answer with the 6 bits in order.
sample.explanation: Feedback = 0, which enters $Q_1$; the rest shift right: 000011.

concepts.label: LFSR periods and primitive polynomials
concepts.definition: A pattern generator is only useful if it cycles through many states before repeating.

sample.question: An LFSR with 12 stages has a primitive characteristic polynomial and starts from a nonzero state. How many clocks pass before its state first repeats?
sample.explanation: A primitive polynomial makes the LFSR visit every nonzero state once: $2^{12} - 1 = 4095$. The all-zero state is excluded because it maps to itself.

concepts.label: Signature aliasing
concepts.definition: A MISR compresses millions of response bits into a few dozen, so information is lost.

sample.question: A long response stream is compressed into a MISR of 11 bits. Assuming every faulty response is equally likely, what is the aliasing probability, in parts per million? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Aliasing approaches $2^{-11}$ for long streams: 488.281 ppm.

concepts.label: Logic BIST and test points
concepts.definition: Logic BIST applies pseudorandom patterns from an on-chip generator to the scan chains and compacts the responses in a MISR, with no tester data beyond a seed and a signature.

sample.question: A STUMPS logic BIST controller applies 100000 pseudorandom patterns. Each pattern shifts 53 cycles to fill the longest internal chain (the unload of the previous response into the MISR overlaps) and takes one capture cycle. At 100 MHz, how long is the session, in milliseconds? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $100000 \times (53 + 1)$ cycles at 100 MHz is 54 ms.

concepts.label: Memory fault models
concepts.definition: Embedded memories occupy a large share of a modern die and are built at the tightest design rules, so they collect a large share of defects.

sample.question:
A cell can be written to 1 but a write of 0 after a 1 leaves it at 1. Which memory fault is this?

A) A down transition fault

B) An inversion coupling fault

C) A stuck-at-1 fault

D) An address decoder fault
sample.answer: A down transition fault
sample.explanation: The cell can hold either value from initialization but cannot make the 1 to 0 transition; a stuck-at-1 cell could never be 0 at all.

concepts.label: March tests for memories
concepts.definition: A March test applies a fixed sequence of reads and writes to every address in a fixed order, then the same for the next element.

sample.question: A March test is written $\{\Updownarrow(w0);\ \Downarrow(r0,w1,r1,w0,w1);\ \Downarrow(r1,w0,w1,w0,w1);\ \Uparrow(r1,w0);\ \Updownarrow(r0)\}$, where $\Uparrow$ and $\Downarrow$ are ascending and descending address orders and $\Updownarrow$ means either. How many operations does it apply per memory cell (its complexity is that number times n)?
sample.explanation: Each element applies all its operations to every address, so the complexity is the total operation count, 14n.

concepts.label: Simulating a March test on a faulty memory
concepts.definition: Knowing which faults an algorithm detects is a theorem about March tests; checking it is a simulation.

sample.question: March X, $\{\Updownarrow(w0);\ \Uparrow(r0,w1);\ \Downarrow(r1,w0);\ \Updownarrow(r0)\}$, runs on a memory of 6 one-bit cells at addresses 0 to 5 ($\Uparrow$ ascending; $\Updownarrow$ also taken ascending). Operations are numbered from 1 in execution order: element by element, address by address, operation by operation. The memory powers up holding all 0s, and cell 4 cannot make a 1 to 0 transition (down transition fault). Which operation number is the first read that returns the wrong value? Answer 0 if no read fails.
sample.explanation: Simulating the memory, operation 35 is r0 at address 4 in element 4 and reads 1.

concepts.label: Redundancy allocation and memory repair
concepts.definition: Large embedded memories rarely come out of the fab perfect, so they are built with spare rows and spare columns.

sample.question: Memory BIST on an 8 by 8 array logs faulty cells at (row, column) (1, 2), (1, 7), (2, 5), (5, 5), (6, 3). The array has spare rows: 2, spare columns: 1. In the first must-repair pass, a row with more faulty cells than there are spare columns must take a spare row, and a column with more faulty cells than spare rows must take a spare column. How many lines are must-repair in that pass?
sample.explanation: Rows with more than 1 faults: 1. Columns with more than 2 faults: 0. Total 1.

concepts.label: Error-correcting codes for memories
concepts.definition: Some memory errors appear after test: soft errors from particle strikes, retention loss, and wear.

sample.question: A memory word holds 26 data bits. How many check bits does a SEC-DED code (single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting extended Hamming code) need?
sample.explanation: SEC needs the smallest r with $2^r \ge m + r + 1$: r = 5 for m = 26. One overall parity bit adds double-error detection: 6.

concepts.label: Boundary scan and JTAG
concepts.definition: Boundary scan, standardized as IEEE 1149.1 and known as JTAG, puts a scan cell on every digital pin of a chip and links them into a shift register reached through a four- or five-wire test access port.

sample.question: A board's JTAG chain links U1 (boundary register 586 cells) in BYPASS, U2 (boundary register 181 cells) in EXTEST, U3 (boundary register 284 cells) in EXTEST, U4 (boundary register 262 cells) in BYPASS. How many bits long is the selected data-register path from TDI to TDO?
sample.explanation: EXTEST selects a device's boundary register; BYPASS selects its 1-bit bypass register. The sum is 467.

concepts.label: The TAP controller state machine
concepts.definition: Every IEEE 1149.1 device contains the same 16-state finite-state machine, clocked by TCK and steered only by the value of TMS on each rising edge.

sample.question:
A TAP controller is in Select-DR-Scan. TMS takes the values 1, 1, 0 on successive rising edges of TCK. Which state is it in afterwards?

A) Pause-DR

B) Run-Test/Idle

C) Update-IR

D) Test-Logic-Reset
sample.answer: Run-Test/Idle
sample.explanation: Following the 1149.1 state diagram edge by edge from Select-DR-Scan ends in Run-Test/Idle.

concepts.label: JTAG instructions and registers
concepts.definition: What the TAP controller shifts depends on the instruction loaded into each device's instruction register.

sample.question:
What does the BYPASS instruction select, and why does it exist?

A) The instruction register, for reloading

B) A 1-bit register, so devices not under test add only one bit to the chain

C) The full boundary register, for safety

D) No register: TDI connects to TDO by a wire
sample.answer: A 1-bit register, so devices not under test add only one bit to the chain
sample.explanation: Bypass shortens long board chains; the single flop also keeps TDO registered for timing.

concepts.label: Core wrappers and IJTAG networks
concepts.definition: A modern SoC holds dozens of reused cores and hundreds of embedded instruments: BIST engines, sensors, PLL controls, debug blocks.

sample.question:
A core vendor ships a core with an IEEE 1500 wrapper and its test patterns. What does the integrator gain?

A) The patterns can be reused at chip level by mapping them through the wrapper, without regenerating them

B) The chip needs no scan chains

C) The core no longer needs testing

D) ATPG must be run on the whole chip anyway
sample.answer: The patterns can be reused at chip level by mapping them through the wrapper, without regenerating them
sample.explanation: Test reuse is the point: the wrapper defines a known boundary at which core-level patterns are valid.

concepts.label: Wafer probe, final test and burn-in
concepts.definition: Patterns become quality only on the test floor. A die is tested on the wafer by a prober, tested again after packaging, and, for high-reliability parts, stressed in burn-in.

sample.question: Wafer probe applies 5404131 scan cycles at 50 MHz plus 222 ms of parametric and handling overhead per touchdown, testing 2 dies in parallel. The tester and prober cost 3 cents per second. What is the test cost per die, in cents? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Touchdown time = 108.083 ms + 222 ms = 330.083 ms; cost per touchdown = 0.9902 cents, shared by 2 dies: 0.495 cents.

concepts.label: Test pattern languages: STIL
concepts.definition: ATPG tools and testers come from different vendors and speak different languages, so patterns travel in a standard interchange format.

sample.question:
Why does STIL describe scan with procedures such as load_unload and shift instead of listing every shift cycle as a vector?

A) Procedures are required by the netlist

B) A scan load is a repeated shift; describing it once and passing chain data keeps files compact and lets the tester use scan memory

C) Scan chains have no timing

D) Testers cannot apply individual vectors
sample.answer: A scan load is a repeated shift; describing it once and passing chain data keeps files compact and lets the tester use scan memory
sample.explanation: Expanding every shift would multiply file size by the chain length; procedures capture the repetition explicitly.

concepts.label: Defect level and the Williams-Brown model
concepts.definition: Customers buy quality, not coverage. The defect level, the fraction of shipped parts that are defective, is usually quoted in defective parts per million (DPPM), and it depends on two quantities a test engineer knows: process yield and fault coverage.

sample.question: A process yields 50 percent good dies and the test set has 95.73 percent fault coverage. Using the Williams-Brown model, what is the defect level of shipped parts, in defective parts per million? Round to the nearest integer.

concepts.label: Fault diagnosis and yield learning
concepts.definition: When a die fails, the tester log says which patterns failed at which outputs. Diagnosis turns that log into candidate defect locations, and volume diagnosis across thousands of failing dies turns those candidates into the yield-learning signal that tells the fab which layer and mechanism to fix.

sample.question: A failing die fails patterns {P1, P5, P8} out of P1 to P8. A pass/fail fault dictionary lists the failing patterns each candidate fault predicts: C1 predicts {P1}; C2 predicts {P1, P2, P3, P5, P8}; C3 predicts {P1, P2, P3, P5, P8}; C4 predicts {P1, P3, P5, P8}. Scoring each candidate by the number of patterns where prediction and observation disagree, which candidate number matches best?
sample.explanation: Mismatch counts (size of the symmetric difference): C1: 2, C2: 2, C3: 2, C4: 1.

concepts.label: Silicon debug and post-silicon validation
concepts.definition: First silicon runs real software at full speed, billions of cycles per second, and finds bugs that pre-silicon simulation never reached.

sample.question:
A failure appears at low voltage and high frequency but disappears at nominal. What kind of issue is suspected?

A) A logic design bug independent of conditions

B) An electrical or timing marginality, often investigated with shmoo plots

C) A March test failure

D) A broken scan chain
sample.answer: An electrical or timing marginality, often investigated with shmoo plots
sample.explanation: Condition-dependent failures point to speed paths, noise or power integrity; shmoo plots map pass and fail across voltage and frequency.

concepts.label: ATPG as a callable skill
concepts.definition: In an agent-first flow, ATPG is not a program an engineer babysits but a skill that agents select and call: a compiled engine with golden tests and a manifest that states what it does, what it takes, what it returns and what may be tuned.
key_ideas: The manifest and the typed interface

sample.question:
An ATPG skill is exposed as a typed tool to other agents. Which output field matters most for a downstream test-time agent?

A) The license server address

B) The ATPG run's log verbosity

C) The source file names of the engine

D) The pattern count and per-pattern shift length, alongside the coverage achieved
sample.answer: The pattern count and per-pattern shift length, alongside the coverage achieved
sample.explanation: Test time is pattern count times shift cycles; a typed result lets the next agent compute cost without parsing logs.

concepts.label: Agents that insert and verify test logic
concepts.definition: DFT insertion, scan stitching, compression, test points and wrappers, is a natural target for agents: it is configuration-driven, it has clear rules, and it has strong automatic checks.

sample.question:
An agent inserts scan into a netlist. Which check proves it did not change the design's function?

A) Static timing analysis alone

B) Running ATPG and looking at coverage

C) Comparing file sizes

D) Combinational equivalence checking between the pre- and post-insertion netlists with scan enable tied to functional mode
sample.answer: Combinational equivalence checking between the pre- and post-insertion netlists with scan enable tied to functional mode
sample.explanation: With scan enable at 0 the scan muxes are transparent, so the two netlists must be equivalent; a miter-based checker proves it.

concepts.label: Golden tests on coverage and pattern counts
concepts.definition: When an agent changes an ATPG or DFT skill, the evidence that it helped and did not hurt is a golden suite: reference designs with known baseline coverage and pattern counts, and tolerances the new run must meet.

sample.question: An agent changed the ATPG skill's fault-ordering policy. The golden suite fails a design if test coverage drops by more than 0.1 percentage points or the pattern count grows by more than 3 percent. Results: D1: baseline 99.83 percent with 18380 patterns, new 99.84 percent with 19262 patterns; D2: baseline 97.78 percent with 18419 patterns, new 97.8 percent with 18234 patterns; D3: baseline 98.09 percent with 5590 patterns, new 98.18 percent with 5550 patterns; D4: baseline 98.27 percent with 15385 patterns, new 98.28 percent with 15661 patterns; D5: baseline 99.36 percent with 7488 patterns, new 99.36 percent with 8019 patterns. How many designs fail?
sample.explanation: Failing: D1, D5. Both limits are checked per design; a gain on one design does not excuse a regression on another.

concepts.label: Diagnosis agents that read failure logs
concepts.definition: Volume diagnosis produces thousands of candidate lists, and someone must decide which dies go to physical failure analysis, a slow and destructive lab step.

sample.question: A diagnosis agent reads a failure log and ranks candidate defects. Prior weights (proportional, not yet normalized) come from layout-weighted defect statistics; likelihoods from how well each candidate accounts for the log. C1: prior weight 3, likelihood 0.3; C2: prior weight 4, likelihood 0.81; C3: prior weight 6, likelihood 0.7; C4: prior weight 1, likelihood 0.51. What is the posterior probability of the most probable candidate, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Posterior is prior times likelihood, normalized: C3 gets 47.46 percent.

concepts.label: Fast fault-sampled coverage in an agent loop
concepts.definition: An agent exploring DFT configurations cannot afford full fault simulation of millions of faults for every candidate.

sample.question: Inside an agent's DFT exploration loop, a fast mode fault-simulates a uniform random sample of 2000 faults out of 833243 instead of all of them, and 1902 of the sample are detected. What coverage does the fast mode report, in percent? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The sample proportion 1902/2000 = 95.1 percent is an unbiased estimate of the full coverage.

domains.name: Floorplanning and Placement
domains.description: Floorplan representations, wirelength models, quadratic and electrostatic placement, legalization, detailed and timing-driven placement.
covers: Physical design overview; floorplanning objectives; die, core, rows and sites; LEF/DEF as the physical representation (what LEF abstracts, what DEF records)
Floorplan representations: slicing floorplans, Polish expressions, sequence pairs, B*-trees; floorplanning by simulated annealing
Macro placement, pin assignment, I/O placement, power planning handoff
Wirelength models: HPWL, clique/star, Steiner estimates; partitioning-based (min-cut) placement

Global placement: quadratic placement (B2B net model), force-directed placement, analytical nonlinear placement (log-sum-exp and weighted-average wirelength, density penalty), electrostatics-based placement (ePlace/RePlAce, FFT Poisson solve, Nesterov), DREAMPlace
Legalization (Tetris, Abacus) and detailed placement (cell swapping, sliding windows, independent-set matching)
Timing-driven placement (net weighting), congestion-driven and routability-driven placement
Placement optimization: buffering and sizing during placement

concepts.label: The physical design flow
concepts.definition: Physical design turns a gate-level netlist into geometry. Floorplanning fixes the chip outline, the core, the rows, the macros and the I/O; placement gives every standard cell a legal location; clock tree synthesis buffers the clock to the placed flip-flops; routing draws the wires.

sample.question:
What does placement take as input that floorplanning produced?

A) The core area, rows, fixed macros, I/O pins and placement blockages

B) The clock tree and its skew targets
