concepts.definition: Beyond spacing, modern rule decks constrain the shape of every wire end. Minimum-area rules forbid tiny isolated metal, end-of-line rules require extra room in front of a line end, and via enclosure rules require metal around each cut.

sample.question: A metal layer's minimum-area rule requires every isolated shape to have area at least 15000 $\text{nm}^2$. A detailed router leaves a 28 nm wide stub only 238 nm long. By how many nm, rounded up to a whole nm, must it extend the stub?
sample.explanation: The stub needs length at least 15000 / 28 = 535.71 nm, so 536 nm after rounding up, an extension of 298 nm.

concepts.label: Search-and-repair DRC loops
concepts.definition: No detailed router produces a clean layout in one pass. After initial routing, a search-and-repair loop finds the remaining violations, rips up the nets around them, raises the cost of the offending locations and reroutes, over and over, until the violation count reaches zero or stops falling.

sample.question: A search-and-repair detailed router marks every grid cell touched by a DRC violation. Each cell costs 2 to cross, plus a marker penalty on marked cells that is 8 in repair iteration 1 and is multiplied by 2 at each further iteration. How much does crossing one marked cell cost in iteration 5?
sample.explanation: The penalty in iteration 5 is 8 x 2^4 = 128, so the cell costs 2 + 128 = 130. Growing penalties push the nets causing the violation away from it a little more each pass.

concepts.label: Coloring-aware detailed routing
concepts.definition: At advanced nodes the tightest metal layers are printed with multiple masks: features too close for one exposure are split between masks.

sample.question: A layer is printed by multiple patterning. Its wires are w1 on track 1 over [24, 66]; w2 on track 1 over [126, 211]; w3 on track 1 over [251, 334]; w4 on track 2 over [28, 96]; w5 on track 2 over [136, 212]; w6 on track 3 over [19, 91]; w7 on track 3 over [151, 234]; w8 on track 3 over [264, 343] (x in nm). Two wires must go on different masks if they are on adjacent tracks with overlapping x ranges (positive overlap length), or on the same track with a tip-to-tip gap below 50 nm. What is the fewest masks that print the layer with no same-mask conflict?
sample.explanation: Build the conflict graph (7 edges) and find its chromatic number: 2. Adjacent-track conflicts alone are 2-colourable by track parity; it is tip-to-tip conflicts on one track that close odd cycles. A colouring-aware router avoids creating such cycles.

concepts.label: Channel density
concepts.definition: Channel routing is the classical detailed-routing problem: a rectangular region with pins on its top and bottom edges, nets that enter at those pins, horizontal trunks on tracks and vertical branches down to the pins.
key_ideas: Channel density as a lower bound

sample.question: A channel has columns 1 to 10. Reading columns left to right, the top-side pins are 3, 0, 1, 0, 4, 4, 3, 0, 1, 2 and the bottom-side pins are 0, 3, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 2, 0, where a number names a net and 0 means no pin. Each net's horizontal trunk spans from its leftmost to its rightmost pin column, inclusive. What is the local density at column 2, the number of nets whose span includes that column?
sample.explanation: The spans are net 1 [3, 9], net 2 [9, 10], net 3 [1, 7], net 4 [5, 6]. 1 of them include column 2.

concepts.label: Horizontal and vertical constraint graphs
concepts.definition: Channel routing has two kinds of constraint. Horizontal constraints say two trunks that overlap cannot share a track.
key_ideas: Longest chain as a lower bound

sample.question: A channel has columns 1 to 9. Reading columns left to right, the top-side pins are 0, 5, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0, 5 and the bottom-side pins are 4, 2, 3, 3, 0, 4, 0, 0, 0, where a number names a net and 0 means no pin. In the vertical constraint graph, a column with net a on top and a different net b at the bottom forces a's trunk above b's, an edge from a to b. How many distinct edges does the VCG have?
sample.explanation: Read each column with two different nets; repeated pairs give the same edge. There are 4 distinct edges.

concepts.label: Channel routing by the left-edge algorithm
concepts.definition: The left-edge algorithm is the first and simplest channel router: sort trunks by left end and pack them greedily onto tracks.
key_ideas: The top track and its limits

sample.question: A channel has no vertical constraints. Its nets' trunks span the inclusive column ranges net 1 [9, 10], net 2 [2, 3], net 3 [2, 6], net 4 [7, 12], net 5 [2, 3], net 6 [5, 10]. The left-edge algorithm sorts the nets by left end and fills one track at a time, adding each net whose left end lies to the right of the last net placed on the track. How many tracks does it use?
sample.explanation: The tracks fill as track 1 {2, 6}, track 2 {3, 4}, track 3 {5, 1}. Without vertical constraints the left-edge algorithm is optimal: it uses exactly the density, 3.

concepts.label: Cyclic vertical constraints
concepts.definition: If net a must be above net b in one column and b above a in another, the vertical constraint graph has a cycle and no assignment of one trunk per net can satisfy both.
key_ideas: How many nets must be split

sample.question: A channel has columns 1 to 10. Reading columns left to right, the top-side pins are 0, 5, 0, 0, 3, 1, 0, 2, 0, 3 and the bottom-side pins are 4, 1, 5, 3, 0, 5, 4, 0, 1, 2, where a number names a net and 0 means no pin. In each column with two different nets, the top net's trunk must lie above the bottom net's: an edge of the vertical constraint graph. How many nets lie on at least one directed cycle of the VCG? Answer 0 if it is acyclic.
sample.explanation: A net is on a cycle exactly when it can reach itself. The nets on cycles are {1, 5}, 2 in all. Any such cycle makes a dogleg-free routing impossible.

concepts.label: Dogleg channel routing
concepts.definition: A dogleg breaks a net's trunk into pieces at its intermediate pin columns, letting each piece sit on a different track.

sample.question: A channel has columns 1 to 10. Reading columns left to right, the top-side pins are 0, 3, 0, 0, 4, 1, 3, 2, 0, 0 and the bottom-side pins are 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 1, 4, 0, where a number names a net and 0 means no pin. A dogleg router splits every net at each of its pin columns, so a net with pins in m distinct columns becomes m - 1 subnets, each spanning two consecutive pin columns; subnets of different nets that cover the same column inherit that column's vertical constraint. How many subnets result?
sample.explanation: Count each net's distinct pin columns and subtract one: 4 subnets in all.

concepts.label: Switchbox routing
concepts.definition: A switchbox is a routing region with fixed pins on all four sides, typically where channels meet.

sample.question:
How does a switchbox differ from a channel?

A) A channel has pins on all four sides

B) A switchbox has fixed pins on all four sides; a channel has pins on two sides and open ends

C) A switchbox has no pins

D) A switchbox has pins on one side only
sample.answer: A switchbox has fixed pins on all four sides; a channel has pins on two sides and open ends
sample.explanation: With pins on all sides a switchbox cannot grow or shift its ends, so it cannot simply add tracks the way a channel can.

concepts.label: Timing-driven routing
concepts.definition: For most nets the router minimises wirelength, but for timing-critical nets the shape of the routing tree decides delay.
key_ideas: Elmore delay through a shared trunk

sample.question: A driver of 600 ohm drives two sinks. Wire has 1 ohm/um and 0.2 fF/um, modelled as distributed RC, and delays are Elmore. Sink 1 (the critical one) has 9 fF of pin capacitance and sink 2 has 2 fF. Topology A runs a 200 um trunk to a Steiner point, then 150 um to sink 1 and 200 um to sink 2. Topology B runs separate wires from the driver, 350 um to sink 1 and 400 um to sink 2. One ohm times one fF is one fs. What is the delay to sink 1 under topology A, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Driver: 600 x 121 fF. Trunk: $r l_0 (c l_0/2 + C_{below})$ where everything past the Steiner point hangs below it. Branch: $r l_1 (c l_1/2 + C_1)$. Total 96400 ohm-fF = 96.4 ps.

concepts.label: Prim-Dijkstra routing trees
concepts.definition: A minimum spanning tree minimises total wirelength; a shortest-path tree gives every sink the shortest path from the source.

sample.question: The Prim-Dijkstra construction grows a routing tree from the source at (20, 14) over the sinks (7, 18), (4, 13), (1, 8), (13, 17) with Manhattan distances. At each step it adds the outside pin v and tree pin u minimising $c \cdot pl(u) + d(u, v)$, where $pl(u)$ is the tree path length from the source to u. With c = 0 the rule is Prim's algorithm. What is the total wirelength of the tree?
sample.explanation: With c = 0 only the edge length matters, so the tree is a rectilinear MST of length 33. Its radius, the longest source-to-sink path, is 33.

concepts.label: Crosstalk-aware routing
concepts.definition: Wires on adjacent tracks are coupled through their sidewall capacitance. When a neighbour switches, it injects charge into the victim, changing its delay and possibly causing a glitch.
key_ideas: Miller factors and the delay window

sample.question: To first order, coupling capacitance between parallel wires scales with their parallel run length and inversely with their spacing: at the minimum spacing it is 0.1 fF/um. A victim runs parallel to an aggressor for 1100 um at 3 times the minimum spacing. What is their coupling capacitance, in fF? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Antenna-aware routing
concepts.definition: During fabrication, metal is patterned one layer at a time with plasma etching, which deposits charge on exposed conductors.

sample.question: A net drives 3 identical gates of width 0.3 um and length 0.1 um. During etch of a metal layer, the metal of that layer connected to the gates but not yet to any diffusion collects charge; its partial antenna ratio is that metal's top area divided by the total gate area. On metal 2, the gate-connected piece is 580 um long and 0.1 um wide, and no diffusion is connected until a higher layer. What is its partial antenna ratio? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: Metal area 580 x 0.1 = 58 um^2; gate area 3 x 0.3 x 0.1 = 0.09 um^2. Ratio 644.4.

concepts.label: Router core versus change surface
concepts.definition: An agent that customises a router must know which parts it may change freely and which it must never touch.
key_ideas: The four layers of a router
Why legality stays in the core
Performance and determinism at the seam

sample.question:
The history-cost increment and the present-cost growth rate of negotiation belong to which layer?

A) Strategy, needing a new plug-in

B) Parameters, changed by configuration without recompiling

C) Observation hooks only

D) Immutable core
sample.answer: Parameters, changed by configuration without recompiling
sample.explanation: These are numbers that tune a fixed strategy, so they are configuration.

concepts.label: Cost functions as router plug-ins
concepts.definition: The router's cost function is its most customer-specific behaviour: every team wants to penalise something different, from vias on critical nets to wiring over an analog block.

sample.question:
A team registers a Tier 2 edge-cost plug-in in a router's cost seam: $cost(e) = b_e(1 + 2\max(0,\ d_e + 1 - c_e)^2) + 0 h_e$, plus 4 for every via on a timing-critical net. The router core calls it for each edge it expands and keeps its own legality checks. All edges have $b_e = 1$, and the net being routed is timing-critical. Candidate paths: path A: via (demand 4, cap 4, history 3), via (demand 2, cap 3, history 2); path B: wire (demand 3, cap 2, history 3), via (demand 3, cap 2, history 3); path C: via (demand 1, cap 3, history 0), wire (demand 2, cap 3, history 2), wire (demand 5, cap 4, history 0). Which path does the router choose?

A) Path A

B) No path: the plug-in must first reject the overflowed edges

C) Path C

D) Path B
sample.answer: Path A
sample.explanation: Plug-in costs: A = 12, B = 22, C = 15. The core takes the cheapest, path A. The plug-in changes only prices; it cannot make an illegal path legal, which stays the core's job.

concepts.label: Layer directives as Tier 1 changes
concepts.definition: Many routing requests are about layers: route this block only on M2 to M6, keep clocks above M5, reserve capacity on M2 for pin access, give these nets double width.

sample.question:
A team reduces the usable capacity of M2 by 30% to leave room for pin access. Which tier is this?

A) Tier 1: a layer capacity adjustment

B) Tier 2: a new congestion model

C) A change to the cell library

D) Tier 3: a change to legality
sample.answer: Tier 1: a layer capacity adjustment
sample.explanation: Layer adjustments are parameters that scale gcell capacities.

concepts.label: DRC-clean as the router's golden test
concepts.definition: A router change is accepted only if routed reference designs come out clean. DRC-clean, connected and within a quality-of-results tolerance is the router's golden test, and a differential comparison against the baseline proves the change touched only what it was meant to.

sample.question: A router change is checked on a golden reference design. The baseline routing has 549642 um of wirelength; the new build routes it DRC-clean with 549323 um. What is the wirelength change, in percent of the baseline? Round to 2 decimal places (negative means shorter).
sample.explanation: (549323 - 549642) / 549642 x 100 = -0.06%. A QoR gate compares this against a tolerance only after the hard gates, zero DRC violations and zero opens, have passed.

concepts.label: Agentic DRC-repair loops
concepts.definition: After detailed routing, a few hundred violations often remain, clustered around crowded cells and macros.

sample.question:
The loop's violations fall from 40 to 3 and then oscillate between 3 and 5. What should it do?

A) Delete the remaining nets

B) Keep the same move forever

C) Escalate: widen the repair window, change strategy, or hand the residual to a human

D) Declare success at 3
sample.answer: Escalate: widen the repair window, change strategy, or hand the residual to a human
sample.explanation: Oscillation means the current move is not converging; a different move or a human decision is needed.

concepts.label: Fast congestion estimators in modeling loops
concepts.definition: An agent exploring placement and flow options cannot afford a full global route for every candidate.
key_ideas: When to recurse to the accurate router

sample.question: RUDY estimates routing demand by spreading each net's wire area uniformly over its bounding box: for a box W by H um and wire pitch 0.14 um, the density inside the box is $p(W + H)/(WH)$, the fraction of the area the net's half-perimeter wire would occupy. What is the RUDY density inside the box of a net spanning 32 um by 3 um? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: 0.14 x (32 + 3) / (32 x 3) = 0.051. Small boxes are dense; long, thin nets spread thin.

domains.name: Extraction, Signal Integrity and Signoff
domains.description: Parasitic extraction, SPEF, RC reduction, crosstalk and noise, ECOs and the signoff checklist.
covers: Parasitic extraction: resistance, capacitance (ground, coupling, fringe) and inductance extraction
Pattern-matching (rule-based) extraction vs field solvers (random-walk, boundary element, FEM)
SPEF: what it records; RC network reduction
Signal integrity: crosstalk, coupling-induced delay change, glitch/noise analysis, Miller factor
Signoff: timing, power, EM/IR, SI, physical; engineering change orders (ECO), PPA closure, the signoff checklist

concepts.label: Sheet resistance and counting squares
concepts.definition: Every resistance an extractor reports starts from the same idea: a metal layer of fixed thickness has a sheet resistance, and a wire's resistance is that number times how many squares of its own width fit along it.

sample.question: A straight wire on one metal layer is 20 um long and 0.1 um wide. How many squares does it contain?
sample.explanation: Squares are length over width: 20 / 0.1 = 200. Sheet resistance times squares gives the resistance, whatever the absolute size of each square.

concepts.label: Wire and via resistance
concepts.definition: A routed net is a chain of wire segments on several layers joined by vias. Its resistance is the series sum of every segment and every via level, with parallel via cuts dividing a via level's resistance.
key_ideas: Vias in series and in parallel

sample.question: A copper wire has effective resistivity 0.04 ohm-um, width 0.05 um, thickness 0.08 um and length 70 um. What is its resistance, in ohms? Round to 1 decimal place.

concepts.label: Temperature dependence of wire resistance
concepts.definition: Metal resistance rises with temperature, roughly linearly over the operating range.
key_ideas: What scales and what does not

sample.question: A wire measures 100 ohm at 25 C. Its temperature coefficient of resistance is 0.0035 per C. What is its resistance at 125 C, in ohms? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Barrier layers and size effects in copper
concepts.definition: A modern copper wire is not all copper. A thin barrier liner, needed to stop copper diffusing into the dielectric, coats its sides and bottom and conducts poorly.

sample.question: A copper wire is drawn 0.024 um wide and 0.05 um thick. A resistive barrier liner of 0.002 um coats both sidewalls and the bottom, and it carries no current. What percentage of the drawn cross-section is conducting copper? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: The copper is $(W - 2b)(T - b)$ = 0.02 x 0.048 = 0.00096 um^2 out of 0.0012 um^2, which is 80%. The liner does not shrink with the wire, so its share grows at every node.

concepts.label: Area capacitance to the layer below
concepts.definition: The simplest capacitance a wire has is the parallel-plate part: the field running straight down from its bottom face to a wide conductor below, such as the substrate or a dense layer of crossing wires.

sample.question: A wire 0.2 um wide and 120 um long runs 0.08 um above a wide grounded plane, in a dielectric of relative permittivity 2.7. Using the parallel-plate formula with $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-3}$ fF/um, what is its area capacitance, in fF? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $C = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r W L / h$ = 0.008854 x 2.7 x 0.2 x 120 / 0.08 = 7.17 fF.

concepts.label: Fringe capacitance
concepts.definition: The field from a wire does not stop at its bottom face. Field lines leave its sidewalls and top and curve down to the conductor below, adding fringe capacitance along each edge.

sample.question: A wire 0.1 um wide and 30 um long has area capacitance 110 aF/um^2 to the plane below and fringe capacitance 35 aF/um along each of its two edges. What is its total capacitance to ground, in fF? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Area: 110 x 0.1 x 30 = 0.33 fF. Fringe: 2 x 35 x 30 = 2.1 fF. Total 2.43 fF.

concepts.label: Coupling capacitance
concepts.definition: Two wires side by side form a capacitor through the dielectric between their facing sidewalls.

sample.question: Two parallel wires of thickness 0.05 um face each other across a spacing of 0.03 um for 40 um, in a dielectric with $\varepsilon_r = 3$. Treat the facing sidewalls as a parallel-plate capacitor with $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-3}$ fF/um. What is the coupling capacitance, in fF? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $C_c = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r T L / s$ = 0.008854 x 3 x 0.05 x 40 / 0.03 = 1.77 fF. Fringe fields add to this, so a field solver would report somewhat more.

concepts.label: The Maxwell capacitance matrix
concepts.definition: A set of conductors over ground is described exactly, in electrostatics, by its capacitance matrix: the linear map from conductor voltages to conductor charges.
key_ideas: Ground capacitance as a row sum

sample.question: A field solver returns the Maxwell capacitance matrix of three conductors over a ground plane, in fF: row 1: [20, -7, -1]; row 2: [-7, 19, -1]; row 3: [-1, -1, 6]. What is the coupling capacitance between conductors 2 and 1, in fF?
sample.explanation: Off-diagonal entries are the negatives of the coupling capacitances: $C_{c} = -C_{21}$ = 7 fF.

concepts.label: Total capacitance of a net
concepts.definition: A driver's load is the sum of everything it must charge: wire capacitance to ground, coupling to every neighbour, and the input capacitance of every sink pin.

sample.question: A net is 130 um of wire with 72 aF/um to ground (area plus fringe), 45 aF/um of coupling to the neighbour on one side and 28 aF/um to the neighbour on the other. It drives one sink pin of 2 fF. What is the net's total capacitance with all coupling counted to quiet neighbours, in fF? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Wire: 130 x (72 + 45 + 28) aF = 18.85 fF. Pins: 2 fF. Total 20.85 fF.

concepts.label: Field-solver capacitance extraction
concepts.definition: A field solver computes capacitance from first principles: it solves the electrostatic potential around a set of conductors and integrates the resulting surface charges.

sample.question:
Why does a capacitance solver only need the geometry and permittivities, and not the frequency?

A) Because the solver averages over all frequencies

B) At on-chip dimensions far below the wavelength, the quasi-static electric field decouples from the magnetic field

C) Because dielectrics have no frequency dependence

D) Because capacitance is defined only at DC by convention
sample.answer: At on-chip dimensions far below the wavelength, the quasi-static electric field decouples from the magnetic field
sample.explanation: When structures are electrically small, capacitance is an electrostatic quantity. Frequency effects enter through inductance and resistance (skin effect), extracted separately.

concepts.label: Rule-based extraction by pattern matching
concepts.definition: Full-chip extraction cannot solve a field problem for billions of wire segments.
key_ideas: Two indices and a run length

sample.question: A rule-based extractor's coupling table (aF/um of parallel run) has, at width 0.06 um: 68 aF/um at spacing 0.02 um and 31 aF/um at spacing 0.03 um; at width 0.08 um: 71 aF/um at spacing 0.02 um and 34 aF/um at spacing 0.03 um. It interpolates linearly in each index. A wire of width 0.06 um runs 120 um beside a neighbour at spacing 0.025 um. What coupling per length does the extractor use, in aF/um? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: On the width-0.06 row, interpolate in spacing: $t = 0.5$, giving 68 + 0.5 x (31 - 68) = 49.5 aF/um.

concepts.label: Floating random-walk capacitance solvers
concepts.definition: The floating random-walk method computes capacitance by Monte Carlo instead of meshing.

sample.question: A floating random-walk solver estimates the coupling between conductors i and j. Each walk starts on a surface around conductor i, hops through the dielectric, and contributes a score (in fF) when it lands on conductor j, and zero otherwise. 6 walks scored 3.1, 2.1, 0.3, 0.4, 3.6, 2.8. What is the coupling estimate, in fF? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The estimate is the sample mean of the walk scores: 12.3 / 6 = 2.05 fF. Each walk is independent, so the estimate is unbiased and its error shrinks as walks are added.

concepts.label: Boundary-element versus finite-element solvers
concepts.definition: Deterministic field solvers come in two main families. Boundary-element methods discretize only conductor surfaces and produce small, dense systems.

sample.question: A boundary-element solver meshes only conductor surfaces, into square panels of side 0.05 um. A wire is a box 1 um long, 0.1 um wide and 0.15 um thick. How many panels cover its whole surface?
sample.explanation: Surface area is $2(LW + LT + WT)$; in panel units that is 2 x (20 x 2 + 20 x 3 + 2 x 3) = 212 panels. A finite-element mesh of the surrounding volume would need far more unknowns.

concepts.label: Calibrating extraction to a golden solver
concepts.definition: A fast extractor is trusted only because it has been compared with a golden field solver on many structures and adjusted until the two agree within a stated tolerance.

sample.question: A fast rule-based extractor is compared with a 3D field solver on a set of nets: net 1: fast 5.9 fF, golden 5.84 fF; net 2: fast 2.2 fF, golden 2.27 fF; net 3: fast 3.6 fF, golden 3.53 fF; net 4: fast 6.5 fF, golden 6.31 fF. What is the largest relative error of the fast extractor against the golden values, in percent of the golden value? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: For each net compute |fast - golden| / golden. The largest is 3.08%.

concepts.label: Loop and partial inductance
concepts.definition: Inductance belongs to a current loop, not to a wire, so it depends on where the return current flows.

sample.question: A signal wire has partial self inductance 550 pH, its return wire has partial self inductance 630 pH, and their partial mutual inductance is 210 pH. Current flows out on the signal and back on the return. What is the loop inductance, in pH?
sample.explanation: With opposite currents the mutual term subtracts: $L_{loop} = L_s + L_r - 2M$ = 550 + 630 - 2 x 210 = 760 pH.

concepts.label: When on-chip inductance matters
concepts.definition: Most on-chip nets are resistive enough that an RC model is accurate. Inductance matters on wide, low-resistance wires carrying fast edges: global clocks, wide buses and power distribution.

sample.question: A clock driver produces edges with a 10 to 90 percent rise time of 80 ps. Using the knee-frequency rule $f \approx 0.35/t_r$, what is the highest significant frequency in the signal, in GHz? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: 0.35 / 80 ps = 4.37 GHz. Above this frequency the edge carries little energy, so this is the frequency at which to compare inductive and resistive impedance.

concepts.label: SPEF
concepts.definition: The Standard Parasitic Exchange Format (SPEF, IEEE 1481) is how an extractor hands parasitics to timers, signal-integrity tools and power analysis.
key_ideas: What SPEF does and does not carry

sample.question:
Which information does a standard SPEF D_NET not record?

A) Resistances between nodes

B) Ground capacitances

C) Coupling capacitances to other nets

D) The wire's layer geometry and coordinates, unless optional extensions are used
sample.answer: The wire's layer geometry and coordinates, unless optional extensions are used
sample.explanation: SPEF is an electrical netlist of R and C elements. Geometry is abstracted away, which is why a tool cannot re-extract from SPEF alone.

concepts.label: Reading a SPEF net section
concepts.definition: Reading SPEF fluently means predicting its contents from a net's topology and computing timing quantities directly from its entries.

sample.question: An extractor writes the D_NET of a net with one driver pin and one sink pin. Its resistor network is a tree spanning the pins and 5 internal nodes. It puts one ground capacitor on every internal node and none on the pins, and the net has one coupling capacitor to other nets. How many entries does the CAP section have?
sample.explanation: 5 ground capacitors plus 1 coupling capacitors: 6 entries.

concepts.label: SPEF name maps and file size
concepts.definition: Full-chip SPEF files run to tens of gigabytes, and most of their bytes are names: long hierarchical instance and net names repeated in every entry.

sample.question: In a SPEF file, a net's full hierarchical name is 53 characters long. With a name map, each reference is replaced by an index token of 4 characters (the asterisk and digits), and the map adds one line per net: the token, a space, the full name and a newline. The net's name appears 11 times in the body. How many bytes does the name map save for this net?
sample.explanation: Each reference saves 53 - 4 = 49 bytes: 11 x 49 = 539. The map entry costs 4 + 1 + 53 + 1 = 59 bytes. Net saving 480 bytes.

concepts.label: RC network reduction
concepts.definition: A detailed extraction can produce tens of millions of RC nodes, far more than a timer needs.

sample.question:
Why must a reduced RC network be passive?

A) Timers reject any network with resistors

B) Passivity guarantees zero error

C) A non-passive model can generate energy and make a downstream simulation unstable

D) Passivity makes the file smaller
sample.answer: A non-passive model can generate energy and make a downstream simulation unstable
sample.explanation: RC interconnect is passive. A reduced model that is not can produce growing responses when combined with drivers, which is why PRIMA's passivity guarantee matters.

concepts.label: Moments of an RC tree
concepts.definition: The moments of a network's impulse response are the coefficients of its transfer function's Taylor expansion in $s$.

sample.question: An RC tree has resistors 0.2 kohm from the driver to node 1 (6 fF), 0.3 kohm from node 1 to node 2 (2 fF), 0.4 kohm from node 1 to node 3 (6 fF), each node with the stated capacitance to ground. One kohm times one fF is one ps. What is the first moment of the impulse response at node 3 (its Elmore delay), in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $m_1(i) = \sum_k R_{ik} C_k$, where $R_{ik}$ is the resistance shared by the paths to i and k. At node 3 this is 5.2 ps.

concepts.label: Node elimination by star-mesh transform
concepts.definition: The workhorse of local RC reduction is eliminating one internal node at a time. Removing a node is Gaussian elimination on the network's nodal equations, which for a resistive star becomes the star-mesh transform: new resistors between every pair of former neighbours.

sample.question: Internal node x has 7.5 fF to ground and resistors 90 ohm to node a, 130 ohm to node b, 190 ohm to node c. A reducer eliminates x with the star-mesh transform, which connects every pair of former neighbours i, j by $R_{ij} = R_i R_j \sum_k 1/R_k$ and splits x's capacitance among them in proportion to their conductances. What is the new resistance between nodes c and b, in ohms? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: Elmore-preserving elimination in an RC chain
concepts.definition: The conductance-proportional split of an eliminated node's capacitance is not just a heuristic: on an RC chain it preserves the Elmore delay at every downstream node exactly.

sample.question: An RC chain runs from a driver through 0.3 kohm to node n1 (5 fF), then 0.7 kohm to node n2 (9 fF). kohm times fF is ps. A reducer eliminates n1: it replaces the two resistors around n1 with one of 1 kohm and splits n1's capacitance between the driver end and n2 in proportion to the conductances of the two removed resistors. How much capacitance is added to n2, in fF? Round to 3 decimal places.
sample.explanation: n2's share is $(1/R_2)/(1/R_1 + 1/R_2) = R_1/(R_1+R_2)$ = 0.3 / 1, so n2 gains 1.5 fF; the driver end gets the remaining 3.5 fF.

concepts.label: The moment-matched pi model
concepts.definition: A cell's delay depends on its load, but a resistive wire shields the driver from the far capacitance, so the total capacitance overstates the load.

sample.question: A uniform distributed RC line has total resistance 1600 ohm and total capacitance 48 fF. Its driving-point admittance has moments $y_1 = C$, $y_2 = -RC^2/3$ and $y_3 = 2R^2C^3/15$. The pi model matching them has $C_{far} = y_2^2/y_3$, $C_{near} = y_1 - C_{far}$ and $R_{\pi} = -y_3^2/y_2^3$. What is $R_{\pi}$, in ohms? Round to 2 decimal places.

concepts.label: The Miller factor of a coupling capacitor
concepts.definition: A coupling capacitor's effect on its victim depends on what the other end does. If the neighbour is quiet, the capacitor acts like one to ground.

sample.question: A victim net rises while its neighbour, coupled through 0.5 fF, switches in the opposite direction at the same time. Modelling the coupling capacitor as a grounded capacitor scaled by a Miller factor, what effective capacitance does it add to the victim's load, in fF? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The Miller factor is 2: the voltage change across the capacitor is 2 times the victim's own swing. Effective coupling 0.5 x 2 = 1 fF.

concepts.label: Switching-dependent effective capacitance
concepts.definition: Once each coupling has a Miller factor, a victim's effective load is its ground and pin capacitance plus every coupling scaled by its factor.

sample.question: A victim net has 3.6 fF of wire capacitance to ground and 3.6 fF of sink pin capacitance. During its transition, aggressor 1 (3.9 fF) switches in the same direction at the same time, aggressor 2 (2.4 fF) stays quiet, aggressor 3 (0.8 fF) stays quiet. Using Miller factors 0, 1 and 2, what effective load capacitance does the victim's driver see, in fF? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: Add ground and pin capacitance, then each coupling times its Miller factor: 10.4 fF.

concepts.label: Crosstalk-induced delay
concepts.definition: When an aggressor switches during a victim's transition, the victim's delay changes: slower if the aggressor opposes it, faster if it helps.

sample.question: Model the victim's driver as 2.2 kohm driving a lumped load, with 50% delay $t = 0.69 R C$ (kohm times fF is ps). The victim has 6.4 fF to ground (including pins) and 3.4 fF of coupling to one aggressor. What is the victim's delay with the aggressor quiet, in ps? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: A quiet aggressor acts as ground, Miller factor 1: 0.69 x 2.2 x (6.4 + 3.4) = 14.88 ps.

concepts.label: Crosstalk glitches
concepts.definition: A quiet net is not safe from its neighbours. When an aggressor switches, charge injected through the coupling capacitor bumps the victim's voltage, a glitch.

sample.question: A quiet victim with 7.7 fF to ground is coupled through 0.5 fF to an aggressor that switches from 0 to 0.8 V. Treating the victim as floating (its driver too weak to respond during the fast edge), what glitch peak appears on the victim, in mV? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: The capacitive divider gives $V_p = V_{DD} C_c/(C_c + C_g)$ = 0.8 x 0.5 / 8.2 = 48.8 mV. This is the upper bound on the glitch; a holding driver reduces it.

concepts.label: Glitch peak with a holding driver and noise immunity
concepts.definition: A real victim is not floating: its driver holds it at its rail through a finite resistance, and that resistance drains injected charge during the aggressor's edge.

sample.question: A quiet victim is held low by a driver of resistance 3.9 kohm and has 3.4 fF to ground. An aggressor coupled through 3.6 fF ramps from 0 to 1 V in 30 ps. For a linear ramp, the victim voltage peaks at the end of the ramp at $V_p = V_{DD} \frac{R C_c}{t_r}\left(1 - e^{-t_r/\tau}\right)$ with $\tau = R (C_c + C_g)$; kohm times fF is ps. What is the glitch peak, in mV? Round to 1 decimal place.

concepts.label: Timing windows and aggressor filtering
concepts.definition: Assuming every aggressor switches against every victim at the worst moment is safe but very pessimistic.
key_ideas: The windowed delta and the iteration

sample.question: A victim switches somewhere in the window 250 to 300 ps. Its aggressors are aggressor 1: 1.7 fF, switching window 210 to 240 ps; aggressor 2: 2.6 fF, switching window 120 to 130 ps; aggressor 3: 1.8 fF, switching window 240 to 250 ps. An aggressor can affect the victim's delay only if its window overlaps the victim's (windows that touch count as overlapping). Non-overlapping aggressors are treated as quiet. How many aggressors survive the timing-window filter?
sample.explanation: Check each window against [250, 300]: 1 overlap.

concepts.label: RC corners and signoff scenarios
concepts.definition: Interconnect varies with the process just as transistors do: metal width, thickness and dielectric height all have tolerances.

sample.question: A chip has 4 functional modes. Setup is signed off at 2 PVT corners, each with 3 RC corners; hold is signed off at 5 PVT corners, each with 2 RC corners. Every mode is checked at every corner combination for its check type. How many timing scenarios must be run?
sample.explanation: Setup: 4 x 2 x 3 = 24. Hold: 4 x 5 x 2 = 40. Total 64. Multi-mode multi-corner analysis multiplies quickly, which is why extraction runs once per RC corner and its results are shared across the PVT corners that use it.

concepts.label: Electromigration and IR-drop signoff
concepts.definition: Extracted resistance feeds two reliability and power checks. Electromigration (EM) signoff checks that current densities in wires and vias are low enough for the chip to last its rated lifetime.

sample.question: A power strap 0.2 um wide and 0.08 um thick carries a DC current of 3.6 mA. Its electromigration limit is 200 mA/um^2. What is the current density in the strap, in mA/um^2? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: $J = I/(WT)$ = 3.6 / (0.2 x 0.08) = 225 mA/um^2, which exceeds the 200 mA/um^2 limit.

concepts.label: The signoff checklist
concepts.definition: Signoff is the set of checks a design must pass before tape-out, each run with the qualified tools at the worst conditions for what it checks.

sample.question:
Which signoff check proves that the layout implements the netlist that was timed?

A) Layout versus schematic (LVS)

B) Design rule checking (DRC)

C) Logical equivalence checking between RTL and netlist

D) Static IR-drop analysis
sample.answer: Layout versus schematic (LVS)
sample.explanation: LVS extracts devices and connectivity from the layout and compares them with the netlist. DRC checks manufacturability, not connectivity.

concepts.label: Engineering change orders
concepts.definition: An engineering change order (ECO) is a targeted change to a nearly finished design: a logic fix found late in verification, or a timing or noise fix found at signoff.

sample.question:
Why are late changes made as ECOs rather than by re-running synthesis and place-and-route?

A) A full re-run perturbs the whole design and throws away its closure, while an ECO touches only what must change

B) ECOs are always more optimal

C) Synthesis cannot be run twice on one design

D) Re-running the flow is forbidden by the foundry
sample.answer: A full re-run perturbs the whole design and throws away its closure, while an ECO touches only what must change
sample.explanation: Timing, SI and physical closure took weeks. A local change preserves them everywhere else.

concepts.label: Metal-only ECOs with spare cells
concepts.definition: A metal-only ECO is a small physical design problem with tight constraints: find spare cells of the right types close to where the fix belongs, wire them in with new metal, and change as few mask layers as possible.

sample.question: A metal-only ECO needs one NOR2 near the point (330, 50) um. The unused spare cells are: NAND2 at (400, 60), NOR2 at (460, 300), NOR2 at (140, 370), NOR2 at (190, 280), INV at (40, 480). Using Manhattan distance, how far is the nearest usable spare cell, in um?
sample.explanation: Only NOR2 spares qualify. The nearest is 370 um away by Manhattan distance, which is what a router would roughly have to wire.

concepts.label: PPA closure
concepts.definition: Closing a design means meeting its performance target within its power and area budgets, all measured by signoff tools: PPA closure.

sample.question:
What does PPA closure mean at signoff?

A) Meeting the timing target while keeping power and area within budget, all at signoff accuracy

B) Passing DRC and LVS

C) Minimizing area while ignoring timing

D) Meeting timing at any power cost
sample.answer: Meeting the timing target while keeping power and area within budget, all at signoff accuracy
sample.explanation: Power, performance and area trade against each other. Closure means all three meet their targets together, measured by signoff tools.

concepts.label: The extractor's core and change surface
concepts.definition: An extractor built for an agent-first flow is split into a small immutable core and a change surface that agents and engineers can adjust without touching the core.

sample.question:
Why must netlist correctness stay in the extractor's core, not in a plug-in?

A) Netlist building is the slowest step

B) A parasitic attached to the wrong net corrupts every downstream analysis, whatever the accuracy mode

C) Customers never ask to change it

D) Plug-ins cannot read layout
sample.answer: A parasitic attached to the wrong net corrupts every downstream analysis, whatever the accuracy mode
sample.explanation: Connectivity is an invariant. A fast or approximate mode may trade accuracy, but never which net a resistor or capacitor belongs to.

concepts.label: Calibration as a Tier 1 change
concepts.definition: Calibration is the extractor's most frequent change, and it should never require a recompile.

sample.question: An extractor's fast mode applies one scale factor per pattern class, stored in a configuration table. For the class M2 coupling at minimum spacing, new golden 3D-solver samples give: 2.2 fF fast vs 2.22 fF golden; 1 fF fast vs 1.01 fF golden; 7.6 fF fast vs 7.91 fF golden. What least-squares scale factor $k$ (minimizing $\sum (k x_i - g_i)^2$) should the Tier 1 table entry hold? Round to 4 decimal places.
sample.explanation: $k = \sum x_i g_i / \sum x_i^2$ = 66.01 / 63.6 = 1.0379. Writing it into the table is a configuration change: no recompile, only a validation run.

concepts.label: Fast and accurate extraction in an agent loop
concepts.definition: An agent that optimizes a layout cannot wait for signoff extraction after every move.

sample.question: Fast extraction is within 4% of the accurate extractor on net capacitance. A net's interconnect-driven delay is 53 ps and scales linearly with its capacitance. What delay error bound, in ps, should an agent attach to this net's fast-mode timing? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: 4% of 53 ps = 2.12 ps. Slack within this band of zero cannot be trusted from fast mode.

concepts.label: Differential parasitic checks for ECOs
concepts.definition: When an agent claims that an ECO rerouted three nets, the claim is checkable: re-extract, compare every net's parasitics before and after, and confirm that only the claimed nets and their geometric neighbours moved.

sample.question: An agent's metal-only ECO claims to reroute n15. Its geometric neighbours, whose coupling may legitimately change, are n11. Re-extraction gives total net capacitance before and after, in fF: n10 3.1 to 1.1; n11 11.1 to 11.1; n12 3.1 to 3.09; n13 2.9 to 2.89; n14 4.3 to 4.3; n15 1.7 to 1.71; n16 10.7 to 10.71. A net has moved if its capacitance changed by more than 0.01 fF. How many nets moved?
sample.explanation: Compare |after - before| with 0.01 fF for each net: 1 moved.

concepts.label: Agentic signoff and ECO loops
concepts.definition: An agentic signoff loop reads the engines' reports, timing and SI violations, IR and EM hot spots, DRC markers, proposes ECOs, runs them through extraction and analysis, and iterates until the checklist is clean, with a human approving the final change.
key_ideas: Fast engines, accurate signoff, and the flywheel

sample.question:
In an agentic signoff loop, what does the agent read at each iteration?

A) Typed reports from the engines: timing and SI violations, IR and EM hot spots, DRC markers

B) Only the final tape-out checklist

C) The RTL source code

D) The raw layout polygons of the whole chip
sample.answer: Typed reports from the engines: timing and SI violations, IR and EM hot spots, DRC markers
sample.explanation: The agent reasons over the engines' outputs. Compact, structured reports let it localize problems and propose targeted ECOs.

domains.name: Physical Verification and DFM
domains.description: GDSII and OASIS, DRC engines, LVS as graph matching, antenna and fill, hotspots and tape-out.
covers: Physical verification overview; GDSII and OASIS: what a layout stream preserves
Design rule checking: width, spacing, enclosure, extension, density, antenna; rule decks; edge-based and hierarchical DRC engines
Layout versus schematic: device recognition, netlist extraction, graph-isomorphism matching (Netgen-style partition refinement)
Electrical rule checking
Antenna effects and fixes, metal fill and density rules
DFM: lithography hotspot detection, double-patterning coloring checks, critical area, recommended rules
Tape-out, mask data handoff, signoff physical checks
KLayout, Magic, Netgen in practice

concepts.label: GDSII records and stream structure
concepts.definition: Physical verification starts from the layout stream that will become masks. GDSII, the oldest and most widely exchanged stream format, is a flat sequence of binary records that describe libraries, structures (cells) and the elements inside them.
key_ideas: The byte size of a structure

sample.question: A GDSII BOUNDARY element is written as the records BOUNDARY, LAYER, DATATYPE, XY and ENDEL. Every record has a 4-byte header (2-byte length, record type, data type); LAYER and DATATYPE each carry one 2-byte integer, and XY carries 4-byte x and y integers for every point, with the first point repeated at the end to close the ring. How many bytes does a polygon with 8 vertices occupy?
sample.explanation: BOUNDARY 4 + LAYER 6 + DATATYPE 6 + XY (4 + 8 x 9 points) + ENDEL 4 = 96 bytes. The XY record lists 9 points because the ring is closed by repeating the first vertex.

concepts.label: GDSII and OASIS
concepts.definition: OASIS is the newer stream format designed to replace GDSII for very large layouts, especially post-OPC mask data.

sample.question:
OASIS writes an unsigned integer in 7-bit groups, one group per byte, with the top bit of each byte marking whether another byte follows. GDSII writes every coordinate as a fixed 4-byte integer. How many bytes does OASIS need for the value 5 (for example a coordinate delta in DBU)?

A) 0 bytes

B) 4 bytes

C) 1 bytes

D) 2 bytes
sample.answer: 1 bytes
sample.explanation: 5 needs 3 bits (it lies in [2^2, 2^3)), and each byte carries 7 payload bits, so ceil(3 / 7) = 1 bytes. Small deltas between neighbouring vertices therefore cost one or two bytes instead of four.

concepts.label: Database units and the manufacturing grid
concepts.definition: Layout databases store integers, not lengths. The stream's UNITS record says how long one database unit (DBU) is, and every coordinate counts those units.

sample.question: A layout's UNITS record sets the database unit to 0.25 nm, and every coordinate is stored as an integer count of database units. A vertex sits at x = 31.5045 um. What integer is stored for its x coordinate?
sample.explanation: One um is 4000 database units of 0.25 nm, so 31.5045 um is 31.5045 x 4000 = 126018.

concepts.label: Hierarchy with SREF and AREF
concepts.definition: A layout is a directed acyclic graph of cells: a cell holds shapes and placements of other cells.
key_ideas: Placements as paths in the cell DAG

sample.question: Cell LEAF holds 29 shapes. Cell MID holds 14 shapes and 3 SREFs of LEAF. Cell TOP holds 13 shapes, 7 SREFs of MID and one AREF of LEAF with 8 columns and 2 rows. How many shapes does TOP contain once fully flattened?
sample.explanation: Flatten bottom-up: MID expands to 14 + 3 x 29 = 101 shapes. TOP = 13 + 7 x 101 + 8 x 2 x 29 = 1184. The hierarchy stores only 56 shapes.

concepts.label: Design rule types
concepts.definition: Design rules are the foundry's contract with the designer: if every rule passes, the layout is manufacturable with acceptable yield.

sample.question:
One U-shaped metal polygon has its two prongs 25 nm apart, inside the same shape. Which rule type covers that gap?

A) Notch, the spacing between facing edges of one polygon

B) Enclosure of the prongs

C) Minimum width of the prongs

D) Minimum area of the polygon
sample.answer: Notch, the spacing between facing edges of one polygon
sample.explanation: A notch is same-polygon spacing. Engines that check spacing only between different shapes must check notches separately.

concepts.label: Width and spacing checks
concepts.definition: Width and spacing are the bulk of any rule deck and the first checks an engine must get exactly right.

sample.question: The minimum width rule on metal 1 is 40 nm. The layer holds the separate wires W1 = $[71, 87] \times [0, 257]$, W2 = $[10, 375] \times [400, 474]$, W3 = $[18, 92] \times [800, 1123]$, W4 = $[69, 309] \times [1200, 1233]$ (nm). How many wires violate the width rule?
sample.explanation: A rectangle's width is its shorter side. 2 of the wires have a shorter side below 40 nm; their length does not matter.

concepts.label: Enclosure and extension rules
concepts.definition: Enclosure and extension rules relate two layers. They keep a via cut inside the metal it lands on despite misalignment, and keep a poly gate long enough past diffusion that the transistor does not leak at its ends.

sample.question: A via cut is $[261, 311] \times [159, 209]$ and the metal above it is $[254, 321] \times [138, 211]$ (nm). What is the via's enclosure by the metal, the smallest distance from a via edge to the corresponding metal edge, in nm?
sample.explanation: The four margins are left 7, right 10, bottom 21, top 2 nm; the enclosure is the minimum, 2 nm.

concepts.label: Notch, end-of-line and run-length rules
concepts.definition: Simple spacing rules treat every pair of facing edges alike. Edges of the same polygon, wire ends, and long parallel runs of wide wires all have their own rules, because lithography and etch treat them differently.

sample.question: A comb-shaped polygon is one horizontal spine with 5 vertical prongs rising from it; the prongs span x-ranges [0, 70], [140, 280], [350, 410], [510, 570], [680, 800] (nm). The notch rule requires at least 90 nm between two edges of the same polygon that face each other. How many notches violate it?
sample.explanation: Each gap between neighbouring prongs is a notch: the edges belong to one polygon, so a merged-shape spacing check sees it. 2 of the 4 gaps are below 90 nm.

concepts.label: Minimum area and via rules
concepts.definition: Area and via rules are where routers most often produce violations: short wire stubs are too small, and wide wires need more than one via cut.

sample.question: An isolated metal stub is 50 nm wide and 72 nm long. The minimum area rule is 8000 square nm. By how many nm must the stub be lengthened, keeping its width, to meet the rule? Give the smallest whole number of nm.
sample.explanation: The stub has area 50 x 72 = 3600. It needs length ceil(8000 / 50) = 160 nm, so 88 nm more.

concepts.label: How a DRC engine works
concepts.definition: A DRC engine turns a rule deck and a layout into a list of violations. Its core is a small set of geometric primitives (merging, Boolean operations, sizing, edge-pair distance queries) driven by spatial data structures so that each shape is compared only with nearby shapes.

sample.question:
A DRC engine checks a 27 nm Euclidean spacing rule. Before computing exact distances it keeps only pairs whose bounding boxes, one of them expanded by 27 nm on every side, overlap with positive area. The shapes are R1 = $[18, 56] \times [80, 94]$, R2 = $[79, 103] \times [95, 111]$, R3 = $[33, 72] \times [14, 27]$, R4 = $[127, 141] \times [60, 86]$, R5 = $[11, 32] \times [49, 59]$, R6 = $[27, 57] \times [104, 131]$ (nm). How many pairs reach the exact distance test?

A) 15 pairs

B) 5 pairs

C) 6 pairs

D) 7 pairs
sample.answer: 6 pairs
sample.explanation: A pair survives when both its x gap and its y gap are below 27 nm. That keeps 6 of the 15 pairs. The exact test then confirms 6 of them as violations: a diagonal pair can pass the box filter yet be 27 nm or more apart.

concepts.label: Sweep-line spacing checks
concepts.definition: Batch DRC engines process a layer with a sweep: a vertical line moves across the die, and only shapes near the line are compared.

sample.question: A sweep-line spacing check for a 22 nm rule moves a vertical line left to right. A shape enters the active set at its left edge and leaves at its right edge plus 22 nm, so it stays available for comparison with shapes starting within the rule distance (closed intervals). The shapes are R1 = $[15, 33] \times [67, 124]$, R2 = $[43, 99] \times [10, 30]$, R3 = $[159, 169] \times [9, 19]$, R4 = $[119, 173] \times [69, 114]$, R5 = $[92, 140] \times [95, 151]$ (nm). What is the largest number of shapes active at once?
sample.explanation: Each shape is active on [x1, x2 + 22]. The maximum number of overlapping intervals, found by scanning the event points, is 3. The active set, not the whole layer, bounds the memory and the per-event work.

concepts.label: Hierarchical DRC
concepts.definition: A modern chip repeats a few thousand cells billions of times. Hierarchical DRC checks each cell once and reuses the result wherever the surroundings are the same, checking only the regions where instances interact.

sample.question:
Cell A has 3 internal spacing violations and is placed 123 times; cell B has 2 internal violations and is placed 26 times; the top cell adds 4 violations between instances. No instance's context changes the internal results. How many violations does a hierarchical DRC run report, listing each cell's errors once in the cell's own coordinates?

A) 9

B) 10

C) 425

D) 5
sample.explanation: Each cell's internal errors are reported once: 3 + 2, plus the 4 top-level ones, 9. A flat run would report 425.

concepts.label: Rule decks and derived layers
concepts.definition: A rule deck is a program. It names the stream's layers, derives new layers by Boolean and sizing operations, and runs checks on them, each tagged with a rule name.

sample.question:
A rule deck derives GATE = POLY AND ACTIVE. POLY is $[71, 90] \times [1, 113]$ and ACTIVE is $[11, 112] \times [50, 85]$ (nm). What is the area of GATE, in square nm?

A) 4998 square nm

B) 3535 square nm

C) 665 square nm

D) 2128 square nm
sample.answer: 665 square nm
sample.explanation: AND keeps the region covered by both layers: the intersection, area 665.

concepts.label: Device recognition from layer Booleans
concepts.definition: LVS compares the circuit drawn in the layout with the schematic. The layout has no devices, only shapes, so the first step is recognizing devices from layer combinations: a transistor is wherever poly crosses diffusion, typed by the well and implant layers around it, with W and L measured from the gate region.
key_ideas: Device types from wells and implants

sample.question: An LVS deck recognizes a transistor wherever POLY crosses DIFF completely (GATE = POLY AND DIFF). The diffusion regions are D1 = $[82, 464] \times [50, 190]$, D2 = $[68, 448] \times [350, 485]$ and the vertical poly lines are P1 = $[495, 515] \times [-7, 531]$, P2 = $[201, 221] \times [-2, 224]$, P3 = $[166, 186] \times [308, 530]$, P4 = $[284, 304] \times [321, 521]$ (nm). How many transistors does device recognition find?
sample.explanation: A poly line that spans several diffusion rows makes one gate in each row it crosses inside the row's x-range, and none where it passes beside a row. Counting crossings gives 3 transistors from 4 poly lines.

concepts.label: Layout netlist extraction
concepts.definition: After devices are recognized, the extractor builds the nets: which shapes are electrically connected through overlaps and vias.

sample.question: Metal 1 wires (horizontal centerlines): h1 at y = 1 from x = 3 to 8; h2 at y = 3 from x = 2 to 6; h3 at y = 2 from x = 1 to 7. Metal 2 wires (vertical): v1 at x = 9 from y = 0 to 4; v2 at x = 2 from y = 5 to 8; v3 at x = 3 from y = 0 to 2. Vias between metal 1 and metal 2 at: none. Two wires on the same layer and the same track connect when their ranges overlap or touch; a metal 1 and a metal 2 wire connect only through a via at a point on both, never by merely crossing. How many nets does connectivity extraction find?
sample.explanation: Union the wires that overlap on a track and the wire pairs joined by each via; 6 wires collapse into 6 connected components, each one net. Crossings without a via stay separate.

concepts.label: Device reduction and property comparison
concepts.definition: Layouts draw devices differently from schematics: one schematic transistor becomes four parallel fingers, a resistor becomes a serpentine of segments.

sample.question: An extracted netlist (W and L in nm) is: M1 nmos g=C s=Y d=VDD W=160 L=60; M2 nmos g=C s=Y d=VDD W=130 L=60; M3 nmos g=C s=Y d=VDD W=130 L=60; M4 pmos g=B s=Z d=Y W=250 L=60; M5 pmos g=A s=Y d=Z W=240 L=30; M6 pmos g=A s=Y d=Z W=150 L=30; M7 pmos g=A s=Y d=Z W=130 L=30; M8 pmos g=B s=Z d=Y W=140 L=40; M9 pmos g=B s=Z d=Y W=300 L=40; M10 pmos g=A s=Y d=Z W=260 L=30; M11 nmos g=C s=Y d=VDD W=370 L=60. The LVS tool merges devices in parallel: same type, same gate net, the same pair of source and drain nets in either order (source and drain are interchangeable), and equal L; the merged device's W is the sum. How many devices remain after parallel merging?
sample.explanation: Group the devices by (type, gate, unordered source/drain pair, L). There are 4 groups; a device with a different L stays separate. Merging is what lets a 4-finger layout transistor match one schematic device.

concepts.label: LVS as graph matching
concepts.definition: LVS asks whether the layout netlist and the schematic netlist describe the same circuit.

sample.question:
LVS models a netlist as a bipartite graph with one vertex per device and one per net, and one edge per device terminal (gate, source, drain; bulk ignored). For the netlist M1 pmos g=A s=VDD d=Y1; M2 pmos g=B s=VDD d=Y1; M3 nmos g=A s=GND d=n1; M4 nmos g=B s=n1 d=Y1, how many edges does the graph have?

A) 16

B) 8

C) 12

D) 10
sample.explanation: Each of the 4 transistors contributes three terminal edges: 12. The graph has 6 net vertices.

concepts.label: Partition refinement in netlist comparison
concepts.definition: Partition refinement is the algorithm at the heart of LVS tools such as Netgen and Gemini.

sample.question: A transistor netlist is: M1 pmos g=A s=VDD d=Y1; M2 nmos g=A s=GND d=Y1; M3 pmos g=Y1 s=VDD d=n1; M4 pmos g=B s=n1 d=Y2; M5 nmos g=Y1 s=GND d=Y2; M6 nmos g=B s=GND d=Y2. Treat the netlist as a bipartite graph of devices and nets. Initially devices are coloured by type, VDD and GND each form a class of their own (they are matched by name), and every other net is coloured by its number of device terminals. In each round, every vertex gets a new colour made of its current colour plus the multiset of (terminal kind, neighbour colour) over its edges, where the terminal kinds are gate and source/drain (source and drain are interchangeable). The initial partition has 7 classes. How many classes are there after one round?
sample.explanation: Recolouring by (colour, neighbour multiset) splits classes whose members see different neighbourhoods. The class counts by round are 7, 12, 13.

concepts.label: Symmetry and ambiguity in LVS matching
concepts.definition: Refinement cannot separate vertices that are truly symmetric: two identical inverters with private inputs and outputs look the same from every angle.

sample.question:
A layout netlist is: M1 pmos g=A s=VDD d=Y1; M2 nmos g=A s=GND d=Y1; M3 pmos g=B s=VDD d=Y2; M4 nmos g=B s=GND d=Y2. Treat the netlist as a bipartite graph of devices and nets. Initially devices are coloured by type, VDD and GND each form a class of their own (they are matched by name), and every other net is coloured by its number of device terminals. In each round, every vertex gets a new colour made of its current colour plus the multiset of (terminal kind, neighbour colour) over its edges, where the terminal kinds are gate and source/drain (source and drain are interchangeable). Refinement runs until the number of classes stops changing. Only VDD and GND are matched by name; no other port names are used. How many classes of the stable partition still contain more than one vertex?

A) 2

B) 6

C) 4

D) 0
sample.explanation: Identical gates with private inputs and outputs are automorphic images of each other, so refinement can never separate them. The stable partition has 6 classes, 4 of them with more than one member; the matcher must break each tie by an arbitrary choice and refine again.

concepts.label: Diagnosing LVS errors
concepts.definition: An LVS report is a list of symptoms: unmatched nets, unmatched devices, property errors.

sample.question:
Schematic net OUT appears in the layout as two nets, one with the driver and one with the loads. What is the error?

A) A short between OUT and another net

B) An open: a missing via or a gap breaks OUT in two

C) A swapped gate connection

D) A floating well
sample.answer: An open: a missing via or a gap breaks OUT in two
sample.explanation: One schematic net matching two layout nets is the signature of a break in connectivity.

concepts.label: Electrical rule checking
concepts.definition: Electrical rule checks look for circuits that are connected as drawn but electrically wrong: floating gates, untapped wells, two drivers on one net, devices exposed to voltages beyond their rating.

sample.question:
An ERC deck flags a floating gate net: a net that reaches only gate terminals and is not a port of the cell. The netlist is M1 pmos g=A s=VDD d=Y1; M2 pmos g=B s=VDD d=Y1; M3 nmos g=A s=GND d=n1; M4 nmos g=B s=n1 d=Y1; M5 pmos g=C s=VDD d=n2; M6 pmos g=Y1 s=n2 d=Y2; M7 nmos g=C s=GND d=Y2; M8 nmos g=Y1 s=GND d=Y2. Besides VDD, GND and the outputs, the cell's input ports are: B, C. How many floating gate nets are flagged?

A) 0

B) 3

C) 1

D) 2
sample.explanation: The nets that touch only gates are A, B, C. Those not listed as input ports have no driver at all: 1 floating nets, which would leave both transistors partly on.

concepts.label: Antenna rules
concepts.definition: During manufacturing, plasma etching of each metal layer charges the exposed metal.

sample.question: When metal 2 is etched, a net's metal 2 pieces 85 by 0.28 um, 16 by 0.4 um are connected to the gates W = 0.65 um, L = 0.13 um; W = 1 um, L = 0.13 um and to no diffusion. Using the area antenna ratio (connected metal area over total gate area), what is the net's metal 2 antenna ratio? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: Metal area = 30.2 square um; gate area = 0.2145 square um (W x L summed over the gates). Ratio = 140.8. All gates on the net share the collected charge, so their areas add.

concepts.label: Partial and cumulative antenna ratios
concepts.definition: Antenna damage happens layer by layer. When metal $i$ is etched, the layers above it do not yet exist, so only metal connected to the gate through layers 1 to $i$ is electrically attached.

sample.question: A gate of area 0.07 square um connects to this metal: metal 1: 54 square um connected through layers up to 1; metal 2: 21 square um connected through layers up to 2; metal 3: 15 square um connected through layers up to 3; metal 4: 49 square um connected through layers up to 4; metal 3: another 55 square um that reaches the gate only through metal 4. The partial ratio of layer i counts only the layer-i metal already connected to the gate when layer i is etched, that is, connected through layers 1 to i. The cumulative ratio at layer i is the sum of the partial ratios of layers 1 to i. What is the partial antenna ratio of metal 4? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: Metal 4 counts 49 square um. Ratio = 49 / 0.07 = 700.

concepts.label: Antenna diodes
concepts.definition: The standard antenna fix is a reverse-biased diode on the gate's net: a small diffusion region that leaks the plasma charge to the substrate before it can stress the oxide.
key_ideas: Diodes on nets with several gates

sample.question: A net has 241 square um of metal 3 connected to a single gate of area 0.225 square um. The metal 3 area ratio limit without protection is 450. How much metal 3 area, in square um, would have to be moved off the net's metal 3 to meet the limit? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The allowed area is 450 x 0.225 = 101.25 square um, so 241 - 101.25 = 139.75 square um must go (in practice by a layer jump rather than by deleting wire).

concepts.label: Layer jumpers and antenna repair
concepts.definition: A layer jumper breaks a long lower-layer route near the gate and carries it over a higher layer.
key_ideas: How a jump cuts the antenna

sample.question: A 276 um long metal 1 route, 0.2 um wide, connects to a gate of area 0.065 square um. The router breaks it 12 um from the gate and carries the rest over metal 2, dropping back to metal 1 only at the far end. What is the metal 1 partial antenna ratio seen by the gate after the jump? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: Before the jump the gate saw 849.2; after it, only the 12 um stub is connected when metal 1 is etched: 0.2 x 12 / 0.065 = 36.9. The far metal 1 piece joins only through metal 2, too late to charge the gate.

concepts.label: Metal fill and density
concepts.definition: Chemical-mechanical polishing removes material at a rate that depends on the local pattern density: sparse regions dish, dense regions erode.

sample.question: A density window is $[0, 70] \times [0, 70]$ um. The metal shapes near it are R1 = $[13, 41] \times [1, 23]$, R2 = $[38, 51] \times [22, 53]$, R3 = $[-8, 24] \times [41, 54]$ (um); some overlap each other and some extend past the window. What is the metal density of the window, in percent? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: Clip every shape to the window (AND), merge the clipped shapes (OR) so overlaps count once, and take the union area: 1328 square um out of 4900, 27.1 percent.

concepts.label: Fill insertion to a density target
concepts.definition: Fill tools add electrically inactive metal shapes to windows below the minimum density.

sample.question: A $170 \times 170$ um window holds 7819 square um of metal, and the minimum density is 50 percent. Fill squares are 1 by 1 um and are placed only in empty space. How many fill squares are needed?
sample.explanation: Target area 50 percent of 28900 = 14450 square um; deficit 6631; ceil(deficit / 1) = 6631 squares.

concepts.label: Sliding density windows and gradients
concepts.definition: Density rules apply to windows that slide across the die with a fixed step, not to a fixed tiling.
key_ideas: The minimum window by tile sums

sample.question: A density rule uses a 50 by 50 um window stepped by 25 um in x and y over a 250 by 675 um die. How many window positions are checked?
sample.explanation: Per axis (D - w) / t + 1: (250 - 50) / 25 + 1 = 9 in x and 26 in y, so 234 positions.

concepts.label: Fill side effects and fill-aware flows
concepts.definition: Fill is metal, so it changes capacitance, and it lives in the same layout as signal wiring, so it must be removed and regenerated when routing changes.
key_ideas: Where fill lives in the flow

sample.question:
A signal wire has a neighbour 50 nm away on one side and empty space on the other. Fill is inserted on the empty side, 40 nm from the wire. Using a sidewall model in which each side's coupling capacitance is proportional to 1 / spacing (same run length and thickness), by what percent does the wire's total sidewall capacitance increase?

A) 80 percent

B) 125 percent

C) 63 percent

D) 20 percent
sample.answer: 125 percent
sample.explanation: Before: k / 50. The fill adds k / 40, which is 50 / 40 = 125 percent of the original. Fill-aware flows keep fill away from critical nets or extract it before signoff timing.

concepts.label: Lithography hotspot detection
concepts.definition: Design rules are a simplified contract with lithography. Some rule-clean patterns still print badly: lines pinch, spaces bridge, line ends pull back, especially at the edges of the process window.
key_ideas: Precision and recall of a detector

sample.question:
A hotspot detector is run on clips whose true status is known from lithography simulation. It flags 69 true hotspots and 9 clips that print correctly, and it misses 25 true hotspots. What is its recall, in percent, rounded to 1 decimal place?

A) 80.2 percent

B) 73.4 percent

C) 26.6 percent

D) 88.5 percent
sample.answer: 73.4 percent
sample.explanation: Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 69 / 94 = 73.4 percent: the share of real hotspots caught. Missed hotspots become yield loss, so recall is the metric a signoff flow cannot trade away.

concepts.label: Pattern matching for DFM
concepts.definition: Pattern matching scans a layout for every occurrence of a known problematic pattern.
key_ideas: Exact matching of a raster pattern

sample.question: A layer is rasterized into a 6 by 5 grid of pixels (1 = metal), rows top to bottom: 01110, 01110, 10101, 00010, 01001, 01000. A hotspot pattern is the 2 by 2 block 10, 10. At how many positions does the pattern match the grid exactly (no rotation)?
sample.explanation: Slide the block over all 20 positions and compare every pixel: 2 match. Production matchers hash each window so a lookup replaces the pixel comparison.

concepts.label: Double-patterning coloring conflicts
concepts.definition: When features are packed tighter than one exposure can print, double patterning splits a layer onto two masks.

sample.question: In double patterning, two features closer than 43 nm (Euclidean) cannot be printed on the same mask, so a conflict edge joins them. The features are F1 = $[96, 123] \times [2, 16]$, F2 = $[98, 130] \times [24, 52]$, F3 = $[5, 28] \times [55, 95]$, F4 = $[51, 82] \times [14, 39]$, F5 = $[74, 94] \times [94, 105]$, F6 = $[111, 140] \times [60, 91]$ (nm). How many conflict edges does the graph have?
sample.explanation: Test all 15 pairs against the same-mask spacing 43 nm: 8 pairs are closer, each one an edge that forces the two features onto different masks.

concepts.label: Critical area of a layout
concepts.definition: Random particle defects cause shorts and opens. Whether a defect of a given size kills the chip depends on where it lands: the critical area is the area of positions where its centre causes a failure.
key_ideas: Critical area at one defect size

sample.question: Two parallel wires run side by side for 360 um with a 125 nm gap. A circular conducting defect of diameter 225 nm shorts them if it touches both. Ignoring end effects, what is the critical area for shorts at this defect size, in square um? Round to 2 decimal places.
sample.explanation: The defect centre must fall in a band of width x - s = 100 nm along the run (zero if the defect is smaller than the gap): 360 um x 100 nm = 36 square um.

concepts.label: Recommended rules and DFM scoring
concepts.definition: Beyond mandatory rules, foundries publish recommended rules: larger spacings, longer extensions, redundant vias.

sample.question:
The minimum metal spacing is 50 nm and the recommended spacing is 80 nm. A block's neighbouring-wire spacings, in nm, are 85, 60, 55, 70, 75, 80. What percent of them meet the recommended value? Round to 1 decimal place.

A) 100 percent

B) 66.7 percent

C) 28.6 percent

D) 33.3 percent
sample.answer: 33.3 percent
sample.explanation: 2 of 6 spacings are at least 80 nm: 33.3 percent. All of them pass the mandatory rule; the recommended rule measures margin.

concepts.label: Tape-out
concepts.definition: Tape-out is the handoff of the final layout to the foundry for mask making. Everything physical verification does converges here: the signed-off stream, the agreed layer map, documented waivers, and proof that nothing changed after signoff.

sample.question:
Why does a tape-out require a single top cell in the stream?

A) LVS needs exactly one transistor

B) GDSII cannot store more than one cell

C) Mask generation starts from one root of the hierarchy; extra top cells are ambiguous

D) Fill requires it
sample.answer: Mask generation starts from one root of the hierarchy; extra top cells are ambiguous
sample.explanation: Orphan top cells in a stream are a classic tape-out mistake, often flagged by the foundry's intake checks.

concepts.label: Mask data preparation and fracturing
concepts.definition: Between tape-out and the mask writer lies mask data preparation: deriving mask layers, applying OPC, and fracturing polygons into the simple figures a writer exposes.

sample.question: A variable-shaped-beam mask writer exposes rectangles of at most 2000 by 2000 nm per shot. How many shots does it need for one 3255 by 5018 nm rectangle, split on a regular grid of maximal shots?
sample.explanation: ceil(3255 / 2000) = 2 columns and ceil(5018 / 2000) = 3 rows: 6 shots. Write time grows with the shot count, not the area.

concepts.label: Layout XOR between versions
concepts.definition: An XOR compares two versions of a layout: it reports the area covered by exactly one of them.
key_ideas: XOR of two versions of a layer

sample.question: A tape-out XOR compares a shape in the signed-off layout, $[7, 20] \times [19, 27]$, with the same shape in the final stream, $[6, 24] \times [14, 27]$ (um). What area, in square um, does the XOR report?
sample.explanation: XOR = A + B - 2 (A AND B) = 104 + 234 - 2 x 104 = 130 square um. Any nonzero XOR on a layer that should be unchanged stops the tape-out until it is explained.

concepts.label: KLayout, Magic and Netgen in practice
concepts.definition: Open-source physical verification rests on three tools. KLayout is a layout viewer and editor with DRC and LVS engines scripted in a Ruby-based language.

sample.question:
How does a KLayout LVS script build the layout netlist?

A) With device-extraction and connect statements over derived layers, then it compares against a SPICE netlist

B) It simulates the layout

C) It reads the netlist from the GDS file

D) It asks the router for connectivity
sample.answer: With device-extraction and connect statements over derived layers, then it compares against a SPICE netlist
sample.explanation: Like any LVS flow, it recognizes devices from layer Booleans and extracts connectivity before comparing.

concepts.label: Agentic DRC fix loops
concepts.definition: Signoff DRC on a large block can report thousands of violations after routing. An agentic fix loop reads the report, classifies each violation, routes it to the engine that owns the geometry, reruns the checks and iterates, with a human approving the final ECO.
key_ideas: Routing violations to the right fixer

sample.question:
A signoff DRC report lists 23 metal spacing, 3 short, 6 minimum-area and 2 via-enclosure violations on routed metal, 11 antenna violations and 0 density-window violations. Of the spacing violations, 4 lie entirely inside standard-cell layouts. The agent's policy: violations on routed metal go back to the detailed router as a Tier 1 rerun of the affected region; antenna violations go to the antenna-repair step; density goes to the fill step; anything inside a cell layout is escalated to a human. How many violations does the agent send to the router?

A) 30

B) 41

C) 34

D) 45
sample.explanation: Routed-metal violations: (23 - 4) + 3 + 6 + 2 = 30. The 4 in-cell spacing violations are not the router's to fix: the router treats cell layouts as fixed, so changing them is a core library change.

concepts.label: Change tiers for verification engines
concepts.definition: Verification engines follow the same four-layer model as implementation engines: an immutable geometry and matching core, policies such as check plug-ins and device extractors, parameters such as rule values and switches, and observation hooks over results.

sample.question:
A new foundry rule changes the density window from 50 to 100 um with a 50 um step. Which tier?

A) Tier 3: a change to the Boolean core

B) Tier 1: window size and step are parameters of the density check

C) A layout change

D) Tier 2: a new density algorithm
sample.answer: Tier 1: window size and step are parameters of the density check
sample.explanation: Density engines take window and step as parameters.

concepts.label: Clean results as golden and differential tests
concepts.definition: For physical verification, the golden test is simple to state: the reference designs must stay DRC-clean and LVS-clean, and the regression designs must produce exactly the expected markers.

sample.question: An agent's change is checked by a differential DRC run. The baseline markers are M2.S.1 at (100, 200), M3.S.2 at (200, 200), M2.S.1 at (300, 300), M2.S.1 at (400, 300). The new run's markers are M2.S.1 at (100, 200), M2.S.1 at (350, 350), M3.S.2 at (200, 200). A marker matches only if the rule and the position are identical. How many markers did the change introduce?
sample.explanation: Introduced = new markers with no identical baseline marker: 1. A golden test for a fix requires this to be zero, whatever happened to the old markers.

concepts.label: Fast hotspot prediction versus signoff
concepts.definition: Learned hotspot predictors are the fast engine of lithography verification: milliseconds per clip against seconds for simulation.

sample.question: A full lithography simulation takes 5200 ms per clip and a learned hotspot predictor 2 ms per clip. A layer has 80000 clips. The fast flow runs the predictor on every clip and simulates only the 8000 clips it flags. What is the speedup of the fast flow over simulating every clip? Round to 1 decimal place.
sample.explanation: Full: 80000 x 5200 ms. Fast: 80000 x 2 + 8000 x 5200 ms. Ratio 10. The speedup is bounded by the flag rate: if the predictor flags more, the accurate engine dominates again.

concepts.label: Rule decks and the IP boundary
concepts.definition: Physical verification touches the most sensitive data in the chain: the foundry's rule decks, device recognition and hotspot libraries, and the customer's complete layout.

sample.question:
An agent fixes DRC violations on site. Which data may leave the site under a strict IP boundary?

A) The GDS of the failing region

B) The full DRC results with cell names

C) The rule deck

D) Nothing design-specific; at most generic, reviewed skills or anonymized metrics agreed in advance
sample.answer: Nothing design-specific; at most generic, reviewed skills or anonymized metrics agreed in advance
sample.explanation: Design and process data stay on site. Know-how can flow back only as skills and approved metrics.

domains.name: PCB Design
domains.description: Schematic to layout, stackups and controlled impedance, differential pairs, vias, manufacturing outputs and board-level SI.
covers: Printed circuit boards, schematic capture, component libraries, footprints and land patterns, bill of materials
PCB layout, autorouters, PCB stackup, controlled impedance, differential signaling and differential pairs, length matching
Vias: through-hole, blind, buried, microvias; HDI; flexible and rigid-flex PCBs
Through-hole vs surface-mount technology, design for assembly, pick-and-place, reflow soldering
PCB DRC/ERC, design for test, Gerber and ODB++ outputs, IPC standards
Board bring-up and hardware debugging; signal and power integrity at board level (IBIS, IBIS-AMI, Touchstone)
Tools: open-source (KiCad, LibrePCB, gEDA/Lepton) and commercial PCB suites

concepts.label: The PCB design flow
concepts.definition: A printed circuit board flow takes a circuit drawn from purchased parts and turns it into copper, holes and assembly instructions.

sample.question:
Which statement draws the boundary between chip EDA and board EDA correctly?
